guide.title: About CAF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CAF file?

CAF, Core Audio Format, is a container Apple designed as a flexible home for audio. Core Audio support dates to OS X 10.4, with OS X 10.3 support through QuickTime 7. Where older containers use small size fields, CAF uses 64-bit offsets, so it has no 4 GB ceiling.

A CAF can hold compressed audio or uncompressed samples, with multiple channels and optional channel-layout information. A mandatory audio-description chunk identifies the stored audio encoding, and information and edit-comment chunks can carry descriptive text.

You meet CAF as audio on macOS and iOS, as long recordings and as sound effects in Apple apps. Many codecs fit inside it, so two CAF files can hold very different audio, and the format is also described as supporting metadata and markers. It is an Apple format.

### Programs that open CAF files

QuickTime Player, Apple Music, Logic Pro and Audacity open CAF files. The format's fact sheet adds these programs:

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- FFmpeg: handles Core Audio Format containers in both directions.
- ffplay: uses FFmpeg demuxers and decoders to play supported CAF audio.

### CAF and WAV compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .caf for CAF; .wav for WAV, with audio/wav and audio/x-wav as common media-type labels.
- **Origin**: CAF is Apple's format. WAV comes from a Microsoft and IBM multimedia specification of August 1991.
- **Structure**: CAF uses 64-bit offsets. WAV is a RIFF-based wrapper for sound rather than one particular audio encoding.
- **Contents**: a CAF can hold compressed or uncompressed audio. WAV often holds linear PCM, though compressed encodings are possible as well.
- **Size limit**: CAF has no 4 GB limit. WAV has a 4 GB file size limit.
- **Metadata**: CAF has information and edit-comment chunks. What a WAV does with metadata varies, as INFO chunks and the Broadcast WAVE extensions store different details.
- **Typical use**: WAV serves audio recording and editing and professional sound production.

WAV, short for Waveform Audio File Format, is a RIFF-based sound wrapper described in the multimedia specification Microsoft and IBM published in August 1991. It usually holds uncompressed PCM audio, so files are large but exact. Broadcast WAVE carries production and preservation metadata. The Library of Congress names WAVE its recommendation for digital audio collections.

The conversion is a decode and rewrite. FFmpeg in your browser reads the CAF and writes 16-bit little-endian PCM into a WAV, dropping any video stream. The page passes no quality setting. No tag options are passed either; FFmpeg's defaults decide, and in a test the CAF's title and artist arrived in the WAV. The CAF stays unchanged, and the download takes its name with a .wav ending. A batch of CAF files runs in sequence and yields a separate WAV for each.

### Other ways to convert CAF to WAV

- **FFmpeg (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `ffmpeg -i field-recording.caf -c:a pcm_s16le field-edit.wav`. 16-bit output can reduce the source depth.
- **Switch (Windows):** add the CAF, choose WAV as the output format, set the encoder options and an output folder, then click Convert. NCH lists CAF input and WAV output for Windows, Mac and Android versions of the program.

### Problems with CAF files

- **It opens but there is no sound**: opening the container does not guarantee that a system can decode the audio codec inside it.
- **The channel layout is not what you expected**: CAF can hold optional channel-layout information. Check the channel order in your editor after converting a multichannel recording.
- **A 24-bit recording loses depth**: the page writes 16-bit PCM, so a deeper CAF is reduced to 16 bits.
- **The WAV is much larger than expected**: the CAF held compressed audio, and PCM is uncompressed.
- **CAF notes are missing from the WAV**: information and edit-comment chunks in a CAF can carry descriptive text, but this page promises only what FFmpeg's defaults copy, such as global tags. Check the WAV in your editor if the notes matter.
- **A program cannot open the CAF at all**: FFmpeg reads and writes the Core Audio Format container, so it can turn the file into a WAV from the command line, and ffplay can play supported CAF audio.
- **A damaged or cut-short CAF**: such a file usually still converts, giving a shorter WAV, so compare its running time with the CAF.

guide.title: Understanding CDR for JPEG output
guide.markdown:
### What is a CDR file?

CorelDRAW saves its drawings as CDR by default. Corel calls the format primarily vector, with shapes, text and effects, though bitmap content can live in a drawing as well. Saving can compress bitmaps and graphic objects, which reduces the file size but slows opening and saving. Properties such as a title and subject can be stored, and fonts are embedded unless they are Asian fonts or lack embedding permission. For compatibility, the Save As dialog lists earlier CDR versions.

### Programs that open CDR files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - LibreOffice Draw: opens CDR by way of the libcdr library.
- **Windows and Mac:**
  - CorelDRAW: opens its native drawings,.

### CDR and JPEG compared

- **Names**: .cdr is a proprietary Corel file, and JPEG goes by .jpg or .jpeg.
- **Structure**: a CDR holds shapes, text and pages that stay editable. A JPEG is a single flat picture and keeps no editable layers.
- **Transparency**: a JPEG can't store an alpha channel, so see-through areas are lost.

This converter cannot read CDR files. If you add a CDR, the page stops with "Image decode failed." Export the JPEG from a program that understands CorelDRAW drawings instead.

### Other ways to convert CDR to JPEG

- **CorelDRAW:** open the drawing and choose File > Export. Pick the folder, set Save as type to JPG and type a file name. Two optional check boxes limit what is exported: Export this page only, for the current page of a multipage file, and Selected only, for the selected objects. Neither is available for every format. Click Export.
- **Corel PHOTO-PAINT:** choose File > Import, pick CDR - CorelDRAW (*.cdr) in the list next to the File name box, click the filename, click Import, then click the image window. In the Convert to bitmap dialog, adjust the width, height, resolution or color mode. Then choose File > Export, pick a JPEG format in the Save as type list, type a file name and click Save.

### Problems with CDR files

- **A newer drawing won't open**: an earlier CorelDRAW release can refuse it, and the documented workaround is a copy saved for the older version.
- **Saving backward changes the drawing**: Corel warns that the copy can lose effects, change how items look or limit editing.
- **PHOTO-PAINT lost the vectors**: imported CDR files are rasterized, so shapes cannot be edited afterward.
- **Fonts**: embedding is limited by each font's permissions, and Asian fonts are not embedded, so check them before you share the CDR.

guide.title: About CDR files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CDR file?

The default drawing format of CorelDRAW is CDR. Corel calls it a primarily vector format: instead of a grid of pixels, the drawing is kept as shapes, curves, text and effects, across multiple pages and layers. Bitmap content can sit inside a drawing next to vector effects, and the save options offer compression for bitmaps and for graphic objects.

Properties like a title and subject can be stored in a CDR, and fonts can be embedded where permissions and other restrictions allow. In the Save As dialog you can pick an earlier CDR version for compatibility, which matters because an older CorelDRAW may reject a drawing from a newer one.

You meet CDR files as logos, illustrations, signage and print design. CDR is a proprietary Corel format, and LibreOffice Draw and Inkscape read it through libcdr.

The target, JPEG, is a raster format with lossy compression, which the Joint Photographic Experts Group specified as ISO/IEC 10918-1. Web photographs, camera files, mailed attachments and shared pictures commonly use it, and its quality can be adjusted.

### Programs that open CDR files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- LibreOffice Draw: imports CDR through libcdr.
- Inkscape: uses libcdr for CDR input.

**Windows and Mac**

- CorelDRAW: opens its native drawings.

**Web**

- The web edition, CorelDRAW Web: documentation covers CDR support in compatible browsers; qualifying Graphics Suite subscribers and maintenance customers get access as a benefit.

### CDR and JPG compared

- **Names and types**: .cdr is CorelDRAW's native format. JPEG files end in .jpg or .jpeg, which mean the same thing.
- **Kind**: CDR is primarily vector. JPEG is a raster format designed for photographs, so shapes become pixels.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy, with no alpha transparency, so transparent pixels cannot survive a JPEG export.
- **Pages and layers**: a CDR can have multiple pages and layers. JPEG is one flat raster picture with no editable layers, so keep your CDR.
- **Support**: a JPEG is supported everywhere, and you can view it in Windows Photos, GIMP, Preview on macOS or a browser. A CDR opens in CorelDRAW, LibreOffice Draw and Inkscape.

This page cannot do the conversion. It runs in your browser, has no CDR reader of its own, and hands the file to the browser's image decoder, and the attempt ends with an 'Image decode failed.' error. Your file is not uploaded and is not changed. Pick one of the programs below, or ask whoever sent the drawing for a JPG. Once the drawing is a JPG its vector shapes are pixels, so pick the export size you need before saving, because enlarging the JPG afterwards cannot restore sharp edges.

LibreOffice Draw can export to any of the graphics formats BMP, EMF, EPS, GIF, JPEG, PNG, SVG, TIFF and WMF. CorelDRAW itself offers JPEG in its export dialog, with options for the current page or only the selected objects.

### Other ways to convert CDR to JPG

- **CorelDRAW on Windows or Mac:** open the drawing, choose File > Export, set Save as type to JPEG, type a file name, optionally tick Export this page only or Selected only, and click Export.
- **LibreOffice Draw on Windows, Mac or Linux:** open the CDR, then export it as JPEG. LibreOffice's guide lists JPEG among the graphics formats Draw exports and Corel Draw (*.cdr) among the formats it opens.

### Problems with CDR files

- **An older CorelDRAW will not open it**: the drawing was probably saved by a newer version. Ask for a copy saved in an earlier version, which the newer program offers.
- **The vectors are gone after PHOTO-PAINT**: that program turns an imported CDR into pixels. Keep the CDR for later vector edits.
- **Lettering changes on another computer**: fonts embed only where font permissions and other restrictions allow, so a drawing sent to someone else may not bring its fonts along.
- **This page stops with a decode message**: nothing here can read the format, so the file never reaches a JPG.
- **The JPG cuts off part of the design**: CorelDRAW can export only the selected objects or the current page, so check which option you picked before saving.
- **The JPG differs from what another program makes**: equal quality numbers in two programs do not mean equal compression or looks.
- **You only need a preview**: ask whoever made the drawing for a JPG.

guide.title: About CDR files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CDR file?

Drawings made in CorelDRAW are stored as CDR, the program's default format. Corel calls the format primarily vector, meaning shapes, curves and text that stay crisp at any size, though a drawing can also contain bitmaps and vector effects. Saving can compress the bitmaps and graphic objects. The file can carry reference properties such as a title and a subject, and embedded fonts, within their permissions.

To share a drawing with someone on an older release, the Save As dialog offers earlier CDR versions. Corel says CorelDRAW files do not work backwards; saving to an earlier version can change newer effects or limit editing.

A CDR usually arrives from a designer, a sign shop, a print vendor or a client who works in CorelDRAW. It is the working file, so a PNG is what people want when they need to show or place the design instead of editing it.

### Programs that open CDR files

- **Windows and Mac:** CorelDRAW created the format and opens it natively. Double-click a file, or use File > Open.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** LibreOffice Draw lists Corel Draw (*.cdr) among the formats it can import.

### CDR and PNG compared

- **Extensions**: .cdr for the drawing; .png and image/png for the picture.
- **What each holds**: a CDR keeps editable shapes, text and effects, whereas a PNG keeps one flat picture made of pixels.
- **Scaling**: drawings scale without loss, but a PNG turns soft when enlarged, so choose the final size at export.
- **Compression**: PNG always compresses without loss, through the DEFLATE method, so the picture matches what the program drew.
- **Structure**: a PNG opens with a fixed signature and continues as chunks: an IHDR chunk describes the image, IDAT chunks hold its compressed pixels, and an IEND chunk ends the file.
- **Bit depth**: indexed, grayscale and truecolor PNGs can use between 1 and 16 bits per sample.
- **Reach**: every major browser displays PNG, and it carries no known royalty-bearing patents.
- **Animation**: the current specification includes animated PNG, with a default image shown by software that cannot play the animation.
- **Transparency**: PNG supports an optional alpha channel, so a see-through background is possible if the export is set up for it.
- **Editing**: all object structure is gone in a PNG. Keep the CDR as the master.

What matters is the program that draws the file, since it decides how the drawing looks as a picture. Image decoding on this page belongs to the browser itself, and for a CDR you should expect "Image decode failed." instead of a picture, so use one of the methods below.

### Other ways to convert CDR to PNG

- **CorelDRAW, single export:** choose File > Export (Ctrl+E on Windows, Cmd+E on Mac), select PNG in the Save as type list, click Export, then set the options in the Export to PNG dialog and click OK. Corel's Export command provides raster formats, while Save As offers only vector ones.
- **CorelDRAW, asset export:** choose File > Export For > Multiple Files, add the objects or page in the Export docker, pick PNG for each and export.
- **LibreOffice Draw:** open the CDR, then use File > Export, choose PNG and set the options. The PNG dialog covers compression and interlacing, plus width, height and resolution of the picture, and the help page for it lists them.

### Problems with CDR files

- **The page shows an error**: its decoder is the browser's own, and it reports "Image decode failed." for this file. Export from CorelDRAW or LibreOffice Draw instead.
- **An older CorelDRAW rejects the file**: ask whoever made it for an earlier-version copy. Newer effects may look different in that copy.
- **A renamed file stays unreadable**: calling the file .png leaves the drawing data untouched, and image viewers reject it.
- **The text looks wrong**: the drawing may use fonts that were not embedded, and a program without them swaps in others. Ask the sender to embed the fonts, which CorelDRAW allows subject to font permissions, and install them before you export.
- **You want to keep editing**: a PNG is a flat picture with no objects left in it. Keep the CDR, and export a new PNG whenever the design changes.
- **The PNG is blurry**: it holds a fixed number of pixels. Export again at a larger size from the program.

guide.title: CDR to SVG: formats and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is a CDR file?

CDR is CorelDRAW's default drawing format, and the format is proprietary to CorelDRAW. Corel describes it as a primarily vector drawing format, and a drawing can contain bitmap content as well as vector effects. A drawing can store reference properties such as its title and subject. Its save options include bitmap and graphic-object compression, font embedding is available subject to font permissions and other restrictions, and the Save As dialog offers earlier CDR versions for compatibility.

This page can't read CDR files. The converter here has no reader for the format, and a CDR you choose ends in the error "Image decode failed." Open the file in one of the programs below instead.

### Programs that open CDR files

- **Windows and Mac:** CorelDRAW opens its native drawings. Corel says CorelDESIGNER and CorelCAD open CDR files too, and that other viewers exist with restricted features.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Inkscape uses libcdr for CDR input, and LibreOffice Draw imports CDR through libcdr as well.
- **Web:** Compatible browsers can open CDR in CorelDRAW Web, which has documented CDR support. Access is a benefit for qualifying Graphics Suite subscribers and maintenance customers.

Corel PHOTO-PAINT turns an imported drawing into pixels, so it keeps no vector objects and isn't a route to vector output.

### CDR and SVG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .cdr is a proprietary Corel format, listed by LibreOffice as application/vnd.corel-draw. .svg is image/svg+xml, plain XML text.
- **Text**: CorelDRAW's SVG export can write text as editable characters, known as glyphs, or as curves. Characters stay editable and searchable. Curves become vector shapes and are no longer editable as text.
- **Effects**: CorelDRAW exports objects with mesh fills or drop shadows as bitmaps. An SVG can mix those pictures with paths.
- **Fonts**: CorelDRAW can embed fonts in a CDR when the font's permissions allow it. When text is exported as characters, you can embed fonts for viewers who may not have them installed.
- **Where it works**: every major browser displays SVG. CDR is proprietary to CorelDRAW, and the other programs above read it through an importer.

A real conversion has to read the drawing's objects, which is what CorelDRAW, Inkscape and LibreOffice do. This site's converter has no CDR reader, so it can't make the SVG for you.

### Other ways to convert CDR to SVG

- **CorelDRAW (Windows, Mac):** use File > Export and set Save as type to SVG - Scalable vector graphics. The dialog also offers SVGZ, a compressed SVG. Under Compatibility you select the SVG version, and UTF-8 encoding is the default and gives a smaller file than UTF-16. Choose the text option, as text or as curves, before you export.
- **Inkscape (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open a supported CDR, then save it and choose the .svg (Plain SVG) type, which Inkscape's manual recommends for sharing a drawing with people who may not use Inkscape. Its documented import list has two CorelDRAW entries, one marked UQ, and both name versions 7 to X4. The manual adds that some imports display an options dialog before the file opens.
- **LibreOffice Draw (Windows, Mac, Linux):** LibreOffice imports CDR through libcdr, and its filter list shows the Corel Draw document type for import and an SVG export filter. From a terminal, the pattern is `soffice --convert-to svg drawing.cdr`, because --convert-to takes the output extension after it, as in `--convert-to pdf *.doc`. Without --outdir, the result is written to the current working directory, and --outdir picks another folder.

Compare the result with a PDF or screenshot the designer exported, so you can spot misplaced objects.

### Problems with CDR files

- **This page can't read it**: there is no CDR reader here. Use a program above, or ask the designer for an SVG.
- **An older CorelDRAW rejects the file**: a CorelDRAW file does not open backward in older versions, and an older save can change newer effects or limit editing.
- **Text shifts after export**: a viewer that lacks the font can't draw the text as designed. Export text as curves, or embed the fonts when you export it as characters.
- **Some objects became pictures**: shadows and mesh fills arrive as bitmaps, so check them at the largest size you will use.
- **Inkscape or LibreOffice shows a different layout**: both read the file through libcdr, so features may differ from the designer's own export.

guide.title: About JPEG compression
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

Its name is short for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which began its work in 1986. JPEG is lossy and made for photos. ITU-T standardized it as T.81 in 1992, and ISO as 10918-1 in 1994. Cameras and scanners write it, and every major browser can show it. The idea is to keep what the eye notices and drop what it doesn't. First the picture is split into small 8x8 pixel squares; a discrete cosine transform turns each square into frequencies, and Huffman coding packs the remainder.

The quality number controls how much of the fine detail is rounded off. A high quality keeps almost everything and makes a big file; a lower one rounds harder and the file shrinks. Quality is usually a 0 to 100 scale, though two programs given the same number can write different files. GIMP's default is 85.

Some arithmetic shows why the setting matters. A 12-megapixel photo is 12 million pixels with three color values each, about 36 MB before compression. Typical settings, a tenth to a twentieth of that, land between 1.8 and 3.6 MB.

The endings .jpg and .jpeg stand for one format, with image/jpeg as its media type, and US patent protection for it ended on 27 October 2006.

Compressing a JPEG that already exists means decoding it to pixels and encoding those pixels again with harder rounding. Progressive order is another way to save a JPEG: a blurry first pass appears, then detail fills in as the rest downloads.

### Programs that compress JPEG files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: the JPEG export dialog offers Quality, Progressive and Optimize settings.
- ImageMagick: reads JPG files in a terminal window.

**Mac**

- Preview: re-exports a JPEG with an adjustable quality.
- Photos: exports a batch of photos as JPEG, with JPEG Quality and Size choices.

**Web**

- Firefox: shows JPEG files.
- This page: MozJPEG at a fixed quality of 82, with several files at once.

**Web and Mobile**

- Chrome: shows JPEG files.

**Mobile**

- Safari: shows JPEG files.

### Original and compressed JPEG compared

- **Quality**: the copy is saved at quality 82, with no slider. Another program's 82 may not match it.
- **Progressive order**: the copy is a progressive JPEG, so a viewer can paint a rough picture first.
- **Metadata**: EXIF, XMP and the ICC color profile are left out. The decoded pixels are all that is encoded.
- **Orientation**: the EXIF orientation tag is not applied and not kept.
- **Pixel size**: the width and height don't change.
- **What stays the same**: the result is still image/jpeg, with 8 bits per color channel and no transparency or layers.
- **When the copy isn't smaller**: you get your original file back.

### Other ways to compress a JPEG

- **Preview (Mac):** go to File > Export, switch the Format pop-up menu to JPEG, move the quality control, then click Save.
- **Photos (Mac):** open File > Export > Export Photos, choose JPEG in the Photo Kind menu, reveal the options with the arrow beside it and reduce JPEG Quality or Size, then click Export.
- **GIMP (Linux, Mac and Windows):** pick File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E), choose JPEG, and in its dialog reduce Quality from the 85 it starts at.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **A form rejects .jpeg but takes .jpg**: the format is the same. Rename the ending, or convert with the [JPEG to JPG converter](/jpeg-to-jpg/).
- **The file is still too large after compressing**: this page changes only the quality. Resize the picture in an editor, then compress again.
- **A logo lost its transparent background**: JPEG has no alpha channel. Keep such images as PNG or WebP, and shrink a WebP with the [WebP compressor](/compress-webp/).
- **The compressor returned the file unchanged**: the new encode wasn't smaller than your file.
- **The photo is rotated wrongly**: the copy no longer carries its orientation tag. Apply the rotation in an editor first.
- **The camera details are missing**: EXIF isn't in the copy. Keep your original for the date and location.
- **Colors look different**: the ICC profile stays behind in your original. Keep it when color accuracy matters.
- **Many files at once**: pick them together, and each is compressed in turn and downloads as its own JPEG, with no ZIP to unpack.
- **Squares appear after many rounds**: detail is lost at each save. Return to the original instead of squeezing an already compressed file.

guide.title: About JPG compression
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

Work on JPEG began in 1986 with the Joint Photographic Experts Group, whose initials give the format its name. T.81, the ITU-T text from 1992, and ISO/IEC 10918-1, adopted in 1994, define its core standard. Cameras and scanners commonly produce it, all major browsers show it, and the US patents that covered it ran out on 27 October 2006. Both .jpg and .jpeg are the same format, and image/jpeg is its media type.

Baseline JPEG is lossy. The picture is grouped into 8x8 blocks; a discrete cosine transform is applied to every block, and Huffman coding packs the result as the finest detail is rounded off. The quality number says how coarse that rounding is. The scale commonly spans 0 to 100, yet one program's 80 need not match another's; GIMP starts at 85. A picture saved at ordinary settings is typically a tenth to a twentieth the size it would be uncompressed.

In a JPG each color channel is 8 bits wide, and neither an alpha channel nor layers exist. Progressive mode is optional: a rough picture shows first and gains detail while the rest of the file arrives. Compressing a JPG means decoding it and saving it again at a lower quality, which is a new lossy save.

### Programs that compress JPG files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: its JPEG export dialog has a Quality setting that defaults to 85, Progressive and Optimize options, and a choice of which metadata to keep.
- ImageMagick: reads JPG files from the command line.

**Mac**

- Preview: File > Export saves a JPEG and lets you adjust its quality.
- Photos: File > Export > Export Photos offers a JPEG Quality and a Size choice.

**Web**

- Firefox: displays JPG files.
- This page: MozJPEG at quality 82, run by your browser.

**Web and Mobile**

- Chrome: displays JPG files.

**Mobile**

- Safari: displays JPG files.

### Original and compressed JPG compared

- **Format**: both are JPEG files, image/jpeg. The download ends in .jpg.
- **Pixels**: the width and height are the same. Nothing is cropped or scaled.
- **Encoder and quality**: the copy is written by MozJPEG at quality 82. Quality numbers aren't a shared scale, so 82 here and 82 in another program can give different results.
- **Layout**: the copy is a progressive JPEG with optimized Huffman tables.
- **Metadata**: the copy carries no EXIF, ICC profile or XMP. Camera settings, the date taken and GPS location stay only in your original.
- **Orientation**: the page neither applies nor saves the EXIF orientation tag, so a photo that relies on it to look upright may come out turned.
- **Size**: if the copy isn't smaller than your file, the page returns your file instead.

Every JPEG save is lossy, including this one. Compress from the best copy you have, once, rather than squeezing the same file again and again.

### Other ways to compress a JPG

- **Preview (Mac):** with the image open, choose File > Export, set the Format pop-up to JPEG, change the quality, then press Save.
- **Photos (Mac):** select the photos and choose File > Export > Export Photos. Pick JPEG from the Photo Kind menu, open the options with the arrow beside it to set JPEG Quality and Size, then click Export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac and Linux):** open the image and use File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E); in the JPEG options, set Quality below its default of 85 and export.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Still over an upload limit**: this page changes only the quality. Shrink the photo's pixel dimensions in an editor, then compress the smaller copy.
- **The same file came back**: the quality 82 encode wasn't smaller than your file, so there was nothing to save.
- **Text and sharp lines look smudged**: JPEG is lossy. Keep screenshots, logos and diagrams as PNG and shrink them with the [PNG compressor](/compress-png/).
- **The location and camera details are gone**: EXIF is not written to the copy. Keep your original when you need them.
- **Colors look different**: no ICC profile goes into the smaller copy. Keep the original when color accuracy matters.
- **The photo comes out sideways**: the orientation tag is dropped. Rotate the picture in an editor before you compress it.
- **Blocky patches show up after repeats**: every save costs more detail. Start again from the original instead of recompressing a compressed copy.

guide.title: Understanding CR2 for JPEG output
guide.markdown:
### What is a CR2 file?

CR2 is Canon's camera-raw format, used by numerous EOS models from the mid-2000s and later superseded by CR3. It is a TIFF-based file made of unprocessed sensor data, and it is proprietary to Canon. The Library of Congress groups it with the other camera raw formats and notes that its extension identifies a Canon raw file.

A raw file keeps what the sensor captured through the camera's color filter array, with very little processing. Turning it into a picture takes demosaicing, then white balance, a gamma curve and noise reduction, all done on a computer. That is the point of shooting raw: you choose those settings later instead of letting the camera bake them in. The cost is that almost no website, printer or phone gallery wants the file as it is, so a JPEG is the usual way to share the result.

You find a CR2 on the memory card of a Canon camera set to record raw, or in a folder of shots someone sent for editing.

Raw files bring a preservation risk too. Makers seldom publish their specifications, and the layouts shift as new camera models arrive. The Library of Congress warns that a format may lose support if its maker stops supporting it. Adobe's DNG is one attempt to normalize raw data, and a DNG may hold a copy of the original raw file inside it.

### Programs that open CR2 files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- darktable names CR2 among its import extensions, and its RawSpeed library does the raw decoding. The documentation says most modern cameras work, though sensors that aren't Bayer (apart from Fujifilm X-Trans) are not decoded.
- ImageMagick lists CR2 as read-only and needs the explicit specifier cr2:image.cr2.

**Windows and Mac:**

- Canon's Digital Photo Professional names .CR2 among its supported raw extensions, next to CR3 and CRW.

### CR2 and JPEG compared

- **Extensions and MIME types**: .cr2 for Canon raw; .jpg or .jpeg with image/jpeg.
- **Contents**: a CR2 carries sensor measurements that need processing before they look like a photograph. A JPEG carries a finished, rendered picture.
- **Interpretation**: a raw workflow leaves color and tone choices to the processing software, while a JPEG has them baked in.
- **Compression**: JPEG is defined by ISO/IEC 10918-1 and is lossy, with an adjustable quality setting. This page sets none.
- **Transparency**: a JPEG has no alpha channel.
- **Support**: a recognized CR2 suffix doesn't guarantee that a program supports the camera behind it.

In this page ImageMagick, built for WebAssembly, runs inside your browser, reads the CR2 and saves a JPEG with no quality value set. None of the usual raw-developer adjustments are offered. You can add several CR2 files; they are processed one after another and each downloads as a separate JPEG. The result also won't necessarily match a camera's preview image, since a preview and a developed picture can differ.

### Other ways to convert CR2 to JPEG

- **Canon Digital Photo Professional (Windows, Mac):** pick the CR2 and use File > Convert and save, then set the image type to JPEG and save. The camera must be supported by that version, and the conversion applies your development recipe.
- **darktable (Windows, Mac, Linux):** select the image and, in the export module, send it to a file on disk with JPEG as the format, then press start export. Camera support, development history and the export profile all affect the result.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick cr2:photo.cr2 photo.jpeg`. The cr2: prefix names the format outright, which ImageMagick needs here.

### Problems with CR2 files

- **A program won't open it**: a recognized .cr2 suffix does not guarantee that your version supports the camera. Update the software or check its list of supported cameras.
- **The JPEG looks different from the camera preview**: develop the CR2 in darktable or Canon's software when the look matters.
- **It looks different in every program**: programs differ in how they turn the raw data into color and tone.
- **A giant file fails**: the page gives up at about 537 megapixels and shows a "too large to convert here" notice. Develop such a file in desktop software instead.
- **Keeping it for later**: keep the CR2 even after you make a JPEG, because only the raw file allows new white balance and tone choices.

guide.title: About CR2 files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CR2 file?

CR2 is Canon's raw image format, the one many EOS cameras wrote from the mid-2000s until CR3 replaced it. Raw means the file holds the sensor's measurements instead of a finished picture. Software has to process them, choosing white balance, tone and color, before they look like a photograph.

A CR2 is built on TIFF, and it carries an embedded JPEG preview next to the sensor data. Canon's own Digital Photo Professional lists .CR2 among the raw extensions it reads.

You usually meet a CR2 when you copy a shoot off the memory card of a Canon camera and find that your phone, an email program or an upload form will not show it. A JPG fixes that.

Raw files exist so you can make those choices after the shot. The catch is that CR2 is a proprietary camera format. A program that recognizes the extension may still not support the camera that made the file.

### Programs that open CR2 files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** darktable lists CR2 as an import extension, and decoding depends on camera support.
- **Windows and Mac:** Canon Digital Photo Professional is Canon's own program and reads CR2 files from the cameras it lists. Adobe Camera Raw supports Canon cameras by model and by minimum plug-in version, so check Adobe's supported-camera list.
- **Linux:** LibRaw's dcraw_emu is a command-line raw developer; LibRaw lists the Canon cameras it supports.
- **Web and mobile:** browsers do not display CR2. This page decodes it with ImageMagick inside the page.

### CR2 and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .cr2 is Canon-specific; .jpg or .jpeg is image/jpeg.
- **What is stored**: a CR2 holds unprocessed sensor data and a small preview. A JPG holds a processed picture.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. The raw data in a CR2 is not a rendered picture at all.
- **Editing room**: raw leaves white balance and tone adjustments open until you process it. A JPG has them baked in.
- **Color depth**: JPEG stores 8 bits per channel, and this page works at 8 bits.
- **Reach**: all major browsers show JPEG, and it comes straight out of most digital cameras and scanners. CR2 needs a decoder that knows your camera.

Its name comes from a committee, the Joint Photographic Experts Group; the ISO/IEC 10918-1 standard dates from 1994. Most programs expose quality as a number from 0 to 100, yet equal numbers in two programs can look different.

The step from CR2 to JPG is a processing step as well as a format change. After it, you have one picture, not a file you can re-develop. For a result you control, develop the CR2 in a raw editor first, then export the JPG from there. If you only need a quick copy to share or to check focus, the converter on this page is enough.

### Other ways to convert CR2 to JPG

- **darktable (Windows, Mac, Linux):** import the CR2 and select it. In the export module, target storage is set to file on disk; then JPEG is chosen as the format, and you press export. The module has a quality setting for JPEG, which defaults to 95.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick cr2:portrait.cr2 portrait.jpg`. ImageMagick's format list says CR2 needs the explicit `cr2:` specifier before the file name. In a test with a sample CR2 this wrote a JPG.

### Problems with CR2 files

- **The program says it cannot read the file**: the extension is recognized but your camera model is not. Update the program, or convert with a decoder that lists the camera.
- **Brightness and color differ from your camera**: the camera, this page and your editor each turn the sensor data into a picture in their own way, so the results will not match.
- **"The RAW file is damaged." or "ends before its picture does"**: the decoder reports the file as cut off or corrupt. Copy it from the card again.
- **Too large to convert**: roughly 537 megapixels is the ceiling; above it you see a message that the picture is too big for this page.
- **You worry the CR2 will not open in future**: it is a proprietary camera format, so long-term access depends on programs keeping support for it. Hold on to the original file.
- **The JPG looks flat**: this page has no tone or color controls. Use darktable to adjust the picture and export your own JPG.

### What is a CR2 file?

Canon RAW version 2, or CR2, is the raw image format of many Canon EOS cameras from the mid-2000s until CR3 replaced it. Inside a TIFF-based file sit unprocessed sensor readings and an embedded JPEG preview. The Library of Congress notes that raw formats need special software to turn them into usable images. - **Linux:**

guide.title: Understanding CR2 to PNG
guide.markdown:
### What is a CR2 file?

The CR2 extension identifies a Canon camera-raw format. Raw files retain sensor measurements that require processing to produce a viewable photograph, so a CR2 differs from a finished JPEG: a raw workflow leaves image interpretation to processing software. Raw processing permits choices such as white balance and tone adjustment after capture. Canon's Digital Photo Professional lists .CR2 among its supported raw-image extensions.

Long-term access depends on support for a proprietary camera format, which is a preservation concern. A CR2 is best treated as the master, with PNG or JPG as copies made from it.

### Programs that open CR2 files

- **Windows and Mac:** Canon Digital Photo Professional reads supported CR2 files, and Adobe Camera Raw covers Canon files too; its supported-camera list tells you which models it handles.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** darktable accepts CR2 among its import extensions, though whether a given file decodes depends on camera support. On Linux, the dcraw_emu sample program in LibRaw is a command-line raw developer, and the LibRaw site lists the Canon bodies it supports.

### CR2 and PNG compared

CR2 is capture-oriented material that requires development. PNG stores already interpreted raster samples. PNG came about as a patent-free GIF replacement; it compresses losslessly with DEFLATE and stores between 1 and 16 bits per sample, with an optional alpha channel. Past its opening eight-byte signature, the file is made of named chunks, with the image header in IHDR, compressed pixels in IDAT, and IEND as the terminator. PNG shows up in every major browser, and macOS uses it for screenshots unless told otherwise. Its media type is image/png. The conversion commits to one rendition of the photograph, including the color and tone decisions of the decoder.

Lossless PNG compression applies to the developed pixels, not to the sensor data. A PNG cannot be turned back into the CR2, and it does not keep the adjustments a raw processor could make. A raw preview and a developed output can differ because the raw data still requires color and tone processing.

On this page, ImageMagick reads the CR2 in your browser and writes the PNG. The page has no white balance, exposure or quality controls. Since the ImageMagick build here is an 8-bit one, the PNG has 8 bits per channel. It reads a single image from the file. Anything above roughly 537 megapixels stops with a "too large" message, since the pixels alone would use over half of the 4 GB the engine can address.

### Other ways to convert CR2 to PNG

- **RawTherapee:** open the photo in the Editor, click the small hard disk icon below the preview to open the Save window, choose PNG and a bit depth there, and save at once or send it to the queue. You decide the rendition, instead of accepting one automatic development.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick cr2:photograph.cr2 photograph.png`. ImageMagick's format list marks CR2 as read-only and says it needs the explicit `cr2:` prefix, and it lists PNG as readable and writable.

### Problems with CR2 files

**The camera is not supported.** A recognized CR2 suffix does not guarantee support for the camera that made it. Check the decoder's model list, update the software and try a different raw processor. Canon's own Digital Photo Professional is a sensible second opinion, and darktable offers a third route; try both before concluding that the file itself is damaged. Renaming the file to another image extension does not develop its sensor data.

**The colors or brightness look wrong.** Because the data needs color and tone processing, a PNG can look different from the camera preview. Open the CR2 in a raw editor, adjust exposure and white balance there, and compare with the look you intended.

**The file will not convert.** A very large picture can stop with a "too large" message, so try a desktop raw workflow when a file fails. Check dimensions and visible detail in the exported PNG before you replace a working copy.

**The PNG is larger than the raw file.** PNG compresses losslessly, so a full-size photograph can make a big file. Keep the CR2 as the master, since long-term access to a proprietary camera format is a preservation concern, and make PNG or JPG copies from it.

CR2, or Canon RAW version 2, was the raw format of many Canon EOS cameras until CR3 took over. Inside is unprocessed sensor data in a TIFF-based layout. - **Origin**: Aldus published TIFF, and Adobe now maintains it.

guide.title: About CR3 files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CR3 file?

CR3 is the camera RAW format Canon introduced in 2018 for newer EOS cameras; Canon ties the .CR3 extension to EOS models released since then. It uses a container based on the ISO base media file format, with lossy or lossless compression.

RAW records the sensor's data, and that needs image processing before ordinary delivery. The camera can also write Compact RAW, called C-RAW, which makes smaller files than the normal RAW option by using lossy compression. Shooting RAW+JPEG makes the camera write two separate files under one image number.

CR3 is used for photography with recent Canon cameras and for editing photos before conversion to JPEG. Canon Digital Photo Professional, Adobe Lightroom, Adobe Photoshop and darktable open it. Processing a RAW file into a JPEG can leave the original RAW unchanged.

### Programs that open CR3 files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- RawTherapee: CR3 decoding arrived in version 5.8, and that release lacked metadata support.
- darktable: gained CR3 support in version 3.8, subject to camera and dependency requirements.

**Windows and Mac**

- Canon Digital Photo Professional: processes supported Canon RAW images.

**Mobile**

- Adobe Lightroom for mobile: for iOS and Android; it edits camera RAW only from supported camera files and with premium access. Check the Canon model; Android file-picker recognition may require share-to-Lightroom or camera PTP import.

### CR3 and JPEG compared

- **Extensions and names**: .cr3 is Canon's RAW format. The .jpg and .jpeg extensions both mean JPEG here, and .jpg is what the page writes.
- **Contents**: CR3 holds unprocessed sensor data. JPEG holds a processed picture and is designed for photographs.
- **Compression**: CR3 has lossy and lossless options. JPEG is lossy, with adjustable quality in general.
- **Container and standard**: a CR3 is an ISO base media file. ISO/IEC 10918-1 is the standard in which the Joint Photographic Experts Group describes JPEG.
- **Typical use**: CR3 serves photography with recent Canon cameras. Typical JPEG uses are web photos, camera output, mail attachments and sharing pictures.
- **Support**: JPEG is supported everywhere. Third-party RAW support must be checked for the particular camera model.

The page reads the CR3 with ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly, which uses the LibRaw library for camera RAW, and writes a JPEG. ImageMagick reads one image from the file and passes no quality setting, and nothing is stripped on purpose. A frame bigger than roughly 537 megapixels is turned away, and the page says the picture is too big for this converter. The work happens in your browser on the main thread, with no server involved. Your CR3 is not changed; you download a new JPEG next to it, named like the CR3 but ending .jpeg.

If you shot RAW+JPEG, look next to the CR3 first: Canon writes a separate file with the same image number, and the JPEG may already be what you need.

### Other ways to convert CR3 to JPEG

- **Canon Digital Photo Professional on Windows or Mac:** select an image, choose File > Convert and save, pick a destination, enter a file name and select an image type.
- **RawTherapee (Windows, Mac, Linux):** click the disk icon to open a Save As dialog with the name, location, format, bit depth and compression level, then save immediately or put the image at the head or tail of the processing queue. The gears icon queues it.
- **darktable (Windows, Mac, Linux):** in the export module, switch the target to file on disk, pick JPEG, adjust quality (default 95) and size, and press Export.

### Problems with CR3 files

- **Your editor does not know your camera**: an older Digital Photo Professional build may fail to understand RAW files from a newer camera.
- **A third-party program shows nothing**: see whether that program supports your particular camera model.
- **RawTherapee 5.8 lacks metadata**: it decoded CR3 pixels without CR3 metadata, and its release notes describe selecting an input profile manually.
- **Lightroom for mobile does not list the file**: on Android, the file picker may only recognize it after share-to-Lightroom or a camera PTP import.
- **The file will not convert here**: one message says the file may be incomplete, meaning it was cut short, and another says it is damaged. Copy it from the card again.
- **The picture is too large**: a result over about 537 megapixels is refused here, and the page says it is too big.

### What is a CR3 file?

Canon brought in CR3 as a raw image format in 2018, for its newer EOS cameras. Its container follows the ISO base media file format, the family that MP4 belongs to, and the compression inside can be lossy or lossless. It is a proprietary Canon format and the successor to CR2.

A raw file holds sensor readings rather than a finished photograph. The Library of Congress describes camera raw data as captured through the sensor's color filter array with very little processing, so demosaicing, white balance, gamma correction and noise reduction all still lie ahead. Those choices are what a raw editor lets you make after the shot.

You find CR3 files on the cards of recent Canon cameras, or in a folder of shots sent over for editing. Almost nothing outside a raw editor displays one directly, which is why people convert them. Because the conversion makes a new file, the CR3 on your disk is not touched.

Raw formats also carry a long-term risk. Manufacturers rarely publish the specification, and the formats change as new models arrive, so support can fade. Keeping the CR3 next to a PNG protects you if software later stops reading it. Adobe's DNG is another attempt to reduce that risk, since it normalizes camera raw data and can embed a copy of the original raw file.

### Programs that open CR3 files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- darktable imports CR3 files and decodes them through its RawSpeed library.

**Windows and Mac:**

- Canon's Digital Photo Professional names .CR3 among its supported raw extensions, beside CR2 and CRW.

### CR3 and PNG compared

- **Extensions and MIME types**: .cr3 for Canon raw; .png with image/png.
- **Container**: CR3 is an ISO base media file. A PNG begins with an eight-byte signature followed by chunks, among them IHDR first, IDAT for the image data and IEND last.
- **Compression**: PNG always compresses losslessly, using DEFLATE, so re-saving a PNG never costs quality. A CR3 may be lossy or lossless.
- **Color depth**: PNG samples run from 1 to 16 bits, but the picture this page writes has 8 bits per channel.
- **Origins**: PNG was designed as an open, patent-free alternative to GIF. The W3C published its Third Edition as a Recommendation on 24 June 2025, and the Library of Congress notes it is not yet an International Standard.
- **Color types**: PNG supports indexed-color, grayscale and truecolor images. Optional chunks can carry gamma, chromaticity and an ICC profile.
- **Transparency**: PNG can carry an alpha channel. A camera photograph has no transparency to carry.
- **Metadata**: the Library of Congress notes that practices for storing Exif or XMP data in PNG have been inconsistent, and this page doesn't copy metadata across.

The conversion develops the raw data into an ordinary picture and then stores that picture without further loss. After that you can edit it in any program, but you cannot go back to the sensor values or change the white balance as a raw editor would. Select a group of CR3 files and each is rendered in turn, giving a separate PNG for every one. The page reads each file in your browser with ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly, and it offers no development options.

### Other ways to convert CR3 to PNG

- **darktable (Windows, Mac, Linux):** after developing the CR3, open the export module, pick file on disk as the target storage, choose PNG as the file format, set the bit depth and profile, then press start export. The camera must be one that darktable supports.

### Problems with CR3 files

- **A program says the file is not supported**: an older version of a raw editor may not understand files from a newer camera. Update the software.
- **A third-party program shows no preview**: its CR3 support has to cover your exact camera model, so check its list.
- **Colors differ from the camera screen**: the raw data requires color and tone processing, and this page applies none of your choices.
- **The result is lossless but not raw**: the PNG stores every developed pixel exactly. If you want different tone or white balance later, go back to the CR3.
- **"Too large to convert here"**: the page refuses files declaring more than about 537 megapixels; develop those in desktop software.

guide.title: About CR3 files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CR3 file?

CR3 is the extension Canon uses for camera RAW images, tied to EOS cameras released since 2018. It stores sensor data, so the picture needs image processing before ordinary delivery. Compact RAW produces smaller files than the normal RAW option, using lossy compression.

A CR3 is QuickTime-based, CR2 is TIFF-based and CRW is CIFF-based, so renaming a file never turns it into one of the others. Processing a RAW file into another format can leave the original RAW unchanged.

### Programs that open CR3 files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** darktable has read CR3 since version 3.8 when camera and dependencies allow, and RawTherapee decodes it from version 5.8, without CR3 metadata in that first release.
- **Windows and Mac:** Digital Photo Professional is Canon's program for supported Canon RAW files.
- **Mobile:** On iOS and Android, Lightroom for mobile edits camera RAW if the camera files are supported and premium access is in place.

### CR3 and TIFF compared

- **History**: Aldus and Microsoft developed TIFF, revision 6.0 came out in 1992, and Adobe controls it today.
- **Flexibility**: compression and color representation both come in several varieties inside TIFF's tag-based wrapper.
- **Naming**: .tif and .tiff name one format, typed image/tiff.
- **Contents**: one TIFF can hold many images.
- **Limit**: BigTIFF extends the offset fields that confine classic TIFF, which uses 32 bits, to roughly 4 GB.

ImageMagick, running in your browser, reads the CR3 and writes the TIFF. The page sets no bit depth, profile or compression.

### Other ways to convert CR3 to TIFF

- **Canon Digital Photo Professional:** pick the CR3 images and open File > Batch process. Set TIFF as the output, then click Execute.
- **darktable:** with the CR3 open in darktable, go to the export module, select file on disk as storage target and TIFF as format. Check the bit depth and profile settings, then export.

### Problems with CR3 files

- **A new camera's file is refused**: your copy of Digital Photo Professional may be too old to read RAW from a newer body.
- **Third-party support is model by model**: check the exact camera.
- **No CR3 metadata in RawTherapee 5.8**: only pixels were decoded, and selecting an input profile by hand is the workaround its release notes describe.
- **A cut-off file**: the reader flags it as possibly incomplete, and a fresh copy from the card is the remedy.
- **A very large picture**: the too large to convert here message covers a RAW file, or the picture it declares, beyond what the converter handles.

guide.title: About CRW files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CRW file?

CRW is a Canon camera RAW format built on CIFF, short for Camera Image File Format. The header specifies the byte order and points to a root directory, and the records inside are organized in a hierarchy of directories. Canon's EOS Digital Rebel is one camera that records its RAW images as CRW.

Structurally, CRW differs from CR2, which is TIFF-based, and from QuickTime-based CR3.

### Programs that open CRW files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick is a free command-line reader that lists CRW as read-only. ExifTool inspects CRW and CIFF structure and tags, but is not a photo editor.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe Camera Raw has a camera table naming the older Canon models it supports and the version each needs. Canon Digital Photo Professional lists .CRW among its Canon RAW image types.

### CRW and JPG compared

- **Origin**: the committee that wrote JPEG began work in 1986, ITU-T T.81 appeared in 1992 and ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994.
- **Method**: after dividing the picture into 8x8 pixel blocks, baseline JPEG applies a discrete cosine transform and Huffman coding.
- **Depth**: 8 bits for every channel, with no alpha channel.
- **Size**: ordinary settings leave an image at a tenth to a twentieth of its uncompressed size.
- **Reach**: every major browser displays a JPG, and cameras and scanners build it in.
- **Names**: .jpg and .jpeg are the same format, registered as image/jpeg.

ImageMagick, running in the page, decodes the CRW picture. The JPG is then written from it, with no quality setting from this page.

### Other ways to convert CRW to JPG

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick older-canon.crw older-canon.jpg`. In its format table, CRW is marked read-only and JPEG read and write.
- **Canon Digital Photo Professional:** with the CRW selected, choose File > Batch process, pick JPEG and finish with Execute.

### Problems with CRW files

- **Support depends on the model**: RAW support varies with the camera and with the library version bundled in each program.
- **A preview is not the photo**: metadata and an embedded preview do not replace decoding the RAW picture.
- **A renamed file fails**: CRW, CR2 and CR3 are separate structures.
- **Cut-off copies**: the reader says when the file ends early or is damaged, so retry with the original from the card.
- **A very large picture**: anything beyond what the converter can hold is reported as too large for it.

guide.title: About CSV and JPG
guide.markdown:
### What is a CSV file?

CSV exchanges rows of text fields between databases and spreadsheets. RFC 4180 documented a common representation in October 2005 rather than inventing the older format, and the registered media type is text/csv. A header record may come before the data rows, and double quotes protect fields that contain commas or line breaks. Dialects differ in delimiter and quoting, and a spreadsheet export stores one sheet's data without workbook formatting.

### Programs that open CSV files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** LibreOffice Calc opens Text CSV through an import dialog with delimiter and column-format choices.
- **Windows and Mac:** Microsoft Excel imports and exports CSV; choose text handling with care for identifiers.
- **Linux:** the Python csv module reads records with configurable dialects.
- **Web:** Google provides a documented Apps Script for importing CSV into Google Sheets.

### CSV and JPG compared

- **Content**: CSV is text you can sort and calculate with. JPG holds pixels, so the numbers in the picture cannot be selected as data.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy and has no alpha.
- **Types**: text/csv against image/jpeg; .jpg and .jpeg are the same format.

The page reads the CSV with the same parser the table converters use and draws it on a canvas. The picture is saved at JPEG quality 0.92, with no other setting to choose. Several CSV files selected together become one JPG each.

### Other ways to convert CSV to JPG

- **Calc and ImageMagick:** in Calc, choose File > Open for the CSV, then File > Export As > Export as PDF. Turn the first PDF page into an image with `magick 'table.pdf[0]' table.jpg`. ImageMagick relies on Ghostscript to read PDF.
- **Excel and GIMP:** open the CSV in Excel with File > Open, select the cells, and choose Home > Copy arrow > Copy as Picture. In GIMP choose File > Create > From Clipboard, then File > Export As and type a name ending in .jpg.
- **Python and Pillow:** read the rows with `csv.reader`, draw them on an image with `ImageDraw.multiline_text` and save with `image.save("table.jpg", "JPEG")`. You choose the canvas size, fonts and column widths in the script.

### Problems with CSV files

- **Everything lands in one column**: the delimiter does not match what the program expects. Set the separator in the import dialog.
- **Dates or IDs changed**: Excel can reinterpret them on opening. Import with the column formats you want.
- **Rows split in the wrong place**: a parser must honor quoted line breaks rather than treat each physical line as a record.
- **Formatting is gone**: CSV saves the current sheet's data alone.

guide.title: About CUR files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CUR file?

CUR is the Windows cursor container. It resembles ICO, but a CUR also stores the coordinates of the pointer's active location, called the hotspot. A single CUR can embed images of several sizes, each with hotspot information of its own.

Animated cursors belong to ANI, which is a separate workflow from ordinary CUR files. Because CUR is specialized for pointer assets, a conventional image format suits a picture you only want to view or share.

### Programs that open CUR files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads CUR, which makes it a way to inspect or render cursor images.
- **Windows:** Visual Studio Image Editor handles cursor resources, but a 32-bit image can only be viewed, not edited.
- **Mac and Linux:** XnView MP lists CUR among its supported formats. Private and educational use is free.

### CUR and GIF compared

- **Origin**: CompuServe introduced GIF in 1987. The GIF89a version, dated July 1990, added transparency, frame timing, comments and application data.
- **Compression**: lossless LZW, for which Unisys began charging license fees in 1994.
- **Palette**: each image uses at most 256 colors.
- **Transparency**: a GIF marks one palette color as fully clear and has no partial transparency.
- **Motion**: many images fit in one GIF, and the delay between them is set in hundredths of a second.
- **Reach**: every major browser displays it, and its media type is image/gif.

Once the browser has decoded the CUR, ImageMagick in the page encodes the GIF. The page sets no quality of its own.

### Other ways to convert CUR to GIF

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick pointer.cur pointer.gif`.
- **Pillow:** open the file with Image.open and save it with a .gif name. Pillow lists CUR as read-only, and its decoder reads the largest cursor. Animated cursors are not supported.
- **ImageMagick and GIMP:** run `magick pointer.cur pointer.png`, open the PNG in GIMP and export it as GIF. The dialog offers Interlace and Save comment, and GIMP exports a maximum of 256 colors.

### Problems with CUR files

- **Clicks land off target**: when the hotspot is misplaced, a click lands away from the point the pointer seems to indicate, so check each frame's coordinates.
- **Resized cursors misalign**: every embedded size needs its own valid hotspot, and coordinates copied blindly between sizes can leave the pointer misaligned.
- **Soft edges turn blocky**: a GIF cannot keep partial opacity, and its 256-color palette can change gradients.

faqs.question: Does the cursor keep its transparency?
faqs.answer: Yes. The cursor's outline sits on a clear background in the PNG, because the page keeps transparency when it writes PNG.

faqs.question: What happens to the hotspot?
faqs.answer: It is dropped. The hotspot marks the active pointer pixel, and CUR stores its coordinates beside the image. The PNG has no field for it, so write the coordinates down before converting if you plan to rebuild a cursor.

faqs.question: My CUR has several sizes. Which one do I get?

faqs.question: Can a PNG become a cursor again?

faqs.question: Does an animated cursor work?

faqs.question: Is the metadata kept?
faqs.answer: No. Only raw pixels reach the PNG writer, so metadata does not come along.

faqs.question: Is a CUR the same as an ICO?
faqs.answer: They are related, with CUR adding the active pointer position. For that target, use [CUR to ICO](/cur-to-ico/).

faqs.question: Does the PNG have a quality setting?

faqs.question: Why does the page say the picture could not be decoded?

guide.title: About CUR and PNG
guide.markdown:
### What is a CUR file?

Windows stores custom mouse pointers and cursor themes in the CUR container. Its layout resembles ICO, with the addition of coordinates for the active pointer location. Those coordinates name the hotspot, the one pixel treated as the click point.

A single CUR can hold images at different dimensions, and every one has its own hotspot data. Animated cursors belong to ANI and not to the usual CUR workflow. The format is built for pointer assets, so an ordinary image format fits better when you have no use for the hotspot, which is the usual reason for converting. When you convert a CUR, you are generally after the picture, for use as artwork, in documentation or as a reference.

The hotspot is the part that trips people up. A misplaced hotspot makes clicks land away from the visually expected point, and a multi-size cursor needs a valid hotspot in every embedded image. Copying coordinates blindly between sizes can misalign the pointer.

### Programs that open CUR files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - ImageMagick lists CUR as a readable format, so you can use it to inspect or render cursor images.
- **Windows:**
  - Visual Studio Image Editor can view and edit cursor resources; 32-bit images can be viewed there but not edited.
- **Mac and Linux:**
  - XnView MP, a viewer that lists CUR as a supported format, costs nothing for private and educational use.

### CUR and PNG compared

- **Names and types**: .cur for a Windows cursor, .png for a Portable Network Graphics image.
- **Structure**: a CUR holds the same layout as an ICO, with a hotspot for each image and several sizes per file. A PNG holds one picture and no hotspot.
- **Transparency**: both can carry alpha transparency. PNG compression is lossless.
- **Standard**: PNG appeared in the mid-1990s to replace GIF without patent worries, and it is an ISO/IEC 15948 standard as well as a W3C Recommendation.
- **Support**: every browser displays PNG, while CUR mostly serves Windows pointers.

Your browser's own image decoder reads the CUR and hands the pixels to the page, which writes the PNG with a canvas. Transparency is kept and PNG has no quality setting, so nothing is traded away for file size. Pixels pass through as 8-bit RGBA, and since only pixels travel, metadata does not. The work happens in your browser, in a Web Worker that falls back to the main thread if the worker fails, so the file is not uploaded.

Several CUR files may be selected in one go. The page handles them in order and saves a PNG for each, named like the source but ending in .png. Nothing is zipped, the CUR files stay as they were, and the page applies no file-size cap of its own.

A PNG of a cursor is a picture only. It shows what the pointer looks like, but the click point is stored in the CUR and not in the PNG. That is fine for documentation, screenshots or a reference image, and it is the reason to keep the CUR if you plan to install the cursor again. The PNG also holds a single picture. If a CUR contains several sizes, use a tool from the list below to choose the one you want.

### Other ways to convert CUR to PNG

- **ImageMagick:** `magick 'input.cur[0]' output.png` names the first embedded image explicitly. ImageMagick's documentation says an index in square brackets selects an image from a multi-image file and that numbering starts at zero, so changing it to `[1]` takes the second image. ImageMagick lists CUR among the formats it reads.
- **Pillow:** `python3 -c "from PIL import Image; Image.open('input.cur').save('output.png')"` saves the cursor as a PNG. Pillow's documentation says its CUR decoder reads the largest available cursor and that animated cursors are not supported. CUR is on its read-only list, so it can open the format but not write it.

### Problems with CUR files

- **Clicks land in the wrong place after you rebuild a cursor**: the hotspot is not stored in the PNG. Set it again in your cursor editor and check each frame's coordinates.
- **You wanted a different size**: the page saves one picture. Use ImageMagick with an index to pick another image from the file.
- **The page says decoding failed**: your browser could not read the file. Try another copy, or a current browser.
- **You only have an animated .ani cursor**: that is a separate format, and this page reads CUR.
- **A hotspot looks misplaced in your own cursor**: open the cursor in an editor and compare the point for each size.
- **You do not need the hotspot at all**: a conventional image format such as PNG is the better choice for artwork.

guide.title: About DCM and JPEG
guide.markdown:
### What is a DCM file?

DCM is the usual ending for DICOM, the standard that defines medical objects such as images, waveforms and reports. The ACR-NEMA predecessor appeared in 1985 and the renamed DICOM standard followed in 1993. The registered media type is application/dicom, and the registration recommends .dcm for disk files other than DICOMDIR, which can index a collection of related files. A Part 10 file begins with a 128-byte preamble followed by the DICM marker. A DCM stores an image together with patient and study metadata, and its pixels can be 16-bit grayscale.

### Programs that open DCM files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** 3D Slicer imports DICOM studies into a database and then loads the series you choose. ImageMagick can read DICOM images, and its notes list window center and width tag handling.
- **Windows:** MicroDicom is a viewer, free for noncommercial use, for CT, MRI and other DICOM studies. IrfanView lists DCM, ACR and IMA among its formats, which need its plug-ins.

### DCM and JPEG compared

- **Content**: a DCM holds the image and its attributes. A JPEG holds only a picture.
- **Depth**: DICOM pixels can be 16-bit grayscale, while a JPEG has no transparency and is always lossy.
- **Compression**: DICOM has many compression options.
- **Types**: application/dicom against image/jpeg.

No conversion happens on this page: with no DICOM reader, the file is rejected with "Image decode failed." Do the export in a program that understands the format.

### Other ways to convert DCM to JPEG

- **MicroDicom (Windows):** open the images, or a disc or folder with File > Scan for DICOM files, then choose File > Export > To a picture file or press Shift+P. Pick a destination folder, what to export and JPG as the image format, then click Export. More settings sets the JPEG quality and whether annotations and overlay text are drawn.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick image.dcm image.jpeg`. ImageMagick reads DICOM images and recognizes window center and width tags.
- **IrfanView (Windows):** install the plug-ins IrfanView needs for DCM, open the file, then use File > Save as and choose JPG as the output format.

### Problems with DCM files

- **Only one slice opens**: a series often spans many files. Open the folder in a viewer.
- **Can't tell whose study it is**: file and folder names do not reliably identify the patient, study or series. Use the DICOM attributes.
- **Some objects will not load**: certain information objects need 3D Slicer extensions instead of its core importer.
- **Patient details travel with the study**: DICOM objects can contain demographic information, so sharing an exported image and sharing the source study have different privacy consequences.

guide.title: Understanding DCM for JPG output
guide.markdown:
### What is a DCM file?

A .dcm file is usually a DICOM object. DICOM stands for Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine, and the DICOM site calls it the international standard for medical images and related information. ISO recognizes it as ISO 12052, and it is built into almost every radiology, cardiology imaging and radiotherapy device. The format reference adds that it stores X-rays, CT and MRI scans together with patient and study metadata, and that its image data can be 16-bit grayscale with many compression options.

The media type is application/dicom, and IANA recommends .dcm for saved files. Data inside a saved file follows a 128-byte preamble and then the text DICM. A DICOMDIR file is different: it indexes a collection, and the files it names must be present. Medical datasets are organized as patients, studies, series and instances, and a series can span many files. Converting one file to a picture therefore does not necessarily export an examination or even a complete series.

This page does not promise to convert a DCM. It reads pictures with your browser's own image decoder, and a DICOM file can end with the message "Image decode failed." The sections below cover programs that open a DICOM and export a JPG.

### Programs that open DCM files

**Windows:**

- MicroDicom is a DICOM viewer for the Windows platform, and its File > Export > To a picture file dialog writes JPG pictures.
- RadiAnt has an Export button that writes JPEG copies of what you are viewing.

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- 3D Slicer imports DICOM folders into a local database organized by patient, study and series. Its core handles images, segmentations, parametric maps and some structured reports, and other object types need extensions.
- ImageMagick lists DCM as read-only and notes that its reader handles window center and width tags. It does not browse a whole study.

### DCM and JPG compared

- **Purpose**: a DICOM object carries image samples together with patient and study attributes. A JPG carries one rendered picture.
- **Standard**: DICOM is maintained by NEMA. JPEG is defined by ISO/IEC 10918-1.
- **Compression**: a DCM may use many compression options. A JPG is always lossy and has an adjustable quality.
- **Depth**: DICOM data can be 16-bit grayscale. A JPG is a presentation of the image, not the original sample values.
- **Transparency**: a JPG has no alpha channel.
- **Frames and slices**: a multi-frame DICOM can be exported as separate pictures, and a series needs an intentional export scope. A single JPG cannot stand in for the structure of a study.

Annotations and metadata are separate matters. MicroDicom can draw annotations onto the pictures it exports, and RadiAnt's annotation options are Full, Basic (anonymous) or Disabled. Inspect the actual output and the export settings before sharing a derivative. Keep the original dataset when the recipient requires DICOM, rather than assuming a JPG serves the same purpose.

### Other ways to convert DCM to JPG

- **MicroDicom (Windows):** with the images open, use File > Export > To a picture file (the shortcut is Shift+P). Set a destination folder, how much to export, from one image up to every patient, and JPG as the format; then click Export. More settings cover separate files for multi-frame images, annotations, image size and JPEG quality.
- **RadiAnt (Windows):** click the Export button or press Ctrl+E. Choose JPEG, the scope (current image, current series or all opened series), click Export and select a folder. More options set the filename prefix, image size, annotations and JPEG quality.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick scan.dcm preview.jpg`. Check the result, because the command is not a replacement for study browsing, frame selection or review in a DICOM viewer.

### Problems with DCM files

- **This page reports a decode error**: the page does not promise to read DICOM. Use one of the applications above instead.
- **Only one slice appears**: check whether the study includes other instances in the series or whether one object contains multiple frames. Use the viewer's scope controls to export what you need.
- **The picture is the wrong size**: check the image size option in the export settings of your viewer.
- **Names or measurements remain visible**: inspect annotations and the image itself before sharing.
- **A recipient asks for the original study**: supply the DICOM dataset through the appropriate workflow. RadiAnt can copy the source DICOM files when you choose DICOM as the export format.
- **A file doesn't open as a picture**: a DICOM file begins with its own header, so a viewer that understands DICOM has to render it. Renaming it to .jpg changes nothing inside.

guide.title: About DDS files
guide.markdown:
### What is a DDS file?

DirectDraw Surface, abbreviated DDS, is Microsoft's texture container, first made for DirectX and used for cubemaps too. Inside, the data may be plain pixels or compressed texture blocks, and the DXT or BC block formats meant for GPUs are common. Game textures and other GPU-ready assets are its typical uses.

Beside the largest surface a file may carry a chain of mipmaps, and cube maps and volume textures also fit. With Direct3D 10 and 11 came an extra header that adds texture arrays. This DX10 header can name formats the original pixel-format structure cannot express.

### Programs that open DDS files

**Windows, macOS and Linux**

- GIMP: built-in DDS support arrived in GIMP 2.10.10.
- ImageMagick: reads and writes DDS, including documented DXT compression and mipmap options.

### DDS and JPEG compared

- **Purpose**: a DDS is a texture container for graphics hardware. A JPEG is a photographic image format.
- **Compression**: a DDS commonly uses DXT or BC blocks. A JPEG is lossy with an adjustable quality.
- **Extras**: a DDS can hold mipmaps and cube maps. A JPEG is one image.
- **Alpha**: a DDS can have an alpha channel. A JPEG has none.
- **Support**: JPEG opens everywhere.

The page has ImageMagick read a single picture from the DDS and write it out as a JPEG.

### Other ways to convert DDS to JPEG

- **texconv:** run texconv -ft jpg review-texture.dds. This Microsoft DirectXTex tool takes a DDS as input, and -ft sets the output file type.
- **GIMP:** open the DDS, then choose File > Export As, use a .jpeg ending and click Export. The JPEG dialog offers a quality value from 0 to 100, and JPEG cannot hold transparency or multiple layers.
- **ImageMagick:** run magick review-texture.dds texture-report.jpeg. ImageMagick lists DDS with DXT and mipmap support.

### Problems with DDS files

- **A reader refuses it**: tools that reject the DX10 extension may accept a legacy RGB or DXT1 to DXT5 header instead.
- **The header is truncated**: a plain DDS header takes at least 128 bytes, and 148 with the DX10 extension.
- **The texture looks scrambled**: a wrong pitch value can throw off how a reader interprets scan lines, so compute it for the stored format.
