guide.title: About GIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF, short for Graphics Interchange Format, was created at CompuServe in 1987. It stores a picture as a grid of palette indexes, compressed with LZW, and every frame may use only 256 colors. The GIF89a version of the specification added blocks that let a file hold several frames with a delay between them, and mark one palette entry as transparent. That is how GIF became the web's looping cartoon format, and it is still common for reaction images, stickers and small diagrams.

The extension doesn't tell you whether a file is a still or an animation. Open it in a browser to see whether it moves.

A multi-frame GIF carries more than pictures. Each frame can have its own local palette, a delay, and a disposal method that says how the frame is treated after it is shown. An interlaced GIF stores its rows out of order. All of that is detail a still copy doesn't need, which is why this page drops it.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP exports a GIF as a still picture or as an animation made from several layers. ImageMagick reads GIF on the command line.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome displays GIF, animation included, in web pages.
- **Web:** Firefox displays GIF, animation included. Dragging a file into a browser window is the quickest way to see whether it moves.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays GIF in web pages. A screenshot of an animated GIF is a still, so keep the file itself.

### GIF and GIF compared

Input and output are the same format here, so the extension (.gif) and the media type (image/gif) don't change. What changes is the file itself.

- **Frames**: the page reads the first frame of the input. The new GIF has one frame, so there is no animation, delay or loop.
- **Palette**: one frame can use 256 colors at most, and the new file follows the same rule.
- **Transparency**: GIF transparency is on or off for each pixel, with no partial opacity, so a soft shadow can't be stored.
- **Compression**: GIF's LZW is lossless. The file is written again, so its bytes need not match the original's.
- **Metadata**: the picture passes through raw pixels, so comments and other embedded information are left behind.
- **Size in pixels**: unchanged. The page doesn't scale the picture.

Because source and target match, the page offers no quality choice, and what is lost is the frames after the first. If you start with an animation, the new file shows only its first frame.

In short, this conversion turns any GIF into a still copy of its first frame, and nothing else.

### Other ways to convert GIF to GIF

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** choose File > Export As to open the GIF export dialog. For an animation, tick As animation; the option is disabled when the image has only one layer.
- **gifsicle (command line):** run `gifsicle -O3 input.gif -o optimized.gif` to rewrite a GIF with several optimization methods tried. The manual notes that -O3 can occasionally make a file larger.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.gif rewritten.gif`, the same input-then-output form its manual uses for converting between formats.

If your GIF moves and you want it to keep moving, use gifsicle or the [GIF compressor](/compress-gif/), not this page.

### Problems with GIF files

- **The result doesn't move**: this page keeps one frame. Go back to the original file.
- **Trails behind moving objects**: frame disposal is wrong. GIMP offers "Cumulative layers (combine)" and "One frame per layer (replace)"; pick the one that matches how the animation was drawn.
- **Banding in a gradient**: 256 colors can't hold a smooth blend. Use PNG, or JPG for a photo.
- **Soft edges turn jagged**: a GIF pixel is either transparent or not, so partial opacity can't be kept. Use PNG instead.
- **A comment goes missing in GIMP**: GIF comments support only 7-bit ASCII, so GIMP exports without a comment that has other characters.
- **Colors shift after exporting from GIMP**: GIMP writes a GIF with at most 256 colors, so a gradient can band.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the browser was unable to read the file. It may be damaged, or it may not be a GIF at all. Fetch a fresh copy from the original source.

guide.title: About GIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF is an indexed-color raster format that supports both individual pictures and timed image sequences. Every picture in a GIF draws from a palette limited to 256 entries, and transparency works by flagging one entry as clear, so soft edges cannot keep partial opacity. That suits flat logos and badges better than photographs.

For an icon, the real question is which frame carries the drawing.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP can export a single picture or a multilayer animation as GIF, and ImageMagick reads GIF, though your install's own format list is the final word on support.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox display GIF files in the page.
- **Mobile:** Safari shows GIF files, as does Chrome on a phone.

### GIF and ICO compared

- **Names and media types**: .gif and .ico; the registered media type for ICO is image/vnd.microsoft.icon.
- **Content**: a GIF is a palette-based sequence of frames. ICO files may include several pictures and are little-endian.
- **Typical use**: ICO is Microsoft's format for interface icons, and it is widely associated with website favicons.

The page decodes the GIF to pixels and keeps its first frame; delays and looping are not carried over. An image taller or wider than 256 px is shrunk to fit a 256 by 256 square with its shape unchanged, a smaller one stays as it is, and a full-size image goes into the ICO as PNG data. Metadata is dropped.

### Other ways to convert GIF to ICO

- **Pillow:** `Image.open("reaction.gif").save("reaction.ico", sizes=[(16,16),(32,32),(48,48)])` writes several sizes from one frame. The GIF loader supports seek() and tell(), so you can move to another frame before saving.

### Problems with GIF files

GIMP caps GIF exports at a 256-color palette, and gradients may shift as a result; the banding shows up once the picture is small. Look at the result on both light and dark backgrounds at its real size.

High-DPI screens show a small icon blurry, so prepare the largest clean still you have.

Because the output holds one image, prepare the version you want as a still first. A small logo or badge converts best; an animated reaction rarely makes a readable icon.

guide.title: GIF to JPG: formats and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

CompuServe released GIF, the Graphics Interchange Format, in 1987. GIF89a, a July 1990 revision, introduced extensions that cover transparency, frame timing, comments and application-specific data. LZW coding compresses the images without loss, and each image uses a palette of up to 256 colors. One GIF can hold many images with a pause between them, given in hundredths of a second, and that sequence is the animation.

For transparency, one palette color is flagged as fully clear, which leaves no partial transparency. In 1994 Unisys began to charge for licenses to use LZW. The relevant US patent ended in 2003, with European and Japanese ones following in 2004. Each frame also carries a disposal setting that tells a viewer what to do with the picture before drawing the next one. image/gif is the registered media type, and all major browsers display GIF. GIF is old and widely supported, which is why animated GIFs are still shared everywhere, while JPEG remains the usual choice for a single still picture.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP exports still pictures or multilayer animations, and can set an animated GIF to loop forever. ImageMagick reads GIF from a terminal.
- **Web:** GIF displays in Chrome and Firefox.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays GIF on iPhone and iPad.

On a Mac, Preview opens an animated GIF too, and shows its frames in the sidebar when you choose View > Thumbnails.

### GIF and JPEG compared

- **Extensions**: .gif is image/gif; .jpg and .jpeg are one format, image/jpeg.
- **Colors**: each GIF image draws from a small palette, against 8 bits for each color channel of a JPEG.
- **Compression**: GIF loses nothing. Baseline JPEG is lossy and works on 8x8 pixel blocks.
- **Transparency**: a GIF can flag a single palette color as clear, with no partial opacity. A JPEG lacks an alpha channel altogether.
- **Animation**: GIF stores many images, JPEG only one.
- **Patents**: the GIF LZW patents lapsed in 2003 and 2004, and JPEG's US patents on 27 October 2006.

Your browser decodes the GIF and the page keeps one picture, the first frame, so an animated GIF yields a still JPEG. The browser writes that frame as a lossy JPEG at quality 0.85, which is a fixed encode rather than a setting you choose. A JPEG cannot restore colors the GIF never had. Transparent areas can't stay transparent in a JPEG. Comments and other metadata are not copied. A set of GIFs is processed in sequence. Every JPEG is saved on its own with the .jpeg ending, named after its GIF, and no ZIP is made. Nothing is uploaded, since the whole conversion stays in your browser.

### Other ways to convert GIF to JPEG

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick "reaction.gif[0]" reaction.jpeg`. The frame number goes in brackets right after the input name, and frames are counted from 0. Quote the name so your shell doesn't read the brackets as a pattern.
- **Preview (Mac):** open the GIF, choose File > Export, choose JPEG from the Format pop-up menu, then click Save. To handle more than one file, open them all in a single Preview window, then select them in the sidebar before you export.

The bracket number is the way to pull a specific frame, since this page always takes the first. Preview is handy for a quick one-off export, while a terminal suits repeat jobs. Use ImageMagick when you need a later frame or a whole folder converted with a single command.

### Problems with GIF files

- **The JPEG shows only the first frame**: JPEG cannot animate. ImageMagick's bracket number exports the frame you want.
- **Banding or speckles**: a GIF frame has only 256 colors, and JPEG compression cannot add colors back. The limit comes from the GIF.
- **A transparent background is lost**: JPEG has no transparency, and soft transparent edges cannot retain partial opacity in a GIF to begin with. Convert to PNG instead if you need see-through areas.
- **Frames look wrong after combining**: when you open an animation as layers, disposal settings decide whether each layer replaces or builds on the one before, so match that choice in your editor.
- **A GIF comment goes missing**: a GIF comment with characters beyond seven-bit ASCII is left out by GIMP, and this page copies no metadata at all.

guide.title: About GIF and JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF, the Graphics Interchange Format, was introduced by CompuServe in 1987. The 89a revision of July 1990 introduced extensions for clear pixels, frame delays, comments and application data. A GIF compresses images losslessly with LZW coding, and every image draws from a palette of 256 colors at most. Its registered media type is image/gif. Those extensions are what make animated GIFs possible.

A GIF is a stack of images, each held for its own delay in hundredths of a second, and that stack is the animation. Only one palette color can be flagged clear, which leaves every pixel either fully clear or fully opaque. That palette limit is why GIF suits flat-color graphics better than photographs. Browsers all show GIF. Colors come from color tables, and an image may use a table of its own instead of the one for the whole file, so the frames of one GIF can differ in color.

You meet GIFs as short looping animations, reaction images, stickers and simple graphics.

### Programs that open GIF files

**Mac, Linux and Windows**

- GIMP: an image editor named in the format reference.
- ImageMagick: a command-line tool whose supported formats include GIF.
- Mozilla Firefox: shows GIF in the browser.

**Mac**

- Preview: listed in the format reference for GIFs.

**Web and Mobile**

- Google Chrome displays GIF.

**Mobile**

- Safari displays GIF.

### GIF and JPG compared

- **Names**: .gif is image/gif, while .jpg or .jpeg is image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: GIF is lossless but limited to 256 colors per image. JPEG is lossy: it works on 8x8 pixel blocks, runs a discrete cosine transform on each and finishes with Huffman coding.
- **Color**: GIF is indexed color. JPEG keeps 8 bits for each color channel.
- **Transparency**: a GIF can mark one color as transparent. JPEG has no alpha channel.
- **Animation**: a GIF holds timed frames, one after another. A JPG is a single still.
- **Good for**: GIF for simple graphics and short loops. JPEG for photographs.
- **Metadata**: only pixels are written, so blocks such as EXIF, ICC and XMP are left behind, along with the GIF's comments.
- **Patents**: the LZW patents behind GIF expired in 2003 and 2004. JPEG's US patents expired in 2006.
- **Quality numbers**: GIF has none, since it is lossless. JPEG quality usually runs from 0 to 100, though one number gives different results in different programs.

On this page your browser decodes the GIF, then the canvas writes its first frame as a JPG at quality 0.85. Pixels that were see-through can't stay see-through, and an animation is cut to its first frame. EXIF, ICC and XMP metadata is dropped.

The download takes the GIF's name with .jpg in place of .gif. Several GIFs are handled in sequence, and every JPG lands in its own download.

### Other ways to convert GIF to JPG

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the GIF and pick File > Export As. Select JPEG from the file-type list, press Export, and a JPEG settings dialog follows, with 85 as its default quality.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick 'input.gif[0]' output.jpg`. The [0] picks the first frame by number, and the quotes keep the brackets from being read by the shell.

Both give you control that this page does not, such as the quality setting.

### Problems with GIF files

- **Only one frame came out**: that is how a JPG works. Keep the GIF if you need the motion.
- **The see-through parts changed**: the GIF had transparency, which a JPG cannot hold. If you need it kept, convert to PNG instead with the [GIF to PNG converter](/gif-to-png/).
- **The first frame looks blank**: a GIF's first frame can be mostly see-through, and a JPG cannot keep see-through pixels, so check that the first frame is the one you want.
- **The timing is gone**: a GIF keeps a delay in hundredths of a second for each frame, and a JPG has nowhere to keep it.
- **Gradients look banded**: a GIF palette has at most 256 colors, and the JPG cannot restore the in-between shades.
- **A GIF will not open**: the file may be damaged, which the page reports as "Image decode failed." Re-download it from its source.
- **You need a different frame**: this page always takes the first. Use an editor that shows each frame separately.

### What is a GIF file?

GIF came out of CompuServe in 1987. Pixels are compressed losslessly with LZW against a palette that holds at most 256 colors, and one palette entry can be flagged transparent, meaning a pixel is fully clear or fully solid, never partly see-through. A file may hold several images in sequence, which is how a GIF animates. The registered media type is image/gif.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens GIF, and ImageMagick reads it.
- **Web and mobile:** Chrome handles GIF in a browser tab as well as on a phone, Firefox does so on the web, and Safari does so on a phone.

### GIF and JXL compared

- **Compression:** JPEG XL is designed for both lossy and lossless coding, and it can losslessly recompress existing JPEG files.
- **Features:** it supports alpha transparency and animation, and it is used for high-bit-depth and HDR images. A GIF palette stops at 256 colors.
- **Loading:** JPEG XL allows progressive decoding, so a viewer can show an image before it has fully downloaded.
- **Metadata:** a JXL file can contain Exif, XMP and JUMBF metadata.
- **Names:** the extension is .jxl and the media type is image/jxl.
- **Support:** Safari, GIMP, XnView MP and IrfanView are listed as programs that open it.

The page decodes your GIF with the browser's own image decoder and reads only the first frame, so a JXL made here is a still. The pixels pass through 8-bit RGBA. ImageMagick, running in your browser, writes the JXL. No server is involved. The page puts no size limit on a file, and a large one just takes longer.

### Other ways to convert GIF to JXL

- **cjxl:** run `cjxl -d 0 loop.gif loop.jxl`. The command line tool accepts GIF input, and `-d 0` selects mathematically lossless coding. It compresses an image or an animation, so it is the route to an animated JXL.
- **GIMP:** open the GIF in GIMP, pick File > Export As, give it a name that ends in .jxl and click Export. The JPEG XL export dialog has a Lossless checkbox.

### Problems with GIF files

- **Soft edges turn hard:** a GIF has no partial opacity, so a soft transparent edge loses its fade.
- **Gradients change:** exporting to GIF in GIMP leaves at most 256 colors, and that can alter gradients.
- **Frames cover each other oddly:** with frame disposal, later images cover earlier ones in different ways, so pick combine or replace to match the animation.
- **A comment goes missing:** GIF comment text must be seven-bit ASCII, so GIMP leaves out any comment with other characters.

- **Codecs:** Matroska supports almost any codec and fixes none.
- **Sound:** a GIF has none, so the MKV from this page is silent.
- **Compression:** the GIF's LZW is lossless but caps color at 256. The MKV holds lossy H.264.

FFmpeg's WebAssembly build re-encodes the GIF locally with libx264 at CRF 32 in the ultrafast preset. Each side stays within 1920 pixels and is rounded down to an even number, and the video plays at no more than 30 frames per second. A smaller picture is never scaled up, a slower rate is never raised, and a faster GIF has frames dropped. Nothing is uploaded.

### Other ways to convert GIF to MKV

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i drawing.gif -an -c:v libx264 -crf 20 drawing.mkv`. The `-an` option leaves out audio, and `-c:v libx264` picks the H.264 encoder.
- **Shotcut:** open the GIF, click Export, then Advanced. In Format / Codec set the container to mkv, and export.
- **ImageMagick and FFmpeg:** run `magick sequence.gif -coalesce 'frame-%04d.png'`, then `ffmpeg -framerate 10 -i 'frame-%04d.png' -c:v libx264 frames.mkv`. The `-coalesce` option fully defines each frame as its own picture, and the second command sets one fixed frame rate in place of the GIF's own delays.

### Problems with GIF files

- **Fading edges do not survive:** GIF has no partial opacity, which means a soft transparent edge cannot hold its fade.
- **Colors drop to 256:** In GIMP the cap on a GIF export is 256 colors, so gradients may look different.
- **Overlapping frames:** a frame's disposal setting decides how later images sit over earlier ones; combine or replace should match the animation.
- **Comment text:** GIF comments only take seven-bit ASCII, so GIMP exports the picture without a comment using other characters.

guide.title: About GIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

The Graphics Interchange Format, or GIF, is a raster format that CompuServe introduced in 1987. It compresses with LZW and limits each frame to a palette of at most 256 colors. It also supports simple animation, which is why GIFs became the format for short looping clips such as reaction images and stickers.

That makes a GIF a series of palette images, not a video stream, and a GIF has no soundtrack. A silent reaction clip, a screen recording of an interface or a small looping illustration may all be GIFs.

Transparency in a GIF is all or nothing. One palette color can be marked transparent, but soft, semi-transparent edges cannot keep partial opacity.

Disposal settings decide whether a new image combines with the previous one or replaces it. That is how a GIF builds an animation from partial frames, and it is one reason a GIF can look wrong in a viewer that handles it differently.

### Programs that open GIF files

**Mac, Linux & Windows**

- GIMP: exports still pictures or multilayer animations.
- ImageMagick: reads GIF. Check which formats your installation supports.

**Web and Mobile**

- Google Chrome: displays GIF.

**Web**

- Mozilla Firefox: displays GIF.

**Mobile**

- Safari: displays GIF.

A browser is the easiest way to check the original before converting, since it shows the animation as the GIF stores it.

### GIF and MOV compared

- **Structure**: a GIF is a series of palette images. A MOV is a QuickTime container, introduced in 1991, built from objects called atoms.
- **Colors**: GIF frames are limited to 256 colors. A MOV can hold H.264 video, which is not limited that way, but it cannot recover colors the GIF never held.
- **Sound**: GIF has none. A MOV can carry audio such as AAC, but this one will not, since the source has none.
- **Transparency**: a GIF has a single transparent color, and the video this page writes has no alpha channel at all.
- **Support**: browsers handle MOV only patchily, and Apple now mostly favors MP4. MOV and MP4 stay separate formats that cannot replace each other.
- **Names**: .gif with image/gif, against .mov or .qt with video/quicktime.

H.264 encoding runs on the ultrafast preset at constant quality 32, and the index is relocated to the head of the file. That is tuned for a quick result in a browser, so very fine detail may soften. A frame beyond 1920 px on its long side is shrunk, and a clip faster than 30 fps gives up frames while keeping its running time. The audio settings in the command have nothing to act on, because a GIF has no audio.

The work happens in your browser. FFmpeg is compiled to WebAssembly and runs single-threaded in its own worker, so nothing is uploaded. A small frame is not enlarged, and the file you download is your GIF's name with .mov at the end. Your original file is not changed, and you can pick several GIFs together to get a separate MOV for each.

### Other ways to convert GIF to MOV

- **FFmpeg (command line):** run ffmpeg -i input.gif -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p output.mov. The pixel format may require even dimensions. No audio is created, since the GIF has none.

This page does the same kind of job without an install, and it also caps the frame at 1920 px and 30 fps. With FFmpeg you set those yourself. Play the result before using it in an edit, since looping and frame timing are handled by the player.

### Problems with GIF files

- **Banding and dithering**: with at most 256 colors per frame, gradients and photos look rough. Converting to MOV does not restore the missing colors.
- **Soft edges look jagged**: a GIF cannot keep partial transparency, so edges are hard.
- **Frames overlap wrongly**: disposal settings control how a new image covers the last. A smeared GIF may be read differently in another viewer.
- **A comment is missing**: GIMP omits a GIF comment that contains characters outside seven-bit ASCII.
- **The MOV looks different from the GIF**: the clip is encoded again as H.264, which is a new lossy version of the animation rather than the original frames.
- **The MOV is a few pixels narrower**: the last pixel of an odd side is cut off.
- **The video does not loop**: it plays once at its fixed length. Set repeat in your player or editor.

guide.title: Understanding GIF to PDF
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF was introduced by CompuServe in 1987. GIF89a, from July 1990, added extension blocks for transparency, frame delays, comments and application data. LZW coding compresses each GIF image without loss, and a palette may hold no more than 256 colors. Transparency is done by flagging a single palette color as fully clear, which rules out partial transparency. Many images fit in one GIF, with the pause between them set in hundredths of a second; that is the mechanism behind GIF animation. The media type is image/gif.

License fees for LZW were first demanded by Unisys in 1994. The US patent expired in 2003, with the European and Japanese equivalents lapsing in 2004. GIF displays in every major browser.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP exports stills or multilayer animations and opens a GIF's frames as layers. ImageMagick reads GIF.
- **Web:** GIF shows in Mozilla Firefox and in Google Chrome.
- **Mobile:** Chrome and Safari display GIF on phones.

### GIF and PDF compared

PDF is a document format created by Adobe to keep text, fonts, images and layout the same on any device. A PDF page can hold text, vector graphics and raster images, and images inside it can use lossless Flate compression or JPEG. This page uses the raster option only. Links, bookmarks, form fields and annotations also have a place in PDF, though none is added here. Its media type is application/pdf.

Your browser decodes the GIF, and the first frame goes into the PDF. It is embedded as a lossless PNG. The palette still limits the picture to 256 colors, so nothing is smoothed or recovered. The page takes its width and height from the image, one pixel for one point, with no margin and no sheet size. Transparent pixels stay transparent, stored as a soft mask.

A GIF's other frames, their timing and the loop setting are left out. PDF is a page-based document family, not an animation format. If the motion carries the meaning, such as a process shown step by step, the PDF shows only one moment of it. Nothing recognizes text in the picture, and no metadata is copied.

With only 256 colors available to every GIF image, a photograph saved as GIF has already been reduced, and the PDF keeps it that way. If you have the original image, start from it instead for a better result.

### Other ways to convert GIF to PDF

- **GIMP:** open the GIF, then choose File > Export As and type a filename that ends in .pdf. The PDF dialog offers Layers as pages, which creates a page for each layer, starting from the bottom layer, and GIMP's GIF export page describes an animation as one frame per layer. Frames that depend on earlier ones can look incomplete as separate pages.
- **Preview on Mac:** open the GIF, choose File > Export and set the format to PDF.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick 'animation.gif[0]' still.pdf`. The bracketed number picks one image from the sequence, and zero is the first. ImageMagick's format list says PDF needs Ghostscript.

### Problems with GIF files

**The PDF shows the wrong moment.** Only the first frame is exported here, and an animation may start from a blank or partial picture. Use GIMP to choose the frame you want, or ImageMagick with a different bracketed number.

**Frames look partial in an editor.** Frame disposal controls how each new image covers the one before. In GIMP, choose combine or replace to match the animation before you export layers as pages.

**Edges look rough.** A GIF cannot hold partial opacity on soft edges, and Gradients can change when GIMP saves a GIF, because that export allows 256 colors at most. The PDF cannot smooth either. Look for the original artwork if you have it.

**A comment goes missing.** Characters beyond seven-bit ASCII in a GIF comment make GIMP leave the comment out, and this page writes no metadata of its own.

**The text is not selectable.** A caption in a GIF is a picture of text. Use OCR if you need to search or copy it.

**The page size follows the pixels.** The PDF page follows the pixel count, not a paper standard, so a small GIF makes a small page and a large one makes a large page.

guide.title: Understanding GIF for PSD output
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

CompuServe introduced GIF, the Graphics Interchange Format, in 1987. Images are packed losslessly with LZW, each palette tops out at 256 colors, and simple animation is part of the design: one file can carry many images, spaced by delays measured in hundredths of a second. The July 1990 GIF89a revision added transparency, per-frame delays, comments and application data blocks. Transparency means choosing a single palette color to be invisible, so partial opacity is impossible. License fees for LZW from Unisys began in 1994, and the patents expired in 2003 and 2004. You see GIF in reaction images, stickers, icons and short looping clips.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - GIMP: can export a still picture or a layered animation.
  - ImageMagick: handles GIF input.
- **Web:**
  - Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox: display GIF.
- **Mobile:**
  - Safari and Chrome: display GIF on a phone.

### GIF and PSD compared

- **Names and types**: .gif is image/gif. .psd is Photoshop's native document, image/vnd.adobe.photoshop.
- **Color**: a GIF frame is capped at 256 palette entries. A PSD header lists one, eight, 16 and 32 bits as possible sample depths.
- **Structure**: a PSD keeps layers, masks and image resources in separate sections. A GIF holds frames.
- **Compression**: a PSD stores pixel data raw or encoded with RLE or ZIP, while GIF uses LZW.
- **Limit**: a PSD side can be no longer than 30,000 pixels, and PSB removes that cap.

Your browser decodes the GIF, and only its first frame is kept, so an animated GIF gives one still picture. The pixels pass through 8-bit RGBA, and ImageMagick writes the PSD. The page builds no layers and no animation frames.

### Other ways to convert GIF to PSD

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick sticker.gif sticker.psd` in a terminal. ImageMagick lists GIF and PSD as readable and writable.

### Problems with GIF files

- **Comments can drop out**: GIMP leaves out a GIF comment that uses characters beyond plain seven-bit text.
- **Soft edges look hard**: a GIF cannot retain partial opacity.
- **Banding**: a GIF holds at most 256 colors, so gradients can shift, and the PSD cannot restore the missing shades.
- **Later frames look partial**: frame disposal changes how later images cover earlier ones.

guide.title: About GIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

The GIF format came out of CompuServe in 1987 for pictures stored with a color palette. A GIF holds either one still picture or several images separated by delays counted in hundredths of a second; that timing is what makes GIF animation. Colors in every GIF image come from a table of no more than 256 entries, and LZW coding compresses the data without loss. Transparency works by marking one palette color as fully transparent, so there is no partial transparency.

Version GIF89a, dated July 1990, brought extensions covering transparency, frame timing, comments and application data. LZW license fees from Unisys began in 1994, and the patent behind them expired in the US in 2003. A GIF is a pixel format with a small palette, so it turns blocky when enlarged. That is why people ask for an SVG, and it is worth knowing before you convert that an SVG made from a GIF does not fix it.

### Programs that open GIF files

**Linux, Mac and Windows:**

- ImageMagick reads GIF. To see what your install supports, run `magick identify -list format`.
- Inkscape imports GIF files, but not their animation.
- GIMP exports still pictures or multilayer animations as GIF.

**Web and mobile:**

- Chrome, Firefox and Safari all show GIF, as does every other major browser.

A browser is the simplest way to check what the first frame of a GIF looks like.

### GIF and SVG compared

- **Kind**: a GIF is a grid of pixels. SVG is XML text for two-dimensional graphics built from shapes, text and embedded images. Its registered media type is image/svg+xml.
- **Scaling**: because SVG shapes are stored as instructions, they can be drawn at any size without losing sharpness. Pixels in a GIF do not scale that way.
- **Animation**: a GIF loops its frames. This page keeps only the first frame.
- **Transparency**: GIF has one transparent palette color. The SVG made here keeps transparency inside the embedded picture.

This page does not trace the GIF into shapes. Your browser decodes the GIF, and the SVG that comes out has one image element inside it. That element carries the picture as a base64 PNG sized exactly like the GIF, with no resizing and no color reduction. Because the picture is still made of pixels, it does not scale the way a drawing does, and it looks just as blocky when zoomed as the GIF did.

From an animated GIF the page keeps the opening frame alone; later frames and their delays are dropped, so what you download is a still. EXIF, ICC profile and XMP data are not carried over. A file the browser cannot decode stops with "Image decode failed.", and no SVG is made.

### Other ways to convert GIF to SVG

- **Inkscape:** use File > Import to bring in the GIF, choose to embed it in the dialog that follows, then save the drawing as SVG. Embedding stores the image inside the SVG file. Inkscape's manual says its GIF support does not include animation. To get paths, select the picture and use Path > Trace Bitmap.
- **LibreOffice Draw:** select the bitmap, go to Shape > Convert > To Polygon, adjust the settings in the dialog, and then use File > Export and choose a graphics file type.

Embedding keeps the picture as pixels inside the SVG, while tracing and converting to polygons make vector shapes.

### Problems with GIF files

- **The SVG no longer moves**: it holds a single frame, so keep the GIF itself for the animation.
- **The first frame is not the one you want**: open the GIF in an editor, save the frame you need as a still, and convert that.
- **Zooming shows squares**: the SVG holds a raster picture, so it stays pixelated. Use a tracing tool to get shapes.
- **Soft edges turn jagged**: a GIF cannot keep partial opacity, so soft transparent edges lose it.
- **Gradients change**: GIMP's GIF export caps the palette at 256 colors, which can alter smooth gradients.
- **You need editable curves for a cutter or a logo**: this page cannot make them. Trace the image in Inkscape or LibreOffice Draw.
- **The GIF will not open**: your browser has to be able to decode it. A file that cannot be read stops with "Image decode failed" instead of an SVG.

guide.title: Understanding GIF for SWF output
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF dates to 1987 and CompuServe. Its GIF89a revision of July 1990 introduced transparency, animation timing, comments and application blocks. Compression is lossless LZW, but every image has a palette of 256 colors at most. Many images in one file, separated by delays in hundredths of a second, make a GIF animate. The media type is image/gif, and every major browser displays it.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - GIMP: writes still pictures or multilayer animations as GIF.
  - ImageMagick: supports reading GIF.
- **Web:**
  - Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox: show GIF in a tab.
- **Mobile:**
  - Safari and Chrome: handle GIF on a phone.

### GIF and SWF compared

- **Names and types**: .gif is image/gif. SWF has the media type application/vnd.adobe.flash.movie.
- **Color**: GIF frames use palettes capped at 256 colors, while the SWF here carries video.
- **Sound**: a GIF is silent. SWF can carry audio, but the file made here has none.
- **Animation**: GIF repeats a stack of images. A SWF is a timeline-based legacy format that can also hold vector graphics and bitmap video.

Shockwave Flash started at Macromedia, which Adobe acquired in 2005, and carried Flash animations, games and interactive content with ActionScript behind them. Adobe Flash Player reached end of life on 31 December 2020. This page makes a video SWF, so no ActionScript is added.

In your browser, FFmpeg runs as WebAssembly and chooses the video codec itself: its default for SWF is Sorenson Spark (FLV1) video at 200 kbit/s. Interlaced frames are deinterlaced, and the picture is capped at 1920 pixels and 30 frames per second, with each side trimmed to an even value.

### Other ways to convert GIF to SWF

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i badge.gif -an -c:v flv badge.swf`. The `-an` option skips audio, and `-c:v` selects the video encoder. FFmpeg lists GIF and SWF as both readable and writable.
- **SWFTools gif2swf:** run `gif2swf -o badge.swf badge.gif`. The `-o` option sets the name of the SWF output file, and the GIF is the input file.

### Problems with GIF files

- **Banding in gradients**: a GIF is limited to 256 colors, which changes smooth gradients.
- **Frames overlay wrongly**: disposal settings decide how later images sit over earlier ones.
- **Comments can drop out**: an export from GIMP skips a GIF comment holding characters outside the seven-bit range.
- **Large GIFs**: a long, large GIF becomes many video frames, so conversion takes longer on a slow device.

guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

CompuServe introduced GIF in 1987. Every image in a GIF is limited to a 256-color palette and compressed without loss using LZW. One GIF can store many images, each with a delay measured in hundredths of a second, which is how it animates. GIF89a, released in July 1990, let files carry transparency flags, frame delays, comments and application data. Transparency works by flagging a single palette entry, so a pixel is either clear or opaque. Every major browser displays GIF, and its media type is image/gif.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** In GIMP you can export a single image or a layered animation to GIF and make the animation repeat endlessly. ImageMagick reads GIF.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox display it.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Google Chrome display it too.

### GIF and TGA compared

- **Color**: a GIF is limited to a palette. A 24-bit TGA stores 8 bits per color component, and a 32-bit TGA adds an 8-bit alpha channel.
- **Animation**: a GIF can animate. A TGA is a single still image.
- **Compression**: GIF uses LZW. TGA can use optional run-length encoding.
- **Use**: video editing and game development workflows still use Targa images.

The page decodes the GIF in your browser and ImageMagick writes the TGA. Only the first frame of an animated GIF is converted, so open the TGA in an image viewer afterwards to confirm it shows the frame you wanted.

### Other ways to convert GIF to TGA

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick 'animation.gif[0]' still.tga`. ImageMagick counts frames from zero, so `[0]` is the first image, and a different number picks a later one. ImageMagick reads and writes both GIF and Truevision Targa.

### Problems with GIF files

- **Soft edges turn hard**: partial opacity is impossible in a GIF, so transparent edges are clear or opaque before the page reads them.
- **Gradients look banded**: GIMP reduces a GIF export to a palette, which can change gradients.
- **Frames cover each other wrongly**: each frame carries a disposal setting that controls what happens to the previous image, so a wrong setting smears the animation.
- **A comment is missing**: GIMP leaves out a GIF comment that has characters outside seven-bit ASCII.

guide.title: About GIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

CompuServe published the GIF format in 1987. Pixels index into a palette with no more than 256 colors and are packed with lossless LZW. A single file can hold a run of images, and each carries its own delay in hundredths of a second. One palette entry can be declared transparent. A GIF has no sound and is labeled image/gif.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens GIF, and ImageMagick reads it.
- **Web and mobile:** Chrome plays GIF on the web and on mobile devices. Firefox handles the web side, and Safari handles mobile.

### GIF and TIF compared

- **Origin:** TIFF dates from Aldus in 1986 and is maintained by Adobe today. It stores one or more images with a tag-based structure.
- **Pages:** a TIFF file can hold several images, but the converter on this page writes one still.
- **Compression:** GIF always uses LZW. TIFF compression may be lossless or lossy; the choices in GIMP's TIFF dialog are None, LZW, Pack Bits, Deflate, JPEG and CCITT fax.
- **Color:** a TIFF may use high bit depth, or CMYK for print. A GIF converted here still has its palette's colors, in an 8-bit file.
- **Use:** TIFF is common in scanning and archiving, in professional photography and print, and in fax and document imaging.
- **Names:** .tif and .tiff are the same format.

Your browser's own image decoder reads the GIF and takes just its first frame. That frame passes through 8-bit RGBA, then ImageMagick, running in your browser, writes the TIFF with no quality setting. EXIF, ICC and XMP data are dropped. A file the decoder rejects gives the error "Image decode failed." Nothing is uploaded.

### Other ways to convert GIF to TIF

- **GIMP:** open the GIF in GIMP, then choose File > Export As and save as TIFF. The TIFF dialog has a Compression list and a Save layers option, which stores each layer as a separate page starting from the bottom.
- **IrfanView:** open the GIF and choose File > Save As. Pick TIF as the format, and tick Show format options dialog to see its saving options. IrfanView's format list shows both GIF and TIF as readable and savable.

### Problems with GIF files

- **No partial opacity:** a GIF cannot hold it, so soft transparent edges lose their fade.
- **256-color ceiling:** A GIF export from GIMP keeps no more than 256 colors, and gradients can change as a result.
- **Disposal settings:** disposal changes how later frames cover earlier ones, so combine or replace should fit the animation.
- **Comments with other characters:** only seven-bit ASCII fits a GIF comment, and GIMP exports without a comment containing anything else.

guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF came from CompuServe in 1987. LZW compression, at most 256 palette colors per frame and basic animation define it. Transparency is all or nothing, since a color is either clear or solid. Looping clips, simple graphics, reaction images and stickers are typical jobs.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Mac, Windows and Linux:** GIMP exports stills or multilayer animations as GIF, and ImageMagick reads GIF.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome and Firefox display GIFs on the web, and Chrome and Safari do on mobile.

Aldus first published TIFF in 1986, and Adobe maintains it today. It stores one or more images in a tag-based structure, with lossless or lossy compression, high bit depth and even CMYK. It serves scanning and archiving, print and professional photography, and fax or document imaging. Because a TIFF can contain several images, scanned document sequences fit well, and preservation masters are another established use. Either .tif or .tiff marks a TIFF file.

Here your browser decodes the GIF and keeps its first frame as 8-bit RGBA, then ImageMagick writes an uncompressed TIFF with an alpha channel. A transparent GIF pixel stays transparent. Expect a file larger than the GIF and no animation. EXIF, XMP and color profiles are dropped. The result opens in Preview on a Mac, in Windows Photos, in GIMP and in Photoshop.

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick "input.gif[0]" still.tiff`. Index 0 is the first image in the file, and `[1]` would pick the second.

Partial opacity at soft edges is lost in a GIF. A GIF exported from GIMP is held to 256 colors, which can change gradients. How later images cover earlier ones depends on the disposal setting, so one frame pulled out alone can look incomplete. GIMP also omits a GIF comment with characters outside the seven-bit ASCII range.

guide.title: About GIF and WebM
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF stands for Graphics Interchange Format. CompuServe introduced it in 1987. Every picture in a GIF is LZW-compressed and drawn from a palette limited to 256 colors. The GIF89a version added extensions for frame delays and for marking one palette color as transparent, which is what made short animations possible. Transparency is all or nothing: one palette color is declared transparent, and nothing can be partly see-through. The delay between pictures is set in hundredths of a second. Unisys' LZW licensing, which started in 1994, faded as patents lapsed, in the US in 2003 and a year later in Europe and Japan.

You meet GIFs as reaction clips, looping demos, stickers and small icons. The format stores pictures and timing, not sound. A GIF made from a movie clip lost its audio when it was made, and no converter can bring it back.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows:** Photos opens GIFs.
- **Mac:** Preview opens GIFs.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP can export layered animations and still pictures, and an exported animated GIF can be set to loop forever. ImageMagick reads GIF.
- **Web and mobile:** every major browser displays GIFs; the ones named here are Chrome and Firefox on desktops and Safari and Chrome on phones.

### GIF and WebM compared

- **Extensions and types**: .gif is image/gif; .webm is video/webm.
- **What it is**: GIF is an image format that can animate. WebM is a video container based on Matroska, and it can hold VP8, VP9 or AV1 video.
- **Compression**: GIF compresses without loss, but only inside its 256-color palette. The WebM this page writes uses VP8 video.
- **Color**: the GIF palette limit is gone in the video, but colors that were already reduced in the GIF stay reduced.
- **Transparency**: GIF allows one fully transparent color. The WebM here is yuv420p, which has no alpha.
- **Sound**: GIF has none. The WebM from this page has none either, because the conversion switches audio off.
- **Looping**: the WebM from this page carries no loop setting, so a video repeats only if the page or player is told to.

FFmpeg decodes the GIF and passes its frames to the VP8 encoder (libvpx) at a fixed quality of CRF 40. The WebM follows the GIF's size and rate, but never exceeds 1920 px on its long side or 30 fps. Dimensions are rounded down to even values, which matters when a GIF is, say, 481 px wide. Interlaced frames, if a file has any, are deinterlaced first.

The file you get is a video, not an image. It opens in a player or sits in a video tag, and it has a play bar. To check it, play it in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or VLC media player; on a phone, try VLC for Android or VLC for iOS. Keep the GIF when the destination only accepts images.

### Other ways to convert GIF to WebM

- **FFmpeg (command line):** type `ffmpeg -i reaction.gif -c:v libvpx -pix_fmt yuv420p -an reaction.webm`. The command writes opaque VP8 video.
- **GStreamer (command line):** run `gst-launch-1.0 filesrc location=reaction.gif ! gifdec loop=force-no ! videoconvert ! vp8enc ! webmmux ! filesink location=reaction.webm`. It needs the gif, vpx and Matroska plug-ins.

### Problems with GIF files

- **The clip plays once and stops**: the converted file has no loop setting, so switch on repeat in your player or on the page's video tag.
- **Colors look speckled**: the GIF's 256-color palette causes dithering that no conversion removes. Go back to the original video if you still have it.
- **A site only accepts image uploads**: a form that wants .gif or an image type can reject video/webm. Keep the GIF there.
- **The picture has no transparent background**: a GIF marks one palette color as transparent, and the video here can't hold that. Place the clip on a matching background.
- **The GIF has no sound**: the format has no audio, so the WebM stays silent.
- **A very large GIF gets smaller**: a GIF wider or taller than 1920 px is shrunk to fit, and a smaller one is never scaled up.
- **A long GIF takes a while**: nothing on the page limits file size or running time, so a long GIF takes as long as your device needs.

guide.title: About GIF and WebP
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

GIF is the Graphics Interchange Format, introduced by CompuServe in 1987. A GIF compresses each picture with LZW and holds at most 256 colors per frame, drawn from a palette. It can hold several pictures with delays between them, which is how a GIF animates, and it can mark one palette color as fully transparent. GIF89a added the control blocks for delays and transparency.

GIFs are everywhere short, looping clips are shared: reaction images, stickers, instructions and small animated graphics. Because the palette is limited, a photograph in a GIF often shows dithering, and a smooth gradient shows bands. Converting the file does not undo that. The picture you start from is the palette picture, and WebP simply stores it in a different way.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows:** Windows Photos opens GIF files. GIMP exports GIF as either a still picture or a multilayer animation.
- **Mac:** Preview opens GIF files, and GIMP exports GIF the same way.
- **Linux:** GIMP and ImageMagick, which reads GIF and can be scripted from the command line.
- **Web and mobile:** Chrome and Firefox show GIF on desktop websites; on phones, Chrome and Safari show it too.

To check the WebP you get from this page, open it in a current browser, since Chrome, Firefox and Safari all display WebP. GIMP has opened and saved WebP natively since 2.10, and Preview on macOS and Windows Photos open it as well.

### GIF and WebP compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .gif and image/gif; .webp and image/webp.
- **Compression**: GIF is lossless inside a 256-color limit. WebP offers a lossless mode and a lossy one, and the lossy one borrows its compression from the VP8 video codec.
- **Color**: WebP is not limited to a palette.
- **Transparency**: GIF has 1-bit transparency, a pixel either shows or does not. WebP has an alpha channel.
- **Animation**: both can animate. This page does not write an animated WebP.
- **Size limits**: WebP stops at 16,383 pixels per side, so anything larger cannot be stored as WebP.

The page decodes the first frame of the GIF with your browser's own image decoder and encodes it as a WebP with a browser canvas or ImageMagick, passing no quality setting. Metadata is not copied, and your original GIF is untouched. The picture passes through 8-bit RGBA, so a GIF's palette colors arrive as ordinary 8-bit pixels.

Google developed WebP and released it in 2010. Its lossy mode comes from the VP8 video codec; it also has a lossless mode, transparency and animation. It is used for web images with smaller files, for images that need transparency and for short animations.

A still WebP is useful when you want a web-friendly picture from the opening frame of an animation, for a thumbnail or a poster, for example. It keeps see-through pixels and sits comfortably on a page next to ordinary photos. If the motion matters, this page is the wrong tool; try one of the methods below.

### Other ways to convert GIF to WebP

- **gif2webp (Google):** run `gif2webp animation.gif -o animation.webp` from the WebP tools. It converts a GIF to WebP and offers -lossy and -mixed options, where mixed picks lossy or lossless for each frame.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick animation.gif -coalesce animation.webp`. The -coalesce option fully defines the look of each frame of a GIF animation, and your ImageMagick needs WebP support, so check its format list.

### Problems with GIF files

- **The WebP is a single picture**: that is how this page works. Use one of the command-line methods above to try for the motion.
- **The first frame is not what you expected**: this page converts only the first frame, so pick the frame in an editor and save it as its own picture first.
- **Soft edges look jagged**: GIF transparency is on or off, so a soft shadow can't be partly see-through. The WebP can't add that back.
- **Colors look blotchy**: the 256-color palette is the cause. GIMP also limits a GIF export to 256 colors, which alters gradients.
- **Frames overlap or leave trails after an edit**: frame disposal sets how later images cover earlier ones. Pick combine or replace in GIMP to match the animation.
- **An old browser balks at the WebP**: a browser from some years back can show still WebP yet lack animation support. Convert the first frame to PNG or JPG if a viewer will not open it.
- **A comment you wrote in the GIF is gone**: GIMP drops a GIF comment with characters outside seven-bit ASCII, and this page drops metadata altogether.

guide.title: About GIF and WMV files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

From CompuServe in 1987 comes GIF, a raster image format. Each frame uses LZW compression and a palette limited to 256 colors at most, and simple animation is supported. Short looping animations, reaction images and stickers are common uses.

### Programs that open GIF files

- **Windows, Linux and Mac:** GIMP exports GIF as stills or multilayer animations, and ImageMagick reads GIF files.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome, Firefox and Safari handle GIF display.

### GIF and WMV compared

WMV, short for Windows Media Video, is a family of Microsoft video codecs usually kept in the ASF container. It was widely used for Windows video and streaming, and today it is a lossy legacy format. A WMV may hold Windows Media Video 7, 8 or 9 content, and ASF itself was designed for storing synchronized media and sending it across networks. Windows Media Player and VLC media player open WMV, which people mostly meet in older Windows video, screen recordings and Windows Media streaming.

In this converter FFmpeg, built for WebAssembly, re-encodes the GIF inside your browser. A GIF side beyond 1920 px shrinks to fit, a smaller GIF stays at its own size, and a rate above 30 fps sheds frames without shortening the clip. Because both sides are made even, an odd one loses a pixel. A GIF has no audio, so the WMV has none either. FFmpeg's defaults write MS-MPEG4 v3 video at 200 kbit/s, and the page offers no codec, bitrate or quality setting. Several GIFs convert as a batch, but each yields a separate video and they are not joined.

### Other ways to convert GIF to WMV

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i input.gif -an output.wmv` on your computer. The output format is guessed from the extension, and `-an` leaves audio out.

### Problems with GIF files

A GIF cannot keep partial opacity along soft transparent edges, and a GIMP export caps its palette at 256 colors, which can change gradients. Frame disposal decides how later images cover earlier ones, so a lone frame can look incomplete. GIMP drops a GIF comment holding characters beyond seven-bit ASCII.

guide.title: About GSM and MP3
guide.markdown:
### What is a GSM file?

GSM here means GSM 06.10, a lossy speech codec specified by ETSI for mobile telephony. Its RPE-LTP algorithm squeezes telephone speech into 13 kbit/s at an 8 kHz sample rate, packing each 160-sample block into a 264-bit frame. It turns up in voice recordings, telephony systems and voicemail, and it is a legacy format. The toast utility from libgsm writes compressed speech with the .gsm ending.

### Programs that open GSM files

- **Windows:** FFmpeg reads raw .gsm frames and exposes them as mono speech.
- **Mac:** Audacity opens GSM audio.
- **Linux:** toast and untoast, the libgsm command-line tools that encode and decode raw GSM speech.

FFmpeg is listed for Mac and Linux too, and VLC media player and SoX are also listed as programs that open GSM.

### GSM and MP3 compared

- **Purpose**: GSM is built for narrow telephone speech. MP3 is a general-purpose lossy audio format from MPEG, and it grew into the standard way to distribute downloadable music.
- **Packaging**: raw .gsm files and Microsoft's WAV GSM packing use different framing.
- **Tags**: MP3 keeps tags such as the title in ID3 data inside the file.
- **Playback**: MP3 plays on nearly every device, browsers included. GSM needs a program that knows the codec.

Here FFmpeg works in your browser, asking libmp3lame for 192 kbit/s and leaving out any video. MP3 cannot reach that rate at GSM's 8 kHz, so the file comes out at about 64 kbit/s. Selected files are processed in sequence, and each MP3 downloads on its own.

### Other ways to convert GSM to MP3

- **FFmpeg:** `ffmpeg -i message.gsm -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 192k message.mp3`. The -b:a option sets the bitrate for the libmp3lame encoder.
- **FFmpeg, variable bitrate:** `ffmpeg -i message.gsm -q:a N -c:a libmp3lame message.mp3`, where N is a quality number. The libmp3lame q option sets a constant quality for variable bitrate instead of a fixed bitrate.
- **SoX:** `sox message.gsm message.mp3`. SoX lists GSM 06.10 and MP3 as optional formats, and MP3 writing needs SoX built with the LAME library.

### Problems with GSM files

- **Chirping or thin sound**: repeated GSM compression removes more information and can create audible chirping, so work from the first recording.
- **The file will not open**: raw .gsm and WAV format 49 are not interchangeable byte layouts.
- **A cut-off recording**: FFmpeg's raw reader expects complete 33-byte blocks, and a truncated last block is invalid to it. FFmpeg logs an error, and this page still writes the MP3 from what it could read, so download the file again if the end matters.

guide.title: About HDR and JPEG files
guide.markdown:
### What is an HDR file?

Radiance is a lighting simulation system, and Greg Ward made the .hdr picture format for it. The format is also called RGBE: a pixel is three color bytes plus one exponent that all three share, so a single file spans far more brightness than a 24-bit RGB file does. Radiance uses these pictures for computed brightness, and 3D artists load them as environment maps. Files can use run-length encoding and end in .hdr or .pic. The registered media type is image/vnd.radiance.

### Programs that open HDR files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** the HDR coder in ImageMagick covers this format for reading and writing.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe Photoshop appears in the media type registration as a user of Radiance pictures.
- **Linux:** Radiance itself, the rendering system the format came from, includes RGBE code.

### HDR and JPEG compared

The target JPEG keeps only eight bits per color channel and has no alpha channel, so it holds far less brightness than an HDR file. That gap decides what this converter does. ImageMagick reads the Radiance file in your browser, and this 8-bit build clips each value above white to white. Those linear values then get an sRGB encoding before the JPEG is written, so highlights brighter than white end up white.

### Other ways to convert HDR to JPEG

- **Luminance HDR:** its command-line tool loads the file with `-l environment.hdr`, selects a tone-mapping operator with `--tmo` (mantiuk06 is the default) and names the tone-mapped output with `-o`. The `-q` option sets the quality from 1 to 100.
- **GIMP:** open the HDR, which GIMP loads as Radiance RGBE, and export it as a JPEG. The JPEG dialog offers Quality, Progressive, Subsampling and metadata choices such as Save Exif data.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick environment.hdr preview.jpeg`. Its format list shows HDR and JPEG as both readable and writable.

### Problems with HDR files

- **Bright areas flatten**: squeezing the brightness range into eight bits throws highlight detail away, so pick a rendering on purpose, for instance with a tone mapper, instead of truncating.
- **Colors look wrong elsewhere**: a program must decode the shared exponent, since the bytes are not ordinary packed RGB.
- **The file will not read**: the .hdr name is not proof of the contents, and the registration for the Radiance type recommends looking at the full header.
- **A very large picture**: beyond about 537 megapixels the page stops and reports that the picture is too large.

guide.title: About HDR and JPG
guide.markdown:
### What is an HDR file?

HDR here is Radiance RGBE, a high-dynamic-range image format created by Greg Ward for the Radiance lighting simulation software. Each pixel is stored as red, green and blue bytes plus a shared exponent, four bytes in all, which allows a wider brightness range than ordinary 24-bit RGB. Files use run-length encoding and the extension .hdr or .pic; the registered media type is image/vnd.radiance. Radiance lighting simulations use RGBE images to represent calculated brightness, and the files also serve as environment maps for 3D rendering.

### Programs that open HDR files

- **Windows:** ImageMagick has an HDR coder for Radiance files in both directions.
- **Mac:** Adobe Photoshop is named in the format's registration among the users of the Radiance media type.
- **Linux:** Radiance, the original rendering system, which ships RGBE reading and writing code.

ImageMagick is listed on Mac and Linux as well, and Photoshop on Windows. Blender, GIMP and Luminance HDR are also listed as programs that open HDR.

### HDR and JPG compared

- **Range**: HDR keeps a wide brightness range. JPG is lossy and designed for photographs.
- **Pixels**: HDR bytes are not ordinary packed RGB, so software has to interpret the exponent.
- **Transparency**: JPG has no alpha channel.
- **Storage**: HDR uses four bytes per pixel rather than three single-precision floating-point channels.
- **Support**: JPG is widely supported. HDR opens in the programs listed above.

This page uses ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly on the main thread. It reads a single image and passes no quality or mapping option, so you cannot steer the highlights. Each value above white is clamped to white, and the linear light is encoded to sRGB.

### Other ways to convert HDR to JPG

- **Radiance and ImageMagick:** run `pcond scene.hdr mapped.hdr` to condition the HDR for viewing, `ra_ppm mapped.hdr mapped.ppm` to write a PPM, then `magick mapped.ppm preview.jpg` to make the JPG.
- **ImageMagick:** `magick scene.hdr -colorspace sRGB preview.jpg` on your own machine.

### Problems with HDR files

- **Washed-out or blown highlights**: clipping bright values to the ordinary eight-bit range can discard highlight information. Choose an appropriate rendering instead of truncating samples.
- **Wrong colors in another program**: an HDR image needs software that interprets the shared exponent, because its bytes are not ordinary packed RGB pixels.
- **A file that will not read**: the extension alone does not identify the contents, and the registered Radiance description advises checking the complete header.

guide.title: About HEIC files
guide.markdown:
### What is a HEIC file?

A HEIC file is a photo stored in HEIF, the High Efficiency Image File Format, with its pictures compressed by HEVC, the H.265 video codec. HEIF is a container standard from MPEG, ISO/IEC 23008-12, first published in 2017. Apple made it the iPhone's photo format with iOS 11 and macOS High Sierra, and the iPhone 7 and later capture in it. Apple says HEIF compresses photos better than JPEG.

One HEIF file can hold more than one picture. It can carry several images or an image sequence, an alpha channel stored as an extra image, more than 8 bits per color channel, and Exif or XMP metadata.

On an iPhone set to High Efficiency, new photos are HEIC. Copied to a computer over USB, they can arrive as JPEG instead, unless Keep Originals is chosen in the Photos settings. Some Android phones can save HEIF too, from Android 10 on devices that support it.

### Programs that open HEIC files

- **Windows:** Microsoft Photos opens HEIC once both the HEIF Image Extension and the HEVC Video Extensions are installed from the Microsoft Store.
- **Windows and Linux:** GIMP imports HEIC. ImageMagick reads it too, with the libheif delegate.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe Photoshop opens HEIC on macOS 10.13 or later, and on Windows once both Microsoft codecs are installed.
- **Mac:** Apple Preview opens HEIF and exports JPEG or PNG, from macOS High Sierra 10.13; Photos, on Mac and mobile, also opens HEIF and exports another format.
- **Web and mobile:** Safari displays HEIC images from version 17.
- **Web:** the signed-in OneDrive website previews uploaded HEIF.
- **Mobile:** on Android, HEIF decoding starts at version 9.

### HEIC and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .heic or .heif, with image/heic and image/heif; .jpg or .jpeg, with image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: HEIC pictures are coded with HEVC (H.265). Baseline JPEG cuts the picture into 8x8 tiles, applies a discrete cosine transform to each tile and Huffman-codes the result.
- **What one file holds**: a HEIF can bundle several images and an alpha channel. A JPG holds one picture.
- **Color depth**: HEIF allows high bit depths; JPEG stores 8 bits per channel. This page decodes to 8-bit pixels.
- **Transparency**: a JPG has no alpha channel at all.
- **Metadata**: a HEIF can carry Exif or XMP. The JPG made here doesn't get the HEIC's Exif data or ICC profile.
- **Quality setting**: the same quality figure gives different output from one tool to the next. This page writes each JPG at 0.85, where 1 is the top of the scale.
- **Where it opens**: JPEG displays in each major browser, and cameras and scanners tend to produce it. HEIC needs the support listed above.

The trade is reach for fidelity. Every major browser displays the JPG, and the page asks for no extension. It is lossy at quality 0.85, and it carries none of the HEIC's Exif tags. A HEIC that holds several images gives only its primary picture.

### Other ways to convert HEIC to JPG

- **Finder (Mac):** Control-click the photo, choose Quick Actions > Convert Image, then choose JPEG and a size.
- **Preview (Mac):** open the photo, choose File > Export, and change Format to JPEG.
- **Photos (Mac):** select the photos, choose File > Export > Export Photos, then set Photo Kind to JPEG.
- **iPhone camera setting:** Settings > Camera > Formats > Most Compatible makes new photos JPEG. Photos you already took stay HEIC.

### Problems with HEIC files

- **Windows says it can't open the file**: add the two Microsoft Store codecs, the HEIF and HEVC extensions, or convert here instead.
- **A website won't accept it**: convert it to JPG here, or use the [HEIC to PNG converter](/heic-to-png/) to get a PNG.
- **The page says "No images in HEIF"**: the file contains nothing to decode. Copy the photo off the phone again and retry.
- **HEIC on one computer, JPG on another**: a USB import from an iPhone can produce JPEG instead. Choose Keep Originals in the Photos settings to get the HEIC files.
- **A whole album to convert**: choose all the photos at once. Each JPG downloads as soon as it's ready.
- **The JPG shows less detail than the HEIC**: both formats are lossy, so a conversion can cost some detail. Convert from the original HEIC, not from a copy that was already converted.
- **A HEIC from an Android phone**: some Android phones save HEIF, and this page converts those files the same way.

guide.title: HEIC background and SVG conversion
guide.markdown:
### What is a HEIC file?

The High Efficiency Image File Format (HEIF) is MPEG-H Part 12 (ISO/IEC 23008-12), and its first edition appeared in 2017. It is a container rather than a codec, and HEIC is the variant whose images are coded with HEVC (H.265). One HEIF file may carry multiple pictures, sequences, depth beyond 8 bits, an alpha layer stored as a second image, and Exif or XMP metadata. Apple's photo apps started saving HEIF in iOS 11 and macOS High Sierra, and every iPhone since the iPhone 7 can shoot it. The Camera settings, under Formats, let you pick High Efficiency (HEIF) or Most Compatible (JPEG). The registered media types are image/heic and image/heif.

### Programs that open HEIC files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP can import HEIC files; ImageMagick can read them through libheif.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos needs Microsoft's HEIF and HEVC extensions before it will open HEIC.
- **Windows and Mac:** Photoshop handles HEIC on macOS from 10.13, and on Windows after both Microsoft codecs are added.
- **Mac:** Preview on a Mac can open a HEIF file and export JPEG or PNG copies.
- **Mac and Mobile:** Photos from Apple opens HEIF and exports another format.
- **Web and Mobile:** Safari displays HEIC from version 17.0, and the OneDrive website previews uploaded HEIF photos.

### HEIC and SVG compared

HEIC stores a photograph with lossy HEVC compression. SVG is an XML format that describes shapes, text and embedded images, so it usually scales without losing sharpness. The SVG contains one `<image>` element that carries the picture as base64-encoded PNG data at the picture's own pixel width and height. Pixel images inside an SVG keep their original resolution when enlarged, so the result scales like a photo, not like a drawing. libheif decodes the HEIC's primary image to 8-bit RGB, and EXIF and ICC data are dropped.

### Other ways to convert HEIC to SVG

- **libheif and Inkscape:** run `heif-dec input.heic intermediate.png`. The heif-dec tool writes JPEG, PNG, TIFF, WebP or Y4M output from a HEIF input. Then, in Inkscape, choose File > Import for the decoded PNG and Path > Trace Bitmap. Tracing builds vector paths from the bitmap.

### Problems with HEIC files

- **Windows won't open it**: Windows needs Microsoft's HEIF Image Extension plus the HEVC Video Extensions. The HEIF extensions are free in the Microsoft Store, and the HEVC Video Extensions cost $0.99.
- **iPhone photos arrive as JPEG**: a USB copy can convert them to JPEG unless Photos is set to Keep Originals.
- **Error "No images in HEIF"**: the file holds no image, so fetch a fresh copy of it.

guide.title: About HEIC files
guide.markdown:
### What is a HEIC file?

HEIC is the file type for HEIF images coded with HEVC. Apple uses HEIF for photos from iOS 11 and macOS High Sierra 10.13, capturing it on iPhone 7 and later, and says it gives better compression than JPEG. HEIF is the container and HEVC is the compression inside it, so HEIC is not simply another name for H.265 video. Its formal name is ISO/IEC 23008-12, MPEG-H Part 12, first published in 2017.

A HEIF file can hold several images, image sequences, an alpha channel as an auxiliary image, high bit depths, and Exif or XMP metadata. WebP is an image format developed by Google. Google announced it on 30 September 2010, and its lossy compression is based on the VP8 video codec. WebP can carry transparency and animation whether lossy or lossless, and it can also hold an embedded ICC profile and Exif or XMP metadata.

### Programs that open HEIC files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- GIMP imports HEIC, and version 2.10.22 improved high-bit-depth handling.
- ImageMagick reads it when built with the libheif delegate.

**Windows:**

- Microsoft Photos needs both the HEIF and HEVC extensions to open HEIC.

**Mac, iPhone and iPad:**

- Photos on Apple devices opens HEIF and exports another format.

**Mac:**

- Preview opens HEIF and exports JPEG or PNG.

**Web and mobile:**

- Safari 17 added HEIC display, including on iOS 17 and iPadOS 17; earlier mobile browsers are not covered.
- The signed-in OneDrive website previews uploaded HEIF. Decoding a local file is a separate capability.
- Android has decoded HEIF since version 9.

### HEIC and WebP compared

- **Coding**: HEIC uses HEVC inside HEIF, while lossy WebP is built on the VP8 video codec's intra-frame coding.
- **Container**: HEIF is a container, not a codec, so the HEVC inside it is what the page has to decode.
- **Transparency**: WebP supports alpha, and a HEIF file can carry alpha too.
- **Support**: lossy WebP displays from Chrome 17, Edge 18, Firefox 65 and Safari 14 onward. Safari displays HEIC from version 17.0.
- **File size**: Apple says HEIF compresses better than JPEG, and on average, Google says, lossy WebP comes out about 30% smaller than JPEG. This page promises no size for its WebP.
- **Limits**: WebP stops at 16383 pixels on each side.

The page decodes the HEIC with libheif running in your browser. A HEIC can hold several pictures, but only the primary one is read, so the output is a single still WebP and never an animation. The pixels pass through 8-bit RGB, which means extra depth in the source is lost, and EXIF data and the ICC profile are not carried over. Keep the HEIC if you may need that information later.

A file that holds no image stops with "No images in HEIF". Your original HEIC is not changed; you download a new WebP.

### Other ways to convert HEIC to WebP

- **GIMP:** open the HEIC, choose File > Export As, pick WebP in the file-type list or end the name in .webp, then click Export. The WebP dialog has a Lossless checkbox, which disables the quality settings, plus image quality and alpha quality settings.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick phone.heic published.webp`. Its format page lists HEIC and WEBP as readable and writable, and says HEIC requires the libheif delegate library and WEBP requires a WEBP delegate library.
- **libheif:** run `heif-dec phone.heic published.webp`. The libheif README says heif-dec decodes HEIF images to JPEG, PNG, TIFF, WebP or Y4M, and the tool picks the format from the output file's suffix. If you set no quality, its source default for WebP is 75.

### Problems with HEIC files

- **Windows Photos will not open it**: it can reject HEIC until both Microsoft media extensions, HEIF and HEVC, are installed. Converting here avoids installing them.
- **iPhone import gives JPEG**: a USB import to a computer can convert to JPEG on its own. Choose Keep Originals to receive the HEIC itself.
- **An older Apple system**: HEIF support depends on the system version, so an older Apple system may not open a HEIC.

guide.title: About HEIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a HEIF file?

HEIF, the High Efficiency Image File Format, comes from MPEG as ISO/IEC 23008-12 and was first published in 2017. It uses the ISO Base Media File Format as its base and can store single stills, collections and timed sequences, with metadata and derived images attached. It is a container, not a codec: HEVC (H.265) is one coding it supports, and HEIC is the variant that uses it. Stills carry the media type image/heif and sequences image/heif-sequence.

Apple brought HEIF to photos with iOS 11 and macOS High Sierra, capturing it on iPhone 7 and later. Apple says HEIF gives better compression than JPEG. The container can hold several images, image sequences and depth maps, plus Exif or XMP metadata, high bit depths, and an alpha channel stored as an auxiliary image. A reader needs to understand the container and also the codec of each item.

Phones are where most people meet it. The listed uses are photographs from modern phones and image sequences and bursts.

### Programs that open HEIF files

**Windows, macOS and Linux**

- GIMP imports and exports HEIF since version 2.10.2.
- XnView MP, a viewer with HEIF support, costs nothing for private and educational use on Windows and Linux.

**Windows**

- Photos needs both of Microsoft's media add-ons, one for HEIF and one for HEVC video.

**macOS**

- Preview, Apple's viewer, opens HEIF and exports it as JPEG.

**Web**

- Safari displays HEIC from version 17.0.

**Mobile**

- Android decodes HEIF from version 9, Apple Photos on iPhone and iPad opens them, and Adobe documents HEIF and .heic support in Lightroom for mobile on both iOS and Android.

### HEIF and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: image/heif for .heif and .heic; image/jpeg for .jpg and .jpeg.
- **What they are**: HEIF is a container that can hold many images and extras. A JPG is one picture.
- **Compression**: HEIF files are listed as smaller than JPEG ones, and JPEG is lossy.
- **Transparency**: HEIF can store alpha in an auxiliary image. JPG cannot.
- **Bit depth**: HEIF supports high bit depths. JPG stores 8 bits per channel.
- **Metadata**: HEIF can carry Exif and XMP. This page does not copy them to the JPG.
- **Support**: every major browser shows JPG. HEIF support depends on the Apple system version, and Windows needs two extensions.
- **Typical use**: HEIF is what modern phones store photos in, while JPG is the usual choice for pictures on the web, files from cameras, mail attachments and sharing photos.
- **Extras**: this page decodes only the primary image, so other pictures in the file do not reach the JPG.

The JPG comes out at quality 0.85 from the 8-bit pixels of the primary image only.

### Other ways to convert HEIF to JPG

- **Preview:** on a Mac, open the HEIF in Preview, choose File > Export, and pick a format such as JPEG before saving. Apple describes this in its support article.
- **libheif:** run `heif-dec input.heif output.jpg`. The tool picks the output format from the filename suffix, and jpg, jpeg and png are among the suffixes it recognizes. Its quality option applies to JPEG output, and a file with several images gives numbered outputs ending -1, -2 and so on.

### Problems with HEIF files

- **A program says unsupported**: knowing the HEIF wrapper is not enough, because the program also has to decode the codec stored inside. A HEIC needs an HEVC decoder.
- **Only one photo is exported**: a file can hold several related pictures or a sequence, and a single-image export does not represent all of them.
- **An old Mac or iPhone can't open it**: older Apple systems lack the built-in support Apple added in iOS 11 and macOS High Sierra, which is why conversion helps. Converting to JPG improves compatibility.
- **Photos refuses it on Windows**: Windows Photos may decline HEIC until you add both of the Microsoft media extensions.
- **USB copies turn into JPG**: photos copied from an iPhone over USB may be converted automatically unless Keep Originals is chosen in Photos settings.
- **No EXIF in the result**: this page leaves metadata behind, so use another tool if you need the capture date or location kept.
- **Check before deleting**: because metadata is left behind, look over the JPG before you remove the original HEIF.
- **Future photos**: switch the iPhone camera to Most Compatible if you want JPG at capture time.
