guide.title: About JIF and JPEG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JIF file?

JIF stands for JPEG Interchange Format. It is the original file layout described in the JPEG standard for storing JPEG-compressed images, and JFIF and Exif largely replaced it, so .jif files are rare now. The pictures use ordinary lossy JPEG compression and carry no alpha transparency. The later JFIF convention allows .jif among its extensions, yet a .jif is far less common than the .jpg that most JFIF files carry. JFIF can carry a small embedded thumbnail, and it was standardized as ITU-T T.871 in May 2011.

### Programs that open JIF files

- **Linux, Windows and Mac:** GIMP, which imports JPEG for editing, is listed among the programs that open JIF files, and ImageMagick reads JPG.
- **Mobile and Web:** Chrome, Firefox and Safari can display JPEG.

XnView and IrfanView are listed as openers for JIF as well.

### JIF and JPEG compared

JPEG is named for the committee behind it, the Joint Photographic Experts Group. ISO/IEC 10918-1 defines it, and it is the usual format for digital camera output. The .jpg and .jpeg extensions mean one and the same format. Editors scale quality from 0 to 100, and the same number in two editors need not give the same compression or appearance. Baseline JPEG compresses 8x8 pixel blocks, using a discrete cosine transform plus Huffman coding, and stores 8 bits per color channel. Because JPEG is lossy, keep the JIF if you may want the first pass later.

Here your browser decodes the JIF to 8-bit pixels and saves a JPEG at quality 0.85, so the lossy step runs a second time.

### Other ways to convert JIF to JPEG

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick input.jif compatible.jpeg`; its command-line page shows this `magick in out` form for changing formats.
- **Pillow:** call `Image.open("input.jif").save("compatible.jpeg")`. Pillow reads and writes JPEG, and its quality option defaults to 75.
- **GIMP:** choose File > Open on the JIF, then File > Export As, give the file a .jpeg name and click Export. The JPEG export dialog has a Quality setting.

### Problems with JIF files

A picture that needs transparency has to start in another format, because a JIF has no alpha channel.

guide.title: About JIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JIF file?

JIF is short for JPEG Interchange Format, the first file layout the JPEG standard defined for holding JPEG-compressed pictures. JFIF and Exif largely took its place, and .jif files are rarely seen now. Most files with a JPEG picture inside today use one of those two layouts.

The compression inside is JPEG, a method the Joint Photographic Experts Group started designing in 1986. The core text is ITU-T T.81 from 1992, which ISO and IEC took on as 10918-1 two years later. Baseline JPEG discards detail by design: 8x8 blocks of pixels pass through a discrete cosine transform, and the results are Huffman-coded. Most digital cameras and scanners write JPEG natively. The format itself is free to use now that its US patents have lapsed, and every major browser displays it, so JPEG is rarely the obstacle. That is the usual reason to convert: the picture is fine, the file name is the problem. JIF is also easy to mistake for GIF, a different format with a 256-color palette and optional animation.

A JIF is used for legacy JPEG files and for interchange of JPEG photographs. A JPG is the form of the same compression that cameras, scanners, web pages and photo sharing sites handle every day, and the two endings, .jpg and .jpeg, mean the same thing. The registered media type is image/jpeg. Converting here changes the layout and the name, and the pixels are decoded and compressed again, so the JPG is a new file rather than a renamed copy.

### Programs that open JIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** XnView lists JIF among the formats it opens. The JPG made here opens in any web browser, in Preview on macOS, in Windows Photos and in GIMP.

### JIF and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: the original layout uses .jif, while the file most programs expect uses .jpg or .jpeg, with image/jpeg as its media type.
- **Compression**: identical. A discrete cosine transform works on 8x8 pixel blocks, and Huffman coding packs the result.
- **Transparency**: neither has an alpha channel, so a JPEG cannot hold transparency.
- **Color depth**: 8 bits for each color channel.
- **Layers**: JPEG cannot store layers.
- **Layout**: JIF is the layout from the standard itself. JFIF and Exif largely replaced it.
- **Quality scale**: editors usually offer a 0 to 100 slider, and equal numbers do not mean equal quality across programs. GIMP's default is 85. This page asks the canvas encoder for 0.85 on its 0 to 1 scale.
- **Progressive mode**: a progressive JPEG paints a rough version first and refines it as the rest of the file arrives.
- **Acceptance**: a form that wants a JPG often checks the ending, so a .jif name can be turned away even when the data would display.

Here the page asks your browser's image decoder to read the file, then saves a JPG at quality 0.85 and the original pixel dimensions. Since both formats are lossy, this is a second round of compression, and EXIF, ICC and XMP data stay behind.

### Other ways to convert JIF to JPG

- **GIMP (any desktop):** bring the picture in, go to File > Export As, name the output with a .jpg ending and press Export. A JPEG settings dialog follows, where you choose the quality. GIMP's JPEG export defaults to 85 and keeps neither transparency nor layers.
- **Photopea (web):** choose File > Open for the picture, then File > Export As > JPG and save the download.

### Problems with JIF files

- **Your editor will not open it**: Use the converter above and open the JPG in any viewer.
- **A form rejects the file**: convert it here and upload the .jpg instead.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the browser could not read the picture. Download the file again, since a transfer that stopped early leaves a file that ends in the middle.
- **It turns out to be a GIF**: GIF and JIF differ by one letter, and a GIF is a different format. Check the full extension before converting.
- **Quality settings differ**: a quality number in one program does not match the same number in another, so compare results by eye rather than by number.
- **Camera details are gone**: the conversion passes through raw pixels and drops EXIF. Read those details from the JIF before converting.

guide.title: Understanding JIF for PNG output
guide.markdown:
### What is a JIF file?

JIF expands to JPEG Interchange Format. It was the earliest layout in the JPEG standard for holding JPEG-compressed pictures. Later layouts, JFIF and Exif, largely superseded it, and .jif files are rarely seen.

Behind the JPEG name stands a committee, the Joint Photographic Experts Group; its work started in 1986. The core standard was published by ITU-T as T.81 (1992) and by ISO/IEC as 10918-1 (1994). Baseline JPEG discards information. It tiles the image with 8x8-pixel blocks, gives each block a discrete cosine transform, and Huffman coding closes the process. With usual settings a file shrinks to roughly one tenth up to one twentieth of the uncompressed picture. Most digital cameras and scanners write JPEG, and all major browsers can show it. Whether you see .jpg, .jpeg or .jif, the picture format is JPEG, and its registered media type is image/jpeg.

### Programs that open JIF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports JPEG for editing.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPEG at the command line; its format table lists it as readable and writable.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display JPEG pictures.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome display JPEG pictures.

A progressive mode also exists: a rough picture shows first, then gains detail while the rest loads.

### JIF and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .jif and image/jpeg for JPEG data; .png and image/png.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. PNG is always lossless, using DEFLATE (LZ77 plus Huffman coding).
- **Transparency**: JPEG has no alpha channel. PNG supports an optional alpha channel.
- **Color depth**: PNG samples can be 1 to 16 bits deep, while JPEG uses 8 bits for each color channel.
- **Quality setting**: JPEG encoders accept a quality value, usually from 0 to 100, whose meaning varies by program. PNG has no such setting.
- **Standards**: The aim behind PNG was a GIF alternative free of patents. The W3C issued it as its first Recommendation for an image format in October 1996, and the ISO/IEC 15948:2004 edition came later.
- **Structure**: a PNG file opens with a fixed byte signature, and the rest is a series of chunks: IHDR, then IDAT with the pixels, and finally IEND.
- **Metadata**: this page drops it, so EXIF, color profiles and XMP don't reach the PNG.

Your browser's own image decoder reads the JIF, and the page writes the pixels as a PNG. PNG has no quality setting, and nothing is re-compressed with loss. The picture passes through 8-bit RGBA, which matches the JPEG's 8 bits per channel. The PNG shows what the JPEG shows, flaws included: blocks, ringing around edges and softness are already in the decoded pixels. A photo often grows as a PNG, because lossless storage of a photograph takes more bytes than JPEG. Your JIF isn't changed, and several files are processed one after another, each PNG downloading separately as a new copy named after the original, such as scan.png. The page sets no file-size limit. The PNG makes a good working copy for editing, where saving again would add another round of JPEG loss.

### Other ways to convert JIF to PNG

- **GIMP:** when you open a JPEG, GIMP imports it into its own XCF format as a new project. Next use File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E), the command for saving in any format besides XCF, and pick PNG.

### Problems with JIF files

- **The browser says "Image decode failed."**: the file is damaged, cut short, or not an image. Get a fresh copy from the source.
- **A transparent PNG was expected**: JPEG has no alpha channel, so it cannot hold transparency and the PNG is opaque. Cutting out a background takes an editor.
- **The PNG is bigger**: lossless storage of a photograph can take more space than JPEG. Keep the JIF for storage and use the PNG for editing.
- **A photo frame refuses it**: some older frames reject progressive JPEG. Export a JPEG with progressive mode disabled.
- **Quality numbers differ**: a given value can behave differently across programs, so identical settings may still produce different file sizes and picture quality.
- **You need the layers back**: JPEG doesn't preserve an editable layer stack, and this PNG holds a single picture. Keep the editing project file.

guide.title: Understanding JP2 for JPEG output
guide.markdown:
### What is a JP2 file?

JP2 wraps a JPEG 2000 codestream in the Part 1 file format, developed by the Joint Photographic Experts Group. JPEG 2000 compression can be lossy or lossless, and the codestream inside decides which, not the wrapper. The wrapper can store color profiles, opacity information and other metadata. A JP2 reader ignores wrapper extensions it does not understand. Its standard extension is .jp2 and its registered media type is image/jp2. The Library of Congress serves digitized maps and newspapers as lossy JP2 images.

### Programs that open JP2 files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - ImageMagick: lists read and write support for JP2.
  - OpenJPEG: an open-source JPEG 2000 codec written in C.
- **Windows and Mac:**
  - Adobe Photoshop: opens a JP2 file when you select it in the latest version.

### JP2 and JPEG compared

- **Names**: .jp2 is image/jp2; JPEG uses .jpg or .jpeg.
- **Compression**: JPEG 2000 allows lossy or lossless coding, while JPEG is lossy.
- **Opacity**: a JP2 may store opacity, which JPEG cannot hold because it has no alpha transparency.
- **Metadata**: the JP2 wrapper can carry color profiles and other metadata alongside the picture.
- **Use**: JP2 suits archives and service images, while JPEG is used for web photographs, camera output and email attachments.
- **After converting**: open the JPEG and compare it with the JP2, since a lossy JPEG cannot return to the original and the JP2 should be kept.

The JP2 is opened as a single picture by ImageMagick running inside your browser tab, and the page sets no JPEG quality. The page refuses a file larger than about 537 megapixels.

### Other ways to convert JP2 to JPEG

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick scan.jp2 shared.jpeg`. ImageMagick lists JP2 and JPEG as readable and writable.

### Problems with JP2 files

- **JPX is not JP2**: the JPX variant belongs to Part 2 of JPEG 2000, not the basic wrapper of Part 1.
- **Browsers do not decode it**: the Library of Congress notes that browsers do not natively decode JPEG 2000, so JP2 files are often converted to a web-friendly format.
- **Few cameras write it**: most cameras do not encode JPEG 2000, so a JP2 is rarely straight out of a camera.

### What is a JP2 file?

JP2 is the file format of JPEG 2000, a still-image standard from the Joint Photographic Experts Group. A JP2 wraps a JPEG 2000 compressed image in the Part 1 file format, which can also hold color profiles, opacity and other metadata. The extension is .jp2 and the media type is image/jp2.

JPEG 2000 can compress with or without loss. A lossy JPEG 2000 image does not recover discarded detail simply by being saved as JP2. A JP2 is also not interchangeable with a JPX file, which belongs to Part 2 of the standard. You find JP2 files in archives and libraries, where the Library of Congress uses lossy JP2 service images for digitized maps and newspapers.

### Programs that open JP2 files

**Windows**

- Adobe Photoshop: Adobe documents opening JP2 images.

**Mac**

- ImageMagick: its formats page marks JP2 as readable and writable.

**Linux**

- OpenJPEG: the open-source JPEG 2000 codec, with command-line utilities rather than an interactive viewer.

### JP2 and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .jp2 and image/jp2; .jpg or .jpeg and image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: JPEG 2000 can be lossy or lossless. Baseline JPEG is always lossy and codes small pixel blocks.
- **Transparency**: a JP2 can carry opacity. A JPG has no alpha channel.
- **Color depth**: a JPG stores 8 bits per channel.
- **Metadata**: a JP2 can carry color profiles and other metadata.
- **Layers**: a JPG holds one flat picture with no layer stack to edit.
- **Use**: JP2 turns up in archive and library service copies, while Chrome, Firefox and Safari all display JPG.
- **Age**: JPEG is the older format, and the one built into cameras and scanners. ITU-T standardized its block coding as T.81 in 1992, and ISO/IEC 10918-1 arrived in 1994.

The codec is what really changes. ImageMagick, compiled to WebAssembly, reads the JP2 on this page and writes the JPG itself, and the page passes no quality setting. Because a JPG has no alpha channel, check the result when your JP2 had transparent parts.

The first JP2 you choose makes the page download the ImageMagick engine, which is about 14 MB, so that conversion starts a moment later than the ones after it. Everything runs on your device and the file is not uploaded. If you convert a scanned archive, check one result first: a JPG made from a lossy JP2 cannot look better than the JP2 did. Keep the original JP2 as your master copy, because a JPG cannot return detail that compression dropped.

Anything above about 537 megapixels gets a too-large message instead of a JPG. With several JP2 files selected, the page converts them one at a time and each gets its own JPG download, unzipped.

### Other ways to convert JP2 to JPG

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.jp2 output.jpg`. The command reads the JP2 and takes the output format from the .jpg ending.
- **XnConvert:** load the JP2 files through Add files on the Input tab, select JPEG on the Output tab and press Convert. Errors appear on the Status tab, and the Action tab stays untouched for a plain conversion. XnView's format list shows JPEG 2000 as readable and writable.

### Problems with JP2 files

- **A program says it cannot open the file**: it has no JPEG 2000 decoder. Convert the file to JPG, or open it in Photoshop or ImageMagick.
- **Pillow cannot open the JP2**: Pillow reads JPEG 2000 only through OpenJPEG 2.0.0 or higher, and it reads L, LA, RGB, RGBA and YCbCr images.
- **A JPX file will not open as a JP2**: JPX belongs to JPEG 2000 Part 2, not the basic Part 1 file format.
- **A lossy JP2**: the Library of Congress uses lossy JP2 service images for digitized maps and newspapers, so a JP2 from a library or archive can already be lossy.
- **Transparent areas are not kept in a JPG**: JPEG export cannot keep transparent pixels. Keep the JP2, or use a format with alpha when you need the see-through areas.
- **The JPG looks soft or blocky**: if the JP2 was lossy, the JPG adds a second round of compression. Detail lost in the first pass does not come back.
- **"Too large to convert here"**: the picture is over about 537 megapixels. Use ImageMagick or OpenJPEG on a computer.

guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

JPEG is a lossy raster format from the Joint Photographic Experts Group committee. It suits photographs, and the .jpg and .jpeg endings mean the same thing. It has no alpha transparency and stores a grid of pixels, so camera output, web photographs and email attachments are typical JPEGs.

A JPEG of a logo shows the shapes but holds none of the paths or type that drew them.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens JPEG files for editing; ImageMagick also reads them, but support depends on how your copy was built.
- **Web:** Browsers such as Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox show JPG images directly.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome show them on a phone.

### JPEG and AI compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg on one side, .ai on the other.
- **Contents**: a JPEG is flat pixels. An AI is Adobe Illustrator's native artwork format, where vector objects and placed pixel pictures can share one document.
- **History**: PostScript underlay AI files until Illustrator 9 reworked the format in 2000. Newer files can also include a PDF rendition alongside the Illustrator data.

The AI written here is a PDF made in your browser, with a PNG copy of your picture placed on a page the size of its pixels. It carries no Illustrator data and nothing is traced, so the picture remains pixels and has no editable paths. The JPEG is not uploaded.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to AI

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick photo.jpg photo.ai`. ImageMagick's format list shows both JPEG and AI as readable and writable.

### Problems with JPEG files

Transparent pixels cannot survive JPEG export, so a logo saved as a JPEG sits on a solid background, and that background goes into the AI file too.

A JPEG keeps no editable layer stack. Retain the project file or the original vector artwork when you have one, because nothing in the JPEG can bring it back.

Two editors given an identical quality number may compress differently, so two JPEGs of one logo can look unlike. If the AI file is for print or packaging, start from the original artwork rather than from a picture that already lost detail.

guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

JPEG, from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, is a lossy format defined in ISO/IEC 10918-1 and designed for photographs. It has adjustable quality and no alpha transparency, and it is supported everywhere. Files ending in .jpg or .jpeg are one and the same format. You find JPEGs as digital camera output, as photographs on the web, and in email attachments and photo sharing.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens JPEG files for editing, and ImageMagick can read them.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos opens JPEG files.
- **Mac:** Preview on macOS opens them.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox display JPG in the browser.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Google Chrome for Android display it as well.

### JPEG and AVIF compared

AVIF comes from the Alliance for Open Media and packs AV1-compressed pictures into a HEIF container; people convert JPEGs to it chasing smaller files for the web. AVIF can be lossy or lossless, handles transparency, HDR and wide color gamut, and goes to 10 and 12 bits. A JPEG source brings none of that. This page decodes the JPEG to 8-bit RGBA pixels and encodes them again, so the AVIF is made from decoded pixels, not a repackaged JPEG. Older browsers may fail to show AVIF, so keep a JPEG fallback. Compare the two files at the size visitors will see before you replace one with the other.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to AVIF

- **avifenc (command line):** run `avifenc -q 80 photo.jpg photo.avif`. The `-q` option sets color quality from 0 to 100, where 100 is lossless.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the JPEG and use File > Export As… to write the AVIF. GIMP supports AVIF import and export from version 2.10.22.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick photo.jpg photo.avif`. ImageMagick lists AVIF as a format it can read and write.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Transparency is missing**: a JPEG cannot hold transparent pixels, so nothing transparent carries into the AVIF. Choose a format with alpha if you need it.
- **An old photo frame rejects the JPEG**: some older photo frames will not open a progressive JPEG, so re-save it with progressive mode off.
- **Quality numbers do not match between editors**: the same quality setting can compress differently from one editor to the next.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPEG holds one flat picture, so keep your project file if you still need the layers.

guide.title: About JPEG and BMP files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

JPEG, short for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, began as a 1986 effort, and ITU-T T.81 (1992) and ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994) standardize it as a lossy format. Baseline coding splits the picture into blocks of 8x8 pixels, runs a discrete cosine transform on each block and entropy-codes the result, so a photo shrinks far below its raw size. Typical settings give files between a twentieth and a tenth of the raw size.

The US patents expired on 27 October 2006. Most cameras and scanners write JPEG, and every major browser can show it. Each color channel gets 8 bits, there is no alpha channel and layers do not exist. A progressive mode shows a coarse picture first and sharpens it while the rest loads. The names .jpg and .jpeg mean one format, and this page's file picker takes both. A 0 to 100 quality scale is typical, though 80 in one program need not look like 80 in another.

### Programs that open JPEG files

**Windows**

- GIMP: imports JPEG for editing.

**Mac**

- ImageMagick: reads JPG.

**Web**

- Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox: display JPG pictures.

**Mobile**

- Safari: displays JPG pictures.

### JPEG and BMP compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .bmp with image/bmp; .jpg or .jpeg with image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. BMP commonly stores pixels uncompressed, though lossless compression exists.
- **Transparency**: a JPEG has none. BMP version 5 can record an alpha channel.
- **Color depth**: 8 bits per channel for JPEG. A BMP header describes its own bit depth and color table.
- **Metadata**: JPEG can carry EXIF, ICC and XMP. BMP version 5 can record an ICC profile.
- **History**: Microsoft controls BMP, used first on Windows and OS/2. Version 5 arrived with Windows 98.
- **Older readers**: software that expects an old bitmap header may want BMP3 or BMP2 rather than ImageMagick's default BMP version.

What changes in this conversion is the storage. The browser decodes the JPEG to 8-bit pixels and ImageMagick writes them as a BMP, so the file grows and the photo looks the same as the decoded JPEG. EXIF, ICC and XMP data stay behind.

A BMP will not improve a photo. It gives you a file that any bitmap reader handles, with decoded pixels and no further JPEG compression for the next program to work on. Size is the price: a photo can be many times larger as a BMP, so PNG or JPEG are usually more practical for sharing.

Pick several JPEG files and the page handles them one after another, giving every file its own BMP download. No ZIP and no merge happens.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to BMP

- **XnConvert:** add the JPEG on the Input tab, set the Output tab's format to BMP and press Convert. Nothing else is needed, and XnView lists BMP as readable and writable.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.jpeg output.bmp`. ImageMagick also writes the BMP2 and BMP3 variants, for programs that need an older header.
- **Pillow (Python):** after importing Image from PIL, chain `Image.open("input.jpeg")` and `save("output.bmp")`. Pillow documents BMP writing for 1, L, P and RGB images.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **A clear background is not there**: JPEG stores no alpha, so any transparency has to be added in an editor and saved in a format that has it.
- **An older photo frame will not show it**: some old frames cannot read progressive JPEG, so save again with progressive mode off.
- **One quality number, two results**: identical numbers in different editors do not guarantee the same compression or look.
- **Layers are missing**: JPEG holds a flat picture, so keep the project file if you need the layers.
- **Blocky edges or fuzzy text**: lossy compression put that damage in the JPEG before this page saw it, so look for a less compressed copy.
- **Text in the photo cannot be edited**: a JPEG holds pixels only, with no live text or vector objects.
- **The camera details are gone from the BMP**: the page writes pixels only, so the EXIF, ICC and XMP data in the JPEG stay behind. Keep the JPEG if you need them.
- **A renamed file still fails**: renaming .jpeg to .bmp leaves JPEG data inside, so only a real conversion fixes it.

guide.title: JPG to GIF: formats and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

Joint Photographic Experts Group is the committee behind JPEG, and it began in 1986. Lossy compression is the baseline design: a transform and Huffman coding are applied to every 8x8 pixel block, which ordinarily leaves a tenth to a twentieth of the raw size. Color channels get 8 bits, and without an alpha channel a JPEG simply cannot hold transparency. A progressive variant lets a rough version of the picture show first.

Most cameras and scanners write the format directly. You can write the extension as .jpg or .jpeg, since they mean one thing, and the media type is image/jpeg. Browsers all display it, and the final US patents lapsed on 27 October 2006.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads a JPEG from a terminal, and GIMP imports it for editing.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox display JPEG.
- **Mobile:** Chrome and Safari display JPEG.

GIF is displayed by the same browsers, on phones as well as computers. GIMP exports GIF as a still picture or a multilayer animation, and ImageMagick reads GIF.

### JPEG and GIF compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg and .jpeg are image/jpeg. A GIF is image/gif.
- **Colors**: 8 bits per channel for a JPEG, against a GIF image restricted to a palette.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. GIF is lossless, but mapping a photograph onto a palette discards distinctions first.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has none. A GIF can make a palette color fully clear, with no partial opacity.
- **Animation**: GIF can hold many frames, while JPEG is one picture.
- **Layers**: neither format stores an editable layer stack.

The JPEG is decoded by your browser, and the GIF is then written by ImageMagick inside the page. The result is a single still frame, not an animation, and several JPEGs give several separate GIFs rather than a slideshow. Nothing is uploaded, because the conversion stays in your browser. The page sets no palette options and passes no quality setting. Camera data such as EXIF and the color profile do not carry over. Detail that JPEG compression removed does not come back in the GIF, and the palette adds a further limit on color. The download keeps your file's name with a .gif ending.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to GIF

- **GIMP:** on Windows, Mac or Linux, open the JPEG, go to File > Export As, save it as a GIF and confirm the options in the GIF Export dialog. GIMP exports at most 256 colors, which can change gradients.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick photo.jpeg photo.gif`. It gives a still GIF and does not build an animation.

The GIF Export dialog in GIMP has an Interlace option and a Save comment option, and when the image has several layers it offers As animation, with controls for the delay between frames, the number of repeats and looping forever. ImageMagick suits scripts and whole folders. Both give a still GIF from a single JPEG. Animation takes a separate step in an editor that supports layers or frames, and GIMP's As animation option stays disabled for an image with only one layer.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Transparent pixels cannot be kept**: transparency is impossible to store in a JPEG, so a background you want clear has to be removed in an editor before you save a GIF.
- **Quality numbers do not match across programs**: the same 0 to 100 setting can give different compression and appearance in different editors, so compare the result rather than the number.
- **Some older photo frames reject progressive JPEG**: if a device will not show a file, try saving it again with progressive mode turned off.
- **Gradients change in the GIF**: smooth areas such as a sky have to be mapped onto a small palette, and GIMP warns that this can change gradients.
- **Layers are not kept**: a JPEG has no layers to edit later, so save the project file as well.
- **Camera details are gone after converting**: EXIF is left behind by this page. Keep the JPEG if you need the date, camera or location data.
- **No animation came out**: the page converts one picture. To animate several images, build the frames as layers in GIMP and export a multilayer animation.

### JPEG and HDR compared

A Radiance HDR file is an RGBE image, an idea from Greg Ward. Every pixel is three color bytes with one shared exponent, which gives a brightness range that plain 24-bit RGB cannot reach. The format has run-length encoding, and its files end in .hdr or .pic. Lighting simulations in Radiance use it for computed light levels, and its media type is image/vnd.radiance.

Your browser first turns the JPEG into pixels, and ImageMagick then writes the Radiance file from that 8-bit data. What you get is the same picture in a new container. A window that the camera blew out to white is still white, and nothing here merges exposures or lets you set exposure or tone. Keep the original JPEG too, because the Radiance copy holds no more detail than the source.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to HDR

- **GIMP:** open the JPEG, then export with a .hdr name or pick Radiance RGBE as the file type. No dialog opens and the export starts at once.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick photograph.jpeg environment.hdr`. Its format list shows JPEG and HDR as both readable and writable.
- **OpenCV:** read the JPEG with `imread` and write it with `imwrite` under a .hdr file name; the library lists Radiance HDR as .hdr and .pic.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **No transparency**: a JPEG cannot carry see-through pixels, so a cutout needs another format.
- **Compression damage**: the blocks and banding that lossy coding leaves are part of the picture for good.
- **No layers**: a JPEG is one flat picture, so save the original artwork separately.

guide.title: About JPEG and ICO
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

Three dates frame the history. Work in the Joint Photographic Experts Group began in 1986, ITU-T published its standard as T.81 in 1992, and the same text became ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994. Baseline JPEG discards detail on purpose: blocks of 8x8 pixels get a discrete cosine transform, and Huffman coding packs what remains. Color is stored at 8 bits per channel with no alpha channel, so see-through pixels cannot exist in a JPEG. An optional progressive layout draws a blurry whole first and sharpens it. A 0 to 100 quality scale is common, but the numbers are not comparable across programs, and an ordinary setting turns a photo into roughly 1/10 to 1/20 of its raw size, which is the trade that made JPEG the photo format.

Either ending, .jpg or .jpeg, means the same format. A JPEG cannot store layers. The final US patents on the format ran out on 27 October 2006. Digital cameras and scanners commonly save in JPEG, and it turns up wherever photos live: phones, stock sites, product pages and email attachments.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows:** Photos shows JPEG pictures.
- **Mac:** Preview shows JPEG pictures.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP can import a JPEG for editing, while ImageMagick opens one from the command line.
- **Web and mobile:** every browser displays JPEG, Chrome and Firefox on the web and Safari and Chrome on phones.

### JPEG and ICO compared

- **Extensions and types**: JPEG uses .jpg or .jpeg and image/jpeg; ICO uses .ico and image/vnd.microsoft.icon.
- **Purpose**: JPEG is for photographs. ICO holds icons for Microsoft Windows, and browsers also use it for favicons.
- **Several images**: one ICO may contain many pictures at different sizes and color depths. Microsoft describes typical icon sizes as 16, 32, 48 and 256 pixels. A JPEG contains one picture.
- **Size**: 256 pixels is the largest side this converter writes, which matches the largest of those typical sizes.
- **Transparency**: ICO supports alpha. A JPEG gives it nothing to carry.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. Here, an image of 256 px is written as a PNG entry.

The page decodes the JPEG with your browser, then hands the pixels to ImageMagick, which writes the ICO. One image goes in. A picture wider or taller than 256 pixels is shrunk to sit within 256 x 256 at the same proportions, and a smaller picture keeps its size. No metadata is copied.

If you need an ICO with 16, 32 and 48 pixel images inside, that is a job for a program that writes several sizes into one file, such as the ImageMagick command below. The converter on this page does not crop to a square or add padding.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to ICO

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** after loading the JPEG, File > Export As lets you name the file with an .ico ending; press Export. The export type is called Microsoft Windows icon.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick portrait.jpeg -alpha off -define icon:auto-resize="16,32,48,64,96,128,256" favicon.ico`. This writes seven sizes into one ICO; ImageMagick's page says the input should be square.
- **IrfanView:** choose File > Open for the JPEG, then File > Save as, pick ICO as the output format, set the file name and save. IrfanView lists ICO among the formats it can save.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **The icon has a white or colored box**: a JPEG can't be transparent, so its whole rectangle becomes the icon. Cut the subject out in an editor first.
- **"Image decode failed." appears**: your browser could not decode the file as a JPEG. It may be another format that was renamed to .jpg.
- **Detail disappears at icon size**: a JPEG bigger than 256 px is reduced to fit the 256 x 256 limit, so a detailed photo loses much of its detail. A simple, cropped picture with one clear subject holds up better.
- **The ICO isn't square**: the converter keeps the JPEG's shape, so crop the JPEG to a square before converting.
- **You lose your layers**: a JPEG keeps none, and neither does this conversion. Keep the project file you made it from.
- **EXIF data is gone**: only pixels are passed on, so camera details, ICC profiles and XMP stay behind.

### What is a JPEG file?

The format's committee, the Joint Photographic Experts Group, started in 1986. ITU-T T.81 from 1992 and ISO/IEC 10918-1 from 1994 specify the core. Baseline JPEG discards information: the picture is split into blocks eight pixels square, every block is run through a discrete cosine transform, and the result is Huffman-coded. Each color channel gets 8 bits, and with no alpha channel there is no transparency or layers. A progressive variant exists too, which shows a rough picture first and refines it while the rest downloads. Cameras and scanners have JPEG built in, and its media type is image/jpeg. Both .jpg and .jpeg are used for one and the same format.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens JPEG for editing, and ImageMagick can read it.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox display JPEG.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Google Chrome display it too.

### JPEG and JPEG compared

Both sides of this conversion are the same format, so the only change is a new encode. The page decodes your JPEG in the browser and writes another one at quality 0.85. That number is an encoder setting, and the same value can mean different quality in different programs; GIMP, for example, defaults to 85. EXIF, ICC and XMP data don't come along, and the pixels pass through 8-bit RGBA. Convert once from the original, because each lossy encode starts from what the last one left behind.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to JPEG

- **GIMP:** open the JPEG, choose File > Export As, enter a new name and pick JPEG under Select File Type. In the JPEG options, set the quality level from 0 to 100. GIMP also lets you choose which metadata to keep.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick original.jpeg -quality 90 rewritten.jpeg`. ImageMagick's JPEG writer scales quality by its own rules.
- **Preview:** on a Mac, open the JPEG and choose File > Export. In the Format pop-up menu select JPEG, set the quality, give the copy a new name and click Save.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Transparency is lost**: JPEG stores no alpha channel, so choose another format if you need clear areas.
- **An old photo frame shows nothing**: it may not read progressive JPEG, so export with progressive turned off.
- **Quality numbers don't match**: the same number in two editors does not guarantee the same compression or appearance.
- **Layers are flattened**: only one merged image is stored, so keep your layered project file.

guide.title: JPEG and JPG: one format, two endings
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

JPEG is one image format with several file endings. The name comes from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, and ITU-T T.81 was the 1992 form of its core standard, ISO/IEC 10918-1 the 1994 one. Cameras and scanners usually write it, and all the major browsers display it.

The two endings are not two formats. Both extensions name one format, so a .jpg and a .jpeg file hold the same kind of data. JFIF, the wrapper most JPEG files use, allows .jpg and .jpeg plus .jpe, .jfi, .jfif and .jif, and every one is served as image/jpeg.

The first JFIF came from Eric Hamilton at C-Cube Microsystems; version 1.02 is dated 1992. JFIF became a standard twice over: in May 2011 as ITU-T T.871, and as ISO/IEC 10918-5. It can embed a small thumbnail of the picture. Such a file opens with the start-of-image marker, immediately followed by an APP0 segment that carries the JFIF label.

Work on the standard began in 1986, and its United States patents ran out on 27 October 2006. Ordinary quality settings leave an image at one-tenth to one-twentieth of its uncompressed size. JPEG stores 8 bits per color channel, cannot hold transparency, and offers a progressive mode in which a rough picture shows first and clarifies as the rest downloads.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows:** the Photos app is listed among the programs that open JPEG.
- **Mac:** Apple's Preview viewer can open a JPEG and export a fresh one.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens JPEG for editing and can export a new one. ImageMagick reads JPG, and its `-list format` output names each format your installation reads.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome opens JPEG files.
- **Web:** Mozilla Firefox opens them too.
- **Mobile:** Safari handles JPEG as well.

### JPEG and JPG compared

- **Format**: identical. The same compression, the same data and the same media type, image/jpeg.
- **Extension**: a .jpeg ending has four letters and .jpg has three, and the data inside is the same.
- **Compression**: lossy, in 8x8 blocks with a discrete cosine transform and Huffman coding, with an optional progressive mode that loads a coarse picture first.
- **Color**: 8 bits per channel; there is no alpha channel and there are no layers.
- **Quality setting**: quality is usually set from 0 to 100, but the numbers aren't comparable between programs: GIMP, for one, starts at 85. This page writes every file at 0.85.
- **Metadata**: renaming leaves the file untouched, so whatever it holds stays, while converting here drops Exif, the ICC profile and XMP.
- **What this page changes**: it decodes the image and encodes it again at quality 0.85. You get a new file, not a renamed one, and your original stays as it is.

### Other ways to turn a .jpeg into a .jpg

- **Rename the file:** the two endings are one format, so renaming it in your file manager is enough, and it changes nothing inside.
- **Preview (Mac):** open the file, use File > Export and set Format to JPEG. Re-exporting compresses the image again.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac and Linux):** open the file and choose File > Export As to save a new JPEG. Each JPEG save compresses the image once more.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** `magick input.jpeg output.jpg` writes a new .jpg. It encodes the image again, so rename the file instead when you need an exact copy.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **An upload form wants .jpg**: if a form insists on .jpg, rename the file or convert it here.
- **A .jfif file**: .jfif is one of the JFIF endings, and the data is ordinary JPEG. If the picker doesn't list it, rename it to .jpeg to pick it.
- **The Exif data disappeared**: converting drops Exif. Rename instead when you need to keep it.
- **A renamed file is still rejected**: if a form still refuses the file after a rename, convert it here to write a fresh one, remembering that it is encoded again.
- **The picture looks slightly different**: the new encode at quality 0.85 can lose fine detail, so compare the two at full size before you delete the original file.
- **Quality slips after repeated saves**: every encode loses a little, so don't convert the same file again and again.

Most files called JPEG are JFIF files: a minimal wrapper, which Eric Hamilton of C-Cube Microsystems wrote down first, so the compressed picture can travel between programs and platforms. JFIF later became ITU-T T.871 and ISO/IEC 10918-5.

A JPEG is already lossy, so turning it into a PDF improves nothing; it only wraps the picture in a document. People do it when they want a document rather than a picture, one that looks and prints the same on any machine.

Adobe's PDF grew from Camelot, a 1991 project of John Warnock's, and existed by 1992. The goal was a document that appears and prints the same on any device. A page can combine text with drawings and bitmap pictures, and a PDF may also include bookmarks, links, annotations and fillable fields. Here, each page holds one picture.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Mac:** Apple Preview opens a JPEG and can save it in other formats, among them PDF.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** JPEG files can be edited in GIMP. ImageMagick reads JPG files as well, and it is run from the command line with the magick program.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome shows JPEG images.
- **Web:** Mozilla Firefox shows them as well.
- **Mobile:** Safari opens JPEG too.

Every major browser displays JPEG.

### JPEG and PDF compared

- **File endings**: image/jpeg files end in .jpg or .jpeg, and JFIF files can also use .jpe, .jfi, .jfif or .jif, while application/pdf files end in .pdf.
- **Compression**: JPEG discards fine detail in 8x8 blocks, and normal settings reduce a photo to between 1/10 and 1/20 of its uncompressed size. A PDF can carry JPEG data as it is or store pixels with lossless Flate. This converter does the second: it decodes the photo and embeds it as PNG data.
- **Color**: JPEG stores 8 bits per channel and has no alpha channel, so there is no transparency to carry.
- **Layout**: a JPEG has pixels but no page. The PDF page is cut to the photo's size at one point per pixel, margin-free.
- **Layers and progressive loading**: a JPEG cannot store layers, but it can be saved in progressive mode, which shows a coarse picture first. A PDF made here has a single picture and no layers either.
- **Text**: a PDF can hold real, searchable text, but one made from a photo holds only the picture.
- **Metadata**: any Exif block, ICC profile or XMP in the JPEG stays behind, and none of them reach the PDF.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to PDF

- **Finder (Mac):** select the JPEGs in the order you want, Control-click the selection, then choose Quick Actions > Create PDF. That order sets the pages.
- **Preview (Mac):** open the JPEG, then pick File > Export and choose PDF as the Format.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **The photo is sideways**: [Image to PDF](/image-to-pdf/) turns a JPEG's page to match its Exif orientation tag, so try the photo there.
- **You want the JPEG's own data in the PDF**: this page re-encodes the photo as PNG data. Image to PDF keeps a JPEG's data as it is.
- **A .jfif file doesn't show up**: the picker's list is .jpg and .jpeg. A .jfif file is a JPEG under another ending, so if it doesn't show up, rename it to .jpg.
- **The message "Image decode failed."**: your browser could not decode the JPEG data. Get a fresh copy from its source.
- **Blocky edges or smeared text**: that's JPEG compression in the original, and the PDF shows the same pixels. Start from the sharpest copy you have.
- **The page prints with wide white borders**: the PDF page matches the photo and has no margin, so any border comes from how it is printed.
- **A scanned page is tilted or has dark edges**: the PDF holds the photo's pixels as they are. Crop and straighten the photo in an image editor before converting.

guide.title: About JPEG and PPM files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

Typical settings squeeze a picture to between 5 and 10 percent of its uncompressed size, which helps explain why the format is everywhere: cameras and scanners commonly build it in, and every major browser displays it. The .jpg and .jpeg extensions mean the same format, and work on it began in 1986 under the Joint Photographic Experts Group. The patents covering JPEG in the US ran out on 27 October 2006. Each color channel gets 8 bits, and neither alpha nor layers fit in the file.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Web:** a browser tab shows it directly.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos can look at one.
- **Mac:** Preview can look at one too.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens a JPEG for editing.

### JPEG and PPM compared

In the Netpbm family, PPM is the format for color. A binary PPM begins with P6 and a plain-text one begins with P3. A pixel holds red, green and blue samples, and the highest allowed sample value ranges from 1 up to 65535. A PPM is RGB only, with no alpha channel and no compression.

The browser decodes your JPEG and ImageMagick writes the PPM from the resulting pixels. You get the pixels without JPEG's compression, but the picture itself is not restored, and the page has no controls to change the output. Open the result in a tool that reads Netpbm files, or convert it onward with ImageMagick or Netpbm.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to PPM

- **Netpbm:** run `jpegtopnm photograph.jpeg > samples.ppm`. The tool writes to standard output, and a color JPEG gives a PPM while a grayscale one gives a PGM.
- **GIMP:** open the JPEG and export it to a PPM file. The dialog's Data formatting setting chooses ASCII or RAW, and RAW makes smaller files.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick photograph.jpeg samples.ppm`. Its format list shows PPM, the Netpbm color pixmap format, as readable and writable.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Flattened artwork**: a JPEG cannot store transparency, so cutouts need a format with alpha.
- **Lossy damage**: blocks and banding left by compression stay in every copy you make.
- **No layers**: only one flat picture fits in a JPEG, so keep the original project.

guide.title: JPEG to PSD: format guide
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

A JPEG is a compressed photograph. The Joint Photographic Experts Group defined the format in ISO/IEC 10918-1 for photos, and it trades some detail for small files at an adjustable quality. It has no alpha channel, and almost every program and device can open it. Both .jpg and .jpeg name the same format.

Cameras write JPEG, web pages serve it, and email attachments and shared photos use it. People convert JPEG to PSD to retouch a photo in Photoshop, or to meet a PSD upload requirement.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPEG, and GIMP brings it in for retouching.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos shows a JPEG.
- **Mac:** Preview on macOS shows one too.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox show JPG pictures inline.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Google Chrome for Android do the same.

### JPEG and PSD compared

A JPEG is a lossy picture with no alpha channel and no layers. PSD is Adobe Photoshop's native, proprietary format. It stores layers, masks, adjustment layers, text and color information so a design can be edited later, in RGB or CMYK mode with 16-bit and 32-bit channels.

A PSD made from a JPEG has only the one picture, so the layers are yours to add. This page decodes the JPEG to pixels and writes them with ImageMagick, so the PSD is no sharper than the JPEG. Keep the JPEG as your original.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to PSD

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the JPEG, choose File > Export As… and give the file the .psd extension. GIMP does not convert every Photoshop feature exactly; some blending modes have no exact equivalent.
- **Photopea (browser):** load the JPEG through File - Open, then run File - Save as PSD. Photopea converts every file you open into a PSD document.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **No text or layers**: a JPEG keeps no editable layer stack, so retype or rebuild anything that was flattened into the photo, and retain the project file next time.
- **Compression blocks remain**: wrapping the pixels in a PSD cannot undo lossy damage.
- **Nothing is see-through**: JPEG stores no transparency, so a design that needs it should go to a format with alpha.
- **Quality numbers differ**: equal numbers in different programs can give a different look and size.

guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

A JPEG is the lossy photo format of the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Cameras and scanners commonly produce it, and browsers display it everywhere. Each channel gets 8 bits, so there is no alpha, and layers cannot be stored. IANA registers image/jpeg, and .jpg and .jpeg name one format.

- **Web:** browsers render them inline.
- **Mac:** Preview displays a JPEG.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos displays it too.

An .rgb ending can mean two different things. ImageMagick has a coder it calls Irix RGB for SGI images, and a separate RGB coder for raw sample streams. Raw streams store no dimensions, so a reader must be given the size and depth.

The browser decodes your JPEG, and ImageMagick's raw RGB coder writes the samples from those pixels. Write down the picture's width and height before you convert. The file will not tell you later, and a wrong guess shows up as a striped or sheared image. Reading it back takes those same numbers, in ImageMagick as a -size and -depth setting before the file name.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to RGB

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick photo.jpeg -depth 8 rgb:photo.rgb`, then read it back with `magick -size 640x480 -depth 8 rgb:photo.rgb photo.png`, using the real width and height. ImageMagick's format list describes RGB as raw sample streams that need the size and depth parameters.
- **Pillow:** open the JPEG, write `image.tobytes()` to a binary file and save `image.size` separately.
- **GIMP:** open the JPEG and export as Raw image data. Planar configuration offers Contiguous or Planar, which writes the channels as separate planes.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Quality scales differ**: setting 85 in GIMP is not guaranteed to match 85 in another program, so judge by eye.
- **No alpha**: JPEG has no way to mark pixels transparent, so cutouts need a different format.
- **Lossy compression**: the decoded pixels carry the JPEG's blocks and banding into any raw copy.
- **Single flat layer**: layered artwork is flattened in a JPEG, so keep the source project.

guide.title: About JPEG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

Work on JPEG began in 1986 inside the Joint Photographic Experts Group, whose name it carries. ITU-T T.81 appeared in 1992 as the core standard, and ISO/IEC 10918-1 followed in 1994. The baseline mode is lossy: Baseline JPEG cuts the image into 8x8 pixel blocks, applies a discrete cosine transform to each and finishes with Huffman coding, which is where detail is lost. At typical settings the output ends up 10 to 20 times smaller than the uncompressed image.

Both .jpg and .jpeg are one format, filed with IANA as image/jpeg. A channel stores 8 bits, and since no alpha channel exists, transparency is impossible. A progressive mode first shows a coarse version that sharpens as more data loads.

Programs usually ask for quality as a figure from 0 to 100; GIMP's default is 85. One figure can look different from one program to the next, so compare by eye. Layers cannot be stored in JPEG either.

Most digital cameras and scanners produce JPEG directly, which is why photographs reach you in it. 27 October 2006 marks the expiry of its US patents, and every major browser can display it.

### Programs that open JPEG files

**Windows, macOS and Linux**

- GIMP imports JPEG for editing.
- ImageMagick reads JPG; which formats work depends on your install.

**Web and mobile**

- Desktop Chrome and Firefox display JPG, and on phones Chrome and Safari do.

### JPEG and SVG compared

- **Media types**: image/jpeg for JPEG, image/svg+xml for SVG.
- **Kind of file**: a JPEG stores pixels. An SVG is XML that lays out flat graphics: shapes, text and images placed inside it. The W3C approved SVG 1.0 in 2001 and published version 1.1 in 2003. The standard is open.
- **Sharpness**: shapes stored as instructions can be drawn at any size. A photo embedded in an SVG keeps its original resolution when enlarged.
- **Compression**: JPEG discards detail to shrink. SVG is stored as text, so you can edit it by hand, and it lends itself to searching, indexing and compression.
- **Transparency**: SVG can be transparent where JPEG cannot.
- **Readable source**: you can open an SVG in a text editor and read it, which is how the hand-written method below works.
- **Styling**: CSS and JavaScript can act on an SVG, which makes it styleable, scriptable and animatable. A JPEG cannot.
- **Extras**: SVG adds clipping paths, masks and filters, and a gzipped file takes .svgz.
- **The embedded copy**: PNG compresses without loss, so the pixels your browser decoded are stored exactly, JPEG's earlier losses included.
- **Typical use**: JPEG is for web photographs, camera files, email attachments and sharing pictures. SVG is for logos, icons, illustrations, diagrams, charts and maps.
- **Where it shows**: an SVG can open on its own or sit inside an HTML page, and every major browser draws it.

No tracing happens here. The page decodes the JPEG, then writes an SVG that holds a single image element sized to the picture's pixel width and height, with the pixels embedded as a PNG.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to SVG

- **Text editor, by hand:** save a text file ending in .svg that contains an svg element with a width, a height and the namespace http://www.w3.org/2000/svg. Inside it, add an image element whose href is the JPEG's file name, with width and height set to the picture's pixel size. MDN notes that JPEG, PNG and other SVG files are the formats SVG software must support, and that unlike HTML's img, width and height are required. This links the JPEG instead of embedding it, so keep the two files together or the picture can vanish. Open the finished SVG in any major browser to confirm the photo appears, then place the pair of files wherever the SVG is needed.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Transparent areas are impossible**: a JPEG cannot hold transparent pixels. Remove the background in an editor and start from a format with alpha instead.
- **Layers are gone**: JPEG does not keep an editable layer stack, so retain the project file you exported from. A flattened JPEG cannot be taken apart again.
- **An older photo frame rejects it**: certain frames refuse progressive files; save the picture again with progressive switched off.
- **The quality number misleads**: a setting copied from one editor to another will not reproduce the same file, so judge by the result and not the figure.

guide.title: About JPEG and TGA
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

The committee behind JPEG, short for Joint Photographic Experts Group, issued its core specification first as ITU-T T.81 (1992) and then as ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994). Pixels are grouped in 8x8 blocks, passed through a cosine transform and Huffman coded, which discards detail for good. Every color channel is limited to 8 bits in a JPEG, which also has no transparency and no layers. Both the .jpg and .jpeg endings name this format, whose media type is image/jpeg, and cameras and scanners write it by default.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens a JPEG as an editable image, and ImageMagick can read it.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox show a JPEG directly in a tab.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays JPEG on a phone.

### JPEG and TGA compared

- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy and typically makes an image ten to twenty times smaller than its raw pixels. TGA keeps the pixels as they are, and can add run-length encoding.
- **Transparency**: a 32-bit TGA adds an 8-bit alpha channel to RGB, which a JPEG never has.
- **Color depth**: a 24-bit TGA keeps 8 bits in each color component.
- **Uses**: TGA turns up in video editing and game development, while JPEG is built into cameras and scanners.

The decoding step belongs to your browser; ImageMagick then takes the pixels and produces the Targa file. Everything passes through 8-bit RGBA, which is why the metadata does not follow. Photographs contain few repeated runs for run-length coding to exploit, so expect a file larger than the JPEG.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to TGA

- **GIMP:** Load the JPEG in GIMP, pick File > Export As and export it as TGA. The TGA dialog has a Use RLE compression checkbox and an Origin choice of Bottom left or Top left.
- **ImageMagick:** `magick photograph.jpeg texture_copy.tga` writes the Targa file. ImageMagick reads and writes both JPEG and TGA.
- **Tacent View:** `tacentview -c photograph.jpeg --out tga` runs in command-line mode, so no window opens. Its JPEG load option exifo=true applies the photo's EXIF orientation.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Cutouts are missing**: the JPEG stores no transparency, so any mask has to be drawn in an editor afterwards.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPEG flattens the picture, so an editable stack of layers survives only in your project file.
- **Legacy displays balk**: certain old picture frames cannot show a progressive JPEG, and a baseline copy avoids that.
- **Quality settings are not portable**: one quality figure gives different results from one editor to the next.

guide.title: About JPEG and TIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

The format is named for the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which started work on it in 1986 and saw the core specification appear as ITU-T T.81 in 1992. Baseline JPEG works lossily, applying a discrete cosine transform to 8x8 pixel blocks and then Huffman coding. Its progressive mode first shows a coarse picture, then refines it while more data arrives. Each channel holds 8 bits and there is no alpha. GIMP's default quality is 85 on the usual 0 to 100 scale. The registered media type is image/jpeg.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Linux, Mac and Windows:** GIMP imports JPEG so you can edit it, and ImageMagick reads JPG files.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome renders JPG on both, with Firefox on the web and Safari on mobile.

### JPEG and TIF compared

Aldus and Microsoft developed TIFF as a tag-based raster wrapper. Revision 6.0 dates from 1992, and Adobe now holds the specification. A file can use various compression methods and color representations and can hold several images. Archival master copies and high-bit-depth work are well-established uses. The names .tif and .tiff both mean TIFF, whose media type is image/tiff.

Here your browser decodes the JPEG to 8-bit RGBA and ImageMagick writes the .tif without any compression. The result is larger than the JPEG and holds no more detail. Camera EXIF, XMP and the ICC profile stay behind.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to TIF

- **Preview on a Mac:** open the JPEG, choose File > Export, pick TIFF in the Format pop-up menu, and click Save.
- **GIMP:** open the photograph, choose File > Export As, export it as a TIFF image, and pick the Compression in the TIFF dialog. JPEG is the one lossy choice there.
- **Pillow:** call `Image.open("input.jpeg").save("delivery.tif", compression="tiff_lzw")`. Without libtiff, Pillow writes only uncompressed TIFF files.

### Problems with JPEG files

- A JPEG holds no transparent pixels, so artwork that needs them has to start in another format.
- JPEG has no layer stack; keep the project file if you may edit the artwork again.
- Quality numbers differ between editors, so equal settings do not promise equal compression or appearance.

guide.title: About JPEG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

Behind the name is the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which started on the format in 1986. The specification dates to 1992 as ITU-T T.81 and was adopted internationally in 1994 as ISO/IEC 10918-1. JPEG was designed for photographs. Baseline coding sends 8x8 pixel blocks through a discrete cosine transform, packs the output with Huffman codes and drops the detail the eye is least likely to notice.

People use JPEG for web photographs, pictures straight off a camera, mail attachments and photo-sharing sites, and most cameras and scanners write it. The US patents lapsed in October 2006, and all major browsers show the format. A progressive mode lets a rough image appear first and clear up as the file loads. You will see both .jpg and .jpeg; they are one format, registered as image/jpeg.

### Programs that open JPEG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Preview on macOS and Windows Photos show JPEG, GIMP edits it, and ImageMagick converts it from a terminal.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display JPG in a tab.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays JPG on iPhone and iPad.

### JPEG and TIFF compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg and .jpeg (image/jpeg) versus .tif and .tiff (image/tiff).
- **Compression**: baseline JPEG is always lossy. TIFF is a tag-based wrapper: it can use different compression methods, lossless or lossy, and different color representations.
- **Size**: a TIFF made on this page can be much larger than the JPEG it came from.
- **Quality scale**: JPEG sliders run 0 to 100 and GIMP's default is 85. This page has no quality setting for TIFF output.
- **Pages**: a JPEG is one picture. A TIFF can contain several images, which makes it useful for scanned document sequences.
- **Bit depth**: a JPEG has 8 bits for each channel. TIFF is established for high-bit-depth imaging, though a TIFF written from this page is 8-bit.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has no alpha channel.
- **Standing**: Aldus and Microsoft created TIFF, revision 6.0 is from 1992, and Adobe now controls the specification. Preservation master files are an established use.
- **Limits**: the 32-bit offsets in classic TIFF cap a file at roughly 4 GB, a ceiling BigTIFF lifts with wider ones.

In this conversion the browser decodes the JPEG, and ImageMagick running in the page encodes the pixels as a TIFF. The TIFF holds the decoded pixels as they are, so no second JPEG compression is applied. EXIF, ICC profiles and XMP stay behind. The download takes the JPEG's name with a .tiff ending, and the JPEG file itself is not changed.

The TIFF made here holds one image. A TIFF can hold several, so software that exposes the full image sequence is needed to see them all, and software may skip private tags, such as certain color-profile extensions.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to TIFF

- **Preview (Mac):** open the picture, go to File > Export, set Format to TIFF and save.
- **GIMP (any desktop):** pick File > Export As with a .tiff extension, then select a compression in the TIFF dialog, which offers None, LZW, Pack Bits, Deflate, JPEG and CCITT. LZW and Deflate are lossless; JPEG compression inside a TIFF is lossy.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.jpeg -compress LZW output.tiff`. LZW is one of ImageMagick's listed compression types, and options go before the output file name.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Blocky squares or halos**: heavy compression leaves 8x8 block edges. A TIFF made from that file keeps them, so start from the least compressed version you have.
- **Transparency**: a JPEG cannot hold see-through areas, and a TIFF made from one has none to show.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPEG is one flat picture, so the layered project file is the thing to keep.
- **An old photo frame will not show it**: some older devices reject progressive JPEG, and saving it again without progressive mode fixes that.
- **Quality numbers do not match**: the same quality number in two editors can give different file sizes and looks, so judge the result by eye.
- **A job asks for 16-bit**: a JPEG source has only 8 bits per channel and the TIFF here stays 8-bit, so no extra depth appears. Ask for the original capture if the job needs it.
- **"Image decode failed."**: your browser could not read the JPEG. Download the JPEG again and retry.

guide.title: About JPEG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPEG file?

The Joint Photographic Experts Group wrote JPEG and gave the format its name. Work started in 1986. The core standard is ITU-T T.81 from 1992, matched by ISO/IEC 10918-1 from 1994. In baseline form JPEG is lossy. The picture is cut into 8x8 pixel blocks, run through a discrete cosine transform and then Huffman-coded, typically cutting an image to somewhere from one tenth to one twentieth of its raw size.

JPEG gives each color channel 8 bits and has neither an alpha channel nor layers. Every major browser shows JPEG, and the US patents lapsed on 27 October 2006. Cameras and scanners produce it. Most files people call JPEGs are really JFIF files, a small wrapper around ordinary JPEG data so programs can swap it. Both endings, .jpg and .jpeg, are one format whose media type is image/jpeg.

Quality is usually chosen on a 0 to 100 scale, and GIMP defaults to 85. A progressive mode also exists: a rough version of the picture shows first and sharpens while the rest loads.

### Programs that open JPEG files

**Any desktop**

- GIMP: loads JPEG so you can edit it.
- ImageMagick: handles JPG on the command line.

**Windows**

- Windows Photos: opens JPEG.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens JPEG.

**Web and mobile**

- Chrome and Firefox display JPEG on a computer, and Chrome and Safari do on a phone.

### JPEG and WebP compared

- **Extensions and media types**: JPEG uses .jpg or .jpeg with image/jpeg, WebP uses .webp with image/webp.
- **Compression**: baseline JPEG is lossy. WebP has a lossy mode built on VP8 key-frame coding and a separate lossless mode. Google reports lossy WebP about 30% smaller than JPEG on average.
- **Lossless mode**: WebP's lossless mode relies on LZ77 matching, prefix codes and a cache of recent colors. Baseline JPEG has no lossless mode.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has none. WebP supports it in both modes.
- **Animation**: WebP can hold frames. A JPEG is one still picture.
- **Color depth**: each JPEG channel gets 8 bits.
- **History**: Google unveiled WebP on 30 September 2010, and RFC 9649 documented it in November 2024. A WebP file is a RIFF container.
- **Largest image**: no WebP can exceed 16,383 pixels along either side.
- **Where each is read**: almost every program reads JPEG. WebP needs a current browser (Chrome 17+, Edge 18+, Firefox 65+, Safari 14+), Android 4.0 or later, or a program with WebP support such as GIMP 2.10 or later. Windows opens WebP in File Explorer and Photos once Microsoft's WebP Image Extension is added, and Photoshop opens and saves it from version 23.2.
- **Metadata**: a WebP file can hold an ICC profile, Exif and XMP, but the one made here holds none of them.

For this pair, the page decodes the JPEG in your browser and writes a WebP from the pixels. A JPEG has no transparency, so the WebP is opaque. You cannot change the quality here.

Detail the JPEG already dropped does not return. If you still have the camera original or an editor file, convert from that when quality matters more than a small file.

### Other ways to convert JPEG to WebP

- **cwebp (command line):** run `cwebp portrait.jpeg -q 85 -o portrait.webp`. Add `-lossless` for lossless mode. No metadata is kept by default.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the JPEG, then choose File > Export As to start the export. Its WebP dialog has Lossless and Image quality settings, plus separate switches for color profile, Exif and XMP data.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** `magick portrait.jpeg portrait.webp` does it in one line. WebP writing needs ImageMagick's WebP delegate library.

### Problems with JPEG files

- **Transparency is missing**: JPEG cannot store it. Export from your editor to a format with alpha, such as PNG or WebP, before you convert.
- **An old photo frame refuses the file**: older frames sometimes fail on progressive JPEG. Save the file again with progressive mode off.
- **Quality looks different between programs**: the same quality number can mean different compression in different editors, so judge by eye.
- **You need the layers back**: a JPEG cannot store editable layers, so hold on to the project file.
- **A progressive JPEG looks blurry at first**: progressive mode shows a coarse picture that sharpens while the rest loads. That is how the mode works, not a damaged file.

guide.title: About JPG and AI files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

In short, JPG (also written JPEG) is a lossy picture format whose standard grew out of 1986 work by the Joint Photographic Experts Group. T.81 from ITU-T (1992) and 10918-1 from ISO/IEC (1994) standardize it. The baseline method cuts the image into 8x8 pixel blocks, transforms each one with a discrete cosine transform and applies Huffman coding.

Cameras and scanners commonly produce JPG. It holds 8 bits for each color channel, with no transparency and no layers. The names .jpg and .jpeg are one format, and the patents behind it in the US expired on 27 October 2006. A quality scale of 0 to 100 is common, and equal numbers in different programs can give different results. Compression has already thrown away some detail, and no conversion restores it. People often ask for JPG to AI hoping to get a logo or drawing they can edit. A JPG contains only colored dots and no shapes, so this page gives you the same picture on a PDF page named .ai.

### Programs that open JPG files

**Windows**

- ImageMagick: opens JPG input on the command line.

**Mac**

- GIMP: imports JPEG for editing.

**Web**

- Mozilla Firefox: displays JPG pictures in browser content.

**Mobile**

- Google Chrome and Safari: both display JPG pictures.

### JPG and AI compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg; .ai. The media type of a JPG is image/jpeg.
- **What each is**: a JPG is one pixel picture. An AI file is Illustrator's native document format and can mix vector objects with pixel images.
- **Compression**: a JPG is lossy. An AI document keeps what Illustrator puts in it: editable effects, brushes, layers and transparency.
- **PDF link**: Illustrator can save an AI with a PDF-compatible copy inside. Illustrator 9 changed the format in 2000; earlier files used PostScript.
- **Opening**: a third-party program that can read the embedded PDF does not always get Illustrator's native objects to edit, and an AI saved without the PDF-compatible copy may not open in it at all.
- **Uses**: logos, illustrations and print layouts are what designers keep in AI source files, which is why people expect an editable result from this conversion.
- **Linked images**: Illustrator keeps them external unless Include Linked Files is chosen while saving.
- **Versions**: opening artwork in an older Illustrator can cause problems, and Adobe advises matching or newer versions.
- **Metadata**: the page drops the JPG's EXIF, ICC profile and XMP.

The wrapper is what changes here. The page decodes the JPG, saves the pixels as PNG, places that PNG on a PDF page the size of the picture, one point for each pixel, and downloads the PDF with an .ai name. Saving as AI does not trace a photo.

That makes the .ai file useful when a workflow insists on the extension, or when you want the picture on a page to scale, position and combine with other artwork. It is the wrong tool when you want to recolor, reshape or enlarge a logo, because the picture is still pixels. For paths you need a tracing tool or the original vector file.

Several JPG files are handled one after another, each producing its own .ai download with no ZIP and no merge.

### Other ways to convert JPG to AI

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.jpg output.ai`. The formats page for ImageMagick shows AI as both readable and writable. The output is a raster-based file and nothing is traced, so try it in the program that will open it.

### Problems with JPG files

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG holds a picture squeezed by the method the Joint Photographic Experts Group began developing in 1986. The standard text exists as ITU-T Recommendation T.81 (1992) and as international standard ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994). Baseline compression is lossy. Pixels are handled in 8x8 blocks, a discrete cosine transform turns each block into coefficients, and Huffman codes store them.

JPG is everywhere because cameras and scanners write it natively and browsers draw it without help. US patent protection ended in October 2006. Both .jpg and .jpeg name this one format, served as image/jpeg.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPG on the command line, and GIMP imports the picture if you want to touch it up first.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox draw JPG in a tab.
- **Mobile:** Safari shows JPG on iPhone and iPad.

### JPG and AVIF compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg (image/jpeg) against .avif (image/avif).
- **Compression**: JPEG applies a block-based discrete cosine transform followed by Huffman coding. AVIF packs AV1-compressed images into the HEIF container and offers lossy and lossless modes.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has no alpha channel. AVIF does.
- **Color depth**: 8 bits for each JPEG channel; AVIF goes up to 12 for HDR and wide gamut, though this page writes 8.
- **Quality scale**: editors tend to offer 0 to 100, but a given number does not mean the same quality everywhere. This page has no quality control of its own.
- **Layers**: JPEG cannot store layers.
- **Metadata**: Exif, XMP and an ICC profile all fit in an AVIF file; this page writes none of them.
- **Origins**: the Alliance for Open Media started in 2015 with a goal of royalty-free media formats, and AV1 appeared in 2018.
- **Large pictures**: Baseline-profile AVIF items top out at 8,192 x 4,352 pixels; bigger pictures are tiled as a grid.
- **Licensing**: AVIF is royalty-free.
- **Speed**: AVIF images are slow to decode, and encoding one can take several seconds. JPEG is quick both ways.
- **Progressive display**: a progressive JPG shows a rough picture early, while an AVIF does not render progressively.
- **Support**: every browser shows JPEG. AVIF displays in current Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge, and Android decodes it from version 12. Older browsers may not show AVIF, so keep a JPEG, PNG or WebP copy for visitors whose browser cannot open AVIF. Windows needs two Microsoft add-ons to preview .avif files: the HEIF Image Extension plus the AV1 Video Extension.

For the conversion, your browser decodes the JPG into pixels. If the browser's canvas can encode AVIF, the page asks it for the AVIF. If it cannot, it returns a PNG, and an ImageMagick build running inside the page writes the AVIF from that. Either way the picture keeps its pixel size and loses its metadata, and the AVIF has 8 bits per channel. Nothing leaves your device, because both the decoding and the encoding happen in the browser tab and the original JPG is left as it was. The download uses the JPG's name with an .avif ending.

### Other ways to convert JPG to AVIF

- **GIMP (any desktop):** use File > Export As, enter a filename that ends in .avif, press Export and accept the AVIF settings.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick photo.jpg photo.avif`. ImageMagick's format table marks AVIF as readable and writable.
- **libavif's avifenc (command line):** run `avifenc -q 75 photo.jpg photo.avif`. The avifenc tool must be built with at least one AV1 codec enabled, because none is on by default.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Banding or blocks in smooth areas**: heavy JPG compression leaves 8x8 block edges, and an AVIF made from the file keeps them. Pick the least compressed copy as the source.
- **No transparency**: a JPG cannot hold see-through pixels, so the AVIF will not have any either. Transparent pixels do not survive saving as JPEG in the first place.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPG is one flat picture, so keep the layered project file.
- **An older device rejects the file**: some older photo frames refuse progressive JPG, and saving it again without progressive mode gets around that.
- **Quality numbers disagree**: equal numbers in different editors give unequal results, so compare by eye.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the JPG could not be opened by your browser's decoder. Download the JPG again and retry.
