guide.title: About JPG and BMP
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

JPEG takes its name from the committee that wrote it, the Joint Photographic Experts Group, whose work started in 1986. ITU-T T.81 (1992) and ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994) are the two publications of the core standard. The .jpg and .jpeg extensions name the same format, and its registered media type is image/jpeg. No alpha channel exists in JPEG, and each color channel gets 8 bits, so layers and transparency can't be stored.

Baseline JPEG is lossy. JPEG compression first cuts the picture into 8x8 pixel blocks; a discrete cosine transform follows, then Huffman coding. A progressive mode shows a coarse version of the image first, which sharpens as more data loads. Quality is commonly a number between 0 and 100, but one program's value does not match another's in output. Digital cameras and scanners mostly have JPEG built in, every major browser displays it, and 27 October 2006 was the expiry date of its US patents. The wrapper called JFIF, the JPEG File Interchange Format, is minimal and exists to exchange JPEG data between programs and platforms.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Linux, Mac and Windows:** GIMP takes JPEG files in for editing.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** JPG is among the formats ImageMagick reads, and your install's format list confirms it.
- **Windows:** Windows Paint and Windows Photos open JPG.
- **Mac:** Preview opens JPG.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox open a JPG directly.
- **Mobile:** On phones and tablets, Safari and Chrome both display JPG.

### JPG and BMP compared

- **Extensions and media types**: image/jpeg uses .jpg or .jpeg. The registered BMP media type is image/bmp.
- **Compression**: JPG is lossy. BMP usually holds uncompressed pixels; lossless compression is possible, including optional run-length compression.
- **Size**: expect a big file from an uncompressed BMP; PNG or JPEG can suit distribution better.
- **Color depth**: BMP stores 1 to 32 bits per pixel. A JPG decoded here becomes 8 bits per channel.
- **Transparency**: JPG has none. Windows 98 brought BMP version 5 in 1998, with room for an alpha channel and an ICC profile.
- **Where you meet them**: JPG comes from cameras and websites. BMP is commonly encountered in Windows screen captures and system graphics.
- **Origin**: Microsoft controls the BMP family, used originally on Windows and OS/2.

On this page your browser decodes the JPG and ImageMagick writes the BMP. Conversion runs through 8-bit RGBA, so the JPG's EXIF, ICC and XMP data does not come along. The BMP is a copy of the decoded pixels, and none of the detail the JPG discarded comes back.

### Other ways to convert JPG to BMP

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.jpg output.bmp`. ImageMagick's format list shows BMP as a format it reads and writes, with version 4 as the default, and names BMP3 and BMP2 for versions 3 and 2.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the JPG and choose File > Export As. Give the file name a .bmp extension in the Name field, or select BMP under Select File Type, and export. The BMP dialog has a Write color space information checkbox, which some programs can't read, and an RGB format list such as 24 bit (R8 G8 B8).
- **Pillow (Python):** Pillow reads and writes BMP. Load the JPG using `Image.open`, then `save` to a name ending in .bmp; with no format given, Pillow reads it from the ending.

Whichever route you choose, the BMP holds the decoded picture, so convert from the largest, least compressed JPG you have if quality matters.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Transparent areas vanish**: transparent pixels can't survive JPEG export, so choose a format with alpha when you need see-through pixels.
- **An older photo frame refuses the file**: some older frames reject progressive JPEG. Export again with progressive mode off.
- **The same quality number looks different**: matching quality numbers across editors don't guarantee matching compression or appearance.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPEG can't store an editable layer stack, so save the project file separately.
- **The picture looks blocky**: a low-quality JPG shows blocky patches around edges and in flat areas, and every program that decodes the file shows them.
- **Colors can't go deeper**: JPEG holds 8 bits per channel, so a program that needs more depth has to start from a different source.

### What is a JPG file?

The committee behind JPEG, the Joint Photographic Experts Group, began its work in 1986, and the standard came out twice: T.81 from the ITU in 1992, then ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994. Baseline JPEG is lossy: it divides the image into 8x8 pixel tiles, applies a DCT to every tile and finishes with Huffman coding. A JPG has 8 bits per color channel, no alpha channel and no layers. The .jpg and .jpeg extensions are interchangeable names for it, and image/jpeg is its media type.

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports JPEG for editing, and ImageMagick reads JPG.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome shows JPG.
- **Web:** Firefox shows JPG.
- **Mobile:** Safari shows it as well.

Windows Photos and Preview on macOS also open it.

### JPG and CUR compared

- **Purpose**: JPG stores photographs. CUR is the Windows cursor format, related to ICO but with coordinates for the active pointer location.
- **Hotspot**: the pixel that does the clicking is called the hotspot. One CUR can hold images at several dimensions, each with hotspot information of its own.
- **Transparency**: CUR supports alpha. JPG does not, so the converted image is opaque.
- **Compression**: JPG is lossy, so the picture's quality is already settled before it becomes a cursor image.

The browser decodes the JPG first, and then ImageMagick writes the CUR with a single image in it. A larger JPG is scaled down, with its proportions intact, until both sides are 256 px or less. The page has no hotspot setting.

### Other ways to convert JPG to CUR

- **Transparency is lost**: a JPEG export cannot keep transparent pixels, so a pointer with a shaped outline needs a format that has alpha.
- **Progressive JPEG**: some older photo frames reject it, so try an export with progressive mode turned off.
- **Quality numbers**: editors scale quality differently, so equal numbers can compress differently.
- **Layers**: no layer stack survives inside a JPG, so keep your project file.

guide.title: About JPG and DDS files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

JPEG, the lossy picture format spelled JPG or JPEG, grew out of a 1986 start by the Joint Photographic Experts Group, and it was standardized as ITU-T T.81 in 1992 and ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994. Baseline coding divides a picture into 8x8 blocks, applies a discrete cosine transform and uses Huffman coding on the result.

Digital cameras and scanners build JPG in, and every major browser shows it. It keeps 8 bits per color channel but no transparency or layers, and both .jpg and .jpeg are the same format. A progressive mode displays a coarse version of the picture first and sharpens it as more data loads. The quality scale runs 0 to 100, and GIMP starts at 85. The compression marks of a JPG remain after any conversion.

### Programs that open JPG files

**Windows**

- ImageMagick: can read a JPG.

**Mac**

- GIMP: imports JPEG into an editor.

**Web**

- Google Chrome: displays JPG pictures in browser content.

**Mobile**

- Safari: displays JPG pictures.

### JPG and DDS compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .jpg and image/jpeg; .dds is Microsoft's DirectDraw Surface texture format.
- **Compression**: a JPG is always lossy. A DDS can hold uncompressed pixels or compressed texture data.
- **Mipmaps**: a DDS can include a mipmap chain beside its largest surface. A JPG is a single picture.
- **Other surfaces**: DDS can hold cube maps and volume textures, and Direct3D 10 and 11 add texture arrays through an extra header.
- **Transparency**: a JPG has no alpha channel. A DDS pixel format can carry an alpha mask.
- **Headers**: the DX10 extension is rejected by some DDS readers, while legacy RGB and DXT1 to DXT5 headers work with more tools.
- **Pixel formats**: formats that the original header structure cannot express can be described by the DX10 header.
- **Pitch**: incorrect pitch information can corrupt how a reader interprets scan lines.
- **Validity**: an ordinary DDS needs at least 128 bytes of header, or 148 with the DX10 extension, so a cut-off file is invalid.
- **Metadata**: a JPG may carry EXIF, ICC and XMP, which the page drops.

What changes in this conversion is the container. The browser decodes the JPG to 8-bit pixels, and ImageMagick writes them out as a DDS with its default settings. The page does not choose a compression format, build mipmaps or resize. A DDS can hold either uncompressed pixels or compressed texture data, so two valid DDS files from the same picture can differ widely in size and in how an engine reads them.

That is fine for a quick test or for a tool that reads a plain DDS and does the rest itself. It is not enough when a game or engine documents exact requirements. For those, texconv and GIMP let you set the format and mipmaps. Test one converted file in your engine before you convert a whole set.

Select several JPG files and the page processes them one after another, with each result downloaded as its own DDS and no ZIP.

### Other ways to convert JPG to DDS

- **texconv (DirectXTex):** Microsoft's example is `texconv -pow2 -f BC1_UNORM cat.jpg`. It fits the texture to power-of-two sizes through -pow2, and by default it generates all mipmaps; add `-m 1` to remove them. The default output type is DDS.
- **GIMP:** load the JPG, pick File > Export As, choose DDS, then set Compression and Mipmaps in the export dialog. The DDS exporter is built into GIMP from 2.10.10 on.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.jpg output.dds`. ImageMagick's formats page lists DDS as readable and writable, with compression defines such as dxt1 and dxt5 and mipmaps; check the result against your engine.

### Problems with JPG files

- **No transparency to use**: a JPG stores no alpha, so create the alpha channel in an editor before you export a texture.
- **Progressive files trip some viewers**: some old photo frames cannot show progressive JPEG, so turn progressive mode off when you export.
- **Quality settings are not comparable**: editors that share a quality number can still differ in compression and appearance.
- **Layers are not stored**: a JPG keeps no editable layer stack, so keep your layered project file.
- **Soft or blocky color edges**: JPG compression damaged them before the conversion, and a bigger or cleaner source helps.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

JPG takes its name from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, and most photographs from cameras and scanners are saved in it. The group began in 1986, and the standard is ITU-T T.81 (1992). The format is lossy: pixels are grouped in 8x8 tiles, a discrete cosine transform converts each tile, and Huffman coding packs the output.

All the major browsers show a JPG, and .jpg and .jpeg are interchangeable names, served as image/jpeg. A JPG has no transparency and cannot store layers, which matters when you place it on a colored page. A progressive JPG first draws a coarse version and sharpens it while the file loads. JPG suits web photos, camera output, mailed attachments and photo-sharing sites, and US patent protection ended in October 2006.

Editors often use a 0 to 100 scale, GIMP's default is 85, and equal numbers do not give equal quality in every program. This page has no quality setting, because the original JPG goes into the document untouched.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports a JPG for tidying a picture before it goes into a document, and ImageMagick reads JPG without a window, from the command line.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox show a JPG when you open it in a tab.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome display JPG on a phone.

### JPG and DOCX compared

- **What they are**: a JPG is one picture. A DOCX is a document, so it can hold styles, images and tables.
- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg (image/jpeg) for the picture; .docx for the Word file.
- **Structure**: a DOCX is a ZIP package of XML files built on the Open Packaging Conventions. Its text and formatting are described in WordprocessingML, and images, styles and properties sit in separate parts of the package.
- **Standards**: the format is standardized twice, as ECMA-376 and as ISO/IEC 29500, and Word made it the default for new files with the 2007 release. LibreOffice Writer, ONLYOFFICE Desktop Editors, Apple Pages, Word for the web and Word for Android are listed as opening it, and some formatting attributes may differ between programs.
- **Package**: because a DOCX is a package of related parts, extracting only document.xml does not reproduce the full document.
- **Compression**: the JPG stays lossy, as it was. Placing it in a DOCX does not recompress it, because the page never decodes it first.
- **Editing**: a DOCX supports tracked changes and comments around the picture, which a bare JPG cannot hold.
- **Transparency**: a JPG has none, so the picture shows as a rectangle on the page.

The page builds the document with the docx library in your browser: one paragraph that holds the picture. The JPG's bytes are put into the package unchanged. A picture wider than 6.5 inches or taller than 9 inches is scaled down, keeping its proportions, and a smaller one keeps its size, measured at 96 pixels per inch. No text is read from the picture.

### Other ways to convert JPG to DOCX

- **Microsoft Word (Windows, Mac):** use Insert > Pictures > This Device, select the JPG, click Insert and save the file.
- **LibreOffice Writer (Windows, Mac, Linux):** choose Insert > Image, select the JPG with the Link box unmarked, then File > Save As and pick a Microsoft Word format in the File type box. LibreOffice opens and saves Word DOCX files.

### Problems with JPG files

- **A solid rectangle shows around the picture**: a JPG cannot be see-through, so it always shows as a solid rectangle. Use a format with alpha when the document needs transparency.
- **The text in the picture cannot be selected**: it is part of the image. Run OCR with the JPG to TXT converter to get the words.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPG never had any, so go back to the layered project file if you need them.
- **Blocky squares around text**: heavy compression leaves 8x8 block edges, and the DOCX carries the JPG unchanged, so start from the least compressed copy.
- **Quality numbers disagree**: a 0 to 100 setting is not a shared unit, so two editors can save the same picture at different sizes.
- **Another app changes the layout**: a different word processor can alter some formatting when it opens the DOCX.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG (or JPEG) is a photograph format named for the Joint Photographic Experts Group. The core standard appeared as ITU-T T.81 in 1992, with ISO/IEC 10918-1 following in 1994. Baseline JPEG is lossy: the image is split into 8x8 pixel blocks, put through a discrete cosine transform, then Huffman coded. A typical setting leaves between a tenth and a twentieth of the uncompressed size.

JPEG gives each channel 8 bits, offers no alpha channel and can't store layers. The US patents ended on 27 October 2006. Cameras and scanners write JPEG, which makes it the usual format for photos on the web, in email and in photo sharing. The .jpg and .jpeg endings name the same format, whose media type is image/jpeg. A progressive JPEG paints a rough picture first and refines it as the rest arrives.

### Programs that open JPG files

**Windows / Mac / Linux**

- GIMP: loads JPEG for editing.
- ImageMagick: a command-line reader of JPG files.

**Windows**

- Microsoft's Windows Photos opens JPG.

**Mac**

- Preview opens JPG.

**Web and mobile**

- Firefox and Chrome open a JPG on a computer; Safari and Chrome handle it on a phone.

### JPG and GIF compared

- **Extensions and media types**: JPG is .jpg or .jpeg with image/jpeg, and GIF is .gif with image/gif.
- **Compression**: baseline JPEG is lossy, while GIF uses lossless LZW coding. Unisys charged LZW license fees from 1994, and its patents expired in 2003 and 2004.
- **Colors**: JPEG keeps 8 bits per channel. A GIF image draws from a palette limited to 256 colors.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has none. A GIF may flag one palette color as fully transparent and offers nothing partial.
- **Animation**: a GIF can hold many images and times each frame in hundredths of a second. A JPG is one still picture.
- **Origin**: CompuServe introduced GIF in 1987. GIF89a, the revision of July 1990, brought transparency, per-frame timing, comments and application data.
- **Metadata**: the GIF made here carries none of the JPG's data.
- **Browsers**: Firefox and Chrome display both formats on a computer, and Safari and Chrome display both on a phone.
- **Stills**: a JPG records one picture, so the GIF made from it has a single frame and no timing to set.
- **Layers**: neither format stores layers, so the GIF made here is one flat picture.

What this conversion does is trade color for compatibility with GIF. Your browser decodes the JPG, and the page writes a single-frame GIF with the colors reduced to fit a 256-color palette. Nothing moves, and no transparency appears. Every JPG is converted in turn on its own, and the GIF keeps the JPG's name with a .gif ending. The GIF is a good fit for a flat graphic, a screenshot or a small icon-like picture, and a poor fit for a portrait or a landscape photo.

### Other ways to convert JPG to GIF

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the JPG, choose Export As under File, name it with a .gif ending and click Export. GIMP reduces the image to a palette of 256 colors or fewer, and a multi-layer image can be exported as an animation. GIMP drops a GIF comment that has non-ASCII characters, and its GIF dialog advises converting the image to indexed mode first, since partial transparency cannot be kept.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick portrait.jpg portrait.gif`. ImageMagick reads and writes both JPEG and GIF, with a GIF palette of up to 256 colors, and quantizing to a palette can change the colors of a photograph.

### Problems with JPG files

- **The picture loads in stages**: a progressive JPG shows a rough picture while it downloads. That is a storage mode, and the GIF made here is a single still frame.
- **Transparency is missing**: a JPEG can't hold transparent pixels. If you need them, pick a format with alpha, such as PNG.
- **An old photo frame refuses the file**: progressive JPEG trips up some older frames. Export once more with progressive mode off.
- **Quality numbers don't match**: JPEG quality normally runs from 0 to 100, and an identical number may give different quality in different programs, so judge results by eye.
- **You need the layers**: JPG does not preserve an editable layer stack. Keep the project file.

guide.title: About JPG and HDR
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG file is a photograph saved with lossy compression. The format was defined by the Joint Photographic Experts Group as ISO/IEC 10918-1 and was designed for photographs. The .jpg and .jpeg extensions are the same format.

You meet JPG files as digital camera output, as photos on the web, and as email attachments and shared pictures. The format has no alpha transparency.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports JPEG for editing. ImageMagick reads JPG.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos opens JPG.
- **Mac:** Preview opens JPG.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome shows JPG.
- **Web:** Mozilla Firefox shows JPG.
- **Mobile:** Safari shows JPG.

### JPG and HDR compared

- **Extensions**: a JPG uses .jpg or .jpeg. Radiance HDR uses .hdr or .pic.
- **Pixels**: Radiance HDR stores a red, green and blue byte plus a shared exponent for each pixel, four bytes in all. Compared with ordinary 24-bit RGB, that leaves room for much brighter values.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy. Radiance HDR uses run-length encoding.
- **Media type**: the registered type for Radiance HDR is image/vnd.radiance.
- **Metadata**: EXIF, ICC profile and XMP from the JPG are dropped.

Greg Ward created RGBE for the Radiance lighting simulation system, where it stores calculated brightness. It is relevant when a renderer or lighting tool asks for an .hdr image. The converter hands it the 8-bit pixels of your JPG, so the extra range of the format goes unused.

### Other ways to convert JPG to HDR

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick ordinary_photo.jpg radiance_copy.hdr`. ImageMagick lists HDR, the Radiance RGBE image format, as readable and writable.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** from File > Export As, end the name in .hdr or choose Radiance RGBE as the file type. Confirm the name and the export starts, with no options dialog.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Highlight detail is gone**: a JPG that lost its bright detail can't get it back from a format change. Go back to the original capture if you need that range.
- **Transparency is missing**: JPEG can't hold transparent pixels, so choose a format with alpha instead.
- **A photo frame won't show the file**: older frames can refuse progressive JPEG. Turn progressive mode off and export again.
- **Quality numbers don't match between editors**: a matching number is no promise of matching compression or looks.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPG doesn't keep an editable layer stack, so keep the project file.

guide.title: About ICO files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

Photographs from cameras, phones and scanners almost always end up as JPG, the extension for the picture format that the Joint Photographic Experts Group began designing in 1986. Its US patents lapsed on 27 October 2006, one reason it spread so widely. The compression is lossy, and a progressive JPG shows a rough picture first and sharpens it while the remainder downloads. JPG cannot store layers, and it has no alpha channel for transparency. Editors score quality from 0 to 100, with GIMP starting at 85, though one program's number does not match another's. The registered media type is image/jpeg.

Logos and avatars travel the same way, which is where this conversion starts: you hold a JPG of the artwork, and a browser tab or a Windows program wants an icon instead.

### Programs that open JPG files

**Mac**

- Preview: opens JPG files.

**Web**

- Any web browser: displays a JPG with no extra software.

**Windows**

- Windows Photos: shows JPG pictures.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: opens and edits JPG files.

### JPG and ICO compared

- **Names and media types**: JPEG goes by .jpg or .jpeg and image/jpeg. ICO goes by .ico and image/vnd.microsoft.icon.
- **Compression**: baseline JPEG is lossy and splits the picture into 8x8 pixel blocks. An ICO entry holds a bitmap or a PNG, which don't lose detail the way JPEG does.
- **Images per file**: a JPG holds one picture. An ICO can hold several.
- **Layers**: JPEG cannot store layers, so the picture you hand over is already one set of pixels. An ICO entry is one bitmap or PNG as well.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has none, since it stores 8 bits per channel and no alpha. ICO images can have it.
- **Typical use**: photographs for JPG, interface icons and favicons for ICO.
- **Reach**: every major browser displays JPEG. ICO is the icon format on Windows and a favicon format in browsers.

ICO is Microsoft's image format for the icons in a graphical interface. A single file may contain the same icon at several sizes, and its numbers are stored in little-endian byte order. Windows Vista's icon guidance added a 256-by-256 image for high-DPI displays, and an ICO can store that image as PNG data. You meet ICO as the icon of a Windows program and as a website's favicon.

What this page does: it decodes the JPG, fits it inside 256 x 256 if it is larger, and has ImageMagick write one image into an ICO. A smaller picture keeps its size. The result is a plain, single-size icon, with no transparency added and no metadata.

### Other ways to convert JPG to ICO

- **GIMP (image editor):** open the JPG, then File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E) lets you write an ICO with GIMP's ICO plug-in. Get the artwork and its size right before you export.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.jpg -resize 256x256 output.ico`. The resize fits the picture inside 256 x 256, and it enlarges a smaller picture to fill that box.
- **FFmpeg (command line):** run `ffmpeg -i input.jpg -s 256x256 -frames:v 1 -c:v png -pix_fmt rgba output.ico`. The size is set outright, so a rectangular JPG is stretched into a square. FFmpeg's ICO writer wants PNG images in RGBA with no side over 256 px.

### Problems with JPG files

- **A JPG can't be transparent**: a logo saved as JPG has a solid background, and the icon built from it keeps that background.
- **Blocky edges around text and lines**: the lossy compression shows on sharp logo edges and thin lettering. Start from the largest, least compressed copy you have.
- **Quality numbers don't match**: two programs saving at "85" can produce different results.
- **No layers**: a JPG keeps no editable stack of layers, so go back to the project file if the artwork needs fixing before it becomes an icon.
- **An old photo frame or player refuses it**: some older ones reject progressive JPG. Re-save without progressive mode, then convert.
- **The picture isn't square**: a wide photo produces a wide icon, because the converter keeps the JPG's proportions when it shrinks it to 256 px. Crop first.
- **The icon looks soft on a high-DPI screen**: a small icon enlarged for such a display may look soft. Begin with a big JPG rather than a thumbnail.

- **Windows, Linux and Mac:** GIMP imports JPEG for editing, while ImageMagick can read JPG.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome is a JPG viewer on both web and mobile; Firefox covers the web and Safari covers mobile.

### JPG and JFIF compared

JFIF (JPEG File Interchange Format) is a minimal wrapper that lets JPEG data move between programs and platforms, and it pins down the color space and pixel aspect ratio. JFIF began with C-Cube Microsystems' Eric Hamilton; version 1.02 is from 1992, and it was approved as ITU-T T.871 in May 2011. A JFIF file begins with the JPEG start-of-image marker and then an APP0 segment labeled JFIF. Most files people call JPEGs are JFIF files, so anything that opens a regular JPEG reads one.

The extensions .jpg, .jpeg, .jpe, .jfi, .jfif and .jif are all allowed for JFIF files, sharing the media type image/jpeg. Some browsers and Windows tools save pictures under the .jfif name.

Your browser decodes the JPG into 8-bit pixels and saves a new JPEG named .jfif, at quality 0.85. This is a second lossy pass, and camera tags, XMP and the color profile are not kept.

### Other ways to convert JPG to JFIF

- **Pillow:** call `Image.open("input.jpg").save("output.jfif", format="JPEG")`. Pillow writes standard and progressive JFIF files.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick input.jpg output.jfif`. Its JPEG format, listed as read and write, is described as the JFIF format.
- **libjpeg-turbo:** run `djpeg -outfile pixels.ppm input.jpg`, then `cjpeg -outfile output.jfif pixels.ppm`.

### Problems with JPG files

- Progressive JPEG is refused by some older photo frames, so export without it for such a target.
- Editors do not map one quality number to the same compression or appearance.
- Transparency cannot survive JPEG export; pick a format with alpha instead.
- Any editable layer stack is gone in a JPEG, so retain the project file.

guide.title: About JPG and JPEG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG file is a photograph or other picture saved in the JPEG format. The name honors the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which wrote the standard for JPG files. Work began in 1986. ITU-T T.81 published the core standard in 1992, and ISO/IEC 10918-1 followed in 1994. US patents on JPEG lapsed on 27 October 2006, and all major browsers show it. The registered media type is image/jpeg.

Baseline JPEG is lossy. Pixels are grouped into 8x8 blocks, put through a discrete cosine transform and Huffman coded. Each color channel gets 8 bits in JPEG, and without an alpha channel transparency is impossible. A progressive mode shows a rough picture first, which sharpens while the rest of the data arrives. Most digital cameras and scanners write JPG files.

Both .jpg and .jpeg refer to one and the same format, and JPEG cannot store layers. So the question behind this page is rarely about the picture. It is about a name: an upload form, a script or a folder rule that wants one ending and gets the other.

### Programs that open JPG files

**Windows**

- Windows Photos: named in the format reference.

**Mac**

- Preview: opens JPG files.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: lets you edit JPEG.
- ImageMagick: reads JPG; check the installed format support.

**Web and Mobile**

- Google Chrome shows JPG.

**Web**

- Mozilla Firefox shows JPG.

**Mobile**

- Safari displays JPG.

### JPG and JPEG compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg and .jpeg, with the same media type, image/jpeg.
- **Format**: identical. Both are JPEG, so there is no difference in compression, color depth, transparency or metadata between a file called .jpg and one called .jpeg.
- **Quality**: usually 0 to 100; GIMP defaults to 85, and identical numbers do not guarantee identical quality across programs.
- **Color depth**: 8 bits per color channel in both.
- **Modes**: baseline, which loads top to bottom, and progressive, which paints a coarse version first and refines it as data arrives. Both endings can hold either.
- **Transparency**: neither has an alpha channel.
- **Download name**: this page names the result after your file, with .jpeg in place of .jpg.

A rename is therefore the exact answer to "how do I make my JPG a JPEG", and this page is a second route to the same name. This page does not rename your file. It decodes the JPG to pixels and writes a JPEG again at quality 0.85, which is a second lossy pass. EXIF, ICC and XMP metadata does not carry over to the new file.

### Other ways to convert JPG to JPEG

- **Rename the file:** because the two names are the same format, changing .jpg to .jpeg in your file manager does the whole job and leaves the picture untouched.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** with the JPG loaded, choose File > Export As, set the type to JPEG in the file-type list and press Export. A settings dialog follows, and GIMP accepts both .jpg and .jpeg as the extension.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.jpg output.jpeg`. This writes the picture again, like this page does.

### Problems with JPG files

- **A form rejects .jpg**: a form may check the ending as text and accept only one spelling. A .jpeg ending satisfies a check for that spelling.
- **Transparent pixels cannot survive JPEG export**: choose a format with alpha, such as PNG, if you need see-through areas.
- **An older photo frame rejects the file**: some older frames do not read progressive files. Save it again with progressive mode off.
- **The picture looks softer after repeated saves**: each lossy save compounds the loss. Make copies from the original, not from a copy of a copy.
- **Quality numbers disagree between programs**: one editor's 85 is not another's, so the same number can give different file sizes and looks.
- **Layers are gone**: a JPEG stores no layers, so keep your project file.
- **Many files to fix**: choose a batch and the page works through it, saving each result as its own file.
- **A folder has both endings**: a program or script that matches only *.jpg will skip the .jpeg files, and the reverse. Pick one ending and rename or convert the rest to match.
- **You want to keep EXIF data**: this page drops it. Rename the file instead, or use a desktop program that copies metadata, because renaming leaves every byte of the picture in place.

guide.title: Understanding JPG and JPG
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

JPG, also written JPEG, is the photo format of the web and of nearly every camera. The Joint Photographic Experts Group published the standard as ISO/IEC 10918-1. JPG compresses with loss: the encoder discards fine detail, and the quality setting decides how much goes. The format has no alpha transparency. .jpg and .jpeg are the same format.

You meet JPGs everywhere: camera output, email attachments, photo sharing, product pictures. Because the format is lossy, every new save adds another generation of loss, which makes it a poor choice for a master that you edit again and again. Keep your original and treat the converted file as a delivery copy.

Why would anyone convert a JPG to a JPG? Because a re-save does something a copy does not. Here the browser decodes the photo and writes a fresh JPG at quality 0.85, and the EXIF data, XMP and ICC profile are left behind. People use it to strip location data before posting a photo, or to get a clean file after an upload form rejected the original. The work happens in your browser with its own image decoder, so the photo is not sent to a server, and your original file is left as it was. It will not fix a photo that was already damaged, and it cannot bring back detail that an earlier save discarded.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows:** the Photos app opens JPG files for viewing.
- **Mac:** Preview on macOS opens JPG files for viewing.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP is an editor that opens JPEG files so you can change them, and ImageMagick can read them in a terminal.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox both display JPG.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome show it too.

### JPG and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: both sides use .jpg or .jpeg and image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: both are lossy. The new file is encoded from decoded pixels, not copied from the old stream.
- **Quality**: this page always writes quality 0.85. Quality numbers don't match across programs, so GIMP's 85 and ImageMagick's 85 can look different.
- **Transparency**: neither has any.
- **Color depth**: pixels pass through 8 bits per channel.
- **Metadata**: the original may carry Exif, XMP and a color profile; the new file carries none of them.

The only things that change are the encoded data and the metadata, and a rename would change nothing at all. Choose a handful of photos at once and each photo is processed in sequence, handing back a separate JPG for each rather than a zip. A moving input contributes just its opening frame, since a JPG holds a single picture.

Two of those differences matter most in practice. First, generation loss: a JPG is lossy, so decoding it and encoding it again at 0.85 compresses the picture a second time. The result looks close to the original, but it is never better, and repeated passes add up. Second, the metadata. A camera writes the date, the lens, the orientation and often the GPS position into the file as Exif. The new JPG has none of that, which is the reason many people run the conversion.

### Other ways to convert JPG to JPG

- **GIMP:** on Windows, Mac or Linux, once the photo is open, choose File > Export As, type a new .jpg name and export. In the JPEG dialog you choose a quality between 0 and 100 and pick which Exif, XMP or IPTC metadata is kept.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick camera.jpg -quality 85 fresh.jpg`. This re-encodes with ImageMagick's own quality scale, and unlike this page it lets you choose the number.

### Problems with JPG files

- **The new file is bigger**: an original saved at a lower setting can grow. Converting again won't shrink it; use the [JPG Compressor](/compress-jpg/) instead.
- **Text and edges look blotchy**: compression artifacts from an earlier save are now baked in. Go back to the earliest copy you have.
- **A photo frame or device rejects it**: some older photo frames reject progressive JPEG. Export with progressive mode disabled.
- **Transparent pixels are gone**: JPEG can't hold them. Save as PNG when you need transparency.
- **Layers are gone**: JPEG keeps no layer stack, so keep the project file.

guide.title: About JPG and JPEG XL files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

JPG, or JPEG, is the lossy photo format from the Joint Photographic Experts Group; work started in 1986, and its US patents lapsed on 27 October 2006. The baseline method, covered by ITU-T T.81 (1992) and ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994), cuts the image into 8x8 pixel blocks and applies a discrete cosine transform and Huffman coding to each. A typical setting leaves 1/10 to 1/20 of the uncompressed size. Each channel holds 8 bits, there is no alpha, and .jpg and .jpeg mean the same thing. Cameras and scanners write it widely, and its media type is image/jpeg.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Mac, Windows and Linux:** GIMP can import JPEG for editing, and ImageMagick opens JPG.
- **Mobile and Web:** Chrome displays JPG on web and mobile, Safari does so on mobile, and Firefox on the web.

### JPG and JXL compared

JPEG XL comes from the JPEG committee as ISO/IEC 18181. It handles lossy and lossless coding, alpha channels, animation and progressive decoding, along with high bit depth, wide color gamuts and HDR. Existing JPEG files can be recompressed by it without any loss. A .jxl file is either a bare codestream or a box-based container, and its media type is image/jxl.

This page does not recompress losslessly. Your browser decodes the JPG to 8-bit RGBA pixels and ImageMagick encodes them as a lossy JXL with default settings. Pixel values change, and there is no quality control. Metadata is dropped.

### Other ways to convert JPG to JXL

- **cjxl:** run `cjxl input.jpg output.jxl`; by default it recompresses the JPEG losslessly.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick input.jpg converted.jxl`, which needs the JPEG XL delegate library.
- **GIMP:** open the JPG, pick File > Export As, and save the result as a JPEG XL file. GIMP 2.10.34 added export, limited to 8-bit lossless.

### Problems with JPG files

- JPEG offers no alpha channel, so transparent pixels cannot survive an export to it.
- An editable layer stack is not preserved in JPEG, so hold on to the project file.
- Older photo frames may reject progressive JPEG; turn progressive mode off when you export for one.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

Most photos you handle are JPGs. A committee of photography and imaging experts began work on the format in 1986, ITU-T published it as T.81 in 1992, and ISO followed with part 1 of 10918 in 1994. The compression is lossy and works on blocks of 8x8 pixels, which is why a JPG is far smaller than the raw pixels.

Each color channel gets 8 bits, and there is neither transparency nor a layer stack. The .jpg and .jpeg endings are interchangeable, and most cameras and scanners produce the format. Its media type is image/jpeg.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens a JPEG for retouching, while ImageMagick handles it from the command line.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome displays JPG.
- **Web:** Firefox displays JPG.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays JPG.

### JPG and PBM compared

PBM is the Portable Bit Map of the Netpbm family, a two-tone format that Netpbm uses as an intermediate between programs. A raw PBM begins with P4 and packs its pixels as bits, while the plain variant begins with P1 and spells them as zeros and ones. A one bit means black. The conventional media type is image/x-portable-bitmap, which IANA has not registered.

On this page the browser decodes the JPG and ImageMagick, compiled to WebAssembly, writes the PBM, so every pixel ends up black or white. Open the PBM beside the JPG before you use it, to see what the black-and-white conversion kept.

### Other ways to convert JPG to PBM

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick scan.jpg -colorspace Gray -threshold 50% scan.pbm` to choose the cutoff yourself, and raise or lower the percentage for your scan.
- **GIMP:** with the JPG open, use File > Export As, call the file scan.pbm, and choose ASCII or RAW under Data formatting. The export is black and white, not continuous grayscale.
- **Netpbm:** run `jpegtopnm scan.jpg | ppmtopgm | pamthreshold -simple -threshold=0.5 | pamtopnm > scan.pbm`. The pamthreshold step writes a PAM file, so pamtopnm turns it into the PBM.

### Problems with JPG files

- **No transparency**: a logo that needs a clear background must start from a different format, because a JPG has none.
- **Quality numbers differ**: an 85 in one editor is not an 85 in another, so re-saving the JPG in a different program can change its look.
- **Layers do not survive**: editable layers cannot live in a JPG, so save the project in its own format.

guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

The JPG is a lossy picture file built for photographs, and nearly every camera, phone and scanner can make one. Each color channel takes 8 bits, layers are impossible, and US patent protection lapsed in October 2006. A progressive JPEG shows a coarse picture first and refines it as loading continues.

When you convert a JPG to something older, the lossy damage stays in the pixels: soft blocks and ringing travel along into the new file.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP can import a JPEG and edit it; ImageMagick takes one as input for scripted batches.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome shows the picture.
- **Web:** Firefox shows the picture.
- **Mobile:** Safari shows the picture.

### JPG and PCX compared

ZSoft made PCX for its PC Paintbrush program on MS-DOS around 1984 and 1985. A PCX opens with a 128-byte header and compresses rows with run-length encoding, which pays off on flat colors and does little for photographs. Some variants add a palette at the end of the file.

This page decodes the JPG in your browser and lets ImageMagick, compiled to WebAssembly, write the PCX. A single image goes in and a single image comes out. Open the PCX in a viewer before sending it on, since older programs may not read every variant.

### Other ways to convert JPG to PCX

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick art.jpg art.pcx`. ImageMagick lists PCX as readable and writable.
- **GIMP:** load the JPG, then choose File > Export As and type art.pcx as the name. The export has no settings dialog.
- **Pillow:** in Python, run `Image.open("art.jpg").save("art.pcx")`. Pillow reads and writes PCX files holding 1, L, P or RGB data, and takes the format from the file ending.

### Problems with JPG files

- **An old frame will not show it**: older photo frames sometimes cannot display progressive JPEG, so export with progressive mode off.
- **Quality scales vary**: quality runs from 0 to 100 and GIMP starts at 85, yet one program's value yields another look than the same value elsewhere.
- **Transparency is lost**: transparent pixels cannot survive JPEG export, so choose another format when you need alpha.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

Most cameras and scanners save their pictures as JPG. Each color channel gets 8 bits, transparency is not available, and fine detail is discarded to keep files small. A file may end in .jpg or .jpeg, and its media type is image/jpeg.

Because the compression is lossy, a PGM made from a JPG cannot recover what the JPG already threw away. Pictures are compressed in blocks of 8x8 pixels, and whatever blockiness is present in the color file remains visible in gray.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPG, and GIMP brings one in for editing.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome displays JPG.
- **Web:** Firefox displays JPG.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays JPG.

### JPG and PGM compared

PGM stands for Portable Gray Map, a Netpbm format that stores only gray samples. A raw file starts with P5 and keeps samples in binary, while a plain file starts with P2 and writes them as decimal text. With a maximum value above 255, each raw sample takes two bytes. The conventional media type is image/x-portable-graymap, and IANA has not registered it. Some Netpbm tools reuse the format for opacity masks, reading the samples as opacity, not brightness.

On this page your browser first decodes the picture, then ImageMagick in WebAssembly produces the PGM.

### Other ways to convert JPG to PGM

- **Pillow:** in Python, `Image.open("photo.jpg").convert("L").save("photo.pgm")` applies the ITU-R 601-2 luma transform from the Pillow reference. Pillow reads and writes PGM.
- **Netpbm:** run `jpegtopnm photo.jpg | ppmtopgm > photo.pgm`. The ppmtopgm step weights red, green and blue as .299, .587 and .114.
- **GIMP:** load the JPG, then File > Export As with the name photo.pgm; ASCII or RAW is chosen under Data formatting.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Matching numbers, different results**: two editors set to the same quality may compress differently, so a re-saved copy may not look like the first.
- **A photo frame rejects the source**: some older frames refuse progressive JPEG, so save a copy with progressive mode disabled.
- **No editable layers**: layers are not stored in a JPG, so hold on to the project file you edited.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG is a JPEG image, the lossy photo format standardized by the Joint Photographic Experts Group in the early 1990s. A .jpg file and a .jpeg file hold the same format, and JPEG has no layers.

JPEG splits a picture into 8x8 pixel blocks, converts each block into frequencies with a discrete cosine transform, and then applies Huffman coding; the baseline mode is lossy. A quality number, usually 0 to 100, decides how much goes. GIMP starts at 85, and the same number gives different results in different programs. Because JPEG is lossy, saving an edited JPEG compresses it again. A progressive JPEG is stored in passes: a browser paints a rough version first and sharpens it as the remaining data comes in.

Digital cameras and scanners mostly write JPEG, and all the major browsers display it. A PNG is lossless, so saving the picture as PNG again and again adds no further loss.

PNG, the format you are saving to, began life as a GIF alternative free of patents. October 1996 brought W3C Recommendation status, a first for any format, and ISO followed with 15948 in 2004. Its compression is always lossless DEFLATE, a mix of LZ77 and Huffman coding, so it never discards pixels. The group behind JPEG, formed to write the photo format, began its work in 1986, and its patents ran out in 2006.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows:** Paint lists PNG among the formats it saves, so it can write a copy of a JPG as PNG.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Open a JPG in GIMP to edit it. ImageMagick reads JPG.
- **Mac:** Apple Preview opens a JPG and lists PNG as one of its export formats.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome shows JPG images.
- **Web:** Mozilla Firefox shows them too.
- **Mobile:** Safari opens JPG. An iPhone camera saves JPEG instead of HEIC when Settings > Camera > Formats is set to Most Compatible.

### JPG and PNG compared

- **File endings**: image/jpeg uses .jpg or .jpeg, and image/png uses .png.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy, with a discrete cosine transform and Huffman coding. PNG is lossless DEFLATE: every pixel comes back exactly as stored.
- **Color depth**: JPEG stores 8 bits per channel. PNG offers 1 to 16 bits for each sample, as grayscale, indexed or truecolor.
- **Transparency**: an alpha channel is optional in PNG and absent from JPEG.
- **Animation**: PNG can animate as APNG. JPEG is always a still.
- **Metadata**: the third edition of PNG lets Exif travel in an eXIf chunk, but this converter carries no metadata across.
- **Typical use**: photographs suit JPEG, which was designed for them, and a Mac saves its screenshots as PNG by default.

Converting changes the container, not the picture. The PNG stores the pixels the JPG decodes to: no lost detail returns, no blockiness goes away, and nothing becomes transparent.

### Other ways to convert JPG to PNG

- **Preview (Mac):** open the JPG, pick File > Export, then select PNG as the Format.
- **Finder (Mac):** Control-click the file, choose Quick Actions > Convert Image, then pick PNG and a size; on some macOS versions the command sits under Quick Actions > More.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac and Linux):** open the JPG, then use File > Export As to write a PNG.
- **Paint (Windows):** open the JPG and save a copy with PNG as the file type.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Blocky patches or halos around text**: those are compression artifacts, and a PNG keeps them. Start from the original photo or a higher-quality export.
- **You need a transparent background**: converting won't remove the background. Erase it in an editor, then save as PNG.
- **Quality drops after repeated edits**: each JPEG save compresses again. Convert once to PNG, edit the PNG, and export a JPG only at the end.
- **A JPG that used to be transparent**: transparent pixels can't survive JPEG export, so the PNG starts from the opaque picture.
- **Camera details have gone**: Exif data isn't carried into the PNG, so keep the original if you need it.
- **An "Image decode failed." message**: the browser could not make sense of the JPG's data. Download the file again, and keep the original in case it is the only good copy.

guide.title: Understanding JPG to PPM
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

Its name honors the Joint Photographic Experts Group, a committee that started in 1986. ITU-T T.81 (1992) holds the core specification, and ISO/IEC 10918-1 followed in 1994. Baseline JPEG is lossy. It transforms 8x8 pixel blocks with a discrete cosine transform, then packs the result with Huffman coding. Color channels get 8 bits each, and there is no alpha channel or layer support. Quality usually runs on a 0 to 100 scale, yet one number can mean different results in different programs. Both .jpg and .jpeg name this format. US patents on it lapsed in October 2006.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPG from the command line, and GIMP imports it for editing.
- **Web and Mobile:** Chrome displays JPG on both, Firefox on the web and Safari on phones.

### JPG and PPM compared

PPM is the color member of the Netpbm family. Each pixel carries red, green and blue samples, in a binary form that starts with P6 or a plain-text form that starts with P3. The maximum sample value can run from 1 to 65535, and PPM has no alpha channel. The media type image/x-portable-pixmap is conventional but not registered with IANA, and a raw PPM can hold a sequence of images with no separators.

The browser decodes your JPG and the page writes the pixels out with ImageMagick. Compression is gone, so the file balloons. Metadata is dropped, and quality lost to JPEG stays lost.

### Other ways to convert JPG to PPM

- **Netpbm:** `jpegtopnm photo.jpg > photo.ppm` handles color input. A grayscale JPG yields PGM, not PPM.
- **GIMP:** load the JPG, use File > Export As with a .ppm name, and select ASCII or raw data formatting.
- **ImageMagick:** `magick photo.jpg photo.ppm` converts by extension and writes color PPM.

### Problems with JPG files

JPEG export cannot keep transparent pixels, so for transparency use a format that has alpha. Some older photo frames reject progressive JPEG, and an export with progressive mode disabled fixes that. Equal quality values in two editors need not give equal compression or equal looks. Layers do not survive in a JPEG, so keep your project file for later edits.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

In JPEG, the J is for Joint, the first word of the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Its baseline mode is lossy by design: each 8x8 block of pixels gets a discrete cosine transform, and Huffman coding writes out the numbers. The group started in 1986, and its core text came out of ITU-T as T.81 in 1992; ISO and IEC took it up as 10918-1 two years after that. Cameras and scanners commonly write JPEG, and the US patents lapsed in October 2006. In progressive mode a rough picture appears first and gets sharper while more data arrives. Quality is normally a 0 to 100 slider, GIMP starts at 85, and the same figure can mean different quality in different programs.

JPEG cannot store layers, which is the main thing a designer wants to add back. The extensions .jpg and .jpeg are one and the same format, with image/jpeg as the media type. Photographs on the web, camera output, mail attachments and photo sharing all lean on it, and every major browser displays it.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports a JPG, which is handy for checking the source before you convert, and ImageMagick opens it in a terminal.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display a JPG you open in a tab.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome show a JPG on a phone.

### JPG and PSD compared

- **Purpose**: PSD is Adobe Photoshop's native document format. JPG is lossy and made for photographs.
- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg (image/jpeg); .psd (image/vnd.adobe.photoshop).
- **Layers**: JPG stores a single flat picture. A PSD keeps layers, masks, adjustment layers and text, in sections kept apart from the image resources.
- **Compression**: JPG is lossy. PSD pixel data can be raw or encoded with RLE or ZIP compression. The PSD written here holds the decoded pixels without JPEG compression, and can be much larger than the JPG.
- **Bit depth**: JPEG channels hold 8 bits. A PSD header supports one, eight, 16 or 32 bits, though the PSD written here uses 8.
- **Size limit**: PSD tops out at 30,000 pixels for each side; PSB lifts that.
- **Signature**: a PSD header begins with 8BPS.
- **Other readers**: programs besides Photoshop must interpret Photoshop-specific data structures, so a thumbnail appearing does not prove a program can edit every part of a file.
- **Transparency**: JPG has none.

First the browser decodes the JPG. Then ImageMagick, which runs in the page, encodes those pixels as a PSD. No layers are made from the picture's contents, and EXIF, ICC profiles and XMP stay behind.

A PSD is a container with several sections. Photoshop uses those sections to hold the pieces of a design, such as layers, masks, adjustments, text and color data, so it can be edited later. The format is proprietary to Adobe, and Adobe documents its header and sections publicly.

### Other ways to convert JPG to PSD

- **Photopea (web):** choose File > Open, load the JPG, then File > Save as PSD. Photopea treats PSD as its main document format.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick picture.jpg picture.psd`. According to its format table, ImageMagick can both read and write PSD.

### Problems with JPG files

- **No layers to edit**: a JPG never stored any. The project file you exported from is the only place they can still be.
- **A blocky or smudged photo**: compression artifacts in the JPG pass straight into the PSD. Look for a less compressed copy of the picture.
- **A transparent logo shows a white box**: JPEG cannot keep see-through pixels, so the box was in the JPG before you converted it.
- **An older photo frame shows nothing**: some reject progressive JPEG, and saving the picture again without it helps.
- **Quality numbers disagree**: the same 0 to 100 value can mean different things in different editors.
- **A very large picture**: a document larger than the PSD dimension limit needs PSB or another suitable format.
- **Going back to a flat image later**: flattening a PSD into a plain image discards its structure, so keep the PSD for editing.
- **A file named .psd that will not open**: a real PSD header begins with the signature 8BPS, so a file with another header is not a PSD whatever its name says.

guide.title: About JPG and RGB
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

JPG is the everyday name for JPEG, the format of the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Its specification appeared as ITU-T T.81 (1992), then as ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994). A JPG compresses a picture with a discrete cosine transform followed by Huffman coding, then adds a header that records its width and height. Every color channel gets 8 bits and nothing is kept for transparency. Both endings, .jpg and .jpeg, mean the same thing, and the registered media type is image/jpeg. Cameras and scanners write it by default.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** a JPG opens for editing in GIMP, and ImageMagick can read it.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display a JPG without extra software.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays a JPG on a phone.

### JPG and RGB compared

- **Header**: a JPG records its size and settings inside the file, whereas raw RGB records none.
- **Compression**: JPG is lossy, and raw samples are uncompressed.
- **Samples**: the raw output is red, green and blue values with no alpha, one byte each.
- **Name clash**: an .rgb ending may also mean an SGI image, which is laid out differently.

A raw RGB file is nothing but red, green and blue samples in a row. With no header, nothing in it tells a program the width, height or bit depth. The browser decodes the JPG and passes the pixels to ImageMagick, which writes them as raw samples. They pass through 8-bit RGBA first, so the metadata is left behind. You must tell any reader the width, height and format yourself.

### Other ways to convert JPG to RGB

- **ImageMagick:** `magick photo.jpg -depth 8 RGB:samples.rgb` writes raw red, green and blue samples. The `-depth` option sets the depth of raw formats such as RGB, whose depth the file does not record.
- **Pillow:** `from PIL import Image; pixels=Image.open('photo.jpg').convert('RGB'); open('samples.rgb','wb').write(pixels.tobytes())` saves the pixels as raw bytes. Pillow reads JPEG files, and `tobytes()` returns the unprocessed pixel data.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Blocky or smudged areas**: raw RGB shows the flaws exactly as decoded and can't repair them.
- **No transparency**: a JPG has no alpha channel, so the samples have nothing to hold.
- **Some old players stall**: progressive JPGs can be rejected by aging photo frames, and re-saving without progressive scans fixes it.
- **The quality scale varies**: one editor's quality value is not another's, so identical settings can give different files.

guide.title: Understanding JPG for TGA output
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

The Joint Photographic Experts Group gave JPG its name and started the work in 1986. The core standard was released as ITU-T Recommendation T.81 and as ISO/IEC 10918-1, dated 1992 and 1994 respectively. The endings .jpg and .jpeg name the same format, registered as image/jpeg.

Baseline JPEG is lossy. Pictures are split into 8x8 pixel blocks, transformed with a discrete cosine transform and entropy coded using Huffman tables, which typically cuts the size to between a tenth and a twentieth. JPEG keeps 8 bits per color channel and lacks an alpha channel, so there is no transparency or layer support. Digital cameras and scanners commonly produce JPEG, and each major browser shows it. The last US patents covering JPEG ran out on 27 October 2006.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports a JPEG for editing and exports at quality 85 by default.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPG at the command line.
- **Web:** Firefox and Chrome show JPG pictures in the browser.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome display JPG pictures.

You choose the quality when saving a JPG, normally from 0 to 100, and one number doesn't promise the same look in every program. Progressive JPEGs load as a blurry whole that sharpens as more of the data arrives.

### JPG and TGA compared

- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg for JPG, with the media type image/jpeg; .tga for Targa.
- **Compression**: JPG is lossy. TGA files may be run-length encoded, an optional step that saves space.
- **Transparency**: JPG has none. A 32-bit TGA adds an eight-bit alpha channel to RGB.
- **Color**: a 24-bit RGB TGA stores eight bits in each color component, the same depth as the 8 bits per color channel a JPG stores. TGA also supports indexed-color and grayscale images.
- **Quality setting**: JPG quality is a value, normally 0 to 100, that one program scales differently from another. This page passes no quality setting.
- **Related extensions**: ImageMagick groups ICB, VDA and VST with Truevision Targa, so you may see those endings on files of the same kind.
- **Where each is used**: JPG comes from cameras and scanners. Targa was built for Truevision video boards and survives in video editing and game development.

In this page the browser decodes the JPG, then ImageMagick writes the TGA. The picture passes through 8-bit RGBA and metadata isn't copied, so camera data is not in the TGA. The JPG's blocky artifacts stay too, because they are already in the pixels. Converting to TGA doesn't recompress with loss, and it won't bring back detail. Because a JPG lacks alpha, there is no transparency to carry over.

Choose TGA only when the receiving tool asks for it, since a photo stored this way can take more room. The page doesn't resize the picture or change its color depth beyond the 8 bits per channel it already has. It runs in your browser, and the download is a new file sharing the original's name, such as photo.tga. Pick several JPGs and they are processed in sequence; every TGA downloads separately, with no ZIP.

### Other ways to convert JPG to TGA

- **GIMP:** open the JPG, which GIMP imports as a new project, then use File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E) and select TGA. The Export Image as TarGA dialog has a Use RLE compression checkbox: checked, the image is compressed with Run-Length Encoding, and otherwise it is uncompressed. Its Origin choice of Bottom left or Top left sets how the image data is stored and has no visual effect.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick fabric-reference.jpg fabric-texture.tga`, which follows the `magick input output` pattern of ImageMagick's own examples. Its format table lists Truevision Targa as readable and writable.

### Problems with JPG files

- **No transparency after converting**: JPEG can't hold transparent pixels, so the TGA comes out opaque. Mask the picture in an editor that writes alpha and save it as TGA.
- **A photo frame won't show the JPG**: some older frames reject progressive JPEG, which loads a rough image first. Save the JPG again with progressive mode disabled.
- **Quality numbers don't match between programs**: the same number can mean different compression in different editors.
- **Layers can't be recovered**: a JPEG holds no editable layer stack, so keep the original project file.

guide.title: Understanding JPG to TIFF
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

Behind the JPEG name stands the Joint Photographic Experts Group, a standards committee that got going in 1986. Part 1 of the standard was released by the ITU in 1992 (T.81) and by ISO/IEC in 1994 (10918-1). Baseline JPEG discards information. Square 8x8 tiles of pixels go through a discrete cosine transform, the results are rounded off, and Huffman coding packs what remains. Quality settings in the usual range leave about one-twentieth to one-tenth of the raw pixel data.

Each color channel gets 8 bits in a JPEG, and the format has neither an alpha channel nor layers. A progressive mode also exists, in which a rough version shows first and sharpens as more data arrives. Whether a file ends in .jpg or .jpeg, it is the same format, typed image/jpeg. US patent protection lapsed on 27 October 2006, and the format is built into most digital cameras and scanners.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens a JPEG for editing, and ImageMagick reads JPG at the command line.
- **Mac:** Preview opens JPEG too, and its File > Export menu lists TIFF.
- **Web:** JPG appears in Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox and Safari. Every major browser does.

### JPG and TIFF compared

TIFF is a raster file wrapper driven by tags, first developed at Aldus and Microsoft. Revision 6.0 came out in 1992; the specification is now controlled by Adobe. Different TIFFs use different compression methods and color representations, a single file can contain multiple images, and the format is well established for scanned document sequences, high-bit-depth imaging and preservation masters. You will see both .tif and .tiff; either way the media type is image/tiff. A classic TIFF locates its contents with 32-bit offsets, capping files at roughly 4 GB; BigTIFF exists to lift that cap. Private tags, some of them color-profile extensions, may also be unknown to a given reader.

First the browser decodes the JPG into 8-bit RGBA pixels. Then ImageMagick, compiled to WebAssembly and running in the same tab, writes those pixels out as the TIFF. The TIFF is uncompressed and carries an alpha channel next to red, green and blue. Camera EXIF fields, XMP data and the ICC profile are all left behind. No setting chooses compression, CMYK separation or an archival preset.

That means the conversion meets a file-type requirement without adding information. A TIFF cannot hold more tonal precision than the 8-bit samples that came out of the JPEG, and its ability to carry high bit depth or CMYK data does not create any from a source that lacks them. Start from the original capture whenever one exists.

### Other ways to convert JPG to TIFF

- **Preview on Mac:** show the JPEG, pick File > Export, change Format to TIFF and save the new file.
- **GIMP:** import the photo, choose File > Export As, then pick TIFF; the dialog that follows lets you choose a compression method. Skip its JPEG option when the goal is to stop adding lossy compression.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick portrait.jpg portrait.tiff`. According to ImageMagick's format list, its TIFF support is read-write and includes options for byte order, compression, strips and tiles; set whichever your recipient asks for.

### Problems with JPG files

**Blocks and smeared texture remain.** JPEG is lossy, and what compression discarded is gone. A TIFF can store the decoded picture, but it cannot calculate the exact detail that existed before compression. Find a less-compressed original if it matters.

**Transparent pixels cannot survive JPEG export.** A JPG has no alpha channel, so a TIFF made from it has no real transparency, whatever channels it carries. Choose a format with alpha for artwork on a transparent background.

**A larger file does not mean more detail.** The TIFF here is uncompressed. Judge it by its dimensions and encoding properties, not by its size.

**Old photo frames and viewers reject the JPG.** Some older photo frames reject progressive JPEG. Try an export with progressive mode disabled. The same quality number can also mean different quality in different programs, which is true of GIMP's default of 85.

**Layers are not kept.** A JPEG cannot hold a layer stack you could edit later, so keep the project file if you have one.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

A JPG stores a picture, not words. Even a photographed page of print is, inside the file, a grid of colored pixels squeezed by lossy JPEG compression, which works on 8x8 blocks of pixels. The compression comes from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, a body that started the work in 1986. ITU-T published its core standard in 1992, and ISO and IEC took it on in 1994.

Photographs on websites, in cameras, in email and on photo-sharing sites are commonly JPG, and every major browser displays it. The two names, .jpg and .jpeg, describe a single format registered as image/jpeg. The text in a photo or scan is easy to see but cannot be selected or searched, because it is only pixels. That is the gap this converter fills. A progressive JPG first shows a rough picture, then refines it as the rest arrives.

A JPG can also carry metadata such as Exif. None of that is text from the page, and none of it ends up in the TXT: only the letters the recognizer reads from the pixels do.

### Programs that open JPG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads JPG from the command line, which helps when you want to resize or straighten a batch first, and GIMP imports JPEG for editing.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox show the picture so you can check it is legible.
- **Mobile:** Chrome and Safari show JPG on a phone.

### JPG and TXT compared

- **What they hold**: a JPG holds pixels. A TXT holds characters and nothing else.
- **Extensions**: .jpg or .jpeg (image/jpeg) against .txt (text/plain).
- **Formatting**: plain text carries no commands for typographic formatting, and it does not prescribe a page layout, a font or how images are arranged.
- **Tables and images**: a word processor can place an image or a table on a page, while plain text cannot.
- **Encoding**: a TXT depends on a character set, shown by the charset parameter. The file written here is UTF-8.
- **Editors**: Visual Studio Code and Vim open TXT on Windows, Mac and Linux, and TextEdit opens it on a Mac. Converting rich text to TXT in TextEdit removes styles and formatting.
- **Reversibility**: converting a picture to text is a reading step, not a re-save, so nothing in the TXT tells you how the page looked.

Here the recognition is done by tesseract.js, running in your browser. The worker, engine and English model are served by this site, so the picture is not sent to another site. The recognized text has line-end spaces removed and runs of three or more newlines reduced to one blank line, and it is saved as UTF-8 with a final newline. If no words are found, the page stops with an error rather than writing an empty file.

### Other ways to convert JPG to TXT

- **Tesseract (command line):** run `tesseract page.jpg result -l eng`. The command takes an input image name and an output base name, and English is the default language if -l is left out.
- **Google Drive and Docs (web):** upload the JPG to Drive, right-click it, choose Open with > Google Docs, then copy the recognized text into a plain-text editor. The image is uploaded to Google, which accepts PDF and .jpeg, .png and .gif files, asks for files of 2 MB or less, and needs the document right-side up.
- **OneNote for Mac:** insert the picture, Control-click it, choose Copy Text from Picture and paste into a text editor. Recognition uses Microsoft online services, and handwriting may not be recognized well.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Several pictures at once**: each JPG gives its own TXT, the pictures are processed in sequence, and no ZIP is made.
- **Stray blank space**: spaces at line ends are cut and three or more line breaks in a row collapse to a single blank line, so extra spacing in the picture may not carry over.
- **Other languages**: this page reads with an English model only. Use a tool with the right language data for another language.
- **"No text was found in this image."**: the page stops there instead of saving an empty file.
- **Tables lose their grid**: plain text has no table structure, so copy the result into a spreadsheet and rebuild the columns by hand.
- **Odd characters in the TXT**: an editor that reads the file with the wrong character encoding shows garbled letters. The file here is UTF-8.

guide.title: About JPG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPG file?

Work began in 1986 at the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which is where the name comes from. ITU-T published the core specification as T.81 in 1992, and ISO followed in 1994 with part 1 of its 10918 standard. In the baseline form, an encoder cuts the picture into blocks of 8 by 8 pixels, applies a discrete cosine transform per block and Huffman-codes the result. Because detail is thrown away, a typical file ends up between a tenth and a twentieth the size of the raw pixels.

Every color channel is stored with 8 bits. There is no alpha channel, which rules out transparency, and no layers. A quality scale from 0 to 100 is the usual control, and the same number in two programs does not promise the same look.

Most digital cameras and scanners write JPG, and it is the everyday choice for photos on the web, email attachments and shared pictures. The two extensions, .jpg and .jpeg, are one format. The last of its US patents ran out on 27 October 2006.

### Programs that open JPG files

**Windows, macOS and Linux**

- Editing is GIMP's strength, and its JPEG export dialog offers quality, smoothing, progressive mode, arithmetic coding, optimized entropy coding, restart markers, chroma subsampling and a choice of DCT method.
- ImageMagick reads JPG at the command line. Its format list describes JPEG as lossy, with quality scaling plus Huffman and DCT options.

**Web and mobile**

- On desktops Chrome and Firefox show JPG, and phones do the same in Chrome and Safari. Every major browser handles it.

### JPG and WebP compared

- **Names**: JPG files use image/jpeg. WebP files end in .webp and use image/webp.
- **Compression**: baseline JPEG always discards detail. Lossy WebP is based on VP8 coding, and the format has a separate lossless method.
- **Transparency**: none in a JPG. WebP stores an alpha channel in both its lossy and lossless files.
- **Animation**: a JPG is a single still, whereas WebP can hold an animation.
- **Dimensions**: a WebP's width and height are each capped at 16,383 pixels.
- **Metadata**: WebP can carry an ICC color profile, Exif and XMP.
- **Origin**: Google announced WebP on 30 September 2010. Its lossy mode reuses the intra-frame coding of the VP8 video codec for still pictures, and JPEG is a standard from the early 1990s.
- **Typical jobs**: WebP serves web images with smaller files, images needing transparency and short animations, while JPEG serves photographs.

Moving from one to the other changes the compression. The page decodes the JPG into pixels, encodes those pixels as a WebP, and leaves the metadata behind.

### Other ways to convert JPG to WebP

- **cwebp:** run `cwebp -q 80 input.jpg -o output.webp`. The -q value runs from 0 to 100 and defaults to 75 when you leave it out. Adding `-lossless` encodes without loss, though that preserves what was decoded and not what the JPG had already discarded. The cwebp manual lists JPEG as an accepted input.
- **GIMP:** bring the JPG in, go to File > Export As, and give the new file a name that ends in .webp. In the WebP dialog you can tick Lossless or move the sliders for image quality and alpha quality, and GIMP's page notes that higher quality usually means a larger file.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick input.jpg -quality 80 output.webp`, the pattern ImageMagick's documentation shows with a PNG input. Its format list notes that WebP needs the WEBP delegate library.

### Problems with JPG files

- **Transparency is missing**: JPEG export cannot keep transparent pixels. Pick a format that has alpha when you need see-through areas.
- **An old photo frame or TV rejects the file**: some older devices cannot show progressive JPEG, where a coarse version appears first and sharpens while the rest loads. Export again with progressive mode off.
- **Older software won't open it**: GIMP lists arithmetic coding among its JPEG options, says it can make files 5 to 10 percent smaller, and warns that older software may not open them.
- **The same quality number looks different**: numbers differ between programs, so equal values do not guarantee equal compression or appearance.
- **No layers survive**: a JPEG holds one flattened picture, so keep the project file you edited it from.

guide.title: About JPS and PDF
guide.markdown:
### What is a JPS file?

JPS is a stereoscopic 3D image format that stores the left and right views side by side in one JPEG file. A typical JPS arranges the two eye views for crossed-eye viewing. The VRex proposal described the stereo layout in a JPEG APP3 marker, and a JPS can carry an embedded preview thumbnail. It is used for stereoscopic 3D photos and for 3D viewers and VR headsets, with JPEG compression and lossy quality.

### Programs that open JPS files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** sView reads JPS stereo markers and treats .jps as a crossed-eye image pair.
- **Windows:** StereoPhoto Maker opens JPS directly and lets you pick the stereo arrangement, and Stereoscopic Player documents JPS descriptor support.
- **Mac:** Pro for Mac is the vendor's Wine-based package of StereoPhoto Maker.
- **Mobile:** On a phone, sView for Android.

XnView MP and IrfanView are also listed as programs that open JPS.

### JPS and PDF compared

- **Content**: a JPS is one picture holding two views. A PDF keeps a fixed page layout.
- **Stereo data**: a PDF page here is a flat picture, so the viewer cannot rearrange the eyes.
- **Layout choices**: StereoPhoto Maker supports side-by-side, above/below and interlaced layouts, and treats the file type separately from the stereo layout.
- **Pages**: a PDF can hold many pages, while a JPS is a single picture.
- **Support**: PDF opens in Adobe Acrobat Reader, Preview on macOS and any web browser.

The browser decodes each file and a separate PDF is written for it. The PDF has one page the size of the image, and the picture is embedded losslessly as a PNG. Metadata is not carried over.

### Other ways to convert JPS to PDF

- **Pillow (Python):** call Image.open on the JPS, then save it under a .pdf name.
- **ImageMagick:** `magick stereo.jps stereo.pdf`.

### Problems with JPS files

- **The views look swapped or stretched**: selecting the wrong stereo arrangement displays the eye views incorrectly.
- **A reader will not infer the layout**: a .jps extension does not guarantee that every reader knows it, and StereoPhoto Maker asks you to specify it.
- **Quality drops after editing**: re-saving a JPS through JPEG output applies the selected compression quality again, so keep the source.
