guide.title: Understanding NEF for JPG output
guide.markdown:
### What is a NEF file?

NEF means Nikon Electronic Format. It stores raw photographs from Nikon cameras and retains the captured sensor information together with camera and lens metadata. A NEF is not simply a large JPG: white balance, hue, tone and sharpening choices can be kept as processing instructions that software applies later.

Nikon describes NEF storage in uncompressed and losslessly compressed forms. Depending on the camera, NEF data has 12-bit or 14-bit precision. The format is a TIFF-based file with an embedded JPEG preview, and it is proprietary to Nikon.

NEF files come from professional and enthusiast photography, and they are the starting point for editing photos before conversion to JPEG. Nikon's own processing software can render a NEF as a JPEG or TIFF while retaining the raw original. That is the idea behind the conversion here: the NEF stays as your negative, and the JPG is the print you hand out.

### Programs that open NEF files

**Mac and Windows**

- NX Studio: Nikon's own program for viewing raw photographs and developing them.
- Adobe Lightroom and Adobe Photoshop both open NEF.

**Linux, Mac and Windows**

- ImageMagick: a command-line tool that reads this camera raw format.
- darktable opens NEF.

**Linux**

- XnView MP: a viewer with NEF listed in its supported formats, free for private and educational use.

### NEF and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: a NEF is a proprietary Nikon format. A JPG ends in .jpg or .jpeg, which name the same format, and its media type is image/jpeg.
- **What is stored**: a NEF holds unprocessed sensor data. A JPG holds a rendered picture, so an export does not replace the adjustable sensor data in the original.
- **Precision**: NEF data is 12-bit or 14-bit. JPEG stores 8 bits per color channel, so an export keeps less tonal information.
- **Compression**: a baseline JPEG is lossy. It cuts the picture into 8x8 pixel blocks, puts each block through a discrete cosine transform, and Huffman coding follows. Quality is usually a number from 0 to 100, which this page leaves alone.
- **Transparency and layers**: JPEG carries no alpha channel and holds no layers.
- **Standard**: The name JPEG comes from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which began work in 1986. Its core standard is ITU-T T.81, published in 1992, and ISO/IEC 10918-1, published in 1994.
- **Progressive mode**: JPEG can also be written progressively, so a rough version shows first and then sharpens as the remaining data comes in.
- **Support**: JPEG's US patents expired on 27 October 2006, and every major browser displays it. Cameras and scanners commonly build it in.

The page reads one image from each NEF through ImageMagick and LibRaw, and writes a JPG. A new file downloads, named after the NEF with the .jpg ending, and the NEF is never changed. Several NEF files convert one after another, with one JPG for each.

### Other ways to convert NEF to JPG

- **NX Studio (Windows, Mac):** select the photo, click Export in the toolbar, set Export as to JPEG, and drag the Quality slider or enter a value for the JPEG compression ratio. To resize, turn on Change image size under Resolution and enter a value for Long edge. Then pick a destination under Save in, and click Export. The JPEG copies are saved to the folder you chose.

### Problems with NEF files

- **"Compression can't be decoded here" on a new Nikon file**: the message names Nikon's High Efficiency RAW as one compression it can't read, and it also appears for a damaged file.
- **A cut-short or damaged NEF**: if the page says the file may be damaged or incomplete, copy it from the card again.
- **A very large picture fails**: past roughly 537 megapixels the page stops and says the file is too large to convert here.
- **Colors look different from another program**: the rendering is applied by processing software, so another program may show other colors.
- **The JPG has less shadow and highlight detail than expected**: an eight-bit JPEG export does not retain the original 12-bit or 14-bit raw representation. Develop the NEF in a raw developer if you need to recover tones.
- **You want to edit later**: do it from the NEF. A JPG export can't recover the sensor data.

guide.title: NEF to PDF: format guide
guide.markdown:
### What is a NEF file?

NEF, short for Nikon Electronic Format, is the raw photo file written by Nikon cameras. It preserves the sensor's capture together with camera and lens metadata, either uncompressed or losslessly compressed, at 12 or 14 bits depending on the camera. White balance, hue, tone and sharpening may be recorded as separate instructions rather than applied to the pixels, and Nikon's software can output a JPEG or TIFF while the raw file stays as shot.

### Programs that open NEF files

- **Windows and Mac:** NX Studio is Nikon's program for viewing and developing NEF photos.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads NEF, a read-only format in its formats list.
- **Linux:** XnView MP supports NEF and costs nothing for private or educational use.

### NEF and PDF compared

A PDF is a document format. It came from Adobe's Camelot project under John Warnock, begun in 1991 and named PDF by 1992, aiming for pages that show or print the same everywhere. ISO 32000-1 standardized PDF 1.7 in 2008. A page can mix text, vector art and bitmaps, and bitmaps are compressed losslessly with Flate or with JPEG. The media type is application/pdf.

In your browser, ImageMagick reads one image from the NEF. The PDF gets a single page cut to the picture, one point per pixel and no margin, with the picture stored inside as a lossless PNG. Several files are never merged, and your NEF is left alone.

### Other ways to convert NEF to PDF

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick selection.nef selection.pdf`. Its formats page marks NEF as readable and PDF as readable and writable, and PDF output requires Ghostscript.

### Problems with NEF files

- **It looks different after development:** white balance and other rendering settings are instructions that processing software applies, so the picture can change between programs.
- **The raw data is gone:** a JPEG export or a PDF is a rendered result and cannot stand in for the adjustable sensor data in the NEF. Keep the original.
- **Less tonal range:** tonal depth varies by camera, and an eight-bit export cannot hold the 12-bit or 14-bit depth of the raw file.

guide.title: About NEF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a NEF file?

Nikon cameras write raw photos as NEF, short for Nikon Electronic Format. The file keeps the captured sensor data with camera and lens details, in a TIFF-based structure that includes a JPEG preview. Precision is 12-bit or 14-bit depending on the body, and the data is stored uncompressed or with lossless compression.

Nikon explains that choices such as white balance, hue, tone and sharpening can be kept as processing instructions rather than applied to the sensor values. A raw developer reads those instructions and renders a visible photograph. So converting NEF to PNG means developing the photo, not only changing the container. PNG is a finished picture that opens anywhere, but exposure and color have to be decided before its pixels are written.

A different developer can render the same NEF differently, so the PNG you get is one interpretation of the capture. Your NEF remains the original, and converting never changes it.

Tone matters most. A NEF holds 12-bit or 14-bit data, so a developer decides which part of the range becomes shadows, midtones and highlights. If a PNG looks flat or too dark, that is the development choice and not damage to the file.

### Programs that open NEF files

- **Windows and Mac:** Nikon NX Studio, the company's software for viewing and developing its raw photos.
- **Mac, Windows and Linux:** ImageMagick reads NEF.
- **Linux:** XnView MP opens NEF files and needs no payment for private or educational use.

Adobe Lightroom, Adobe Photoshop and darktable also open NEF.

### NEF and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .nef; .png, image/png.
- **Content**: unprocessed sensor data in a NEF, a finished pixel image in a PNG.
- **Precision**: a NEF's bit depth depends on the camera. PNG supports 8-bit and 16-bit channels.
- **Compression**: PNG is lossless for the pixels it is given. NEF is uncompressed or losslessly compressed.
- **Transparency**: PNG supports alpha transparency, though a camera photo has none.
- **Standard**: PNG is both ISO/IEC 15948 and a W3C Recommendation.

This page reads the NEF with ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly, using its bundled LibRaw decoder, and writes the PNG directly. It reads one picture and sets no quality value. Nothing is stripped on purpose. A file the decoder can't handle, such as a High Efficiency RAW from Nikon or a damaged one, ends with a message about RAW compression.

PNG's lossless compression applies to the pixels it receives. It can't undo choices made during demosaicing or color conversion. A lossless output and a reversible workflow are separate things, so keep the NEF.

Size follows from that. A PNG of a full-resolution Nikon photo stores every pixel, so the file can be large. Pick PNG when you want a lossless copy of the developed picture for editing or for a document, and the lossy JPG when you want something to share.

### Other ways to convert NEF to PNG

- **darktable (Windows, Mac, Linux):** first develop the NEF, then open the export module. Under target storage pick "file on disk", set the format to PNG, then press start export. darktable lists export to PNG among its features and NEF among the raw formats it imports.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick photograph.nef photograph.png`. ImageMagick lists NEF as a format it reads and PNG as one it reads and writes, and its docs show the same input-then-output form.
- **NX Studio and GIMP:** in NX Studio, select the photo and use Export to save a TIFF. NX Studio's saving options include TIFF but not PNG. Then open that TIFF in GIMP, use File > Export As and save it as PNG; GIMP shows its PNG Export dialog.

- **An unreadable result**: the raw decoder may not support that camera or compression. Try an updated raw developer such as darktable.
- **"Compression can't be decoded" message**: the message points to Nikon's High Efficiency RAW, or a damaged file. Open it in a Nikon-supported raw developer, or get another copy.
- **The PNG does not match the preview**: the development differs. Compare exposure, white balance and color in a raw developer instead of re-encoding the PNG.
- **The PNG is huge**: lossless compression doesn't promise a small file. Use the NEF to JPG converter if size matters.
- **Camera details are missing**: the NEF holds the camera and lens details and a PNG may not. Keep the NEF as the record.

guide.title: Understanding NEF for TIFF output
guide.markdown:
### What is a NEF file?

NEF stands for Nikon Electronic Format, the raw format of Nikon cameras. Sensor data arrives unprocessed, together with camera and lens metadata, inside a TIFF-based structure that also carries a JPEG preview. Depending on the camera the data has 12 or 14 bits, and Nikon stores it uncompressed or losslessly compressed. White balance, tone and sharpening can be kept as instructions to apply later, which is why a NEF can look different once it is developed. Nikon's software can turn a NEF into a JPEG or TIFF and leave the raw original untouched.

### Programs that open NEF files

For TIFF output, open the NEF in:

- **Windows and Mac:** NX Studio, Nikon's own software, views and develops NEF files.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads the format.
- **Linux:** XnView MP can browse NEF, and it is free only for private and educational use.

### NEF and TIFF compared

- **Content**: a NEF holds raw sensor data. A TIFF holds finished pixels.
- **Compression**: TIFF supports lossless and lossy methods. The page sets none.
- **Pages**: a TIFF can hold several images. This page reads one picture.
- **Preview**: a NEF carries a JPEG preview, which can look different from the developed TIFF.
- **Origin**: TIFF was published by Aldus and is now maintained by Adobe.

LibRaw, built into ImageMagick for WebAssembly, develops the NEF in your browser. ImageMagick then writes the TIFF. A NEF whose picture needs Nikon's High Efficiency RAW compression fails with a message saying so, and a picture over about 537 megapixels is refused.

### Other ways to convert NEF to TIFF

- **Nikon NX Studio:** select the photograph, click Export, and under Export as choose TIFF (8 Bit) or TIFF (16 Bit). LZW compression is optional. Check the remaining settings and export.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick portrait.nef portrait.tiff`. ImageMagick lists NEF among its readable formats.

### Problems with NEF files

- **The TIFF looks different from the preview**: raw rendering differs between programs. Compare in your editor.
- **A new camera's NEF fails**: use software that supports the model, such as Nikon NX Studio.
- **The NEF is damaged**: the page cannot read a cut-off file.
- **The raw settings are gone**: the TIFF holds finished pixels, so keep the NEF to redo the development.

guide.title: Understanding OGA and MP3
guide.markdown:
### What is an OGA file?

OGA is the general file extension for audio in the Ogg container, made by the Xiph.Org Foundation. Ogg is a wrapper, not a codec, so an OGA can hold audio such as Vorbis, FLAC, Speex or Opus. RFC 5334 registered audio/ogg and the .oga extension in September 2008. That RFC keeps .ogg for Ogg that contains only a Vorbis bitstream.

Every Ogg file begins with the pattern OggS. Plenty of music apps and upload forms accept MP3 but not OGA, which is why people convert. The MP3 is a delivery copy, so keep the OGA if you might want the original sound again.

Since the codec varies, an OGA may be lossy or lossless: Vorbis is lossy, Ogg FLAC is lossless. The Xiph.Org Foundation controls the audio/ogg registration, so the container is open rather than tied to one company. Because an Ogg audio stream can carry different codecs, a program that assumes one codec handles the others badly, which is why the broader .oga name sits beside .ogg.

### Programs that open OGA files

- **Windows, Mac, Linux, iOS and Android:** VLC plays most multimedia files without codec packs, though playback of an Ogg file also depends on the codec inside.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Audacity imports Ogg Vorbis and FLAC without extra software. FFmpeg's table lists Ogg for decoding and encoding and has decoders for Vorbis, FLAC, Speex and Opus.

### OGA and MP3 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .oga with audio/ogg; .mp3 with audio/mpeg.
- **What they are**: Ogg is a container, and the codec inside decides the compression. MP3 is one specific lossy codec.
- **Compression**: an OGA can be lossy or lossless. An MP3 is always lossy.
- **Lossless sources**: an Ogg FLAC file is lossless, so the MP3 trades that sound for a lossy copy.
- **Metadata**: MP3 uses ID3 tags for metadata.
- **Playback**: Nearly every device plays MP3, the main reason to convert to it.

The page decodes the sound with FFmpeg in your browser and encodes it with LAME, asking for a constant 192 kbps, which MP3 cannot reach below 32 kHz. Only audio is written. A Vorbis or other lossy source ends up as a second lossy pass that can't improve the source. The OGA itself is untouched, since you receive a new file, and a multi-file selection is processed in sequence with one MP3 per source.

### Other ways to convert OGA to MP3

- **FFmpeg (command line):** the documented form is ffmpeg -i input output, so run `ffmpeg -i archive.oga -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 192k portable.mp3`. FFmpeg's table lists Ogg as supported and MP3 encoding through the external LAME library. The -c:a libmp3lame option selects that LAME encoder, and -b:a 192k sets the bitrate.
- **Audacity (Windows, Mac, Linux):** load the Ogg audio through File > Import > Audio, then pick File > Export Audio and select MP3 from the Format list; the matching extension is added automatically. The dialog also sets the sample rate and the channels (Mono, Stereo or a custom mapping), which this page does not. Ogg Vorbis and FLAC import without extra software; other codecs can need Audacity's optional FFmpeg library.
- **Switch for Windows:** choose Add or File > Add and select the OGA, pick MP3 in Output Format, check Encoder Options, set the Save to Folder field and click Convert. Switch lists OGA input only for Windows.

### Problems with OGA files

- **The player is silent**: a player that recognizes the Ogg wrapper can still lack the decoder for the particular audio stream. Try VLC, which plays most multimedia files, or convert the file to MP3 here, where nearly every device can then play it.
- **A program treats it as Vorbis**: treating every .oga as Vorbis misidentifies files encoded with other audio codecs, and a codec-specific .ogg assumption can prevent an application from handling general .oga streams correctly.
- **You expected lossless**: an OGA is lossless only if it holds FLAC. Check what it holds in a tool such as FFmpeg.
- **The MP3 sounds worse**: a low-bitrate original carries its artifacts into the MP3. Look for a cleaner copy of the recording, ideally the lossless original.
- **A long file is slow**: the page imposes no size limit, so how long it takes rests on your device.

guide.title: About OGG and M4A
guide.markdown:
### What is an OGG file?

Xiph.Org maintains Ogg, a free container that wraps compressed multimedia. Sound and video streams can be interleaved inside it, and each stream's codec, not the container, sets how it is compressed. Data is read and written in sequence, a design that fits streaming, and every page of it carries a timestamp and an error check.

Ogg is open and patent-free, and its uses include games, open-source music on Linux, and audio on the web. A Vorbis file usually ends in .ogg, whereas .oga is the wider ending for any audio in Ogg. RFC 5334, from September 2008, registered audio/ogg for audio-only streams and video/ogg for video.

### Programs that open OGG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Audacity opens Ogg Vorbis audio for editing, and VLC plays the container and decodes its Vorbis.
- **Web:** Firefox and Chrome open OGG files.

### OGG and M4A compared

- **Container**: Ogg comes from Xiph.Org. M4A is audio alone, stored in an MPEG-4 file.
- **Audio**: an OGG usually holds Vorbis, a lossy codec. An M4A holds AAC or Apple Lossless, with tags and cover art in the wrapper.
- **Fit**: Ogg suits streaming. M4A suits software that expects MPEG-4 audio.

Vorbis and AAC are both lossy, so going from one to the other decodes the sound and encodes it afresh. This page asks for AAC and leaves video out.

### Other ways to convert OGG to M4A

- **FFmpeg (command line):** run `ffmpeg -i recording.ogg -vn -codec:a aac -b:a 192k listening-copy.m4a` to drop video and write the audio as AAC.
- **Audacity (Windows, Mac, Linux):** import with File > Import > Audio, export through File > Export Audio and choose M4A, which needs the optional FFmpeg library.

### Problems with OGG files

- **Your player says it can't play it**: Ogg only packages the audio, so the player must also have a decoder for the codec inside, and the container never names which codec that is.
- **The extension points to the wrong thing**: .ogg normally means Vorbis, but .oga covers other audio and .ogv covers video, as RFC 5334 sets out.
- **Pieces of the recording are missing**: Ogg notices damaged pages, yet it can't rebuild the audio they held.

guide.title: Understanding OGG for WAV output
guide.markdown:
### What is an OGG file?

Ogg is an open container from Xiph.Org for streams of compressed multimedia. Sound and video can be interleaved in one file, and each stream is compressed the way its codec decides. Ogg supports sequential reading and writing, which suits streaming pipelines, and its framing includes timestamps and error detection.

The .ogg extension is conventionally used for Vorbis audio, while .oga is the broader audio extension. The IETF published the Ogg media-type registration in September 2008. An audio-only Ogg stream uses audio/ogg, and video content uses video/ogg.

OGG files turn up in game soundtracks, Linux music libraries and web audio. The format is open and patent-free, and its usual audio codec, Vorbis, is lossy.

Because Ogg is only the wrapper, two files with the same .ogg ending can behave differently. One may hold Vorbis, which nearly every Ogg-aware program reads, and another may hold a codec that a given editor lacks. That is the most common reason an OGG opens in one program and fails in another.

### Programs that open OGG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Audacity imports Ogg Vorbis audio directly for editing, and VLC media player plays Ogg containers and decodes Vorbis audio.
- **Web:** Firefox and Chrome open OGG files.

### OGG and WAV compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .ogg with audio/ogg; .wav with audio/wav or audio/x-wav.
- **Structure**: Ogg is a container whose streams can use different codecs. WAVE is a RIFF-based wrapper for sound, and Microsoft and IBM documented it in their August 1991 multimedia specification.
- **Compression**: .ogg audio is usually lossy Vorbis. A WAV commonly holds linear PCM, though compressed encodings can appear too.
- **Size**: the WAV is much larger, because decoded samples take more room than a compressed stream. A plain WAV also tops out at 4 GB, and very large recordings may need RF64.
- **Odd payloads**: a recorder may use proprietary compression inside a WAV, and for such imports Audacity's advice is to use its FFmpeg library.
- **Metadata**: standard INFO chunks and Broadcast WAVE extensions store different information.
- **Standing**: the Library of Congress recommends WAVE for digital audio collections, and Broadcast WAVE adds metadata for production and preservation.

The page decodes the audio with FFmpeg inside your browser and writes signed 16-bit little-endian PCM. A new WAV downloads under the OGG's name with the .wav ending, and the OGG is never changed. Choose several OGG files and they convert in turn, each with its own WAV and no ZIP.

### Other ways to convert OGG to WAV

- **Audacity (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the OGG, choose File > Export Audio, name the file with the .wav ending, and set Encoding. Signed 16-bit PCM is the default. Then pick the export range: the entire project or the current selection. A Multiple Files option exports several files based on tracks or labels. Audacity's manual warns that WAV files are limited to a maximum size of 4 GB, which it ties to maximum durations.
- **FFmpeg (command line):** run `ffmpeg -i interview.ogg -c:a pcm_s16le interview.wav`. Here -i names the input file and -c:a sets the audio codec, 16-bit little-endian PCM. FFmpeg's general documentation lists Ogg among the file formats it reads and writes, and lists signed 16-bit little-endian PCM among its audio codecs.
- **SoX (command line):** run `sox interview.ogg interview.wav`. Unless you give -t, SoX works out the output type from the file extension, and -t exists for files whose type can't be told from the ending. The first example in the SoX manual turns an AU file into a WAV file in the same way.

### Problems with OGG files

- **An editor says the file is unsupported**: the file may hold a codec that the editor lacks. A player needs the enclosed codec as well as Ogg container support, because Ogg itself does not identify one audio encoding.
- **The extension is misleading**: RFC 5334 distinguishes .ogg Vorbis files from general .oga audio and .ogv video, so the three endings are not interchangeable.
- **Parts of the recording are missing**: the container detects damaged pages, but that does not reconstruct missing encoded audio. Get a fresh copy of the OGG.
- **Audacity will not import it**: Audacity imports Ogg Vorbis directly, so a refusal points to a different codec inside the container.
- **Two OGG files behave differently**: check which codec each holds rather than trusting the ending.

guide.title: Understanding OGV for MP3 output
guide.markdown:
### What is an OGV file?

OGV is the Ogg container used for video, maintained by the Xiph.Org Foundation. It usually holds Theora video with Vorbis or Opus audio, and its media type is video/ogg. Ogg streams begin with the bytes OggS. Xiph recommends .ogv for video, though the older .ogg ending also turns up on video files. An OGV can contain audio, video and timed text, but the extension does not promise that a soundtrack exists.

### Programs that open OGV files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** VLC media player plays Ogg containers with Theora and Vorbis, and FFmpeg can open Ogg streams to inspect or convert them.

One documented pairing for Ogg video is Theora pictures with Vorbis sound, which VLC plays. Even so, a player can understand Ogg yet lack the decoder for one of its streams.

### OGV and MP3 compared

- **Content**: an OGV carries picture and sound. An MP3 carries sound only.
- **Compression**: Vorbis and Opus are lossy, and so is MP3.
- **Metadata**: MP3 uses ID3 tags.
- **Media type**: video/ogg and audio/mpeg.
- **Playback**: MP3 plays on nearly every device.

FFmpeg runs in your browser as WebAssembly. It decodes the sound and encodes it with libmp3lame, asking for 192 kbps, with the video disabled. LAME cannot reach 192 kbit/s below 32 kHz, so a source recorded at a lower sample rate gets a lower bitrate. The command sets no sample rate, channel layout or tag mapping, so FFmpeg's defaults decide.

### Other ways to convert OGV to MP3

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i seminar.ogv -vn -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 192k seminar.mp3`. `-vn` leaves the picture out, and `-b:a` sets the audio bitrate. The OGV needs a sound track.

### Problems with OGV files

- **No MP3 appears**: the OGV may have no audio track, so FFmpeg reports an error.
- **A player opens the file but misses a stream**: Ogg support does not include every codec, so the sound or picture may need a different decoder.
- **Timed text only**: an OGV can carry timed text and other visually presented content, so a file with no audio track gives no MP3.
- **The MP3 sounds rough**: the source was already compressed, and MP3 compresses again.

guide.title: About OGV and MP4 files
guide.markdown:
### What is an OGV file?

The .ogv ending marks video stored in an Ogg container. The Ogg format is maintained by the Xiph.Org Foundation, and RFC 5334 gives video/ogg as the media type. An OGV file can hold audio, video, timed text and other visually presented content. Every Ogg stream begins with the identification bytes OggS. The format is royalty-free, and it is used for open-source video and for web video in Firefox. Theora video with Vorbis or Opus audio is the typical content.

The ending says only that the container is Ogg. One documented combination is Theora video with Vorbis sound, but an Ogg file does not necessarily contain Vorbis, so the codec has to be identified before you decide what to do with a file. Xiph recommends .ogv for video, though older files may end in .ogg.

### Programs that open OGV files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** VLC media player can play an Ogg container holding Theora and Vorbis. FFmpeg demuxes Ogg streams so you can inspect and convert them.

### OGV and MP4 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .ogv with video/ogg; .mp4 or .m4v with video/mp4.
- **Typical codecs**: Theora and Vorbis in OGV. H.264 and AAC in MP4, which can additionally hold AV1, VP9, MP3 or Opus.
- **Standard**: the MP4 specification is MPEG-4 Part 14, published in 2003 as ISO/IEC 14496-14 and layered on the ISO Base Media File Format. Ogg comes from Xiph.Org and is open.
- **Contents**: an MP4 is a container for several codecs, including H.264, H.265 and AV1 video, and it can also hold subtitles, chapters and metadata. An OGV carries Theora pictures along with Vorbis or Opus sound, and sometimes timed text.
- **Structure**: an MP4 is made of nested boxes, the same idea QuickTime calls atoms.
- **Support**: every major browser plays MP4, and from version 5.0 Android also plays HEVC video inside MP4.

A player may understand Ogg while lacking a decoder for one of its streams, so an OGV that opens in one program can show nothing in another.

The page decodes the OGV with FFmpeg and asks for H.264 (ultrafast, CRF 32), AAC at 96 kbps and an index moved to the head of the MP4. Pictures stay at their own dimensions and rate unless they exceed 1920 pixels or 30 fps, and the sides are made even. The page has no quality, size or trim controls. A deinterlacing step handles any frames the file marks interlaced. You do not pick between several audio or video streams.

### Other ways to convert OGV to MP4

- **FFmpeg (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `ffmpeg -i source.ogv -c:a aac -c:v libx264 ogv-delivery.mp4`. It re-encodes instead of copying the Ogg streams, and you can add options to match a receiver's requirements.
- **VLC (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open Media > Convert / Save, add the OGV, set a destination file, choose a profile and press Start. VLC's documentation does not list profile names, so look at what your copy offers before you start.

This page converts the whole OGV. In FFmpeg, writing `-t` ahead of `-i` caps how much input is read, so `ffmpeg -t 10 -i source.ogv short.mp4` converts just the first ten seconds.

### Problems with OGV files

- **A player opens the container but shows nothing**: it may lack a decoder for the video inside. A player understanding Ogg does not guarantee Theora support, so identify the codec first.
- **The ending is .ogg instead of .ogv**: the older .ogg ending is also seen on video, although Xiph recommends .ogv for that role. This page expects .ogv.
- **The codec is not what you assumed**: a file with an Ogg ending can hold a codec other than Vorbis, so find out which codec it uses before you decide what to do.
- **The file holds more than pictures**: besides video, an OGV can carry audio, timed text and other visual content, and this page gives you no choice among them.
- **A renamed file fails**: renaming it to .mp4 changes nothing inside, and the contents are still Ogg.
- **Frame size or rate is capped**: pictures wider or taller than 1920 pixels are reduced here, and anything faster than 30 frames a second is brought down to 30. Keep the OGV if you want the original.

guide.title: OPUS to M4A: format guide
guide.markdown:
### What is an Opus file?

Opus became an IETF standard in September 2012 as RFC 6716, an open, royalty-free audio codec. It builds on SILK from Skype and CELT from Xiph.Org, and works well for speech, music and low-delay use. Bitrates run from 6 to 510 kbit/s. A .opus file commonly stores the sound in an Ogg stream, as RFC 7845 specifies, with descriptive metadata and seeking.

Its uses include voice chat and calls, streaming and low-bitrate speech recordings. People convert Opus to M4A when a music app, editor or device does not accept Opus.

### Programs that open Opus files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** FFmpeg's Ogg muxer accepts Opus, and opusdec, the decoder in the Opus project's opus-tools, decodes .opus files.

### Opus and M4A compared

Opus is a codec, while M4A is an audio-only MPEG-4 file that usually holds AAC, or lossless ALAC. M4A supports metadata tags and cover art, and it is used for iTunes and Apple Music tracks, podcasts and iPhone voice memos. The M4A made here holds AAC, never ALAC, and the page asks FFmpeg for 192 kb/s. Both formats are lossy, so converting adds a second round of compression. Pick M4A when the target app lists AAC but not Opus.

### Other ways to convert Opus to M4A

- **FFmpeg (command line):** enter `ffmpeg -i input.opus -c:a aac -b:a 192k output.m4a`. FFmpeg decodes the Opus audio and writes AAC.
- **opusdec and Audacity:** decode with `opusdec input.opus output.wav`. In Audacity, bring in the WAV via File > Import > Audio, then choose M4A(AAC) Files FFmpeg in the Format dropdown of File > Export Audio. Audacity needs its optional FFmpeg library for AAC export.

### Problems with Opus files

- **A program rejects the Opus**: a program that reads Vorbis in Ogg may still fail on Opus, since Opus uses its own Ogg headers. Converting to M4A avoids the problem.
- **Unwanted leading samples**: a reader that ignores the pre-skip value plays extra samples at the start, and Ogg Opus says how to apply it.
- **A sample rate that looks wrong**: Ogg Opus counts its playback timing at 48 kHz, which is not necessarily the rate the recording started with.

guide.title: About Opus files
guide.markdown:
### What is an Opus file?

An open audio codec built for speech and music, including live calls, Opus was standardized by the IETF. That happened in September 2012 as RFC 6716. Its design joins SILK technology from Skype with CELT technology from Xiph.Org. Opus is lossy, with bitrates from 6 to 510 kbit/s, and it is royalty-free.

A .opus file is normally Ogg Opus: the encoded sound stored in an Ogg stream as RFC 7845 describes, with descriptive metadata and seeking. Its media type is audio/ogg with the opus codec parameter. It works well for speech and music and for low-delay use, and it is used for voice chat and calls, for streaming and for low-bitrate speech recordings. Not every program that reads Ogg Vorbis decodes Opus, because Opus uses its own headers inside Ogg.

### Programs that open Opus files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- FFmpeg: decodes Opus; encoding goes through the external libopus library.
- opusdec: the Opus project's command-line decoder, part of opus-tools. `opusdec input.opus output.wav` writes a WAV when the output name ends in .wav.
- VLC media player: plays .opus.
- Audacity: does not read Opus on its own, but tries the optional FFmpeg library when it is installed.

**Web**

- Firefox and Chrome play Opus in the browser.

### Opus and MP3 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .opus with audio/ogg; .mp3 with audio/mpeg.
- **Origin**: Opus is an IETF standard from 2012. MP3, short for MPEG-1 Audio Layer III, was published as ISO/IEC 11172-3 in 1993 after work at Fraunhofer IIS.
- **Compression**: both are lossy. MP3 relies on a hearing model to throw away sound that most listeners would not notice.
- **Bitrates**: Opus spans 6 to 510 kbit/s. MP3 spans 32 to 320 kbps, with sample rates of 32, 44.1 or 48 kHz.
- **Metadata**: Ogg Opus carries descriptive metadata. MP3 puts titles and other tags into ID3 blocks.
- **MP3 size**: an MP3 at 128 kbit/s comes to about an eleventh of the CD audio it was made from. The MP3 design goes back to work that began late in the 1980s at Fraunhofer IIS, together with colleagues in the MPEG audio group.
- **Patents**: MP3's patent licensing program ran out on 23 April 2017.
- **Playback**: every major browser plays MP3, while Opus is played by Firefox and Chrome among others. Opus needs a player that understands its Ogg mapping.

On this page FFmpeg, running in the browser, decodes your Opus and re-encodes it with LAME, asking for 192 kbit/s. MP3 can't reach that rate below 32 kHz, where LAME writes a lower one. Opus can be far smaller than that, so a speech file can grow. Both formats are lossy, so the result is a second-generation copy.

The page does not trim, normalize or change the volume. It also does not pick between audio tracks: if a file holds more than one, FFmpeg's defaults decide.

### Other ways to convert Opus to MP3

- **FFmpeg from the command line:** run `ffmpeg -i interview.opus -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 192k interview.mp3`. FFmpeg handles the Opus decoding.
- **Audacity with FFmpeg:** Audacity does not support Opus natively, but with the optional FFmpeg library installed it tries FFmpeg to import the .opus file. Then choose File > Export Audio, pick MP3 in the Format menu and select a Bit Rate Mode. Preset is the default and uses settings the LAME developers recommend for music. Variable runs from 0 (highest quality) to 9 (smallest file), Average takes 8 to 320 kbps, and Constant keeps one bitrate so the file size is predictable.

### Problems with Opus files

- **A player ignores the file**: a program that reads Vorbis in Ogg does not necessarily decode Opus. Try VLC, or convert to MP3.
- **The start sounds off**: Ogg Opus has a pre-skip value that readers must apply. A tool that ignores it can add unwanted samples at the beginning.
- **The sample rate looks wrong**: Ogg Opus keeps its playback timing on a 48 kHz basis. That does not tell you the rate of the original recording.
- **The file is tiny**: Opus bitrates start at 6 kbit/s, so a very small .opus file is normal and not a sign of damage.
- **Audacity won't open it**: Audacity needs the optional FFmpeg library for Opus. Install it, or convert the file here first.

guide.title: About Opus and WAV files
guide.markdown:
### What is an Opus file?

Opus is an open codec for speech and music that was built with interactive communication in mind. The IETF standardized its original definition in RFC 6716 in September 2012. It blends SILK, which came from Skype, with CELT, from Xiph.Org. A .opus file commonly stores the encoded sound in an Ogg stream as specified by RFC 7845, and Ogg Opus supports descriptive metadata. It registers as audio/ogg carrying a codecs parameter of opus, and a player can jump within a long recording.

Opus is lossy, since its coding modes give up some signal detail to keep the representation compact. Ogg Opus also counts its playback time in units of 48 kHz, whatever sample rate the original recording had when it was captured.

### Programs that open Opus files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** opusdec is the decoder the Opus project distributes in opus-tools for decoding .opus files, which commonly hold the sound in an Ogg stream. FFmpeg has an Ogg muxer that accepts Opus.

### Opus and WAV compared

- **Names and types**: .opus goes with audio/ogg, and .wav is labeled audio/wav or audio/x-wav.
- **What it is**: Opus is a codec. WAVE wraps sound in a RIFF structure without prescribing one encoding, so compressed encodings can appear in it alongside linear PCM.
- **Size**: Opus compresses and discards detail. A PCM WAV keeps every sample.
- **History**: Microsoft and IBM documented the WAVE format in their August 1991 multimedia specification.
- **Metadata**: Ogg Opus supports descriptive metadata and seeking. In a WAV, INFO chunks and the Broadcast WAVE extension hold different kinds of information, so tag handling varies.
- **Preservation**: WAVE is the format the Library of Congress recommends for digital audio collections.
- **Size limits**: a very large recording may need RF64, because the original RIFF size fields run out.
- **Editors**: Audacity imports most WAV recordings, including PCM variants. A recorder may use proprietary compression inside WAV, and for such files Audacity recommends its FFmpeg library.
- **Phones**: Mozilla lists WAV among the supported audio file types on Android.
- **Timing**: playback timing in Ogg Opus is expressed at 48 kHz, which says nothing about the original recording's rate.

What this page does is run FFmpeg, as WebAssembly in your browser, with the PCM signed 16-bit little-endian codec and the video dropped. That produces uncompressed samples. The command never sets a sample rate or channel layout, so the page has no such options. It also passes -vn, which discards any video stream, so only sound is written. The WAV is uncompressed PCM, so it can be far larger than the Opus original. Decoding does not recover what the Opus encode removed. Files are converted one after another with no ZIP, so a batch gives you one download per file. Each download takes the original's name with a .wav ending, and the source file is left alone. The output is checked against the target format, so a result that is not a WAV fails with a message instead of being saved.

### Other ways to convert Opus to WAV

- **opusdec (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `opusdec message.opus decoded.wav`. opusdec writes WAVE output when the output filename ends in .wav.
- **FFmpeg (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `ffmpeg -i message.opus -c:a pcm_s16le editable.wav`. It will not reconstruct information the source encode discarded.

With FFmpeg, `-vn` removes any video, so a file that carries pictures as well as sound yields only the sound.

### Problems with Opus files

- **A program reads Ogg but not Opus**: software that handles Vorbis in Ogg may not decode Opus, as the Ogg mapping for Opus has its own headers.
- **Unwanted audio at the start**: dropping the pre-skip value can cause unwanted leading samples, and Ogg Opus defines how readers must apply it.
- **The sample rate looks different from your microphone's**: Ogg Opus stores its playback timing on a 48 kHz basis, which should not be confused with the original recording's sample rate.
- **Detail is already gone**: Opus is lossy, so the samples in the WAV are the ones that were left, and decoding cannot bring back the sound before the first encode.
- **The file comes from a video**: choose the audio file itself. Without an audio stream, the run ends in an error.

guide.title: ORF to JPEG: format guide
guide.markdown:
### What is an ORF file?

ORF is the raw-picture extension of Olympus cameras, and of OM SYSTEM cameras since the brand changed. A file stores raw sensor readings in a TIFF-based layout with a JPEG preview embedded. Which cameras a program can read depends on its version; Adobe's table, for example, starts OM-1 ORF support at Camera Raw 14.2. Many photographers shoot ORF so they can edit before exporting JPEGs. OM Workspace, the maker's software, develops ORF files, adjusts white balance and exposure, and keeps a history of your processing so an edit can be undone back to the original settings.

### Programs that open ORF files

- **Windows and Mac:** OM Workspace comes from the camera maker and processes raw files. Adobe Camera Raw reads ORF too, with a minimum version that depends on the exact camera.
- **Linux:** ImageMagick reads ORF as a camera raw format, as long as the needed delegates are installed on your system.

### ORF and JPEG compared

The Joint Photographic Experts Group gave JPEG its name and began its work in 1986; ITU-T T.81 followed in 1992 and ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994. The method is lossy, works on 8x8 blocks and stores 8 bits per color channel. It has no layers and no alpha channel, though an optional progressive mode first draws a rough image and refines it as the file loads. Both .jpg and .jpeg name the format, its media type is image/jpeg, and every major browser displays it. Photos on web pages, in email attachments and on sharing sites are usually JPEG.

ImageMagick, working inside your browser, reads one image from the ORF and writes a JPEG. No quality setting is passed. With several files, each is converted in its turn and saved separately, and the ORF itself is untouched.

### Other ways to convert ORF to JPEG

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick portrait.orf portrait.jpeg`. In the formats list, ORF is read-only while JPEG can be read and written.

### Problems with ORF files

- **Camera not supported:** an older raw plug-in may lack your camera even though it opens other ORF files. Update the plug-in or the software.
- **A missing option:** in OM Workspace, not every processing option works with every raw image.
- **High Res Shot files:** OM Workspace needs 8 GB of memory or more to process them as raw.

guide.markdown:
### What is an ORF file?

Each ORF is a raw photograph from an Olympus or OM SYSTEM camera. It is TIFF-based, holds unprocessed sensor data and carries an embedded JPEG preview. Readers are matched to camera models and program versions, so a brand-new body can need an update before its files open. ORF mainly serves photographers who edit first and export afterwards. Samples run from 1 to 16 bits, and an optional alpha channel gives each pixel its own transparency. Browsers all display it, under the media type image/png. It suits screenshots, logos, pictures that need transparency and web graphics with crisp edges.

ImageMagick picks one image from the ORF and writes it out as PNG. The page passes no quality value, since lossless PNG has nothing to trade. Pick several ORFs if you like: each becomes its own PNG download, and the originals are never altered.

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick landscape.orf landscape.png`. Its formats page marks ORF as read-only and PNG as readable and writable; PNG output requires libpng.

guide.title: Understanding OTF and PNG
guide.markdown:
### What is an OTF file?

OTF identifies an OpenType font. Microsoft and Adobe developed OpenType from the TrueType structure, adding capabilities for glyph descriptions and typographic layout. A font contains information used to draw text; it is not simply a ready-made picture of the alphabet. Its available characters and shaping features vary between typefaces.

### Programs that open OTF files

- **Mac:** Font Book installs and validates OpenType and OpenType-SVG fonts.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** FontForge opens .otf fonts for inspecting and editing, and fontTools TTX dumps a font's binary tables as XML.

### OTF and PNG compared

OpenType stores glyphs and text-layout data in tables, and its outlines may be TrueType, CFF, bitmaps or SVG. PNG stores lossless raster samples. A PNG of a font is a picture, not a replacement for it.

This page makes a specimen sheet: the font's name at 40 pixels, the alphabets and digits at 28, and the pangram at five sizes. ImageMagick draws it in black on white and converts it to grayscale, and the image is as wide as the longest line needs. A specimen is also a selection: it does not show every script, alternate or feature in the font.

Keep the OTF for typing and scalable rendering.

### Other ways to convert OTF to PNG

- **ImageMagick:** `magick -font typeface.otf -pointsize 48 label:'Sample ABC 123' preview.png` draws any text you choose in the font. It sizes the canvas to the text.
- **GIMP:** choose Tools > Text, choose the typeface from the selector of installed fonts, and type your sample. Export the image as PNG with File > Export As.
- **Inkscape:** use the Text tool, choose the installed family in Text > Text and Font, then use File > Export PNG Image. The export dialog lets you pick the page, drawing or selection and set the image size in pixels.

### Problems with OTF files

**An older renderer fails:** a rendering engine of older vintage may not support the font's outline representation.

**A corrupt font:** it can stop text from displaying correctly, and Font Book offers validation.

**Duplicate copies:** two installed copies of one font can conflict, and Font Book can resolve duplicates.

guide.title: About OTF files
guide.markdown:
### What is an OTF file?

An .otf file stores an OpenType font. The format grew out of TrueType through work by Microsoft and Adobe, with a first release in 1997. The registered media type is font/otf.

OpenType files organize glyph and text-layout data into tables. A glyph description may use TrueType outlines, CFF outlines, bitmaps or SVG, so two .otf files from different foundries can be built differently. Variation tables also let several related faces share one font resource. Some OpenType fonts even use SVG for their glyph descriptions, which is a different thing from the SVG file this page makes.

A font file describes how to draw characters, and it is not a drawing. Turning one into a picture means choosing some text to draw, which is the job of this page.

### Programs that open OTF files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- FontForge lists otf among the file types in its Open dialog.
- Binary tables are read by fontTools TTX, which writes them out as XML for inspection.

**Mac:**

- Installing and validating OpenType and OpenType-SVG fonts is what Font Book does.

### OTF and SVG compared

- **Contents**: an OTF holds glyph data and layout rules for many characters. An SVG is XML describing shapes, text and embedded images.
- **Standards**: SVG is an open W3C standard that became a Recommendation in 2001. OpenType came from Microsoft and Adobe.
- **Typical use**: install an OTF to type with it. An SVG is shown as a picture, in a browser or in Inkscape.
- **Scaling**: outlines kept as drawing instructions stay sharp at every size. A raster picture inside an SVG does not.
- **Text**: SVG files are plain text, which can be edited and searched. Pixels embedded in one cannot.
- **Styling**: stylesheets and scripts reach into an SVG, so its look can be changed, driven by code and animated.
- **Media type**: SVG is registered as image/svg+xml.
- **Compression**: a gzip-compressed SVG uses the .svgz extension.
- **Placement**: open an SVG by itself, or embed it in an HTML page.
- **Effects**: SVG supports clipping paths, masks and filter effects.

The two formats do not map one to one. Your font is loaded into ImageMagick in the browser, and FreeType draws a specimen. The first line is the font's own name at 40 pixels, taken from its name table and cut off at 64 characters. A font with no usable name gets the heading OTF font instead. Then come the capital letters, the lowercase letters, then the numerals along with some punctuation marks, each at 28 pixels. A pangram about a fox and a dog follows at 16, 24, 32, 48 and 64 pixels. Ink is black on white, and the sheet is between 400 and 2400 pixels wide. This picture is wrapped inside an SVG file.

So the SVG holds a picture and not the font's outlines. Its letters cannot be edited, which suits a preview, a thumbnail or an illustration. If you need paths, use one of the methods below.

Files convert one after another, each SVG downloads on its own, and your OTF is never changed. The page sets no size limit and nothing is uploaded.

### Other ways to convert OTF to SVG

- **FontForge, export a glyph:** open the OTF with File > Open. With a glyph's outline view, use File > Export and choose SVG. The manual says this exports the splines of the glyph.
- **FontForge, SVG font:** after opening the OTF, choose File > Generate Fonts and pick SVG font. FontForge usually writes contours for each glyph in that format.
- **fontTools:** run `fonttools pens.svgPathPen face.otf "ABC" > letters.svg`. The characters follow the font file, and the paths are printed to standard output.

### Problems with OTF files

- **Older renderer**: a rendering engine can lack support for a font's particular outline representation.
- **Corrupt file**: a damaged font can prevent correct display, and Font Book provides validation.
- **Duplicate copies**: installed twice, a font can cause conflicts, and Font Book can resolve them.
- **Not readable**: if the file is not a font ImageMagick can read, the page says so.
- **No letters**: a font with none of the characters in the sheet gets the message that it has no letters the converter can draw.
- **Outlines wanted**: the specimen cannot supply them, so use FontForge or fontTools.

guide.title: PBM to PNG: format guide
guide.markdown:
### What is a PBM file?

PBM, short for Portable Bit Map, describes two-tone raster images, and Netpbm uses it as the glue between image-processing programs. The raw variant opens with P4 and packs its pixels bit by bit. The plain variant opens with P1 and spells pixels out as zeros and ones, with a one meaning black and a zero meaning white. Raw PBM permits consecutive images, while plain PBM contains one. The customary MIME label is image/x-portable-bitmap, which Netpbm notes is not registered with IANA.

### Programs that open PBM files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads PBM images, and XnView MP lists PBM among its readable formats. XnView MP is free for private and educational use.

### PBM and PNG compared

PNG started as a patent-free alternative to GIF and is standardized as ISO/IEC 15948:2004. Its compression loses nothing, and pictures can be indexed, grayscale or truecolor, with samples from 1 to 16 bits and transparency available through an alpha channel. A PBM carries only black and white, so a PNG made from it is a two-tone picture in a file that more programs can open. Every major browser shows PNG, and the media type is image/png.

Your browser runs ImageMagick here, and it takes one picture from the PBM. No quality setting is passed, since PNG has none to adjust. Add several PBMs and each is processed in turn and saved on its own; the originals stay as they were.

### Other ways to convert PBM to PNG

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick stencil.pbm stencil.png`. Its formats page marks both PBM and PNG as readable and writable.
- **Pillow:** in Python, after `from PIL import Image`, run `Image.open("mask.pbm").save("mask.png")`. Pillow reads plain and raw PBM and takes PNG from the file ending.

### Problems with PBM files

- **No shades:** color and gray shading cannot be represented directly in a two-tone image.
- **Large plain files:** a plain PBM spends a text digit on each pixel, so it takes more space than the raw form.
- **Partial readers:** some programs implement only a restricted part of the specification.
- **Several images in one file:** Netpbm recommends a minimal single-image layout for interoperability.

guide.title: About PCD files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PCD file?

PCD is the image format of Kodak's Photo CD system, introduced in 1992. Each file holds one photo at several resolutions, from a thumbnail up to high resolution. Photo CD defines sizes from 128 by 192 to 2048 by 3072 pixels, and ProPhotoCD adds 4096 by 6144. The image stores luminance at full resolution and chromaticity at half resolution.

A standard Photo CD places numbered .pcd images in photo_cd/images. The overview.pcd file supplies the thumbnails for a contact sheet.

### Programs that open PCD files

- **Windows:** IrfanView is free for noncommercial use and reads PCD. Its Photo-CD plug-in adds high-resolution decoding.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick is a free command-line reader and writer for Photo CD, with a documented write limit of 768 by 512 pixels.
- **Mac and Linux:** hpcdtoppm is the decoder Netpbm documents; it is distributed separately under restrictive licensing.

### PCD and JPG compared

- **Extensions**: .pcd and .jpg. A .jpeg file is the same format as .jpg.
- **Content**: a PCD stores several resolutions of one photo. A JPG stores a single image.
- **Compression**: JPG is lossy and its quality is usually chosen between 0 and 100. Each channel gets 8 bits, and transparency isn't possible.

ImageMagick reads the PCD here and one JPG comes out. No quality value is passed and there is no resolution setting. Above about 537 megapixels, a picture is turned away.

### Other ways to convert PCD to JPG

- **ImageMagick:** `magick family-scan.pcd family-view.jpg`. ImageMagick's format list shows PCD as readable and writable.
- **IrfanView (Windows):** open the PCD, then use File > Save as, choose JPG as the output format, set the name and folder, and save. Install the Photo-CD plug-in for high-resolution decoding.
- **hpcdtoppm and Netpbm:** `hpcdtoppm archive-image.pcd -ppm -5 archive-image.ppm` writes a PPM at the 16Base size, then `pnmtojpeg -quality=90 archive-image.ppm > archive-image.jpg` writes the JPG. Netpbm says hpcdtoppm may not be sold or used in profit-making activity.

### Problems with PCD files

- **A tiny picture**: overview.pcd is only Base/16 resolution. Use the numbered image file for a larger picture.
- **The highest ProPhotoCD size is missing**: it needs its extension files and the original directory layout, so copying one PCD alone can lose it.
- **A program can't open the file**: GraphicConverter's Mac App Store edition doesn't import PhotoCD. IrfanView and ImageMagick do.

guide.title: PCX to JPG: format guide
guide.markdown:
### What is a PCX file?

ZSoft created PCX as the native format of its PC Paintbrush program, which reached MS-DOS in 1984 and 1985. A picture is a raster with run-length encoding, palette-based or truecolor, and some variants add a second palette after the image data. PCX saw wide use on DOS and early Windows, and old clip art collections still turn up in it. A related DCX file bundles several PCX pictures, an arrangement common in fax software.

### Programs that open PCX files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick lists PCX for reading and writing, and Pillow, a Python imaging library, reads and writes PCX in the modes its documentation names.

### PCX and JPG compared

JPEG is named after the Joint Photographic Experts Group, active since 1986, and ITU-T T.81 followed in 1992. Baseline JPEG is lossy: it cuts the picture into 8x8 blocks, runs a discrete cosine transform, then Huffman-codes the result. Each channel gets 8 bits, there is no transparency, and the media type is image/jpeg. The endings .jpg and .jpeg are interchangeable, and web photos, email attachments and shared snapshots are mostly JPEG.

Run-length encoding in a PCX loses nothing, so the step to JPG adds a loss that was not there before. The conversion happens in your browser with ImageMagick, which decodes a single picture from the PCX. The page passes no quality setting. Each file is saved separately and your PCX stays as it is.

### Other ways to convert PCX to JPG

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick archive.pcx archive.jpg`. Its formats page marks both PCX and JPEG as readable and writable.
- **Pillow:** in Python, run `Image.open("clipart.pcx").convert("RGB").save("clipart.jpg")` after `from PIL import Image`. The `convert("RGB")` call turns a palette image into RGB before the JPEG is written.

### Problems with PCX files

- **A program rejects the file:** newer software sometimes drops PCX support while handling modern bitmaps. Convert it with one of the tools above.
- **Saving back to PCX:** Pillow's PCX writer accepts monochrome, grayscale, palette and RGB data, not arbitrary channel arrangements.
- **A DCX read as one PCX:** treating a DCX as a single PCX loses the document's multiple-image structure.

guide.title: About PCX and PNG
guide.markdown:
### What is a PCX file?

PCX is a raster image format created by ZSoft for its PC Paintbrush program. It emerged for MS-DOS around 1984 and 1985 and uses run-length encoding, with 1 to 24 bits per pixel and often a palette. Each PCX opens with a 128-byte header, and some variants carry an additional palette at the end. It survives in legacy DOS and Windows graphics and old clip art collections. A DCX document groups PCX pictures, commonly for fax applications.

### Programs that open PCX files

- **Windows:** ImageMagick lists PCX reading and writing, and IrfanView opens PCX.
- **Mac:** Pillow reads and writes PCX in its documented supported modes, and XnView MP opens PCX.
- **Linux:** GIMP opens PCX.

ImageMagick and Pillow are each listed on all three desktop systems.

### PCX and PNG compared

- **Compression**: PCX is run-length encoded; PNG is a lossless format.
- **Colors**: PCX is often palette-based. PNG supports 8-bit and 16-bit channels and alpha transparency.
- **Origin**: PCX dates from the 1980s on DOS. PNG followed in the mid-1990s and is standardized as ISO/IEC 15948 and a W3C Recommendation.
- **Typical use**: PCX turns up in old clip art collections. PNG suits screenshots, logos and web graphics that must stay sharp.
- **Structure**: a PCX begins with a 128-byte header, while a PNG starts with a fixed signature and is built from chunks.
- **Lineage**: PNG arrived as the patent-free replacement for GIF, and its media type is image/png.
- **Support**: PNG is supported by every browser. Applications may omit PCX even when they open newer bitmap formats.

This page uses ImageMagick as WebAssembly on the main thread. It reads one image and sets no quality.

### Other ways to convert PCX to PNG

- **ImageMagick:** `magick drawing.pcx drawing.png` on your own machine.
- **Pillow (Python):** call Image.open on the PCX, then save it under a .png name.

### Problems with PCX files

- **An application will not open it**: some programs have dropped PCX support while still opening newer bitmap formats, so convert to a current one.
- **A fax set looks like one page**: reading a DCX as though it were one PCX loses the document's multiple-image structure.

guide.title: About PDF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PDF file?

PDF stands for Portable Document Format, and Adobe made it. The idea came out of John Warnock's Camelot project, started in 1991, and by 1992 it was PDF. Warnock wanted one file that any application could produce and any device could show or print identically. The way it draws a page derives from PostScript and is free of any device or resolution. ISO took in PDF 1.7 as standard 32000-1 in 2008, then PDF 2.0 as 32000-2 in 2017.

Inside, a PDF blends text, vector drawings and raster pictures, plus links, bookmarks, form fields, annotations and media. Images in it can be compressed losslessly with Flate or with JPEG. Fonts have to be embedded for the pages to match on every machine. Particular jobs have their own subsets, namely PDF/A to archive, PDF/X to print and PDF/UA for accessibility. You meet PDFs as forms and contracts, as e-books and as print-ready files. The difference between real text and a picture of text matters here: a scanned invoice looks readable to you but gives a converter no characters.

### Programs that open PDF files

**Windows**

- GIMP: brings PDF pages in as images, and wants the password for a protected file.

**Mac**

- Apple Preview: shows pages and thumbnails.

**Linux**

- Evince: the GNOME document viewer.
- Okular: renders through Poppler.

**Web**

- Acrobat online: opens an uploaded PDF in the browser for annotation, and may need an account.

**Mobile**

- Adobe Acrobat Reader shows PDFs on both Android and iOS, and a PDF saved on an Android device opens in Firefox for Android.

**Windows and Mac**

- Firefox: has a built-in PDF viewer with annotations.

### PDF and HTML compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .pdf uses application/pdf.
- **What each stores**: a PDF fixes where each word and picture sits on a page. HTML describes a document's structure with elements and attributes, and CSS supplies how it looks.
- **Who maintains it**: ISO 32000 for PDF, and the WHATWG's Living Standard for HTML.
- **Resources**: a PDF embeds fonts and images. The HTML this page writes holds only text and one inline style, so it has no separate files to lose when you move it.

This converter writes one HTML page from the PDF's text. Each source page becomes a section, and each paragraph a p element. A paragraph breaks at an empty line, at a font size change of more than a fifth, or at a gap well above the page's usual line spacing, and a word split with a hyphen at a line's end keeps its hyphen. Nothing else survives: no images, tables, links, annotations or form fields.

### Other ways to convert PDF to HTML

- **Poppler pdftohtml (command line):** run `pdftohtml input.pdf output.html`. The `-s` option makes one HTML file for all pages, `-c` asks for complex output and `-i` skips images. It writes into the current working directory.
- **pdf2htmlEX (command line):** run `pdf2htmlEX input.pdf`, which writes an HTML file named after the PDF into the current directory, or into the folder you give with `--dest-dir`. For CJK characters it needs `poppler-data`, which it bundles a copy of.

Choose one of these when you need more than the text, for example the images, and this page when you want the words as light HTML.

### Problems with PDF files

- **No words to extract**: the PDF is a scan or blank. Use an OCR program first. When only some pages lack text, this page converts the rest and names the ones without.
- **Two columns run together**: the PDF stores text in a different order than you see it. Compare the HTML with the page, especially where a sentence crosses a column.
- **A password blocks it**: open the PDF with the password in a viewer and save or print an unprotected copy.
- **A damaged PDF is refused**: a file that is empty, isn't a PDF or is cut short past repair stops with a message saying it may be damaged or incomplete.
- **A viewer shows wrong fonts or a blank page**: Firefox can do this with some PDFs. Download the file and try another viewer.
- **A site's PDF won't open in Firefox**: an incorrect MIME type on the server can stop Firefox from using its viewer. Download the file and open it from disk.
- **Asian characters disappear**: those fonts need character-map data this page doesn't include. Use another extractor for that file.

guide.title: About PDF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PDF file?

PDF, the Portable Document Format, is Adobe's answer to an old office problem: a document should look and print the same whatever program made it and whatever device opens it. It began as John Warnock's Camelot project in 1991, which had become PDF by 1992. Its imaging model comes from PostScript and doesn't depend on the screen or printer. ISO took up PDF 1.7 in 2008 as ISO 32000-1; PDF 2.0, ISO 32000-2, followed in 2017. Profiles for narrower jobs include PDF/A for archives, PDF/X for print and PDF/UA for accessibility.

People use PDF for forms and contracts, print-ready files and e-books.

Each page leaves as a PNG, a format made as a patent-free successor to GIF. A PNG is a W3C Recommendation and ISO/IEC 15948:2004, and it never throws pixels away, so the page you see is the page you save. The newest specification, which the W3C finalized on 24 June 2025, covers animated PNG, though a PDF page is a still, and it adds HDR color through the cICP chunk.

### Programs that open PDF files

- **Linux:** Evince and Okular are the Linux viewers; Okular renders PDF with Poppler.
- **Windows, Mac and web:** Mozilla Firefox opens PDFs in its own reader, which supports annotations.
- **Windows:** GIMP imports a PDF's pages as images, asking for a password if the file needs one.
- **Mac:** Apple Preview displays PDF pages and their thumbnails.
- **Web:** Adobe Acrobat online takes an uploaded PDF for annotations, with account requirements to check.
- **Mobile:** Firefox for Android shows PDFs kept on the device, and Adobe Acrobat Reader works with them on Android and iOS.

### PDF and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .pdf with application/pdf; .png with image/png.
- **What the file holds**: a PDF contains pages where text, vector graphics, pictures, links, bookmarks, form fields and annotations can sit together. A PNG holds one grid of pixels.
- **Resolution**: a PDF page doesn't depend on the device or its resolution, while a PNG has a fixed pixel count. Converting therefore fixes the resolution: here, at most twice the page's size.
- **Fonts**: a PDF looks the same everywhere only when it embeds its fonts. A PNG has no fonts, only the drawn result.
- **Compression**: pictures inside a PDF use Flate or JPEG. PNG is always lossless DEFLATE, so the drawn page is saved without further loss.
- **Color**: a PNG may be palette-based, grayscale or truecolor, with a depth of 1 to 16 bits per sample.
- **Transparency**: PNG supports an alpha channel, but pages from this converter get an opaque white background.
- **Inside the file**: every PNG begins with a fixed signature; chunks follow: a header chunk (IHDR), the pixel data in IDAT chunks, and a closing IEND chunk.
- **Pages**: one PDF, many pages; here every page gets its own PNG, called name_page1 for the first, name_page2 for the second and so on, with no page limit.

### Other ways to convert PDF to PNG

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac and Linux):** in the PDF Import dialog, choose the pages and resolution and set Open pages as to Images. Then use File > Export As to save a page as a PNG.
- **ImageMagick (terminal):** `magick input.pdf output.png` does it. ImageMagick lists PDF as readable only when Ghostscript is installed.

### Problems with PDF files

- **A protected PDF**: GIMP's PDF import asks for the password when a file needs one, so open it there and export the pages.
- **Fonts look different from the original**: ask the sender for a copy of the PDF with its fonts embedded.
- **A poster or drawing comes out small**: pages are capped at about 16.8 megapixels, so a very large page gets less than twice its size. GIMP's import resolution gives more pixels.
- **Wrong fonts or blank pages in a viewer**: Firefox can show some PDFs with the wrong fonts or blank pages. Save the PDF and try another viewer before converting.
- **See-through areas came out white**: this page paints every page on white. GIMP keeps them see-through unless you tick its white-fill option.
- **A long PDF floods your downloads**: every page is its own file, so a 100-page PDF gives 100 PNGs. Delete the pages you don't need afterwards.

guide.title: About PDF and TXT files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PDF file?

PDF is a document format made by Adobe. Its roots lie in Camelot, a project John Warnock began in 1991 that had become PDF by 1992. The goal was a file that captures a document from any application and shows or prints it the same way anywhere. The ISO 32000-1 standard of 2008 is PDF 1.7, and ISO 32000-2 of 2017 is PDF 2.0. Its media type is application/pdf.

Besides text, a PDF can hold vector graphics and raster images, plus links, bookmarks, form fields and annotations. To look the same everywhere it needs its fonts embedded. The text is stored as drawing instructions positioned on a page, which is why pulling it out takes some work: a PDF page is not a paragraph in a word processor. Scans are different again, because a scan is an image of text, not text. Adobe's own help notes that scan imagery is distinct from extractable text, so a page can look full of words and still give a TXT nothing.

### Programs that open PDF files

**Windows and Mac**

- Mozilla Firefox: built-in PDF viewing and annotations.

**Windows**

- GIMP: imports PDF pages, and asks for the password of a protected file.

**Mac**

- Apple Preview: shows PDF pages and thumbnails.

**Linux**

- Evince and Okular, which uses Poppler to render PDF.

**Web and Mobile**

- Adobe Acrobat: the online version lets you annotate an uploaded PDF in the browser, and Acrobat Reader views PDFs on Android and iOS.

**Mobile**

- Firefox for Android opens PDFs stored on the device.

### PDF and TXT compared

- **File names and media types**: .pdf is application/pdf and .txt is text/plain.
- **Layout**: a PDF has fixed pages and embedded fonts. A TXT has no layout at all.
- **Content**: a PDF holds text, graphics and images. A TXT holds text only.
- **Encoding**: this page writes the TXT as UTF-8.
- **What carries over**: the words, taken in storage order, which is usually reading order. A line ends where pdf.js marks one, and its spaces are collapsed.
- **What is lost**: layout, fonts, tables, images, links, annotations and form fields.
- **Line breaks**: a TXT can hold only lines and blank lines. A paragraph's lines stay on lines of their own, with a blank line after each paragraph and between pages.
- **Hyphens**: a word broken at a line's end keeps its hyphen in the TXT.

The page reads each page's text with pdf.js. A paragraph ends at an empty line, where the next line is higher up the page, where the font size changes by more than a fifth (a heading), or where the gap to the next line is much larger than the page's usual spacing.

### Other ways to convert PDF to TXT

- **pdftotext (Poppler):** run `pdftotext input.pdf output.txt`. The command converts a PDF to plain text, and without a second name it writes a file named after the PDF with .txt.
- **PyMuPDF (Python):** follow the "Extract all Document Text" recipe. It opens the PDF, joins the page.get_text() string of every page with a form feed and writes the encoded text to a file. The recipe warns that text may not come out in reading order.
- **Preview and TextEdit (Mac):** in Preview choose Tools > Text Selection, select text and use Edit > Copy. Paste into TextEdit and choose Format > Make Plain Text before saving. This suits an excerpt, not a whole PDF.

### Problems with PDF files

- **No text comes out**: a scan or photo has no text layer. Run OCR first, then convert. The converter does none.
- **A password is asked for**: the PDF needs one to open. Remove it in a reader, then convert the copy.
- **Columns come out mixed**: the PDF stores columns a row at a time. Copy the columns by hand or use a layout-preserving tool.
- **Chinese, Japanese or Korean text is missing**: text in a font with no Unicode map that relies on one of Adobe's predefined CMaps is dropped here, and a PDF with only such text is refused as having none.
- **Words are out of order**: pdf.js follows the order inside the file, usually but not always reading order. Check a page or two.
- **A file will not open at all**: the file could be damaged, truncated or not a PDF at all. The page calls it unreadable. Download it again.

guide.title: PES to JPG: format guide
guide.markdown:
### What is a PES file?

A PES file holds embroidery data for Brother's PE-DESIGN workflow, and Brother and Babylock machines use it. It stores stitch coordinates, a thread color palette and a design preview. PE-DESIGN 11 can show PES designs as thumbnails in Explorer in its full edition, and files saved by that version may be larger because they contain more design information. Ink/Stitch can both import and export PES, and Brother's Artspira app accepts PES files on iOS and Android. A PES describes stitches, not a grid of pixels.

### Programs that open PES files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Ink/Stitch is a free embroidery extension for Inkscape with PES import and export.
- **Windows:** PE-DESIGN 11 is Brother's application; its trial has restricted features.
- **Mobile:** Artspira accepts PES uploads on iOS and Android.

### PES and JPG compared

JPEG is a lossy picture format from the Joint Photographic Experts Group, standardized as ITU-T T.81 in 1992. It stores 8 bits per color channel, has no transparency and cannot hold layers. A JPG is a flat picture, so it cannot carry thread colors, stitch order or machine instructions, and it works only as a preview of the design. The media type is image/jpeg.

On this page the browser's own image decoder gets the file, and it stops on a PES with "Image decode failed." To get a JPG of a design, use software that draws the stitches, such as the programs below, and keep your PES for the sewing machine.

### Other ways to convert PES to JPG

### What is a PES file?

Brother created PES for its embroidery machines, and Babylock machines use it too. Inside are the stitch coordinates, the thread colors and a small preview of the design. That is a sewing recipe for a machine, not a grid of pixels. In the full edition of Brother's PE-DESIGN 11, PES designs also appear as thumbnails in Explorer.

### Programs that open PES files

- **Windows:** PE-DESIGN 11, Brother's own application (its trial limits some features).
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Ink/Stitch, a free extension for Inkscape that imports and exports PES.
- **iOS and Android:** Artspira, Brother's own app, takes PES files.

### PES and PNG compared

A PNG is a raster picture, losslessly compressed, with optional transparency, and every major browser shows it. To get from PES to PNG, a program has to draw the stitches as an image. A sewing machine can't use that picture, so hold on to the PES.

Nothing on this page can draw it. Files are opened by your browser's built-in image decoder, and it has no idea what embroidery data is. Choosing a PES ends in the message "Image decode failed." and no PNG appears. The programs below do the job.

### Other ways to convert PES to PNG

- **Ink/Stitch and Inkscape:** use File > Open on the PES; it opens in Manual Stitch Mode. Then press Shift+Ctrl+E to open the Export PNG Image dialog, export the page, all drawn objects, the selected objects or a custom area, then enter the size in pixels, name the file and click Export.
- **pyembroidery:** in this Python library, `pyembroidery.write_png(pyembroidery.read_pes("design.pes"), "design.png")` reads the PES and writes the PNG. PNG is write-only there.

### Problems with PES files

- **Image decode failed:** that is the browser telling you PES isn't a picture format. Use an embroidery program.
- **The machine can't hold the design:** big designs can overflow a machine's USB storage; Brother recommends a USB flash drive where the machine supports one.
- **Large files:** Brother's support page says PE-DESIGN 11 puts more design information into a PES, which can make the file bigger.
- **More than 255 color changes:** Ink/Stitch's FAQ says a PES file can't save more.

guide.title: About PGM files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PGM file?

PGM stands for Portable Gray Map. It is the grayscale member of the Netpbm family and stores one gray value for each pixel. A raw PGM begins with P5 and keeps its samples in binary form. A plain PGM begins with P2 and writes each sample as decimal text. When the Maxval in the header is above 255, every raw sample takes two bytes.

Netpbm also uses PGM for opacity masks, with a different reading of the sample values. The conventional media type is image/x-portable-graymap, which IANA has not registered. People meet PGM in image-processing experiments and in grayscale image interchange.

### Programs that open PGM files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- ImageMagick: reads and writes the PGM member of the Netpbm family.
- Netpbm: provides programs and libnetpbm for processing graymaps.

### PGM and PNG compared

- **Content**: a PGM holds gray samples and nothing else. A PNG can hold gray, color and an alpha channel.
- **Encoding**: PGM is either plain text or binary. PNG compresses its data without loss.
- **Depth**: a raw PGM uses one byte per sample up to a Maxval of 255 and two bytes above it. PNG allows 8-bit and 16-bit channels.
- **Reach**: every browser supports PNG, while PGM belongs to image tools.

Here a PGM goes through ImageMagick in your browser and comes out as a PNG. The step adds no filter, and it writes eight bits per sample.

### Other ways to convert PGM to PNG

- **Netpbm:** run pnmtopng measurement.pgm > measurement.png. The program maps the file's maximum value to a PNG depth.
- **ImageMagick:** run magick measurement.pgm review.png.
- **GIMP:** use File > Export As, add .png to the file name and confirm with Export. GIMP's PNM reader loads plain and raw files, and the export dialog that follows offers PNG options.

### Problems with PGM files

- **A program rejects the file**: older readers may refuse samples deeper than eight bits. The pamdepth program from Netpbm can reduce the Maxval.
- **Only the first image shows**: some readers stop after one image, although a raw PGM may hold a sequence.
- **The grays look wrong**: linear-light and sRGB variants can display differently from the BT.709 reading the specification describes.
