guide.title: Understanding PNG and AI
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

A PNG, short for Portable Network Graphics, stores a picture as a grid of pixels with lossless compression, so the saved samples come back exactly. It supports indexed, grayscale and truecolor images, plus an optional alpha channel for transparency. The first W3C Recommendation for it dates from October 1996.

You come across PNG as screenshots, interface graphics, icons and logos with clean edges. A designer who asks you for an AI file usually wants more than a PNG: paths they can edit, text they can retype and shapes that scale. A PNG cannot give them that on its own, because it holds colored dots and not outlines.

AI is the file designers use for logos, illustrations and print layouts. People search for "PNG to AI" for three reasons: a printer or client asked for an .ai file, they want to open a picture in Illustrator, or they hope to turn a flat logo into editable shapes. This page writes an .ai file that holds your picture. It cannot do the third.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows:** the Photos app opens PNG files for viewing.
- **Mac:** Preview opens PNG files for viewing, and a Mac screenshot is a PNG unless you change the setting.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP loads a PNG for editing, and ImageMagick decodes one in a terminal.
- **Web:** every major browser shows a PNG inline.
- **Mobile:** phone browsers display one too.

### PNG and AI compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .png and image/png; .ai, which this page writes as application/pdf.
- **What each holds**: a PNG is pixels only. A native AI file combines vector objects and pixel images, and it keeps editable effects, brushes, layers and transparency.
- **Origin**: AI is Adobe Illustrator's native artwork format. Illustrator 9 changed it in 2000, and earlier files used PostScript.
- **Color depth**: a PNG can hold more than 8 bits per channel; the file made here keeps 8.
- **PDF compatibility**: Illustrator can save an AI with a PDF rendition inside. An AI file saved without it may fail in third-party software.

The file this page writes is simpler than a native AI. It is a PDF page made by embedding your PNG losslessly, with the .ai extension, and it begins like any PDF. Each pixel of your PNG gets one point of page, with no margin around it. The PNG is first decoded to 8-bit pixels, which leaves metadata and any extra bit depth behind, and see-through areas are carried over as a soft mask.

A program that reads the PDF does not necessarily see native Illustrator objects, because there are none. Nothing is traced and no text becomes editable. You may choose several PNGs together: they are processed in sequence, each producing a separate .ai without any archive.

Two cautions apply to AI files you make yourself in Illustrator. Linked images remain external unless Include Linked Files is selected while saving, whereas the picture here is embedded, so nothing is left to link. And artwork opened in an older Illustrator version can cause compatibility problems, so Adobe advises matching or newer versions.

### Other ways to convert PNG to AI

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick logo.png logo.ai`. ImageMagick's format list marks both PNG and AI as readable and writable, and describes AI as Adobe Illustrator CS2. This keeps the picture as pixels; it does not trace paths, and its output is ImageMagick's own rather than the file this page builds.

### Problems with PNG files

- **The logo looks jagged when enlarged**: a PNG has a fixed pixel count, so enlarging only makes the pixels bigger. Find a larger original or a vector source.
- **The file is bigger than expected**: PNG compression is lossless, so a smaller compression setting does not reduce pixel fidelity.
- **Camera tags and profiles are missing**: GIMP writes them only when its export dialog asks for them, so switch on the metadata options when you need them.
- **Layers sit in the wrong place**: GIMP and other programs can place layer offsets differently, so skip GIMP's PNG offset option.
- **An animated PNG shows one frame**: a viewer with no animation support falls back to the still default image, and this page likewise keeps only the first frame.

guide.title: About PNG and AVIF
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

GIF relied on a patented algorithm, and PNG (Portable Network Graphics) was created to replace it for lossless web images. In October 1996 PNG became the first format to be published as a W3C Recommendation; RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948 followed. A file starts with a fixed signature, then runs in chunks: IHDR holds the header, IDAT carries the image data and IEND closes the file. Its compressor is DEFLATE, which pairs LZ77 matching with Huffman codes, and no pixel data is thrown away.

Samples can be 1 to 16 bits wide, in indexed, grayscale or truecolor images, with an optional alpha channel. The current specification also describes animated PNG (APNG); a viewer without animation support displays a single fallback frame. Since June 2025 the third edition has been a W3C Recommendation; it introduces HDR signaling through a cICP chunk and a place for Exif data, the eXIf chunk. Screenshots, interface art and logos that need clear backgrounds are the typical material, and macOS saves screenshots as PNG by default. PNG is not known to be covered by royalty-bearing patents, and every big browser can show it.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - GIMP imports a PNG for editing.
  - ImageMagick reads PNG from the command line.
- **Web and Mobile:**
  - Google Chrome displays PNG.
- **Web:**
  - Mozilla Firefox displays PNG.
- **Mobile:**
  - Safari displays PNG.

### PNG and AVIF compared

- **Names and types**: PNG files end in .png (image/png, or image/apng for animated ones). AVIF files end in .avif.
- **Compression**: PNG is lossless without exception. AVIF stores AV1-compressed images in the HEIF container and can be lossy or lossless.
- **Alpha**: both support alpha transparency.
- **Depth**: a PNG sample is 1 to 16 bits wide. AVIF supports 10-bit and 12-bit depth, aimed at HDR and wide-gamut pictures.
- **Motion**: PNG has APNG; AVIF can hold image sequences.
- **Metadata**: since its third edition, PNG allows Exif data in an eXIf chunk.
- **Support**: every major browser shows PNG. Chrome 85 and Firefox 93 were the first to decode AVIF, Safari on iOS 16 added still AVIF images, and Android 12 and later decode baseline 8-bit AVIF. A browser that decodes AVIF does not guarantee that every app or operating system viewer opens the same file.

The page decodes the PNG with the browser's own decoder into 8-bit RGBA pixels and encodes those pixels as AVIF. That is why an animated PNG contributes only its first frame and no metadata is copied. The encoder is the browser's canvas where the browser can write AVIF, and ImageMagick where it cannot. AVIF is used for web images that need small files and for HDR and wide-gamut images.

### Other ways to convert PNG to AVIF

- **GIMP:** Open the PNG in GIMP, press Shift+Ctrl+E for File > Export As and pick AVIF as the type. GIMP added AVIF import and export in release 2.10.22, and its news post says HEIF files, AVIF included, can be handled at 10 and 12 bits per channel, so older releases lack the AVIF exporter.

guide.title: About BMP files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

The PNG format was designed to replace GIF without patent worries. In October 1996 it became the first image format the W3C published as a Recommendation, after which it was issued as RFC 2083 and again as ISO/IEC 15948:2004. A third edition of the specification reached Recommendation status on 24 June 2025. Its compression never discards anything; it uses DEFLATE, which combines LZ77 with Huffman coding.

A PNG file starts with a set signature and continues as a series of chunks, among them IHDR (header), IDAT (pixel data) and IEND (the end). Pixel data can be indexed, grayscale or truecolor, at 1 to 16 bits a sample, with an optional alpha channel for per-pixel transparency. The current specification includes animated PNG (APNG); software without animation shows the default still frame instead. All major browsers display PNG, and macOS saves its screenshots as PNG.

People ask for this conversion when a program, device or assignment wants a bitmap. The two formats hold the same kind of thing, a grid of pixels, so the picture stays the same; what changes is how it is stored. PNG's third edition also adds HDR support through the cICP chunk and allows Exif metadata in an eXIf chunk, but neither is carried into the BMP here.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows and Mac**

- GIMP: opens PNG for editing.

**Windows**

- Windows Photos: opens PNG.

**Mac**

- Preview: the built-in viewer on macOS.

**Linux**

- ImageMagick: reads PNG.

**Web**

- Any web browser, such as Chrome or Firefox, displays PNG.

**Mobile**

- Safari and Chrome display PNG on a phone.

### PNG and BMP compared

The BMP raster family belongs to Microsoft, was first used on Windows and OS/2, and reached version 5 with Windows 98 in 1998. Version 5 is able to store an ICC profile and an alpha channel. You will most often run into BMP in Windows screen captures and system graphics. The registered media type is image/bmp. To open the BMP you get, ImageMagick reads it, XnView MP supports BMP too (company use needs a license), and Firefox displays BMP in the browser.

- **Compression**: PNG is always lossless and compressed. A BMP usually holds uncompressed pixels, though lossless compression exists, so it tends to be much larger.
- **Transparency**: PNG has an optional alpha channel. BMP version 5 can record an alpha channel, but this page doesn't keep PNG transparency.
- **Color profile**: BMP version 5 can store an ICC profile. The page drops ICC, EXIF and XMP data.
- **Depth**: A PNG can use up to 16 bits per sample, while this page writes 8 bits per channel.
- **Origin**: PNG is a W3C and ISO standard. BMP comes from Microsoft.
- **Media type**: image/png and image/bmp.

On this page the browser decodes your PNG and ImageMagick writes the BMP from the pixels. There is no BMP version, depth or compression option. An animated PNG gives its first frame only, and the page sets no size limit. The original PNG is not changed, so you can always make another BMP from it later.

### Other ways to convert PNG to BMP

- **GIMP:** load the PNG, pick File > Export As, put .bmp at the end of the Name field, then click Export.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick input.png output.bmp`. ImageMagick's format list says the default is version 4, and that BMP3 and BMP2 write versions 3 and 2. For an older program that expects a version-three header, run `magick input.png BMP3:output.bmp`. In a local run, the default wrote a Windows 98/2000 and newer header and BMP3 wrote a Windows 3.x header.
- **XnConvert:** load the PNG into the Input list, choose a folder and BMP under Output, and click Convert.

### Problems with PNG files

- **Transparent areas change**: the page does not keep PNG transparency in the BMP. Check the result over the background you plan to use.
- **A 16-bit PNG loses depth**: the BMP gets 8 bits per channel, so the extra precision does not survive.
- **Color looks different**: the PNG's ICC profile isn't carried over, and neither are EXIF and XMP.
- **An animated PNG gives one still**: only the first frame is written. Keep the PNG for the motion.
- **A small PNG becomes a large bitmap**: PNG packs repeated colors efficiently, such as flat areas in a screenshot, and a mostly uncompressed BMP doesn't. PNG or JPEG is usually more practical for distribution.
- **An older program refuses the BMP**: it may expect an older bitmap header. This page writes ImageMagick's default version; BMP3 or BMP2 output covers older programs.
- **"Image decode failed." appears**: this browser couldn't read that file. Try the original PNG.

guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

Replacing GIF without its patent problem was the goal of PNG. PNG was the first format to receive W3C Recommendation status, in October 1996, and it was later issued as RFC 2083 and as ISO/IEC 15948:2004. A W3C Recommendation dated 24 June 2025 made the specification's third edition official. Lossless DEFLATE compression, a mix of LZ77 and Huffman coding, is the only kind PNG uses.

Following a fixed signature, a PNG is made of chunks; the header chunk is IHDR, the pixel data lives in IDAT and IEND closes the file. Samples of 1 to 16 bits are supported in indexed, grayscale and truecolor images, with an optional alpha channel giving per-pixel transparency. Registered media types are image/png, with image/apng for animated files. With the third edition, HDR is handled by the cICP chunk and Exif metadata may sit in an eXIf chunk.

No royalty-bearing patents are known to cover PNG, and all major browsers display it. By default, macOS stores screenshots as PNG. Screenshots, interface graphics, logos and images with transparency are common PNG material, which is why a PNG often becomes the starting point for a cursor.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Linux and Mac:** GIMP opens PNG files so you can edit them.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick lists PNG as a readable format, so see your install's format support.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos opens PNG.
- **Mac:** Preview opens PNG.
- **Web:** PNG displays in Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox.
- **Mobile:** Phones show PNG in Safari and Chrome.

To check a finished cursor, ImageMagick lists CUR as a readable format. On Windows, the Visual Studio Image Editor views and edits cursor resources, although 32-bit images can be viewed but not edited there. XnView MP, free for private and educational use, lists CUR among its supported formats on Mac and Linux.

### PNG and CUR compared

- **Extensions and media types**: PNG files use .png, and .cur is the Windows cursor container.
- **Purpose**: PNG is a general image format. CUR is made for pointers, and a conventional image format is more suitable when hotspot information is unnecessary.
- **Hotspot**: a CUR is related to ICO but includes coordinates for the active pointer location. PNG has no such coordinate.
- **Sizes**: a CUR may embed several images at different dimensions, each with its own hotspot. A PNG is one image.
- **Color and transparency**: PNG has an optional alpha channel for transparency, and the CUR sheet lists alpha transparency among the properties of a cursor file.
- **Animation**: animated cursor assets use ANI rather than the ordinary CUR workflow.

On this page, the browser decodes the PNG and ImageMagick writes the CUR. One image goes in and one comes out. A larger picture is scaled down until it fits, because the format stores each side in one byte, and a picture at the full 256 px is held as PNG data. The page has no hotspot control. Metadata is not copied, and the picture is decoded to 8-bit pixels first.

### Other ways to convert PNG to CUR

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the PNG and choose File > Export As. Replace the extension in the Name field with .cur, or choose it under Select File Type, then export. The Windows cursor dialog lets you set the save type for each size, the Compressed (PNG) option, and Hot spot X and Hot spot Y.
- **Axialis CursorWorkshop:** open the PNG, select the area you want, and choose Image > Create New Cursor from Selection. Pick the image formats in the New Cursor From Image dialog, then use Draw > Set Cursor Hot Spot and click at the hotspot position.
- **SixLabors ImageSharp (.NET):** load the PNG, set HotspotX and HotspotY on `image.Frames.RootFrame.Metadata.GetCurMetadata()`, and save with `new CurEncoder()` to a .cur file. ImageSharp's page says to choose hotspots from the cursor design, not to copy them from another size.

### Problems with PNG files

- **A smaller compression setting changes nothing**: PNG compression is lossless, so a smaller setting does not reduce pixel fidelity.
- **Layers sit at the wrong offset**: GIMP and other applications can disagree about layer offsets, so leave GIMP's PNG offset option off.
- **Camera tags are missing**: GIMP exports camera tags and profiles only when asked, so turn on the matching metadata controls if you need them.
- **The picture doesn't move**: software that cannot animate shows an animated PNG's default still image.

guide.title: About PNG and DDS files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

Portable Network Graphics, shortened to PNG, began as a patent-free answer to GIF. October 1996 brought its W3C Recommendation, the first for any format, and RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948:2004 followed. Its compression, DEFLATE, is always lossless, so a PNG can be saved again with no loss of pixels. Every PNG opens with a fixed signature and then runs as a series of chunks: IHDR holds the header, IDAT the image data and IEND ends the file.

Indexed, grayscale and truecolor images are all allowed, using 1 to 16 bits per sample and optionally an alpha channel that gives each pixel its own transparency. Animated PNG (APNG) is covered by the current specification too, and software with no animation support shows the default still image instead. image/png is the media type, and animated files use image/apng. Browsers all display PNG, and screenshots on macOS are saved as PNG unless you change it.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Linux, Mac and Windows**

- GIMP: brings PNG in for editing.
- ImageMagick: reads PNG, so check which formats your install supports.

**Web**

- Mozilla Firefox shows PNG pictures.

**Web and Mobile**

- Google Chrome shows PNG pictures.

**Mobile**

- Safari displays PNG on phones and tablets.

### PNG and DDS compared

- **Extensions**: .png against .dds.
- **Purpose**: PNG is a picture for screens and the web. DDS is Microsoft's DirectDraw Surface texture-file format, made for GPU texture pipelines such as Direct3D.
- **Compression**: PNG is always lossless. DDS stores either plain pixels or compressed texture data, typically the DXT/BC block formats.
- **Mipmaps**: a DDS asset may include a mipmap chain alongside its largest surface. PNG holds one image.
- **Other surfaces**: Cube maps and volume textures fit in a DDS; texture arrays arrive with the extra header of Direct3D 10 and 11.
- **Transparency**: PNG has an alpha channel. A DDS can have one too.
- **Headers**: the DX10 header can describe formats the original pixel-format structure cannot express, and some DDS readers reject it.
- **Metadata**: PNG can carry Exif in an eXIf chunk. Metadata is not carried into the DDS written here.

This page decodes the PNG in your browser to 8-bit RGBA pixels and passes them to ImageMagick, which writes the DDS. The page does not ask for a compression format or mipmaps, and the file you get depends on ImageMagick's DDS writer.

The download takes the PNG's name with .dds in place of .png.

### Other ways to convert PNG to DDS

- **DirectXTex texconv (Windows):** run `texconv -ft dds -f BC3_UNORM input.png`. Add `-m 1` if you want only one mip level. By default it generates all levels, and the format has to match your renderer.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the PNG, choose File > Export As, select DDS among the file types, then click Export. The DDS settings dialog comes up next. The DDS plug-in has been built into GIMP since 2.10.10.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.png output.dds`. Its formats page marks DDS as supported for reading and writing, and mentions dxt1, dxt5 and mipmap defines.

Choose texconv or GIMP when the engine fixes the format, since both let you pick it.

### Problems with PNG files

- **The extra depth of a 16-bit PNG is lost**: the pixels pass through 8-bit color on the way to the DDS, so the DDS holds the 8-bit version.
- **An animated PNG is cut to one frame**: the first. The DDS written here is a single still texture.
- **EXIF, ICC and XMP data does not carry over**: raw pixels are all that is passed along, which leaves camera tags and profiles behind.
- **PNG compression does not reduce fidelity**: a smaller compression setting in an export dialog changes file size, not pixels.
- **Layer offsets differ between programs**: GIMP warns that its PNG offset option may be read differently by other applications, so avoid that option.
- **The PNG is very large**: no limit is built into the page, so time and memory depend on your device.
- **Several PNGs**: each becomes its own DDS, and they download one by one.
- **The PNG will not open**: the page shows "Image decode failed." for a damaged file, or reports that the browser has no decoder for that kind of file. A current release of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari should open it.

### What is a PNG file?

A PNG records an image as a grid of pixels. Whether it holds a screenshot, a scanned letter, a diagram or a logo with see-through corners, the format knows nothing of words, so a screenshot of a paragraph is colored dots and not text.

PNG began as a patent-free replacement for GIF. The World Wide Web Consortium published it as a Recommendation in October 1996, and ISO published it as standard 15948. It compresses with DEFLATE without losing data, stores 1 to 16 bits per sample and may include an alpha channel. A file starts with a fixed signature and then runs in chunks. PNG is the usual choice for screenshots, interface graphics, logos with transparent areas and any web image that must stay crisp, and macOS saves its screenshots as PNG by default. The current specification also covers animated PNG, and its third edition, a W3C Recommendation since June 2025, allows Exif metadata in an eXIf chunk. PNG carries no known royalty-bearing patents, and every major browser displays it.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:**
  - GIMP, a free editor, imports PNG for editing.
  - ImageMagick, a command-line tool, reads PNG.
- **Web and Mobile:**
  - Google Chrome displays PNG.
- **Web:**
  - Mozilla Firefox displays PNG.
- **Mobile:**
  - Safari displays PNG.

### PNG and DOCX compared

- **Names**: .png for the image, .docx for the document.
- **Purpose**: DOCX has been Microsoft Word's default format since Word 2007, and people use it for letters, reports, resumes and contracts. It can hold styles, images, tables, tracked changes and comments.
- **What each stores**: a PNG is one picture. A DOCX is a ZIP-based Open XML package with document parts and media parts, and an image sits in a part of its own.
- **Standards**: DOCX is specified in ECMA-376 and ISO/IEC 29500, while PNG answers to ISO/IEC 15948 and the W3C.
- **Text**: a PNG holds pixels, while the DOCX can hold typed text, styles and tables. This page writes none of that: pixel data differs from document text and layout.
- **Transparency**: a PNG can have an alpha channel, and the DOCX carries the PNG data unchanged.

The page makes a new Word document with one paragraph holding your PNG as an inline picture. Each pixel counts as one 96th of an inch, and a picture too big for the box of 6.5 by 9 inches is shrunk, with its proportions kept, until it fits. It never grows beyond its own size. The PNG is not re-encoded, and no text is recognized from it. You can pick several PNG files at once, and each one becomes its own DOCX while your originals stay as they were.

The DOCX is a document that holds your picture and nothing more. The PNG does not become text, a table or shapes you can edit, so a screenshot of a report stays a screenshot. If you need the words in it, extract the text separately and paste it into the document.

guide.title: PNG to EPUB: formats and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

A PNG file follows the Portable Network Graphics design, created as a replacement for GIF that avoided its patent trouble. Autumn 1996 brought the W3C Recommendation for PNG, a first for any format the W3C had published, and ISO later issued it as ISO/IEC 15948. A PNG always compresses without loss, using the DEFLATE method, and it can carry an alpha channel for per-pixel transparency.

You come across PNG all the time because macOS saves screenshots in it by default. It is also the usual choice for interface graphics and logos, where sharp edges matter more than file size, and every major browser displays it. Newer editions of the specification also allow Exif metadata and animated PNG, and software that can't animate shows the file's default still image instead.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** for batch work, ImageMagick reads PNG from a terminal, which suits preparing many images at once, and GIMP opens it for editing while keeping its transparent areas.
- **Web:** Google Chrome and Mozilla Firefox draw a PNG on the page.
- **Mobile:** on an iPhone or iPad, PNG is displayed by Safari.

### PNG and EPUB compared

- **Extensions**: .png is image/png and .epub is application/epub+zip.
- **What each holds**: a PNG is one picture. An EPUB packages HTML, CSS and images in one ZIP container, with a reading order called the spine.
- **Text**: an EPUB can hold real text that reflows to the reader's screen. Words drawn into a PNG stay part of the picture.
- **Standard**: EPUB 3.3 is maintained as a W3C Recommendation.

This page writes an EPUB 3 package holding a single page. The PNG is stored in it unchanged, with no re-encoding, so the picture inside is byte for byte the PNG you chose. The book takes your file's name as its title, the picture's alt text matches it, and the language is English. It does not read the words in the picture. Pick several PNGs and each one becomes its own EPUB.

To open the result you need an e-book reader, because an image viewer won't show it. calibre's E-book viewer and Adobe Digital Editions run on Windows and Mac, Foliate on Linux, and Google Play Books in a browser or on a phone.

### Other ways to convert PNG to EPUB

- **LibreOffice Writer (Windows, Mac, Linux):** place the PNG with Insert > Image, then choose File > Export As > Export as EPUB. The export dialog has a layout method setting for a reflowable or a fixed layout EPUB. Add real text around the picture if readers need selectable captions.
- **Pandoc (command line):** write page.md with a Markdown image line (an exclamation mark, the description in square brackets, the PNG file name in parentheses), then run `pandoc page.md -o book.epub`. Pandoc includes local images linked from the Markdown in the EPUB it generates.
- **Pages (Mac):** click the Insert Media button, choose Photos or Videos to pick the PNG, then choose File > Export To > EPUB. The export dialog asks for a title and author and offers a cover option, and the Layout setting offers fixed or reflowable for word-processing documents.

These tools build a book around text you supply, so the image can sit between paragraphs, headings and captions. Use one of them when you want an author name, a cover or several images in one book.

### Problems with PNG files

- **Words in a screenshot**: the letters are pixels of the picture, so the book can't search them or read them aloud. Searching and text-to-speech need real text, which means retyping the content or running a separate text-recognition tool first.
- **A transparent diagram looks wrong**: see-through pixels show whatever page color the reader app draws behind them. Check white lines or text on both light and dark pages before you share the book.
- **Several PNGs became several books**: each file converts on its own. Use Writer, Pages or Pandoc when you want one book with a shared table of contents.
- **A PNG is very large**: a big screenshot makes a big EPUB, because the file is copied in whole. Shrink it in GIMP or with ImageMagick first if the book must stay small.
- **Layer offsets differ between programs**: GIMP's PNG export has an offset option, and other applications may place layers differently, so leave that option off if other people will open the file.
- **Camera tags and profiles**: a PNG export from GIMP omits them unless the metadata controls are switched on, so switch them on when you need them.

guide.title: About PNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

Designed to replace GIF without its patent baggage, PNG was published by the W3C as a Recommendation in October 1996, the first format to get that status. RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948:2004 followed, and the third edition of the specification arrived on 24 June 2025. Files start with a signature and continue as chunks; the header lives in IHDR, the pixels in IDAT and a closing IEND.

Nothing is thrown away in PNG: DEFLATE, a blend of LZ77 and Huffman coding, does the compressing. Pictures may be indexed, grayscale or truecolor at between 1 and 16 bits per sample, and an added alpha channel gives every pixel its own transparency. The third edition brought HDR support via the cICP chunk and room for Exif metadata in an eXIf chunk.

That makes PNG a good fit for screenshots and interface graphics, logos and images with transparency, and web graphics that must stay sharp. macOS saves screenshots as PNG by default.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows, macOS and Linux**

- GIMP imports PNG for editing.
- ImageMagick reads PNG.

**Windows**

- Windows Photos opens the format.

**macOS**

- Preview counts among the macOS viewers.

**Web and mobile**

- Chrome and Firefox display PNG in a page, and Chrome and Safari do so on phones.

### PNG and GIF compared

- **Extensions and media types**: image/png for .png (image/apng for animated files); image/gif for .gif.
- **Colors**: PNG allows up to 16 bits per sample and truecolor. A GIF picture draws from a palette capped at 256 colors.
- **Compression**: both are lossless. PNG uses DEFLATE and GIF uses LZW, which Unisys began licensing in 1994 before the patents ran out in 2003 and 2004.
- **Transparency**: PNG has a full alpha channel, so edges can fade out. GIF only lets one palette color be fully transparent.
- **Animation**: GIF can hold many frames with delays set in hundredths of a second. The current PNG specification covers animated PNG too, and software that cannot animate shows the default still image.
- **Typical use**: PNG fits screenshots and graphics you will edit again; GIF is for brief looping animations, plain graphics, icons, reaction images and stickers.
- **Age**: CompuServe introduced GIF in 1987, and the GIF89a version of July 1990 added extensions for transparency, frame timing, comments and application data.
- **Support**: every major browser displays both.
- **Bit depth**: each channel is held at 8 bits on the way through, so a 16-bit PNG loses its extra depth.

What changes in this conversion is the palette. The page decodes the PNG to pixels and writes a GIF, so anything beyond 256 colors is reduced, and animated PNGs reach the GIF as their first frame only.

### Other ways to convert PNG to GIF

- **GIMP:** with the PNG open, pick Export As from the File menu and finish the new name with .gif. The GIF dialog offers interlace, which lets an image on a web page appear progressively as it downloads, a comment, and As animation with loop forever, a delay and frame disposal. GIMP only exports a maximum of 256 colors, and its docs advise indexed mode first.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick input.png output.gif`. Its format list marks both PNG and GIF read and write, with GIF as 8-bit PseudoColor up to 256 palette entries.

### Problems with PNG files

- **Colors look banded after conversion**: the GIF has only 256 colors. A photo is a poor fit.
- **Soft edges turn jagged or gain a halo**: GIF can't keep partial opacity, so shadows and anti-aliased edges are flattened.
- **GIMP export looks different**: GIMP reduces a GIF export to no more than 256 colors, which can change gradients.
- **A palette you didn't pick**: this page reduces colors for you, while GIMP's docs advise setting indexed mode first, so the palette is chosen on purpose.
- **Layer offsets**: they may differ between GIMP and other programs, so avoid the PNG offset option.
- **Metadata is missing**: camera tags and profiles are optional in GIMP's PNG exports and absent from this page's GIF.
- **A comment goes missing**: GIMP omits a GIF comment containing characters outside seven-bit ASCII.
- **An animated PNG shows one frame**: this page keeps the default still image and nothing else.
- **Animation frames cover each other oddly**: GIMP's frame disposal setting decides how each later image covers the ones before, so choose combine or replace to suit.

guide.title: About PNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

GIF's patent trouble led to PNG, designed as a free replacement. It was published by the W3C in the autumn of 1996 as that body's first format Recommendation, and it later appeared as RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948:2004. A fixed signature opens each file, then chunks follow, for example IHDR carrying the header, IDAT the pixels and IEND the closing marker. A third edition reached Recommendation status on 24 June 2025, bringing cICP for signaling HDR and an eXIf chunk for Exif data.

DEFLATE compression is used, and it never discards data. Each sample can be indexed, grayscale or truecolor at depths running from 1 up to 16 bits, and optional alpha stores transparency for each pixel. Animated PNG (APNG) is part of the current specification as well; software unable to animate displays the default still frame.

Browsers of every major kind display PNG, and screenshots on macOS default to this format. Registered media types: image/png, plus image/apng for animated files.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- Editing a PNG is possible in GIMP, which imports it.
- Reading PNG is also something ImageMagick does, though you should inspect which formats your install supports.

**Web:**

- Chrome shows PNG pictures directly.
- Firefox displays them as well.

**Mobile:**

- Safari renders PNG on a phone or tablet.

### PNG and HDR compared

- **Purpose**: PNG is a general lossless image format. Radiance HDR was created for the Radiance lighting simulation software and is also known as RGBE, a scheme created by Greg Ward.
- **Pixels**: a PNG stores samples per channel. An HDR pixel is four bytes: red, green and blue plus one shared exponent. Brightness values computed during Radiance lighting simulation are what such RGBE images hold.
- **Range**: the shared exponent stretches brightness well past what plain 24-bit RGB can express, which is the point of the format.
- **Compression**: PNG always uses lossless DEFLATE, while HDR files use run-length encoding.
- **Extensions**: an HDR file ends in .hdr or .pic, and its registered media type is image/vnd.radiance.
- **Uses**: HDR serves environment maps for 3D rendering, lighting simulation and HDR image storage. PNG suits screenshots, logos and web graphics.
- **Readers**: Blender, GIMP, Adobe Photoshop and Luminance HDR open HDR files.
- **Animation**: a PNG can animate through APNG, but one HDR file holds one picture.

Your browser's own image decoder opens the PNG, and the pixels pass through 8-bit RGBA before ImageMagick writes the Radiance file. A 16-bit PNG therefore loses its extra depth first. The new file cannot contain brightness the PNG never recorded, so nothing is made brighter than white.

The HDR has no transparency, since the page keeps it only when writing PNG or WebP. Metadata is also lost, as the image travels as raw pixels, leaving EXIF, ICC profiles and XMP behind. When the PNG is animated, frame one is what gets written.

The work runs in a Web Worker, and if the worker fails it is retried on the main thread. No quality setting exists. The page handles files one after another, offers each as its own download, imposes no size limit and uploads nothing.

### Other ways to convert PNG to HDR

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick source.png destination.hdr`. ImageMagick's format table lists both PNG and HDR as readable and writable.
- **ImageMagick, format prefix:** use `magick source.png HDR:destination.hdr`. A format name before the file name tells ImageMagick which format to write.
- **ImageMagick and Radiance ra_ppm:** run `magick source.png intermediate.ppm`, then `ra_ppm -r intermediate.ppm destination.hdr`. The -r option converts a pixmap to a Radiance picture, and -g sets gamma with a default of 2.2.

### Problems with PNG files

- **Compression level**: choosing a lower compression setting cannot cost fidelity, since PNG packing is lossless.
- **Layer offsets**: GIMP and other applications can interpret them differently, so skip its PNG offset option.
- **Missing camera tags**: GIMP treats camera tags and profiles as optional, so enable the metadata controls when you need them.
- **Decode message**: the page shows "Image decode failed." when the browser's decoder cannot open the file.
- **Browser message**: when a browser lacks support for the format, the page suggests a recent release of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.
- **Bright areas clipped**: squeezing bright values into the usual eight-bit range may throw away highlight detail.

guide.title: About PNG files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

PNG, short for Portable Network Graphics, was devised to succeed GIF without patent problems. In October 1996 it was published by the W3C as its first format Recommendation, and RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948:2004 came afterwards. All PNG compression is lossless and uses DEFLATE, a blend of LZ77 and Huffman coding.

A PNG begins with a fixed signature and then consists of chunks, among them IHDR (header), IDAT (image data) and IEND (end of file). Bit depth runs from 1 to 16 bits per sample across indexed, grayscale and truecolor images, and an optional alpha channel adds per-pixel transparency. Animated PNG is part of the current specification, and software that cannot animate displays the default still image.

All major browsers display PNG, and no known royalty-bearing patents cover it. Two media types are registered: image/png, plus image/apng for animated files. macOS screenshots are PNG by default, and interface graphics and logos that need transparency commonly use it too.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Mac, Linux and Windows**

- GIMP: reads PNG files into an editable image.
- ImageMagick: reads PNG and writes JPEG from the command line.

**Windows**

- Windows Photos: can show a PNG.

**Mac**

- Preview: shows PNG files and exports other formats.

**Web**

- Firefox: shows PNG images.

**Web and Mobile**

- Chrome: shows PNG images.

**Mobile**

- Safari: shows PNG images.

### PNG and JPG compared

- **Compression**: PNG is always lossless. Baseline JPEG is lossy. 8x8 pixel blocks are cut from the image, transformed with a discrete cosine transform and then Huffman coded.
- **Size**: typical JPEG settings shrink an image to between a tenth and a twentieth of its uncompressed size.
- **Transparency**: PNG has an optional alpha channel. A JPEG stores no alpha channel, so transparency cannot be kept; its color channels are 8 bits each.
- **Quality**: JPEG quality is normally a 0 to 100 setting, but programs disagree about what a given number means. GIMP defaults to 85.
- **Modes**: a progressive mode is available too; a rough image shows first and sharpens as the data loads.
- **Layers**: JPEG cannot store layers.
- **Names**: .jpg and .jpeg name the same format, and the media type is image/jpeg.
- **History**: the Joint Photographic Experts Group, which gave JPEG its name, began work in 1986. T.81 from ITU-T (1992) and ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994) cover the core standard. Patents covering it in the US ended on 27 October 2006.
- **Support**: all major browsers display JPEG, which most digital cameras and scanners build in.
- **Uses**: JPG suits web photographs, camera output, and photos that are emailed or shared. PNG suits screenshots, interface graphics and web graphics that must stay sharp.

What this page does: your browser decodes the PNG, and the page writes a JPEG from the pixels at quality 0.85. Pixels go through 8-bit RGBA, which drops any extra depth in a 16-bit PNG. None of EXIF, ICC profiles or XMP is copied. An animated PNG contributes just its first frame. No size limit is set by the page itself.

### Other ways to convert PNG to JPG

- **Preview (Mac):** open the file, choose File > Export, pick JPEG from the Format pop-up menu, adjust the quality and click Save.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac and Linux):** bring in the PNG and use File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E) to export a JPEG. The JPEG export dialog starts at Quality 85, and JPEG does not support transparency or multiple layers.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick image.png image.jpg`.

### Problems with PNG files

- **The JPG is lossy**: PNG is lossless and JPEG is not, so a conversion back to PNG can't restore detail. Keep the PNG if you may need it.
- **Transparent areas can't stay transparent**: transparent pixels cannot survive JPEG export. Choose a format with alpha instead, such as WebP via [PNG to WebP](/png-to-webp/).
- **The JPG lost its EXIF data, color profile and XMP**: they are not carried over, so keep the PNG if you need that information.
- **An animated PNG gives one picture**: only its first frame is converted.
- **Layers disappear**: JPEG cannot keep an editable stack of layers. Keep the project file.
- **A different quality number gives a different file**: matching quality numbers across editors do not guarantee matching compression or appearance.

### What is a PNG file?

PNG was designed in the mid-1990s as a patent-free stand-in for GIF, whose LZW compression had started to draw license fees. The name is short for Portable Network Graphics. In October 1996 PNG was the first format to be a W3C Recommendation. Later came RFC 2083 and, from ISO/IEC, standard 15948:2004. A third edition, a W3C Recommendation since 24 June 2025, adds HDR color through the cICP chunk, allows Exif metadata in an eXIf chunk and covers animated PNG.

PNG compression is always lossless, using DEFLATE, which is LZ77 plus Huffman coding, so every pixel survives. On a Mac, a screenshot you take is stored as a PNG unless you change the setting.

Adobe created PDF out of Camelot, John Warnock's 1991 project, which had turned into PDF by 1992, so a document would look and print identically on any machine. For that, a PDF has to embed its fonts. Pages may combine type, line art and bitmaps, and the file can add links, bookmarks, form fields and annotations. The ISO versions are ISO 32000-1 (PDF 1.7, 2008) and ISO 32000-2 (PDF 2.0, 2017). Here each page holds one picture, your PNG.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Mac:** Apple Preview opens a PNG and can export it as a PDF, JPEG, TIFF and more.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Edit PNG files in GIMP. ImageMagick reads PNG.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome displays PNG.
- **Web:** Mozilla Firefox displays PNG.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays PNG.

PNG displays in every major browser, and no known patents requiring royalties cover it.

### PNG and PDF compared

- **File endings**: .png is image/png (image/apng once animated), and .pdf is application/pdf.
- **Inside the file**: after its fixed signature, a PNG is a run of chunks, with the header in IHDR, the pixel data in IDAT and an IEND chunk to finish. A PDF describes pages, using an imaging model from PostScript that does not depend on the device or its resolution.
- **Compression**: PNG always uses lossless DEFLATE. A PDF can store a picture with lossless Flate or with JPEG. This converter embeds the PNG losslessly.
- **Color and transparency**: PNG supports indexed, grayscale and truecolor pictures, from 1 to 16 bits for each sample, and may add an alpha channel. In the PDF, the alpha becomes a soft mask.
- **Pages**: a PNG has pixels but no page size. The PDF page takes the image's size, one point per pixel.
- **Color depth**: a 16-bit PNG loses its extra precision, because the conversion goes through 8-bit RGBA.
- **Animation**: the latest specification covers APNG, and a viewer without animation falls back to the default still image. This converter reads only the first frame.
- **Metadata**: EXIF, ICC profiles and XMP don't come across, even though PNG's third edition allows an eXIf chunk for Exif data.

### Other ways to convert PNG to PDF

- **Finder (Mac):** select the PNGs, Control-click one of them and pick Quick Actions > Create PDF. Pages keep your selection order.
- **Preview (Mac):** open the PNG, then use File > Export and set Format to PDF.

### Problems with PNG files

- **A PNG with 16 bits per channel**: 8-bit RGBA is the working format here, so the finer steps between shades are lost in the PDF.
- **The PDF shows an unexpected background**: nothing paints a background, so transparent pixels stay see-through. Fill the PNG with a color in an editor first if you want a solid page.
- **An animation turned into one picture**: an animated PNG gives its first frame.
- **A screenshot shows private details**: the PDF keeps every pixel, so crop out names, addresses and notifications before converting.
- **"Image decode failed." appears**: the PNG's data could not be decoded by your browser. Save a fresh copy from the app that created it.
- **A screenshot comes out large on paper**: the page follows the image's size at one point per pixel, so a large screenshot makes a large page. Scale the print to fit your paper.
- **A page size such as A4 or Letter is wanted**: this page has no page-size setting, and the page always matches the image.
- **Many PNGs, one PDF wanted**: this page makes one PDF per PNG. [Image to PDF](/image-to-pdf/) combines them, one page each.

guide.title: Understanding PNG for PPM output
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

PNG stands for Portable Network Graphics. It came out of the 1990s effort to replace GIF without patent worries, and today it is both a W3C Recommendation and ISO/IEC 15948. The format is lossless, can carry an alpha channel and allows either 8 or 16 bits for each color channel.

### Programs that open PNG files

For PPM output, open the PNG in:

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP opens PNG files for editing, and ImageMagick reads PNG as well.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display PNG in a page.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome display PNG on phones.

PPM has a narrower audience, so use an imaging tool rather than expecting a phone gallery to show it.

### PNG and PPM compared

- **Compression**: PNG is lossless and compact. PPM stores samples with little compression, so files can be large.
- **Transparency**: PNG has alpha. PPM has none.
- **Depth**: PNG allows 8 and 16 bits per channel. PPM allows 8 or 16, and this page writes 8.
- **Encoding**: a binary PPM begins with P6, and the rarer plain-text form with P3.
- **Family**: PPM is the color member of Netpbm, next to grayscale PGM and black-and-white PBM.
- **Samples**: each PPM pixel carries red, green and blue samples, and the maximum sample value can range from 1 to 65535.

The PNG is read into 8-bit RGBA pixels by the browser, then ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly writes the PPM. Metadata stays behind.

### Other ways to convert PNG to PPM

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick diagram.png diagram.ppm`. The output ending selects the format.
- **Netpbm:** run `pngtopam -mix -background=white diagram.png > diagram.ppm` to compose transparency onto white. A grayscale PNG produces PGM instead and a black-and-white one PBM, so check the file header.

### Problems with PNG files

- **A logo gained a background**: the PNG's alpha channel cannot be stored in PPM, so flatten onto a chosen color first.
- **A 16-bit PNG lost depth**: the page writes eight bits per channel.
- **An animated PNG became a still**: the page uses the first frame and ignores the rest.
- **Colors changed**: the embedded profile is dropped.
- **You worry about the PNG's compression level**: PNG compression is lossless, so lowering the setting never costs pixel fidelity.

guide.title: PNG to PSD: formats and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

PNG stores a raster picture without loss, and macOS uses it for screenshots. DEFLATE compresses the pixels, so decoding returns exactly what was saved. The design replaced GIF without its patent issues. The W3C turned PNG into a Recommendation in autumn 1996, a first among its formats, ISO later issued it as ISO/IEC 15948, and a third edition of the specification became a Recommendation in June 2025.

The file starts with a signature and then runs through chunks, with IHDR as the header, IDAT as the pixel data and IEND as the end marker. Images can be indexed, grayscale or truecolor, each sample 1 to 16 bits wide, with an optional alpha channel for transparency. You meet PNG as screenshots, interface graphics and logos, and web graphics that must stay sharp, and every major browser displays it.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** to view or edit, GIMP opens PNG, and ImageMagick can read it from a terminal.
- **Web:** PNG shows up in both Chrome and Firefox.
- **Mobile:** iPhone and iPad display PNG in Safari.

### PNG and PSD compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .png is image/png, while .psd is image/vnd.adobe.photoshop, and the file begins with the signature 8BPS.
- **Purpose**: a PNG stores a finished picture. A PSD is Photoshop's native document, with separate sections for layers, masks and image resources.
- **Bit depth**: a PNG sample is up to 16 bits wide, while a PSD header allows 1, 8, 16 or 32.
- **Size limit**: a PSD holds no more than 30,000 pixels per side, and PSB goes beyond that.
- **Compression**: A PSD may store its pixels uncompressed, or packed with RLE or ZIP. PNG always uses DEFLATE, so both can be lossless.
- **Metadata**: this page doesn't carry EXIF, ICC profiles or XMP across.

Your PNG is already flat, so the PSD this page writes is a flattened copy of the same picture. Your browser decodes the PNG into 8-bit pixels, so a 16-bit PNG loses depth. ImageMagick then writes the PSD, and the page checks that the result starts with the 8BPS signature. Layers that were flattened before the PNG was saved are not in the file, and text stays pixels. Choosing several PNGs gives one PSD for each.

To open the PSD, ImageMagick and XnView MP read it on Windows, Mac and Linux, and Photopea in a browser uses it as its main document format. Programs other than Photoshop have to interpret Photoshop-specific data structures, so a preview opening doesn't prove that every layer feature will edit the same way.

### Other ways to convert PNG to PSD

- **Photopea (web):** choose File > Open and pick the PNG, then choose File > Save as PSD. The page says every file you open in Photopea is converted to PSD, and that the PSD format preserves the document's structure.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick artwork.png artwork.psd`. The format table lists both PNG and PSD as readable and writable. It converts the pixels only, so objects baked into the PNG stay baked in.

A PSD can hold layers and masks, which a flattened export doesn't keep, but neither route can bring back what a PNG no longer has. Add new layers, masks and text on top in the editor after the PSD is open.

### Problems with PNG files

- **The text can't be edited**: saving text to PNG turns the letters into pixels, which are hard to change, and a PNG stores no fonts. Ask whoever made the image for the original design file, or retype the words on a new text layer in Photopea or another editor.
- **The PSD has one layer's worth of content**: the PNG was flattened when it was exported. Hidden layers can't be recovered from it.
- **A 16-bit master lost depth**: this page works in 8 bits per channel, so keep the original PNG if the extra depth matters.
- **Layer offsets differ between programs**: layers can sit differently in GIMP than in other applications, so skip GIMP's PNG offset option if you will share the file.
- **Camera tags and profiles are optional in GIMP exports**: switch on the relevant metadata controls when you need them, and keep in mind that this page drops EXIF, ICC and XMP.
- **The PNG is damaged**: the page says "Image decode failed." Download the file again or check it in GIMP.

- **Samples**: a PNG may hold 1 to 16 bits per sample and an alpha channel. The RGB file has three interleaved 8-bit samples per pixel.
- **Same ending, different file**: an .rgb ending can also mean an SGI image, which Pillow reads and writes. ImageMagick separates the two: its SGI coder writes SGI, and its RGB coder writes raw samples.

In this converter your browser decodes the PNG, then ImageMagick writes the RGB file. The page sets no quality. Files you select together are converted one after another, each downloading on its own.

- **ImageMagick, SGI:** run `magick texture.png sgi:texture.rgb` when the receiving program wants an SGI header.

### Problems with PNG files

- **Layer offset from GIMP**: a PNG exported with GIMP's offset option can place the layer differently in other applications. Leave that option off when exporting.

guide.title: About PNG to SVG
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

PNG, for Portable Network Graphics, was started as a way to replace GIF without its patent problems. The W3C published it as its first Recommendation for a format, in October 1996; RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948:2004 came later. Compression is always lossless and uses DEFLATE, which is built from LZ77 and Huffman coding.

A PNG starts with a signature that never changes, then chunks: IHDR is the header, IDAT carries the pixels and IEND closes the file. A PNG may hold indexed, grayscale or truecolor images, from 1 to 16 bits per sample, and can add an alpha channel so each pixel has its own transparency. All major browsers show PNG, and macOS uses it for screenshots by default.

A PNG is a grid of pixels, and that is its limit when you want an SVG: a vector file describes shapes and stays sharp at any size. SVG is an open W3C standard, an XML language for describing two-dimensional graphics through shapes, text and embedded images. Those embedded images are the heart of PNG to SVG.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Linux, Windows and Mac**

- Inkscape: brings in a bitmap through File > Import and can trace it.
- GIMP: opens PNG for editing.
- ImageMagick: reads PNG files from the command line.

**Windows**

- Windows Photos: shows PNG pictures.

**Mac**

- Preview: shows PNG pictures.

**Web**

- Firefox: renders PNG in the browser.

**Web and Mobile**

- Chrome: renders PNG in the browser.

**Mobile**

- Safari: renders PNG in the browser.

### PNG and SVG compared

- **Media types**: image/png for PNG, and image/svg+xml for SVG. A gzip-compressed SVG uses the .svgz extension.
- **What is stored**: PNG stores pixels. SVG stores shapes, text and embedded images as instructions in XML text.
- **Scaling**: an SVG's shapes redraw cleanly at any size, but a pixel image embedded in it keeps its own resolution however far it is enlarged.
- **Editing**: being plain text, an SVG opens in any text editor, and its contents can be searched, indexed and compressed. They work with CSS and JavaScript, so they can be styled, scripted and animated.
- **Transparency**: PNG has an optional alpha channel. SVG draws only what the file describes.
- **Effects**: clipping paths, masks and filter effects are part of SVG.
- **Browsers**: every major browser displays both.

What this page makes is an SVG that embeds your picture. It does not trace it. The file holds one image element, set to your picture's own pixel width and height, whose data is the picture as a PNG stored as base64 text. Nothing is resized or reduced to fewer colors, and transparency is kept in the embedded PNG. The result is still pixels inside, so it doesn't scale like a vector. If you start from a JPG, the [JPG to SVG converter](/jpg-to-svg/) is the one to use.

Tracing works the other way. A tracing program looks for edges and areas of color and redraws them as shapes. The result is a redrawing rather than a copy, and it works best on dark shapes against a bright background.

### Other ways to convert PNG to SVG

- **Inkscape (Windows, Mac, Linux):** use File > Import to bring in the PNG, select it with the Selector tool, then open Path > Trace Bitmap (Shift+Alt+B). Pick a mode such as Brightness cutoff, which creates a silhouette-like path that follows the shape of your image. Use Update to refresh the preview and click Ok. Tracing works well for dark silhouettes on a bright background; Centerline tracing turns a shape into an open path, a fit for handwriting and line drawings.
- **Potrace (command line):** Potrace reads PNM (PBM, PGM, PPM) and BMP but not PNG. Save a BMP copy of the PNG, then run `potrace -s input.bmp -o output.svg`. It traces in black and white at a cutoff set with `-k`, which is 0.5 by default. The [PNG to BMP converter](/png-to-bmp/) can make the BMP.

### Problems with PNG files

- **The SVG still looks blurry when enlarged**: it holds the original pixels. Trace the PNG if you need clean edges at a larger size.
- **Potrace won't read the file**: it doesn't take PNG. Convert to BMP first.
- **A trace looks wrong**: a trace is a redrawing, so it can differ from the original. Try a different mode in the Trace Bitmap dialog.
- **The SVG file is larger or smaller than the PNG**: it is not a byte copy of your file. The embedded picture is re-encoded and written out as text inside the SVG.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the browser couldn't read the PNG. Save a fresh copy from its source.

guide.title: About PNG and TGA
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

PNG was created as a patent-free successor to GIF, and it was the first format ever published as a W3C Recommendation, in October 1996, and RFC 2083 plus ISO/IEC 15948:2004 followed. PNG compression is lossless, built on the DEFLATE algorithm, a combination of LZ77 and Huffman coding. A fixed signature starts the file, then come chunks such as IHDR for the header and IDAT for pixel data, with IEND at the end.

You can store indexed, grayscale or truecolor pictures with 1 to 16 bits per sample, and add alpha if each pixel needs its own transparency. The newest edition of the specification supports HDR with a cICP chunk and permits Exif data in an eXIf chunk. Screenshots on macOS are saved as PNG by default, and all major browsers display it. The registered media types are image/png and, for animated files, image/apng. A PNG headed for a TGA workflow often comes from a texture artist, a screenshot or an exported graphic, and the reason for converting is usually an older renderer or importer that asks for Targa.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports PNG for editing, which lets you check the image ahead of a texture pipeline.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads PNG, though you should inspect the installed format support first.
- **Web:** Firefox and Chrome display PNG.
- **Mobile:** Safari and Chrome display PNG.

### PNG and TGA compared

Targa is a raster image format associated with Truevision video boards. It supports RGB, indexed-color and grayscale imagery, and it can use optional run-length encoding to reduce storage. Video editing and game-development workflows still use Targa images. In ImageMagick, Truevision Targa shares a group with ICB, VDA and VST.

Each color component of a 24-bit RGB TGA takes eight bits, and the 32-bit kind adds alpha to that. Saving RGB artwork at 24 bits removes the space needed for a Targa alpha channel. Open the result in the application that will use it before relying on it for a decal, cutout or particle texture.

Here the browser's own decoder reads the PNG into 8-bit RGBA pixels, and ImageMagick then writes the TGA. It sets no quality or compression option. Passing through raw pixels costs a 16-bit PNG its extra depth, and EXIF, ICC profiles and XMP do not come along. A format change should not be treated as a color-management operation, particularly for maps where the destination expects a specific interpretation of channel values.

An animated PNG yields only its first frame, not a run of TGA files. For an animated texture, export the frames you need through a workflow that controls filenames and timing.

### Other ways to convert PNG to TGA

- **GIMP:** load the PNG, then File > Export As with a name that ends in .tga. The Targa export dialog has a Use RLE compression option and an Origin setting. Choose what the destination expects. GIMP's Targa plug-in does not preserve every version-2 extension field.
- **ImageMagick:** `magick texture.png texture.tga` converts one file, and ImageMagick's format list shows PNG and TGA as readable and writable.
- **ImageMagick mogrify:** `magick mogrify -format tga *.png` converts every PNG in the current folder. The -format option changes the suffix, so the PNGs stay beside the new .tga files.

### Problems with PNG files

**Layers sit in the wrong place after export from GIMP:** layer offsets may differ between GIMP and other applications, so avoid its PNG offset option when the image will travel.

**Camera tags or profiles are missing:** they are optional in GIMP exports, so enable the relevant metadata controls when you need them. They would not survive this converter in any case, as the TGA is written from raw pixels.

**An animation shows as a still:** a program that cannot play animated PNG shows the default still image, though the specification itself covers animation. This page, too, converts that first frame.

**A smaller compression setting seems to cost quality:** it does not, because PNG compression is lossless and the setting never changes pixel fidelity. Only the size of the PNG changes, and the pixels this page reads stay the same.

**Gradients band after conversion:** PNG can hold up to 16 bits per sample, and this converter works in 8 bits per channel. Keep the 16-bit PNG as the master, and use a desktop workflow when those values matter.

guide.title: Understanding PNG to TIFF
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

PNG, the Portable Network Graphics format, was designed to stand in for GIF without GIF's patent trouble. The W3C issued it in October 1996, the first image format to get that treatment, and it was later republished as RFC 2083 and as the ISO/IEC 15948:2004 standard. The W3C approved a third edition of the specification in June 2025. Squeezing is always lossless and uses DEFLATE, which pairs LZ77 with Huffman coding.

A fixed signature opens every PNG, and chunks follow: the header sits in IHDR, pixel data in IDAT, and IEND marks where the file stops. A PNG may be indexed, grayscale or truecolor, storing between one and sixteen bits per sample, and with an alpha channel each pixel can be partly transparent. In the third edition, HDR is indicated with a cICP chunk, and Exif data may live in an eXIf chunk. Its registered media type is image/png, with image/apng used for the animated kind. PNG carries no known royalty-bearing patents, every major browser displays it, and macOS screenshots are PNG files unless you change the setting.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP turns a PNG you open into a new project in its own XCF format. ImageMagick reads PNG from the command line.
- **Web and mobile:** Firefox and Chrome show PNG files inline on the desktop web; on phones, Chrome and Safari do the same.

### PNG and TIFF compared

Aldus and Microsoft created TIFF, a raster format organized around tags. Its sixth revision dates from 1992, and the specification is now in Adobe's hands. Compression methods and color models vary from file to file, one TIFF can contain many images, and the format is a long-standing pick for high-bit-depth imaging and preservation masters. Both .tif and .tiff name the format, and image/tiff is its media type.

Your browser decodes the PNG into pixel values of 8 bits per channel, then ImageMagick, which runs as WebAssembly in the tab, writes the TIFF from them. The result is an uncompressed TIFF with red, green, blue and an alpha channel, so transparent pixels stay transparent. Depth above 8 bits is lost on the way, EXIF, XMP and the ICC profile do not make the trip, and an animated PNG keeps just its opening frame.

The page has no options for compression, color space or bit depth. If a recipient specifies a compression tag or a profile, use one of the programs below.

### Other ways to convert PNG to TIFF

- **GIMP:** with the PNG open, choose File > Export As and pick TIFF, then set the compression in the TIFF export dialog: no compression, LZW, Pack Bits, Deflate, or JPEG, which is lossy. Picking a compression is the way to a smaller TIFF than this page writes. The CCITT fax options appear only for an indexed image reduced to two colors.
- **Preview on Mac:** open the PNG in Preview, go to File > Export, choose TIFF from the Format menu, give the copy a name and click Save. Apple's page lists HEIC, JPEG, JPEG-2000, OpenEXR, PDF, PNG and TIFF in that menu. It is a quick route when you need no settings.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick graphic.png graphic.tiff`. ImageMagick's format list says its TIFF support has extensive strip, tile, byte order and compression controls; add whichever your recipient requires.

### Problems with PNG files

**An animation shows as one picture.** The current specification covers animated PNG (APNG), and software that cannot animate it shows the default still image. The TIFF here is that first frame. Export the frame you want from an animation tool before converting if it is not the first.

**Camera tags and profiles are missing.** GIMP makes them optional when it exports a PNG, so the file may never have carried them. Turn on the metadata controls when you export if you need them.

**Layers or offsets shift.** GIMP's PNG offset setting records a layer position that other programs may read another way; switch it off before saving a PNG for someone else.

**The PNG is larger than it needs to be.** Every PNG is compressed losslessly, so a stronger compression setting in the program that made it shrinks the file without changing a pixel.

### What is a PNG file?

Made to replace GIF without GIF's patent trouble, PNG stores a picture losslessly. First of its kind at the W3C, PNG became a Recommendation in October 1996, with RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948 after it. Under the hood it is a fixed signature followed by chunks, with the pixel data compressed by DEFLATE. Its pixel layouts are indexed, grayscale and truecolor; each sample takes 1 to 16 bits, and an alpha channel is optional. All major browsers show PNG, and no royalty-bearing patents are known to cover it. image/png is its registered media type, and image/apng is the one for animated files. Software that cannot animate a PNG shows its default still image instead.

Most people meet PNG as a screenshot, because macOS saves screenshots as PNG by default. That is why this pair exists. A screenshot of a web page, a chat or a spreadsheet looks like text, but the file holds only pixels. The letters are not characters a text editor can select. To get them out, the converter has to read the picture, which is called optical character recognition, or OCR.

### Programs that open PNG files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- GIMP imports PNG for editing, so you can crop a screenshot to the lettering before you convert it.
- ImageMagick reads PNG.

**Web and mobile:**

- Google Chrome displays PNG.
- Mozilla Firefox displays PNG.
- Safari, on mobile, displays PNG.

### PNG and TXT compared

- **Extensions and media types**: a screenshot ends in .png and is labeled image/png. The text it becomes ends in .txt and is labeled text/plain.
- **What is stored**: a PNG is a grid of pixels, in indexed, grayscale or truecolor, with an optional alpha channel. A TXT holds characters, and its charset says how the bytes map to them.
- **Compression**: PNG is always lossless, using DEFLATE. A text file is not compressed.
- **Layout**: plain text has no fonts, page layout or picture placement, so columns, tables and styling in the screenshot do not carry over.

Unlike most pairs here, this one does not copy anything out of the PNG; it reads the picture. A text recognizer runs in your browser with an English model only, and the image is not uploaded. When it finds no lettering, you get a message and no file.

### Other ways to convert PNG to TXT

- **Tesseract (command line):** run `tesseract capture.png recognized -l eng`. The `-l` option picks the language, and English is the default when you leave it out. The default output format is text, and it wrote recognized.txt next to the image in a test run. Tesseract and the English language data must be installed.
- **PowerToys Text Extractor (Windows):** show the PNG on screen, press Windows+Shift+T and drag over the text. The text goes to the clipboard; paste it into a text editor and save a .txt file. It reads the screen region, not the file. Microsoft says the text may not be perfect and needs a quick proofread.
- **Preview and TextEdit (Mac):** open the PNG in Preview, drag to select the text, Control-click and choose Copy Text. Paste into TextEdit, choose Format > Make Plain Text and save. Live Text isn't available in all regions or languages.

### Problems with PNG files

- **The text comes out wrong or scrambled**: OCR reads shapes, and small, blurry or slanted letters get misread. Capture the screen at a larger size or scan at a higher resolution, then convert again. Enlarging a blurry image adds no detail.
- **The page finds no text**: the picture has no readable lettering, or the lettering is too faint or small. Try a sharper copy, and crop away borders and busy backgrounds.
- **Letters in another language come out as nonsense**: the model is English. A screenshot in another language needs an OCR program with that language's data.
- **Columns run together**: plain text has no columns. Convert each column or region as its own cropped image and join them in an editor.
- **The recognizer couldn't start**: the recognizer or its English model did not load. Reload the page and try again, or try another browser.
- **A photo gives nothing**: OCR finds letters, not objects, so a picture with no writing in it ends with no text instead of a description of the scene.

guide.title: PNG to XBM: background and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is a PNG file?

Developers designed PNG to replace GIF without the patent worries. It reached W3C Recommendation status in October 1996, the first format to do so, and ISO/IEC 15948 came later. Pixels are always stored losslessly. Color can come from a palette, gray levels or full truecolor, and an alpha channel is available for see-through areas. Every major browser shows PNG, and macOS takes screenshots in this format by default.

### Programs that open PNG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports PNG for editing.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** ImageMagick reads PNG.
- **Web and Mobile:** Google Chrome displays PNG.
- **Web:** Mozilla Firefox displays PNG.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays PNG.

### PNG and XBM compared

An XBM keeps its picture as C source text, not as a binary image. It served the X graphical environment for icons and pointer artwork, and it may include coordinates for a pointer hot spot. Its image is monochrome, so the colors, grays and transparency of a PNG have nowhere to go and color artwork turns monochrome.

On this page your browser decodes the PNG, and ImageMagick then writes the XBM from those pixels. Metadata is dropped along the way.

### Other ways to convert PNG to XBM

- **GIMP:** open the PNG, choose File > Export As, type a name that ends in .xbm and click Export. GIMP offers XBM only for an image with 8 bits per channel. The export options are an X10 format bitmap, an identifier prefix, a comment, hot spot values, and a mask file that is enabled only when the image has an alpha channel.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick picture.png picture.xbm`. ImageMagick reads and writes XBM, for black and white only.
- **ImageMagick, flattened first:** run `magick picture.png -background white -alpha remove -alpha off -monochrome picture.xbm`. Here `-alpha remove` composites the image over the background color, `-alpha off` disables the alpha channel and `-monochrome` transforms the image to black and white.

### Problems with PNG files

- **Compression setting:** pixels come through exactly as saved, because PNG never discards image data.
- **Layer offsets:** the offset option in GIMP's PNG export places layers in a way other programs may not match, so leave it unchecked.
- **Camera tags and profiles:** an export from GIMP carries them only if you enable its metadata controls.

guide.title: About PPM files
guide.markdown:
### What is a PPM file?

PPM is the name of Netpbm's portable color pixel-map format. Each pixel is made of red, green and blue samples, with a maximum sample value that may fall anywhere between 1 and 65535. A normal binary PPM announces itself with P6, while the less common plain-text form uses P3.

Several images can follow one another in a raw PPM without any separator. The usual media type, image/x-portable-pixmap, is conventional and is not registered with IANA.

The design is plain on purpose. A PPM has little metadata and a redundant pixel layout, so files can be large next to images prepared for distribution. That simplicity is also why it appears in scripts and image-processing experiments, and why it is often turned into a JPG before anyone else sees it.

### Programs that open PPM files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- ImageMagick reads and writes PPM color images.
- Provided by Netpbm are the libnetpbm reader and tools for working on PPM files.

### PPM and JPG compared

- **Compression**: PPM stores its samples as they are. Baseline JPEG discards information: the picture is divided into 8x8 pixel blocks, every block is passed through a DCT (a discrete cosine transform) before Huffman coding packs the result.
- **Size**: at everyday JPEG settings the result is a small fraction of the raw size, roughly a tenth to a twentieth.
- **Depth**: a PPM may use sample values up to 65535, whereas JPEG stores 8 bits per color channel.
- **Alpha**: neither format holds transparency, since a PPM is RGB only and JPEG has no alpha channel.
- **Name**: the abbreviation stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group, a body whose effort started in 1986.
- **Standard**: two documents define it, ITU-T T.81 (1992) and ISO/IEC 10918-1 (1994).
- **Progressive mode**: JPEG can show a coarse version of the image first and sharpen it as more data loads.
- **Quality**: the scale generally runs from 0 to 100, GIMP starts at 85, and one number can mean different results between programs.
- **Extensions**: the same format sits behind .jpg and .jpeg, and layers cannot be stored in it.
- **Reach**: JPEG is built into most digital cameras and scanners, and every major browser displays it.
- **Patents**: JPEG's US patents expired on 27 October 2006.
- **Media type**: image/jpeg is registered for JPEG.

ImageMagick, compiled to WebAssembly, decodes the PPM on the main thread of your browser tab and writes a JPG. It reads one image from the file, so a raw PPM holding a sequence of pictures still gives a single JPG. Because the page supplies no quality value and strips nothing explicitly, you cannot pick a JPG quality here. If the picture exceeds about 537 megapixels, conversion fails and a message says it is too large.

Nothing is uploaded and no other size limit applies, so a big file mostly costs time. Files are processed in sequence, every JPG downloads on its own and your PPM stays unchanged.

If you need a particular quality, use one of the commands below on your own computer.

### Other ways to convert PPM to JPG

- **Netpbm:** run `pnmtojpeg -quality=90 image.ppm > image.jpg`. The program reads a Netpbm image and writes JFIF to standard output, and n in -quality runs from 0 (worst) to 100 (best), with a default of 75. Values below about 25 can give images that some interpreters cannot read. For a PPM input the output is in YCbCr format.
- **ImageMagick:** type `magick image.ppm -quality 90 image.jpg`. According to ImageMagick, -quality controls the compression level of JPEG encoders.
- **IrfanView:** load the PPM through File > Open, and under File > Save as pick JPG. IrfanView's format table shows PPM and JPG as readable and savable.

### Problems with PPM files

- **Large files**: the redundant layout and sparse metadata make PPMs big next to compressed images.
- **Eight-bit readers only**: certain readers handle just one eight-bit image. pnmtopnm can normalize awkward input, and pamdepth lowers the depth.
- **Gamma surprises**: files labeled PPM sometimes hold sRGB or linear values rather than the specified transfer function, and pnmgamma can reconcile them.
- **Viewer will not open it**: try GIMP, IrfanView, XnView MP or the Netpbm tools, all of which open PPM.
- **Blocky detail**: the 8x8 block approach of baseline JPEG means hard edges and text can show artifacts.
