guide.title: Understanding SVG to JPEG
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

SVG stands for Scalable Vector Graphics, an open W3C standard. The W3C published SVG 1.0 as a Recommendation in 2001 and SVG 1.1 two years later. The language is XML-based and stores a drawing as shapes, text and embedded images instead of pixels, so the picture can be drawn at any size and stay sharp. The files are plain text: a text editor opens them, and they can be searched, indexed and compressed. Compressed with gzip, an SVG takes the .svgz extension, while image/svg+xml is its media type.

SVG works with CSS and JavaScript, which lets a drawing be styled, scripted and animated, and it offers clipping paths, masks and filter effects. It may be opened as a document by itself or dropped into an HTML page. Every major browser displays SVG. Pixel images can also be embedded in an SVG.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Inkscape works with SVG natively, and Firefox displays it. Open the original in Inkscape when you want to change the artboard size, the background or the text before you export.
- **Web and mobile:** Firefox and Chrome render SVG in a desktop browser; Chrome and Safari handle it on phones and tablets too.

### SVG and JPEG compared

An SVG stores instructions for drawing; a JPEG stores compressed samples of a finished picture. The standards committee that produced JPEG started its work in 1986. The ITU released the specification as T.81 in 1992, and ISO/IEC adopted it as 10918-1 in 1994. Baseline JPEG is lossy: 8x8 pixel blocks undergo a discrete cosine transform before Huffman coding finishes the job. Color is kept at 8 bits per channel, and transparency and layers are not part of the format. Files named .jpg or .jpeg are the same format, identified by the media type image/jpeg.

Your browser does the drawing here. The SVG goes through the browser's own image decoder and is drawn one to one at the size it reports, with no scale factor and no size cap added by the page. Those pixels become a JPEG written at quality 0.85, which is verified as genuine JPEG data before you receive it. JPEG cannot store transparency, and the page paints no background of its own, so place a background shape behind the artwork in the SVG when you want a known color there.

Metadata and structure do not come along. The image passes through raw pixels, so object names, links, scripts and the text itself end up as picture content only. A JPEG made this way is a delivery copy, not something to edit again.

### Other ways to convert SVG to JPEG

- **Inkscape:** open the SVG and use File > Export. The Export dialog lists JPEG among its default formats, and you set the export area and the resolution in DPI before exporting. The notes for Inkscape 1.2 describe this dialog, and add that its JPEG export, which once turned a transparent background black, now uses the document's background color. This is the route when you need a larger picture.
- **GIMP:** open the SVG; GIMP loads it as an image. Then choose File > Export As and save in JPEG format, which brings up a dialog with a Quality setting from 0 to 100 (the default is 85). GIMP's JPEG export supports neither transparency nor multiple layers, and the SVG itself is rasterized, so keep the original.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick drawing.svg picture.jpg`. ImageMagick's format list says an SVG is rendered through Inkscape, RSVG or its own internal MSVG renderer.

### Problems with SVG files

**Fonts change the drawing.** The SVG only names its fonts. A viewer without them substitutes others, and the drawing changes with them. Check the text before converting, because the JPEG freezes whatever was drawn.

**Linked pictures vanish.** Pictures the SVG links from other files are not part of the SVG itself, so a program or converter that draws it as an image has nothing to show for them. Embed them in the file first.

**Embedded photos stay small.** Pixel images can sit inside an SVG, and they stay at their original resolution however far the drawing is enlarged. A low-resolution photo inside the SVG looks soft in a big JPEG.

### What is an SVG file?

Scalable Vector Graphics is an open W3C standard. SVG 1.0 was recommended in 2001 and SVG 1.1 followed in 2003. The XML language lays out shapes, text and embedded pictures, so a drawing stays sharp at any size. The files are plain text that you can edit, search and compress, and a gzipped one ends in .svgz. Its media type is image/svg+xml.

An SVG is shown by itself or inside an HTML page. Because CSS and JavaScript apply to it, it can take styling, scripting and animation, and it also covers clipping paths, masks and filters. It is most often seen as logos and icons on the web, illustrations, diagrams, charts and maps.

### Programs that open SVG files

**Windows, macOS and Linux**

- Inkscape is the native SVG editor.
- Firefox displays SVG.
- Adobe Illustrator and Figma are listed too.

**Web and mobile**

- Chrome and Firefox display SVG in a page, and so does every major browser.
- On phones, Chrome and Safari show it.

### SVG and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .svg is image/svg+xml; JPG files use image/jpeg and the .jpg or .jpeg ending.
- **What they are**: SVG stores shapes and text as instructions. JPG stores a fixed grid of pixels.
- **Scaling**: shapes in an SVG stay sharp however large they are drawn, whereas a JPG has only the pixels it was saved with.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy, splitting the picture into 8x8 pixel blocks. SVG is text.
- **Transparency**: an SVG can leave areas empty. JPG cannot store an alpha channel.
- **Editing**: SVG text and shapes stay editable. A JPG cannot store layers or live text.
- **Typical use**: SVG serves graphics that must stay sharp. JPG serves photographs on the web, camera output, and email attachments and photo sharing.
- **Origins**: work by the JPEG group began in 1986. The core standard was published as ITU-T T.81 in 1992 and as ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994, and 27 October 2006 is when its US patents expired.
- **Quality scale**: programs usually take a quality figure from 0 to 100, and an identical figure can give different results between them; GIMP's default is 85. This page fixes it at 0.85.
- **Browsers**: every major browser displays both formats.
- **Bit depth**: JPG stores 8 bits per channel, and the pixels pass through at 8 bits here.

This converter has your browser draw the SVG at the size it reports for it, then stores the picture with JPEG quality 0.85. The code adds no scale factor and no size cap.

### Other ways to convert SVG to JPG

- **GIMP:** open the SVG as an image, which GIMP's glossary says it can import from vector graphics software. To save, pick File > Export As, type a .jpg name for the file and click Export, which brings up the JPEG options.
- **ImageMagick:** run `magick input.svg output.jpg`. Its format list gives the SVG row read and write mode and says it renders with Inkscape, RSVG or its internal MSVG renderer.
- **Inkscape and Preview:** in Inkscape, open the export dialog with Shift+Ctrl+E (File > Export PNG Image), select Page, Drawing, Selection or Custom, enter the size in pixels, give the file a name and click Export. Next, open that PNG in Preview on a Mac, open the File menu, choose Export and pick JPEG from the Format pop-up menu before clicking Save.

### Problems with SVG files

- **The text looks different**: layout depends on available fonts, so substituted fonts can change the drawing.
- **Images are missing**: this page never draws a picture the SVG links to, even one that is online. Embed each one in the file as data.
- **Embedded pictures look soft**: an SVG can embed pixel images, and those parts retain their original resolution when enlarged.
- **The JPG is tiny**: the output is drawn one pixel to one pixel at the size the browser reports. Set a width and height in the file for a bigger result.
- **An empty background can't stay clear**: JPG has no transparency, so draw your own background shape to control what fills the space.
- **Fonts do not match the web page**: a web font loaded by a page isn't drawn in a standalone SVG.
- **A style sheet is ignored**: an external stylesheet referenced by the file is left out of the drawing, so put the styles inside the SVG.

guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

The letters SVG expand to Scalable Vector Graphics. The format is XML-based and describes two-dimensional artwork made of shapes, text and embedded images. The W3C maintains it as an open standard: version 1.0 was recommended in 2001, and 1.1 followed in 2003. Shapes are stored as instructions, so a single file stays sharp however large it is drawn.

Plain text means an SVG needs no special software to read: any editor will open it, and search, indexing or compression all work on it. The gzip-compressed form is saved with an .svgz extension. CSS and JavaScript apply to SVG, so a drawing can be styled, scripted and animated, and the format adds clipping paths, masks and filter effects. It works as a stand-alone file or as a piece of an HTML page. Its registered media type is image/svg+xml.

Designers meet SVG as logos and icons exported from a drawing program, as charts from a plotting tool, and as artwork on websites. A PDF is the usual way to hand such a drawing to someone who wants a document, a print shop, or a form that takes only PDF.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Mac, Windows and Linux:** Inkscape edits SVG as its native format, and Firefox displays it.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome displays SVG on the web and on phones, and Safari displays it on phones.

### SVG and PDF compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .svg and image/svg+xml; .pdf and application/pdf.
- **What they are**: SVG is XML text that describes a drawing. PDF is a page format created by Adobe and standardized as ISO 32000, built to look the same on any device.
- **Content**: an SVG describes shapes, text and embedded images. One PDF page can combine text, vector graphics and raster images, and the file may also hold links, bookmarks, form fields and annotations.
- **Imaging**: every major browser displays SVG, and a PDF's imaging model comes from PostScript and does not depend on the device or resolution.
- **Fonts**: text layout in an SVG depends on the fonts available, while a PDF needs its fonts embedded to look the same everywhere.
- **Images inside**: a PDF can store its pictures using Flate, which is lossless, or using JPEG.

A PDF can hold vector paths, but this converter does not write them. It draws the SVG in your browser and puts that picture on a page, so you get the fixed layout of a PDF without the scalability of SVG. For vector output, use one of the programs below, and keep the SVG as the source either way.

### Other ways to convert SVG to PDF

- **Inkscape (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the SVG, choose File > Save a Copy and pick Portable Document Format (*.pdf) as the type. The manual advises converting decorative text, such as a logo, to paths, and keeping an SVG master.
- **CairoSVG (command line):** run `cairosvg drawing.svg -o drawing.pdf`. The format follows the output file's extension. CairoSVG's documentation says its text and font support is limited, fonts must be installed on the system, and animation and scripting are not implemented.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick diagram.svg diagram.pdf`. ImageMagick's format list says SVG is rendered by Inkscape, RSVG or its internal renderer, and that PDF support requires Ghostscript.

### Problems with SVG files

- **Text looks wrong**: the drawing depends on which fonts are present, and a replacement font can alter it. Turn the text into paths before exporting, or install the font the SVG names.
- **A picture is missing**: this page renders the SVG as an image, which means a linked picture is not drawn whether or not you are online. Embed pictures in the SVG as data URIs.
- **The PDF is soft when printed**: the picture is embedded at the SVG's pixel size. Use Inkscape instead.
- **Pictures inside the SVG stay pixelated**: pixel images embedded in an SVG keep their own resolution, so enlarging them shows the blocks.
- **The page is much smaller than expected**: the PDF follows the size your browser reports for the SVG, one pixel to one point. If a larger page is needed, set the size in an editor beforehand.
- **The file will not load**: when the browser cannot decode the file, you get "Image decode failed." Check it in a browser or in Inkscape beforehand.

- **How the picture is stored**: SVG keeps shapes and text as instructions. PNG keeps a fixed grid of pixels, compressed losslessly with DEFLATE.
- **Scaling**: an SVG redraws cleanly at any size. A PNG blurs or turns blocky when enlarged past its pixels.
- **Transparency**: both have it. An SVG is clear wherever nothing is drawn; a PNG records an alpha value per pixel.
- **Text**: in an SVG it stays real text. In a PNG it becomes pixels.
- **Motion**: SVG can animate. This page writes a single still PNG.
- **Color depth**: PNG supports between 1 and 16 bits per sample; this page saves 8 bits per channel.
- **Outside files**: an SVG is rendered as a standalone image here, so anything it links to, such as a picture, a stylesheet or a web font, is never fetched. What is embedded in the file, and fonts installed on your device, do appear.

How this page draws it: your browser renders the SVG at the size it reports, one to one, onto a transparent canvas, and the canvas is saved as a PNG. Nothing in this page scales the picture or caps its size.

### Other ways to convert SVG to PNG

- **Inkscape (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the SVG and choose File > Export (Shift+Ctrl+E). On the Single File tab, pick Selection, Document, Page or Custom as the area, set the image size or DPI, choose PNG as the export format and click Export. The Background Color button sets what fills the background.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** bring the SVG into GIMP, then use File > Export As (Shift+Ctrl+E) to save it as a PNG. GIMP is a raster editor, so the drawing becomes pixels.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.svg output.png`. ImageMagick draws SVG with Inkscape, RSVG or its own MSVG renderer.

### Problems with SVG files

- **The PNG is smaller than you wanted**: there is no scale option here. Export from Inkscape and set the image size or DPI there.
- **Text shows in the wrong font**: lettering uses whichever fonts your device has, and a font the file links to over the web isn't loaded here.
- **The background looks black or checkered in some viewers**: the PNG keeps the SVG's empty areas transparent, so what shows behind them depends on the viewer.
- **A linked picture is missing**: pictures the SVG only links to are never loaded here. Embed them in the SVG before converting.
- **Many drawings to convert**: choose them together, and the page draws the SVGs one after another and hands back a separate PNG for each, with no ZIP to unpack.
- **A site won't accept your SVG**: upload the PNG instead, since a PNG is displayed by every major browser.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the browser could not render the file. Fix it in a text editor or re-export it from your design tool.
- **You need a JPG or an icon**: use the [SVG to JPG converter](/svg-to-jpg/) or the [SVG to ICO converter](/svg-to-ico/).

guide.title: Understanding SVG to SVG
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

Short for Scalable Vector Graphics, SVG is a W3C standard vector format written in XML. Shapes, paths and text are described mathematically, so images scale to any size without losing sharpness. It is used for logos and icons on the web, illustrations and diagrams, and charts and maps. An SVG can also embed pictures, and those parts keep their own pixel resolution when the drawing is enlarged.

SVG to SVG sounds like a no-op, but the output is a different kind of file: a picture wrapped in SVG markup.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Inkscape works on SVG natively, while Mozilla Firefox renders it.
- **Web and mobile:** Google Chrome displays SVG on both, and Safari does so on mobile.

### SVG and SVG compared

- **Structure**: your original holds shapes, paths and text. The result holds one `<image>` element with a PNG embedded as base64.
- **Size**: the picture is drawn 1:1 at the dimensions the browser gives the original.
- **Tracing**: none. The picture is not turned back into vector shapes.
- **Transparency**: the canvas starts transparent, so see-through areas survive in the PNG.
- **Metadata**: nothing but raw pixels passes through, so EXIF, ICC and XMP data is gone.
- **Privacy**: the drawing never leaves your device, since the page works in the browser.

### Other ways to convert SVG to SVG

These work on the SVG itself instead of replacing it with a picture.

- **Inkscape:** when you save, choose the Plain SVG type. Its manual describes it as meant for sharing your drawing with people who might not use Inkscape. Work on a separate copy.
- **Scour:** run `scour -i design.svg -o cleaned.svg`. Its options are typically lossless but can be tweaked for more aggressive cleaning.
- **SVGO:** run `svgo one.svg -o one.min.svg`. It has a plugin architecture, and the plugins are set in a config file such as `svgo.config.mjs`.

### Problems with SVG files

- **Pictures in other files vanish**: an SVG drawn as an image never loads them, online or not. Embed such pictures as data.
- **Fonts change the drawing**: the text is laid out with whichever fonts exist, so a stand-in font can alter its look.
- **Embedded pictures look soft when enlarged**: they keep their own pixel resolution. Keep your original for further editing.

guide.title: SVG to TGA: background and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

An SVG file lists shapes, text and embedded images in XML, and a renderer draws them: that is the Scalable Vector Graphics standard from the W3C. Since the shapes are instructions rather than pixels, the drawing keeps clean edges at whatever size you ask for. The file is text, CSS and JavaScript can act on it, and all major browsers show it. A pixel image embedded in an SVG is the exception, because it keeps its original resolution when enlarged.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Inkscape, for native SVG editing.
- **Windows, Mac, Linux and Web:** Mozilla Firefox displays SVG.
- **Web and Mobile:** Google Chrome displays SVG.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays SVG.

### SVG and TGA compared

Targa, a raster format tied to Truevision's video boards, keeps turning up in video editing and in game development. It supports RGB, indexed-color and grayscale images. In a 24-bit file every color component gets eight bits; a 32-bit file adds an eight-bit alpha channel. Run-length encoding is optional. Moving from SVG to TGA locks the drawing to a single pixel size, so it can't be scaled up cleanly or edited as shapes again.

Your browser paints the SVG at its reported dimensions; ImageMagick then writes the TGA from those pixels. Metadata doesn't come along. The browser loads nothing from outside the file, so the TGA shows only what the SVG embeds, plus fonts installed on the device.

### Other ways to convert SVG to TGA

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick -density 144 artwork.svg artwork.tga`. -density controls the resolution at which ImageMagick draws the SVG into pixels.
- **Inkscape and ImageMagick:** use Inkscape to open the SVG, press Shift+Ctrl+E and choose an export area, set the width in pixels, name the file and click Export for a PNG. Then run `magick artwork.png artwork.tga`.

### Problems with SVG files

- **Lettering changed:** text layout depends on the fonts available, so a substitute for a missing one alters the drawing.
- **A picture is missing:** artwork that the SVG only points to stays blank on this page; put the image inside the file.
- **The texture looks soft:** bitmaps embedded in the SVG retain their original resolution when enlarged.

guide.title: SVG to TIF: background and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

The W3C's SVG format uses XML to describe flat graphics through shapes, text and embedded pictures. Stored as instructions, those shapes can be rendered large or small with no loss in sharpness. The format is readable text that CSS and JavaScript can style, and every major browser can display it. Pictures embedded in the file are the exception: they keep their original pixel resolution when enlarged.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Inkscape edits SVG natively.
- **Windows, Mac, Linux and Web:** Mozilla Firefox displays SVG.
- **Web and Mobile:** Google Chrome displays SVG.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays SVG.

### SVG and TIF compared

TIFF wraps raster data in tags, and Aldus and Microsoft were behind its development. The 6.0 revision dates from 1992, and today the specification belongs to Adobe. One format sits behind both file endings, and its media type is image/tiff. Inside, the choice of compression and color representation varies from file to file, several images can share one file, and archivists rely on it for high-bit-depth imaging and preservation masters. An SVG converted to TIF becomes one raster picture at a fixed size, and its shapes are no longer editable.

On this page the browser paints the SVG at the dimensions it reports, then ImageMagick writes the TIF from those pixels. They pass through at 8 bits per channel, so the TIF is not a high-depth file, and metadata is dropped. The browser loads nothing from outside the SVG, so the result shows embedded data plus fonts installed on your device.

### Other ways to convert SVG to TIF

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick -density 180 illustration.svg illustration.tif`. A higher -density value gives a larger canvas when ImageMagick reads the SVG.
- **Inkscape and ImageMagick:** in Inkscape, open the SVG and press Shift+Ctrl+E to get the Export PNG Image dialog. Export a PNG at the pixel width you want, then run `magick illustration.png illustration.tif`.

### Problems with SVG files

- **A font was swapped:** the lettering follows whichever fonts your device has, so the drawing changes when one is missing.
- **A picture went missing:** an outside image the SVG points to is not drawn here; put the picture into the file itself.
- **A photo in the drawing looks soft:** a bitmap inside the SVG stays at its own pixel resolution however far you enlarge it.

guide.title: About SVG files
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

SVG is short for Scalable Vector Graphics. It is an XML-based vector image format and a W3C standard, with SVG 1.0 a Recommendation in 2001 and SVG 1.1 following in 2003. A logo, chart or icon is stored as shapes, paths and text instead of a grid of pixels, which is why an SVG can be enlarged to any size without going soft. Because the format is plain XML text, you can open the file in a text editor and read its shapes, and a text file can also be searched, indexed and compressed. The drawing can be styled with CSS, and the file can include animation and scripting. SVG also supports clipping paths, masks and filter effects. Browsers open an SVG directly, and a web page can embed one too. A gzip-compressed SVG uses the .svgz extension, and the registered media type is image/svg+xml.

Not every SVG is purely vector. Photos can be placed inside one, and they stay at their own resolution however far you zoom. A drawing can also refer to resources outside the file. A font installed on the device shows up, but a linked image or web font never loads when the SVG is drawn as a picture.

### Programs that open SVG files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- Inkscape: edits SVG natively.
- Mozilla Firefox: opens SVG files in the browser.

**Web and mobile**

- Google Chrome displays SVG.
- Safari displays SVG on mobile.

### SVG and TIFF compared

- **Content**: SVG holds shapes, text and styling you can edit. TIFF holds pixels in a tag-based structure, and one file can store several images.
- **Size**: an SVG has no fixed pixel size and scales cleanly. A TIFF is fixed at the pixel dimensions it was saved with, so enlarging it later cannot bring the sharpness back.
- **Compression and color**: TIFF allows several compression schemes, deep color and CMYK separations. SVG is XML text. The extensions .tif and .tiff both name TIFF, with the media type image/tiff, and it was developed by Aldus and Microsoft as a tag-based raster wrapper that can hold different color representations.
- **History**: TIFF began in 1986 at Aldus, and its 6.0 revision dates from 1992. Adobe now controls the specification. Classic TIFF stores file offsets in 32 bits, so a file tops out near 4 GB. SVG is a W3C recommendation.
- **Typical use**: TIFF turns up in scanning, archiving, photography and print work, and document imaging, while SVG is the logo, icon and diagram format of web pages.

The steps are short. Your browser renders the SVG and reports its width and height, and those numbers become the TIFF's pixel dimensions. The page adds no scaling, no size cap and no viewBox logic of its own, and it paints no background, so clear areas remain clear. ImageMagick, running as WebAssembly, then saves the pixels as an uncompressed TIFF whose channels are 8-bit red, green, blue and alpha. Because only raw pixels travel, EXIF data, color profiles and XMP packets stay behind. If you need more pixels, enlarge the width and height attributes in the SVG first. Your original SVG is not changed.

### Other ways to convert SVG to TIFF

- **ImageMagick:** run `magick -density 300 logo.svg logo-print.tiff`. The -density option sets the resolution ImageMagick renders an SVG at, and the default is 72 dots per inch. ImageMagick renders SVG through Inkscape, RSVG or its own internal renderer, so the result depends on the installation.
- **GIMP:** GIMP opens an SVG as an image in the usual way. Choose File > Export As to store it in a format other than XCF, and pick TIFF. The TIFF dialog offers compression such as None, LZW, Pack Bits and Deflate. GIMP opens the SVG as a picture of pixels, so keep the original SVG.

### Problems with SVG files

- **Letters are in the wrong typeface**: text is drawn with the fonts your device has, so a stand-in typeface can alter how the drawing looks. Convert the text to outlines in Inkscape before you start.
- **An image is absent**: a picture the SVG only links to is not fetched. Embed it in the file as data.
- **An embedded photo looks blurry when enlarged**: the pixel parts of an SVG keep their original resolution.

guide.title: About SVG and TTF
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

SVG is an XML format for drawings. It describes shapes, text and embedded images, and the geometry scales without losing sharpness. A font outline is only a filled shape, so strokes, text, colors and masks have no place in it.

This page turns the filled shapes of one SVG into a single glyph. Prepare the icon as one simple filled drawing; the artboard sets the height the glyph gets.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Inkscape edits SVG natively, and FontForge opens the finished TrueType outlines.
- **Web:** Chrome and Firefox display SVG.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays SVG.
- **Windows:** Windows Font Previewer shows a font before you install it.
- **Mac:** Font Book installs and validates font files.
- **Linux:** GNOME Fonts previews installed typefaces.

### SVG and TTF compared

- **What they hold**: an SVG holds drawing instructions. A TTF holds scalable character outlines in tagged tables, with glyph mappings, metrics and naming.
- **Origin**: Apple developed TrueType and licensed it to Microsoft. The media type is font/ttf.
- **Scale**: the font here is built at 1,000 units to the em, with the artboard (the viewBox, else width and height, else the drawing's bounds) at full height and 150 units below the baseline.
- **Limits**: a glyph can have at most 65,535 points, and a drawing past that is refused as too detailed.

The icon lands on U+E000 in a font named after your file.

### Other ways to convert SVG to TTF

- **FontForge interface (Windows, Mac, Linux):** double-click a glyph slot, choose File > Import, change the format to SVG and pick the file. Drag the outline down to the baseline, scale it with Element > Transform, then use the Generate dialog and pick the True Type outline type.
- **FontForge scripting:** `glyph.importOutlines` accepts svg files into the foreground layer, and `font.generate` takes its output type from the extension of the file name you give it.
- **IcoMoon (web):** add SVGs in the Import panel, then open the Export panel, keep the Font format ticked and download the package. Code points are set in the Metadata tab of the Batch panel.

### Problems with SVG files

- **Thin lines disappear**: a stroke becomes nothing. Convert strokes to filled outlines first.
- **Holes fill in**: a very complex shape can run past the page's time or room, and its crossing outlines then fill. Simplify the artwork.
- **Typing a letter shows nothing**: the icon is on U+E000, not on a familiar key. Type that code point to see it.
- **The font won't display**: a damaged font can fail to show; Font Book on a Mac validates font files.

guide.title: SVG to WebP: formats and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is an SVG file?

The Scalable Vector Graphics format is an XML language from the W3C for describing drawings with shapes, paths and text instead of pixels. Because shapes are stored as instructions, a browser can draw an SVG at any size without losing sharpness, and CSS can style it. The W3C made SVG a Recommendation first in 2001 and issued the 1.1 edition in 2003. An SVG can also embed a raster picture, so not everything you see in one is a vector. Keep that in mind before you pick an export size.

SVG turns up in web logos and icons, in illustrations, diagrams, charts and maps alike. Its media type is image/svg+xml, and each major browser can display it. Since the file is plain text, a plain editor opens it, and software can search, index or compress it. A compressed one uses the .svgz extension. The format also covers clipping paths, masks and filter effects, and an SVG can be shown on its own or placed inside an HTML page.

### Programs that open SVG files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Inkscape, the native SVG editor, handles the file, and Mozilla Firefox displays it.
- **Web:** Chrome displays SVG.
- **Mobile:** Safari displays SVG on iPhone and iPad.

### SVG and WebP compared

- **Extensions**: .svg is image/svg+xml, .webp is image/webp.
- **Stored as**: an SVG holds drawing instructions. A WebP holds pixels.
- **Scaling**: an SVG redraws sharply at any size. A WebP has fixed dimensions and softens when enlarged.
- **Transparency**: both can be see-through. WebP supports transparency in lossy and lossless files.
- **Animation and scripts**: SVG supports both. A WebP can hold an animation too, but this page writes a single picture.
- **Editing**: paths, text and object names stay in the SVG. The WebP has none of them.
- **Limit**: a WebP image can be at most 16,383 pixels on either side.

Google announced WebP in 2010, and a WebP file is a RIFF container. RFC 9649 documents the format and registers its image/webp media type.

Your browser draws the SVG first, and the WebP has the pixel size the browser reports for it, 1:1, with no scale factor added by this page. The canvas starts transparent, so empty areas stay see-through. The picture has 8 bits per channel, and nothing from the SVG's metadata is carried over. Choose several SVGs and each downloads as its own WebP, named after its SVG, so a set of icons takes one visit.

To view a WebP, use Chrome or Firefox, GIMP opens it on Windows, Mac and Linux, and XnView MP reads and writes it.

### Other ways to convert SVG to WebP

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick diagram.svg diagram.webp`. ImageMagick's format table marks SVG and WebP as readable and writable, and notes that SVG is drawn by Inkscape, RSVG or its own renderer. Compare the result with the original in a browser tab.
- **Inkscape with cwebp:** export a PNG from Inkscape with File > Export PNG Image, choosing the area and the size in pixels, then run `cwebp -lossless diagram.png -o diagram.webp`. cwebp reads PNG, JPEG and TIFF input, and its -lossless option encodes without loss.

Both routes let you pick the size or a lossless WebP, which this page doesn't offer. Use them when you need an exact pixel size, or a whole folder converted at once.

### Problems with SVG files

- **The WebP is soft or small**: the size comes from the SVG's own width and height. Edit those in a text editor, or export at the size you need from Inkscape.
- **Text looks different**: how text is laid out depends on which fonts exist, and a substituted font changes the drawing. Convert the text to paths before converting the file so the shapes travel with it.
- **A linked picture is missing**: a picture the SVG links to never loads, because the page draws the file as an image whether you are online or not. Embed that picture in the SVG first.
- **An embedded photo looks soft**: a small picture inside the SVG stays at its own resolution, however large the export.
- **"Image decode failed."**: the browser could not draw this file. Try it in a browser tab first, and repair any XML errors in an editor such as Inkscape.

guide.title: About SWF files
guide.markdown:
### What is an SWF file?

Flash animations, games and interactive pages were delivered as SWF files, a format that began at Macromedia. Adobe acquired Macromedia in 2005. The Library of Congress also records the expansion Small Web Format. A file can combine vector graphics, animation and bitmap video. Interactive content uses ActionScript alongside a timeline.

An SWF may refer to external media instead of holding every resource. Flash Player was discontinued by Adobe on 31 December 2020, which leaves SWF mostly as a format for old archived web content.

### Programs that open SWF files

**Windows, macOS and Linux**

- Ruffle: emulates Flash, and how well a file plays depends on the ActionScript features it uses.

**Windows and Linux**

- Lightspark: a Flash implementation that is only partial.

**Mac**

- Adobe Audition: imports SWF to extract audio from a video file if DLMS support is enabled; it does not run interactive Flash.

**Web**

- Ruffle's web player: runs Flash in a browser through WebAssembly, and some APIs are still missing.

### SWF and AVI compared

- **Purpose**: an SWF is a Flash container for vector animation, ActionScript and embedded media. An AVI holds interleaved video and audio.
- **Interaction**: an SWF can respond to clicks through ActionScript. An AVI plays from start to finish.
- **Container**: an AVI is RIFF-based and can hold many codecs. Microsoft introduced it in 1992.
- **Players**: AVI plays in QuickTime Player, in Windows Media Player and in VLC.

Here FFmpeg takes the media streams out of the SWF, encodes the video as MPEG-4 and the sound as MP3, and wraps them in an AVI.

### Other ways to convert SWF to AVI

- **FFmpeg:** run ffmpeg -i clip.swf -c:v mpeg4 -c:a libmp3lame decoded.avi. FFmpeg's SWF reader decodes audio and video tags and skips the rest, so ActionScript does not run.
- **JPEXS Free Flash Decompiler with FFmpeg:** on Linux, run ffdec -export movie extracted presentation.swf. The movie export defaults to FLV without sound. Then run ffmpeg -i extracted-movie.flv -c:v mpeg4 extracted-movie.avi, using the file name the export wrote.
- **Ruffle with OBS Studio and FFmpeg:** play the SWF in Ruffle, then in OBS add a Window Capture or Display Capture source, review the audio settings and begin recording. Then run ffmpeg on the recording file, for example ffmpeg -i your-recording -c:v mpeg4 -c:a libmp3lame performance.avi. This captures a game as it plays.

### Problems with SWF files

- **Nothing runs**: Adobe Flash Player no longer runs Flash content after its end-of-life block. Open the file in Ruffle.
- **A game acts differently**: some Flash APIs are missing from Ruffle, so visuals or behavior can change.
- **Parts are missing**: an SWF that refers to external media may not behave as intended when those files are absent.

guide.title: Understanding SWF and FLV
guide.markdown:
### What is a SWF file?

SWF is the legacy Flash multimedia format associated with Macromedia and Adobe. It can combine vectors, bitmap media, timelines, and ActionScript-driven interaction. An animation, a video wrapper, and an interactive game can therefore share the extension while requiring different ways to interpret their contents.

### Programs that open SWF files

- **Web:** the Ruffle web player emulates Flash inside a browser with WebAssembly, leaving some APIs incomplete.
- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** to watch the SWF before converting, Ruffle emulates Flash, with results that depend on the ActionScript in use.
- **Windows and Linux:** Lightspark implements Flash only in part.
- **Mac:** Adobe Audition can pull the audio out of an SWF, though it is no interactive Flash runtime.

### SWF and FLV compared

FLV is a container from the Flash delivery ecosystem, usually holding H.263 or H.264 video with MP3 or AAC audio. An SWF can be an interactive program, and its ActionScript can even point to an external FLV.

This page runs FFmpeg to re-encode the SWF as H.264 video and AAC sound. Frames wider than 1920 pixels shrink, 30 fps is the ceiling for the rate, and odd edges lose a pixel.

### Other ways to convert SWF to FLV

- **FFmpeg direct encode:** `ffmpeg -i media.swf -c:v libx264 -crf 27 -f flv -c:a aac direct.flv` re-encodes the embedded media with CRF 27 where this page uses CRF 32, and with no size or rate cap.
- **FFmpeg compatible copy:** `ffmpeg -i media.swf -c copy -f flv copied.flv` skips the new encode when the extracted streams fit FLV.
- **FFmpeg lossless intermediate:** decode with `ffmpeg -i media.swf -c:v ffv1 -c:a pcm_s16le intermediate.mkv`, check that file, then encode it to FLV. The review stage costs disk space but no extra loss before the final encode.

### Problems with SWF files

**Flash Player is retired:** Adobe's end-of-life block stopped Flash Player from running Flash content.

**Ruffle differs:** Ruffle leaves some Flash APIs unimplemented, so an SWF may look or act differently.

**Assets are absent:** an intact SWF can misbehave when the external assets it needs are missing.

**Interaction cannot stay:** ActionScript controls do not survive conversion to video.

guide.title: About SWF files
guide.markdown:
### What is an SWF file?

SWF is the file format of Flash, the web animation and games technology that began at Macromedia and passed to Adobe when it bought Macromedia in 2005. The letters are commonly read as Shockwave Flash, and a source also gives the name Small Web Format. One file can combine vector graphics, timeline animation, bitmap video, sound and ActionScript code. Its registered media types include application/vnd.adobe.flash.movie.

Adobe ended support for Flash Player on 31 December 2020, so SWF files now live in archives of old games, cartoons and banner ads, and it is no longer simple to see them play. An SWF may also refer to outside media instead of containing everything, so an old file can be missing parts it once loaded.

### Programs that open SWF files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- Ruffle: a Flash emulator, where compatibility depends on the ActionScript features a file uses.

**Windows and Linux**

- Lightspark: an incomplete Flash implementation.

**Mac**

- Adobe Audition: its SWF import pulls out the audio of video files, and it is not an interactive Flash runtime.

**Web**

- Web player from the Ruffle project: runs Flash in a page through WebAssembly, with some APIs still missing.

### SWF and GIF compared

- **Names and media types**: .swf is application/vnd.adobe.flash.movie. .gif is the Graphics Interchange Format that CompuServe introduced in 1987.
- **Content**: an SWF holds vector graphics, animation, video, sound and code. A GIF holds raster frames and nothing else.
- **Color**: a GIF frame draws from a palette of at most 256 colors. A SWF's vector fills and video are not limited that way.
- **Transparency**: GIF has 1-bit transparency, where a pixel is either clear or solid.
- **Sound and interactivity**: GIF has neither.
- **Compression**: GIF compresses each frame with lossless LZW.

What happens here: FFmpeg opens the SWF and builds a palette from its video frames, sampled at 15 fps and scaled to fit 480 pixels with even sides. A second pass then draws every frame with that palette and writes a GIF that repeats forever, so you do not need to choose a loop count. Only the video stream is used, so the sound is dropped and no ActionScript runs. A SWF that ran faster than 15 fps loses its in-between frames. The SWF you chose is never altered.

### Other ways to convert SWF to GIF

- **JPEXS Free Flash Decompiler:** run `ffdec -format frame:gif -export frame frames-out banner.swf`, using the executable for your platform. The wiki documents the -format option, where frame:gif is one of the frame formats. This writes each frame of the SWF as a separate GIF image in the output folder. For frame export the wiki lists PNG, APNG, GIF, AVI and SVG, with PNG as the default.
- **FFmpeg:** for a SWF with embedded video, run `ffmpeg -i clip.swf flash-preview.gif`. FFmpeg's SWF reader handles bitmap, video and audio data, and it skips vector shape tags, so it is not a Flash renderer. The reader covers FLV1, screen video, JPEG and lossless bitmap pictures, with PCM, ADPCM, MP3 and Nellymoser sound.
- **Ruffle plus OBS Studio and FFmpeg:** open the SWF in Ruffle. In OBS add a window or display capture source, click Start Recording and perform the sequence. Check the recording settings under Settings > Output first. Then encode the saved recording as a GIF with FFmpeg. This captures one playing session, including any errors.

### Problems with SWF files

- **Nothing will open it**: Flash Player was retired at the end of 2020. Use Ruffle or Lightspark instead. Lightspark is an incomplete Flash implementation, so it may not cover everything a file uses.
- **A game or animation looks wrong in Ruffle**: Ruffle has not implemented every Flash API, so graphics or behavior can differ from the original. Its compatibility page says most ActionScript 1 and 2 content will work, with some graphical inaccuracies, and that most ActionScript 3 games run well enough to be played.
- **Parts are missing**: a SWF can depend on external files that no longer exist online. Get the whole set of files.
- **FFmpeg reports an error**: the SWF probably holds no video stream, only sound or vector drawing. Try JPEXS for frames or record it with Ruffle.
- **The buttons don't work**: a GIF has no code, so ActionScript controls cannot carry over.

guide.title: SWF background and MOV conversion
guide.markdown:
### What is an SWF file?

SWF belongs to the Flash ecosystem. Macromedia created the format for Flash animations, games and interactive web content, and Adobe stopped supporting Flash Player on 31 December 2020. A file can combine timeline animation, vector shapes, compressed media and ActionScript code. Some SWFs hold a movie stream, while others draw their scenes from vectors and scripts, and a few carry both. That difference decides whether a media converter finds anything to extract.

MOV is a QuickTime movie container for timed media. It holds a linear recording of pictures and sound, so clickable Flash behavior and branching can't survive in it.

### Programs that open SWF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Ruffle, an emulator for Flash, plays SWF files, though some language and API features are still missing, and the JPEXS Free Flash Decompiler opens them too.
- **Windows and Linux:** Lightspark is an incomplete Flash implementation.
- **Web:** a web player from Ruffle emulates Flash in a browser through WebAssembly.

FFmpeg has an SWF demuxer that reads the media embedded in the file.

### SWF and MOV compared

This page does not render Flash. FFmpeg runs in your browser and reads only the audio and video embedded in the SWF. It doesn't run ActionScript or draw the vector animation, so a SWF without embedded video has nothing for it to read.

When there is media to read, the page encodes H.264 video with x264 and AAC audio at 96 kbps into a MOV, with the moov atom moved to the front (`+faststart`). The long side is capped at 1920 px, the frame rate at 30 per second, and sizes become even.

### Other ways to convert SWF to MOV

- **FFmpeg:** run `ffmpeg -i archive.swf -c:a aac -c:v libx264 extracted-movie.mov`. Check the result by playing the MOV, since only embedded media can appear in it.

### Problems with SWF files

- **The MOV shows no scene**: the SWF draws its scene with Flash features and holds no video to read.
- **Buttons no longer work**: a movie plays straight through and keeps no interaction.
- **The animation does not look like the SWF**: only the embedded audio and video are read, never the vector drawing.

guide.title: About SWF and MP4
guide.markdown:
### What is a SWF file?

An SWF is a Flash file, also known as Small Web Format. It is a legacy multimedia format associated with Macromedia and Adobe Flash, and Adobe acquired Macromedia in 2005. A single SWF may mix vector drawings, animation and bitmap video. Interactive ones put ActionScript on the timeline, and some point to outside media in place of holding every resource. Its registered media types include application/vnd.adobe.flash.movie.

Flash Player was retired on 31 December 2020, after which it no longer ran Flash content at all. That is why SWF files now survive mostly as Flash animations, games and archived web content, and why people look for a way to keep them as video.

### Programs that open SWF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** Ruffle is a Flash emulator. How well a file plays hinges on which ActionScript features it needs.
- **Windows and Linux:** Lightspark is an incomplete Flash implementation.
- **Mac:** Adobe Audition can import an SWF and extract the audio of video files when DLMS support is enabled. It is not an interactive Flash runtime.
- **Web:** a browser can run Ruffle's web player, which uses WebAssembly to emulate Flash. Some APIs remain incomplete, and Ruffle also ships as browser extensions.

### SWF and MP4 compared

An SWF describes a timeline with scripts, while an MP4 records a finished video. MP4 is a container defined in ISO/IEC 14496-14 that can hold video, audio and metadata, and H.264 video with AAC audio is its most common combination. Turning an SWF into an MP4 therefore keeps what can be played back and leaves the logic behind. No video can retain ActionScript interactions as executable controls, so a menu, a button or a game stays in the SWF.

This page reads the video and sound embedded in the SWF with FFmpeg. FFmpeg is not a Flash runtime, so it does not run ActionScript. The picture goes through x264 using CRF 32 and the ultrafast preset, while the sound is encoded by AAC at 96 kbps. The long edge of the frame tops out at 1920 px, and the rate tops out at 30 frames a second. A smaller frame is not enlarged, a slower clip is not sped up, and a faster clip has frames dropped while keeping its length. Both sides then drop to even numbers, which costs an odd side one pixel.

Your download takes the SWF's name plus .mp4, and the original stays as it was. Files in the queue run in turn, each becoming a separate MP4.

### Other ways to convert SWF to MP4

- **FFmpeg (command line):** FFmpeg lists Flash (SWF) among the formats it can demux, so `ffmpeg -i movie.swf movie.mp4` converts the video and sound inside a file. It gives you control over the codecs and size, which this page fixes.
- **JPEXS plus FFmpeg:** JPEXS Free Flash Decompiler exports from the command line with `ffdec -format frame:avi -export frame frames input.swf`. Its sound item type exports audio separately, and movie exports default to FLV without sound. Convert the exported AVI with `ffmpeg -i frames/movie.avi output.mp4`, using the file name JPEXS actually wrote.
- **Ruffle and OBS Studio:** play the SWF in Ruffle, add its window to OBS with the + button under Sources and Window Capture, and press Start Recording. Ruffle's desktop apps for Windows, macOS and Linux suit this best. The capture holds only the route you play through, so it suits a game or a lesson that needs clicks, and OBS shows its recording format under Settings > Output.

### Problems with SWF files

**Adobe's player will not run it:** the retired Flash Player is not an option, so use an emulator such as Ruffle, or convert the video inside the file.

**It plays differently in Ruffle:** Ruffle does not implement every Flash API, so an SWF may show graphical or behavioral differences from the original.

**Pieces are missing:** an SWF can refer to external images, sound or video instead of containing them. Without those files beside it, it can behave incompletely, so keep them together.

**Interactions disappear in a video:** a video conversion cannot retain ActionScript interactions as executable controls. Record the route you want to show, or keep the SWF for the interactive version.

guide.title: About TGA files
guide.markdown:
### What is a TGA file?

Targa, written .tga, began as the picture format of Truevision's video boards, which is where the name comes from. It can hold RGB, indexed-color or grayscale images. In a 24-bit RGB file each of red, green and blue gets 8 bits; a 32-bit file adds an 8-bit alpha channel so pixels can be partly see-through. The data may be run-length encoded, an option that squeezes long stretches of identical pixels.

The boards are history, but the format stuck around. Video editing and game development still use Targa images, so most TGAs people find today are game textures, 3D renders or frames out of an editing project. Hardly any phone, browser or office program shows one, which is the usual reason for wanting a JPG: something to paste into a document, post on a forum or send by email.

### Programs that open TGA files

**Windows, Mac and Linux:**

- GIMP has an official Targa plug-in that both loads and exports the format.
- ImageMagick treats TGA, ICB, VDA and VST as one Truevision Targa family and can read and write it.

**Windows and Mac:**

- Adobe Photoshop can open a Targa and has its own Targa options on save; a 24-bit save leaves no room for an alpha channel.

### TGA and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media type**: .tga for Targa. For JPEG, .jpg and .jpeg are one format, registered as image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: a Targa keeps every pixel, whether or not run-length encoding is used. Baseline JPEG throws detail away by cutting the picture into 8x8 pixel blocks, applying a discrete cosine transform and coding the result with Huffman codes.
- **Transparency**: the alpha channel in a 32-bit TGA has no counterpart in JPEG, which stores no transparency at all.
- **Layers**: JPEG cannot store them.

- **Where each is used**: Targa belongs to production, with game textures, renders and video frames. Most digital cameras and scanners build JPEG in, and browsers all show it, so it travels where a Targa cannot.

How the page does it: ImageMagick, compiled to WebAssembly, reads the TGA on your device and writes the JPG. Only one image is read from the file.

### Other ways to convert TGA to JPG

- **ImageMagick (command line):** `magick texture.tga preview.jpg` does it in one line. ImageMagick's format list shows TGA and JPEG both as readable and writable, and the command ran on a TGA fixture here. Add `-quality 90` before the output name to pick a JPEG quality yourself; ImageMagick scales it from 1, the lowest quality and most compression, to 100, the best quality and least compression.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the TGA, choose File > Export As, give the file a .jpg name and click Export. A JPEG export dialog follows, with quality at 85 by default. The same number can mean a different quality in another program, and JPEG doesn't support transparency or multiple layers.
- **Pillow (Python):** run `from PIL import Image` then `Image.open("texture.tga").convert("RGB").save("preview.jpg")`. Pillow reads and writes TGA, and picks the output format from the file name. Saving an RGBA Targa straight to JPEG raised an error in a test, so the `convert("RGB")` step stays.

### Problems with TGA files

- **Nothing on your computer opens it**: open the TGA in GIMP, Photoshop or ImageMagick, or make a JPG here.
- **The see-through areas are gone**: JPEG has no alpha channel. When transparency matters, take the [TGA to PNG converter](/tga-to-png/) instead.
- **A "32-bit" file looks like ordinary color**: the number counts bits per pixel, so it is four 8-bit channels, not 32 bits for each color.
- **An export lost its alpha**: saving RGB artwork at 24 bits leaves no space for a Targa alpha channel. Write it as 32-bit if you need one.
- **Partial transparency in an indexed Targa**: GIMP cannot export full partial-alpha information in an indexed Targa color map, and only one fully transparent color is allowed in its indexed mode.
- **The JPG looks softer than the texture**: that is the cost of lossy compression. Keep the TGA as the working file.
- **Version 2 extension fields vanish**: GIMP's Targa support does not keep every one of them, so a round trip through GIMP can drop extra data stored in the file.
- **The page refuses a huge image**: shrink the picture in an editor first.

guide.title: About TGA and PNG
guide.markdown:
### What is a TGA file?

Targa, or TGA, is a raster format that Truevision introduced in 1984. Each pixel takes 8 to 32 bits, run-length encoding is optional, and an alpha channel may be included. It has a simple header, and ImageMagick's format list marks it as readable and writable.

Targa survives in game development and in video and 3D rendering, where artists and tools still pass textures and renders around as TGA. ImageMagick groups the ICB, VDA and VST endings with Truevision Targa, so those files are the same family.

### Programs that open TGA files

- **Linux, Mac and Windows:** the Targa plug-in that ships with GIMP loads and exports TGA images.
- **Linux, Mac and Windows:** ImageMagick can read and write Truevision Targa, which covers the TGA, ICB, VDA and VST family.
- **Windows and Mac:** Adobe Photoshop opens Targa images and provides Targa save options.

### TGA and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .tga (also .icb, .vda, .vst) for Targa; .png and image/png for PNG.
- **Compression**: Targa's run-length encoding is optional. PNG always compresses, using DEFLATE (LZ77 plus Huffman coding), and it is lossless.
- **Color depth**: Targa runs from 8 to 32 bits per pixel. PNG supports indexed, grayscale and truecolor images with 1 to 16 bits per sample.
- **Transparency**: both have an alpha channel.
- **Used for**: Targa serves game textures and video and 3D rendering output. PNG is the choice for sharp web graphics, interface art, logos and screenshots, and for pictures that need transparency.
- **Origin**: Targa dates from 1984, and PNG from the mid-1990s, when it was devised as a patent-free successor to GIF. October 1996 saw it become the W3C's first published Recommendation for an image format. Its standards-body editions are RFC 2083 and ISO/IEC 15948:2004.
- **Reach**: browsers of every major kind show PNG, and no known patent on it demands royalties. GIMP, Windows Photos and Preview on macOS open it too, and macOS saves screenshots in PNG by default.
- **Media types**: image/png is registered for PNG, and image/apng for animated files.
- **Structure**: inside a PNG you find a fixed signature and then a run of chunks; the header lives in IHDR, image data sits in IDAT and IEND ends the file.
- **Newer features**: software without animation support shows PNG's default still image, though the specification itself now covers animated PNG. The third edition adds HDR support via a cICP chunk and Exif metadata in an eXIf chunk.

Mostly the wrapper changes here. ImageMagick compiled to WebAssembly reads the TGA and writes a PNG, and the page passes no quality setting. The file is read as a single image, and nothing is uploaded. A picture over about 537 megapixels is turned away. Your original TGA is not changed, since you download a new copy. When you pick several files, they are handled one at a time and no ZIP is made.

### Other ways to convert TGA to PNG

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick texture.tga texture.png`. ImageMagick's format list shows TGA and PNG as both readable and writable, and its quickstart shows the same pattern: `magick rose.jpg rose.png`.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the TGA with File > Open, then pick File > Export As and give it the name texture.png. The PNG dialog that follows lists pixel format and metadata options. The compression level only trades speed for size, since PNG compression is not lossy.
- **IrfanView:** choose File > Open for the Targa, then File > Save as and select PNG. IrfanView's format list marks TGA and PNG as readable and savable, and its FAQ says to set the new file name or folder and save.

### Problems with TGA files

- **An indexed TGA with transparency looks wrong in one program**: programs differ here. GIMP 2.10.32 improved its support for indexed Targa images with an alpha channel, on both import and export.
- **A tool rejects the file by its ending**: the ICB, VDA and VST endings name Truevision Targa too, but this page's file picker lists .tga files.
- **The page calls the picture too large**: reduce the render's pixel count in an editor, then convert again.
- **The PNG has a different file size**: Targa's run-length encoding is optional and PNG always compresses. PNG compression is lossless, so a different size is not a quality loss.
- **A file with several images gives one picture**: only a single image is taken from the file.

guide.title: About TIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a TIF file?

TIF is the short spelling of TIFF, the Tagged Image File Format. It is a raster format first published by Aldus in 1986 and developed with Microsoft, and Adobe now holds its specification. Revision 6.0 came out in 1992. A TIFF is built from tags that say how the pixel data is stored, so two files with the same ending can differ a lot inside.

That flexibility is why scanners, print shops and document-imaging systems use it. A TIFF can use different compression methods and color representations, reach high bit depths, and hold several images in one file, which suits a scanned stack of pages. It is not always lossless, though. The compression is chosen when the file is written.

Photographers and archivists keep TIFFs as preservation masters because high bit depth and lossless storage are established uses of the format. The ending tells you the container, not what is in it: one page or fifty, 8 bits or 16, lossless or not.

### Programs that open TIF files

- **Linux, Mac and Windows:** TIFF opens in GIMP for editing. ImageMagick reads and writes TIFF from the command line, with controls for compression, strips, tiles and byte order.
- **Windows:** Windows Photos opens TIFF.
- **Mac:** Preview lists TIFF among the formats in File > Export, and Adobe Photoshop opens TIFF too.

### TIF and JPG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .tif and .tiff with image/tiff; .jpg and .jpeg with image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: a TIFF can be lossless or lossy, depending on the method used. JPG is always lossy, so detail is traded for a smaller file.
- **Pages**: a TIFF can hold several images. A JPG is one picture, and this page writes one JPG for each file.
- **Bit depth and color**: TIFF can carry high bit depths and CMYK. The converter works at 8 bits for the JPG.
- **Specification**: Adobe controls the TIFF specification, while JPEG is defined by the ISO/IEC 10918-1 standard.
- **Support**: JPG is supported almost everywhere, and every major browser displays it.

ISO/IEC 10918-1, published in 1994, is the core JPEG standard, written by the Joint Photographic Experts Group. Digital cameras and scanners generally produce it natively. A 0 to 100 range is typical, but identical figures can look different between programs. Progressive JPEGs paint a blurry preview first and sharpen it as the remaining data arrives.

The conversion sets no quality, so there is nothing to tune here. For a scan of fine print or line art, look at the JPG at full size before you throw anything away. The TIF on your disk stays as it was; what you download is a fresh JPG that carries its name. Picking several TIFs together runs them one after another with no ZIP. A lossless copy is also possible, because the site has a PNG option for TIF files.

### Other ways to convert TIF to JPG

- **GIMP:** open the TIFF and choose File > Export As. The Quality field in GIMP's JPEG export dialog accepts 0 to 100. GIMP's manual says every format other than XCF loses some image properties, such as layers and transparency, and that exporting does not change the open image.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick scan.tif scan-copy.jpg`. ImageMagick's format list marks TIFF as readable and writable. In a test with a small TIF this wrote a JPG.

### Problems with TIF files

- **A website or form rejects the TIF**: convert the file. Renaming it to .jpg does not change what is inside.
- **Only one picture came out**: a TIFF can hold several images, and this page gives one JPG per file. Use software that exposes the full image sequence if you need every page.
- **A reader does not understand the file**: private tags vary, and a program may not recognize all of them, color-profile extensions included.
- **The page says the picture couldn't be read**: either the file is damaged or it uses a TIFF variant that ImageMagick cannot decode. Try the scanning software that made it.
- **Colors shift on a 16-bit or CMYK scan**: the JPG comes out with 8 bits for each color, so compare it with the original before you rely on it.
- **A very large scan**: original TIFF offsets are 32 bits wide, capping a file near 4 GB, and BigTIFF widens them. Pictures beyond roughly 537 megapixels are declined by the page.

guide.title: About TIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a TIF file?

A .tif file holds a TIFF, short for Tagged Image File Format. Aldus and Microsoft created it, and the specification now belongs to Adobe, which acquired Aldus's PageMaker program. Aldus first published TIFF in 1986. At that point it handled only bilevel images, and grayscale and color came later as scanners and storage improved. Revision 6.0 arrived in 1992, and files that follow earlier versions remain valid TIFF 6.0 files.

You meet a .tif when you scan a document, when a photographer or print shop sends a print master, or when a library or archive hands over a preservation copy. Among the Library of Congress's preferred formats for photographs and other graphic images is TIFF, which it uses as a master format in many digitization workflows. Subtypes such as TIFF/EP, GeoTIFF and Adobe DNG build on it. The long .tiff ending names the identical format, and image/tiff is the media type for both.

### Programs that open TIF files

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: opens a scan for editing, and each export format keeps its own subset of the project's properties.

**Mac**

- Preview: has TIFF in its File > Export menu among the formats it can write.

### TIF and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .tif or .tiff with image/tiff, and .png with image/png.
- **Compression**: a TIFF may be stored uncompressed or with LZW, Group 4 or JPEG, whereas PNG never loses data.
- **Images per file**: one TIF can contain many pictures, which suits a stack of scanned pages. This page reads only a single picture from the file.
- **Color**: color handling is defined by a tag. Plain 8-bit grayscale and 24-bit RGB dominate, yet some workflows go past 8 bits per channel. An embedded ICC profile is possible in a TIF, though not every reader recognizes it, so the format suits high-bit-depth imaging and preservation masters. PNG offers 8-bit and 16-bit channels plus alpha transparency.
- **Age**: TIFF dates from 1986 and grew up with scanning and print. PNG was designed in the mid-1990s to replace GIF without its patent problems, and it is now both a W3C Recommendation and ISO/IEC 15948.
- **Reach**: every browser draws a PNG, while a TIF needs a program that understands it.

On this page ImageMagick runs as WebAssembly inside your browser, so your scan is never sent to a server. It decodes one picture from the TIF and writes it as a PNG, without resizing it or setting a quality value. Only the first file waits for the converter to load. A multi-page TIF gives a single PNG rather than one per page. When you need every page, keep the TIF as your master and treat the PNG as a viewing copy.

### Other ways to convert TIF to PNG

- **Preview (Mac):** open the TIF, choose File > Export, set the Format menu to PNG and press Save. That menu offers PNG next to HEIC, JPEG, JPEG-2000, OpenEXR, PDF and TIFF. For many files, open them in one Preview window, select them in the sidebar and export.
- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the scan, choose File > Export As, type .png after the name in the Name field, then press Export.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick 'scan.tif[0]' scan.png`. The number in brackets selects one image from a multi-image file, counting from zero, so `[1]` is the second. Keep the quotes, since Linux shells treat brackets specially.

### Problems with TIF files

- **A program shows just one image of a multi-page scan**: a TIFF may hold several images, and only software that exposes the whole sequence shows them all. Open the file in such a program, or choose a page with ImageMagick as above.
- **The conversion stops with a size error**: anything over about 537 megapixels is turned back, and you can shrink the scan's resolution in an editor first. Classic TIFF itself tops out near 4 GB because of its 32-bit offsets, and BigTIFF uses 64-bit offsets to lift that.
- **Colors or tags look wrong elsewhere**: some private tags, including certain color-profile extensions, are unknown to other readers. Export from the program that made the TIF.
- **A renamed file still fails**: switching .tif to .png leaves TIFF data inside, so make a real conversion.

guide.title: TIFF to JPG: formats and alternatives
guide.markdown:
### What is a TIFF file?

The Tagged Image File Format, called TIFF, is a tag-based raster wrapper designed by Aldus and Microsoft. Its 6.0 revision appeared in 1992, and the specification is now controlled by Adobe. Each image in a file carries tags that say how its pixels are stored, so one file can use different compression methods and color representations. A TIFF can also contain multiple images, a design that fits scanned documents made of several pages.

People meet TIFF as scanner output, in high-bit-depth imaging, and in preservation master files, where keeping every detail matters. In GIMP, export formats retain different subsets of a project's properties, so check what a given export keeps. Whether you write .tif or .tiff, the format is the same, and image/tiff is its media type.

### Programs that open TIFF files

- **Windows, Mac and Linux:** GIMP imports a TIFF for editing, and ImageMagick reads and writes TIFF and exposes settings for compression, strips, tiles and byte order.
- **Mac:** the File > Export menu of Preview includes TIFF among its formats.

### TIFF and JPEG compared

- **Extensions**: .tif and .tiff are image/tiff, while .jpg and .jpeg are image/jpeg and name the same format.
- **Compression**: a TIFF can use different compression methods. Baseline JPEG is lossy, splitting the image into 8x8 pixel blocks.
- **Images per file**: TIFF can contain several. JPEG stores one.
- **Color and depth**: high bit depths are an established TIFF use. Each color channel of a JPEG has 8 bits, and without an alpha channel it can't hold transparency.
- **Layers**: a JPEG can't store layers.

JPEG is short for Joint Photographic Experts Group, the committee that began its work in 1986. The standard itself came out twice: as ITU-T T.81 in 1992, then as ISO/IEC 10918-1 in 1994. Programs usually offer quality on a 0 to 100 scale, but one number can give different results in different programs. A progressive mode also exists, where a coarse picture appears first and sharpens as the rest loads. Every major browser displays JPEG, and the last US patents on it lapsed on 27 October 2006.

The ImageMagick build inside this page is WebAssembly, running in your browser, and it reads the TIFF as one picture. If the file has several pages, you get a single JPEG, not one per page. This page passes no quality setting, and it leaves your TIFF as it was. Because JPEG is lossy, some detail is traded away. A picture beyond about 537 megapixels is refused, and the page reports that it is too large for this converter. Choose several TIFFs and they run one after another, each saved as a separate JPEG with the .jpeg ending. No ZIP is made, and no file is uploaded, because the whole conversion happens on your device.

### Other ways to convert TIFF to JPEG

- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick "scan.tiff[0]" scan.jpeg`. ImageMagick's format table lists TIFF and JPEG as readable and writable. A frame number in brackets after the input name selects the frame to read. Counting starts at 0, so another number gives another page.
- **sips (Mac, command line):** run `sips -s format jpeg scan.tiff --out scan.jpg` in Terminal. The format option lists tiff and jpeg among its values, and --out names the result.

These help when you need one chosen page of a scan. A multi-page document scan is the usual case where this page's single-image limit matters, and the bracket number is the way around it.

### Problems with TIFF files

- **You wanted every page but got one**: only one image is converted here. Because a TIFF may hold several images, pick software that exposes the whole sequence, for example ImageMagick's bracket selector.
- **A private tag or color profile is ignored**: not every reader understands each private tag, and that includes some color-profile extensions. Check the color settings in GIMP before converting.
- **The file is huge**: 32-bit offsets in classic TIFF limit a file to about 4 GB, and BigTIFF widens those fields.
- **Transparency disappears**: a JPEG export drops transparent pixels. Pick a format with alpha if you need them.
- **The JPEG looks softer**: JPEG is lossy, so keep the TIFF as the archive copy, because converting back cannot restore the detail JPEG discarded.

guide.markdown:
### What is a TIFF file?

Short for Tagged Image File Format, TIFF is a tag-based raster wrapper created by Aldus and Microsoft. The first release dates from 1986 and revision 6.0 from 1992; Adobe now controls the specification. TIFF permits several compression methods and several color representations. Files end in .tif or .tiff, and the media type is image/tiff.

Multiple images per file make TIFF useful for scanned document sequences, and high bit depth imaging and preservation masters are established uses. You meet TIFF from scanners, in print and professional photography workflows, and as the master copy a photographer keeps beside a smaller JPG. The format reference also lists fax and document imaging among its uses. GIMP supports high-precision TIFF import and export. Because a TIFF may hold several images, a converter that reads one has to take a single image from the file.

### Programs that open TIFF files

**Mac**

- Preview: the format list under File > Export offers TIFF.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: imports TIFF for editing, and what an export keeps depends on the format.
- ImageMagick: reads and writes TIFF; compression, strips, tiles and byte order are all adjustable.

**Windows**

- Windows Photos: the format reference lists it.

### TIFF and JPG compared

- **Extensions**: .tif or .tiff is image/tiff, while .jpg or .jpeg is image/jpeg.
- **Compression**: TIFF can be lossless or lossy. JPEG is lossy: the picture is divided into 8x8 blocks that go through a discrete cosine transform before Huffman coding.
- **Pages**: a TIFF may contain several images, whereas a JPG is a single picture.
- **Color depth**: TIFF supports high bit depth and CMYK. JPEG stores 8 bits per color channel.
- **Transparency**: JPEG has no alpha channel. Layers do not survive either.
- **Size limit**: classic TIFF is capped near 4 GB.
- **Support**: JPG opens in every browser and phone. TIFF needs a viewer that understands its tags.
- **Typical use**: TIFF for scanning, archiving and print. JPG for web photos, camera output and email attachments.
- **Quality setting**: TIFF has none for lossless compression. JPEG quality runs from 0 to 100, but programs scale it differently, so equal numbers do not give equal results.

ImageMagick takes one image from the TIFF and saves a JPG. A multi-page TIFF gives one picture, not one per page. Keep the TIFF: a JPG cannot be turned back into it, and saving the JPG again later costs more detail.

The download takes the TIFF's name with .jpg in place of .tif or .tiff, and each TIFF in a batch is converted and saved on its own.

### Other ways to convert TIFF to JPG

- **GIMP (Windows, Mac, Linux):** load the TIFF, go to File > Export As, pick the JPEG entry in the file types and hit Export. The JPEG settings dialog appears next, where the default quality is 85.
- **Preview (Mac):** open the TIFF, go to File > Export, choose JPEG as the Format and save.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick 'input.tiff[0]' output.jpg`. The [0] picks the first image in the file, and the quotes keep the brackets away from the shell.

On a desktop you can set the JPEG quality and see the settings before saving, which this page does not offer.

### Problems with TIFF files

- **It will not open**: viewers can stumble on private tags, some color-profile extensions included. Re-save it from GIMP or a similar editor.
- **Only one page converted**: the TIFF holds several images and this page reads one. Use software that exposes the whole image sequence.
- **Over 4 GB**: classic TIFF uses 32-bit offsets and stops at about 4 GB, and BigTIFF extends those fields.
- **The picture is too large**: pictures over roughly 537 megapixels are refused.
- **A "couldn't be read" message**: the page could not read the picture, which may be damaged or incomplete; save a new TIFF from GIMP or Preview and convert that.
- **Transparent areas change**: a JPG cannot keep transparency. Convert to PNG if you need it.
- **A scanned page looks soft**: JPEG is lossy and works in 8x8 blocks, so thin lines and small text can blur. Keep the TIFF as the master.
- **The colors look off**: a JPG holds 8 bits per channel, so a high bit depth TIFF is reduced. Check the result against the original.

guide.markdown:
### What is a TIFF file?

The Tagged Image File Format, or TIFF, is a raster format from Aldus and Microsoft. Aldus released the first version in 1986, revision 6.0 arrived in 1992, and the specification is now Adobe's. The name comes from its structure: a TIFF is a wrapper of tags that describe the image data, its color and other characteristics. Both .tif and .tiff are used for it, and its media type is image/tiff.

Different compression methods and color representations are possible in a TIFF, and one file may contain several images, which made it a staple for scanned document sequences. Deep bit depths and preservation masters are also long-standing uses. You mostly meet it from scanners, fax and document imaging software, and in professional photography and print. GIMP supports high-precision TIFF import and export, which suits the format's deeper bit depths.

A PDF is a common next step when a scan has to be sent or filed. It turns the image into a document page that PDF readers handle.

### Programs that open TIFF files

**Mac**

- Preview: its File > Export sheet lists TIFF among the formats.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: loads image files for editing; what an export keeps depends on the format chosen.
- ImageMagick: reads and writes TIFF and exposes compression, strip, tile and byte-order controls.

**Windows**

- Windows Photos: appears in the format reference.

### TIFF and PDF compared

- **Extensions**: .tif and .tiff are image/tiff, .pdf is application/pdf.
- **Pages**: one TIFF file may contain several images, while a PDF holds fixed pages; this page writes a single page.
- **Compression**: TIFF can be lossless or lossy, and offers many methods. This page embeds the picture in the PDF losslessly.
- **Content**: a TIFF holds raster pixels alone. A PDF can combine text, vector graphics and images, though the PDF written here carries a single picture.
- **Color depth**: TIFF can use high bit depth and CMYK. PDF images can use lossless Flate compression or JPEG.
- **Size limit**: classic TIFF uses 32-bit offsets, which keeps it to about 4 GB. BigTIFF extends those fields.
- **Who can open it**: the PDF opens in Firefox, Apple Preview, Evince, Okular and Adobe Acrobat Reader, so the person you send it to needs no viewer that understands TIFF tags.
- **Standards**: PDF 1.7 was standardized as ISO 32000-1 in 2008, and PDF 2.0 as ISO 32000-2 in 2017.

ImageMagick reads one image, which the page saves as a PNG and sets on a PDF page matching the image's size. No quality setting is passed, and the pixels are not resampled to a paper size. The result looks like the scan, is not searchable and is not set to A4 or Letter.

The download takes the TIFF's name with .pdf in place of its ending. Several TIFFs convert one after another, and each PDF is saved separately. Nothing is added to the page around the picture: no header, footer or page number.

### Other ways to convert TIFF to PDF

- **Preview (Mac):** open the TIFF in Preview, then File > Export, Format: PDF, and save. The Format menu in the export sheet lists PDF.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick input.tiff output.pdf`, which reads the TIFF and takes the output format from the .pdf ending. ImageMagick's formats page lists TIFF as readable and writable, and PDF as readable and writable but requiring Ghostscript.

### Problems with TIFF files

- **Only one image of a multi-page TIFF came out**: this page reads a single image. Split the TIFF into one file per page first if you need each one.
- **The picture is too large**: a picture over roughly 537 megapixels is refused.
- **A "couldn't be read" message appears**: the file's picture could be damaged or incomplete. Try a desktop program and save a fresh copy.
- **A viewer refuses the file**: some viewers cannot interpret every private tag, color-profile extensions among them. Re-save it from GIMP or another editor.
- **A TIFF over 4 GB**: classic TIFF stops near 4 GB, and BigTIFF extends that.
- **The PDF page is far bigger than A4**: one pixel is one point, so a 300 dpi scan makes a page about four times the size of the paper. Scale it when you print.
- **The text isn't searchable**: it is a picture of text. OCR is needed.
